criminal-law/alabama/expungement.summary: Alabama allows expungement of certain criminal charges that did not result in conviction and, under narrower rules, some misdemeanor and felony convictions under Alabama Code Chapter 15-27, expanded by the 2021 REDEEMER Act. Eligibility depends on the offense, how the case ended, and applicable statutory conditions; a dismissal, acquittal, completed sentence, or pardon does not automatically erase the record. Petitions go to the circuit court in the county where the charges were filed, and expungement does not mean every record is physically destroyed.

facts.label: Misdemeanors and other lower-level charges
facts.value: Section 15-27-1 covers misdemeanor criminal offenses, violations, traffic violations, and municipal ordinance violations. It provides separate eligibility rules for charges without convictions and for qualifying convictions; not every offense or case disposition qualifies. — Ala. Code § 15-27-1.

facts.label: Felony charges without convictions
facts.value: Section 15-27-2 provides routes for qualifying felony charges, including specified dismissals, grand-jury no-bills, acquittals, and completion of qualifying diversion programs. The applicable conditions depend on the particular disposition. — Ala. Code § 15-27-2(a).

facts.label: Felony convictions
facts.value: The felony-conviction route requires a pardon with restoration of civil and political rights and additional statutory conditions. Specified offense categories remain excluded, so a pardon alone does not establish eligibility. — Ala. Code § 15-27-2(b).

facts.label: Conviction exclusions
facts.value: The conviction provisions contain restrictions involving violent offenses, sex offenses, and other specified categories. Their precise application differs between misdemeanor and felony convictions. — Ala. Code §§ 15-27-1(b), 15-27-2(b).

sections.heading: How different case outcomes are treated

rows: A not-guilty verdict is a recognized basis for seeking expungement; a court petition is still required.
A statutory nonconviction pathway, subject to the applicable section's conditions.
Recognized in the nonconviction provisions; it does not itself remove records.
Potentially eligible under the separate conviction provisions, including sentence-completion and financial-obligation requirements.
Requires the statutory pardon-based pathway; completing a sentence alone is insufficient.

facts.label: Supporting records
facts.value: The petition must include the sworn statements and supporting records required by statute, including a certified criminal-history record from the Alabama Law Enforcement Agency. — Ala. Code § 15-27-4.

facts.label: Court review
facts.value: The court considers statutory factors, and the law provides procedures for objections and hearings. Filing an eligible petition does not itself expunge the charge. — Ala. Code § 15-27-6.

facts.label: Not complete destruction
facts.value: Alabama's expungement framework restricts ordinary access but preserves specified records and permits access in circumstances authorized by law. Disclosure exceptions also remain. — Ala. Code ch. 15-27.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Alabama
bullets: The circuit court in the county where the charges were filed receives the expungement petition, including petitions involving qualifying municipal charges. — Ala. Code § 15-27-4.
The Alabama Law Enforcement Agency supplies the certified criminal-history record required for the petition; it does not replace the circuit court as the decision-maker. — Ala. Code § 15-27-4.
Alabama's Administrative Office of Courts publishes expungement forms through its official E-Forms website.

sections.heading: Common questions in Alabama
bullets: Does dismissal automatically clear the record? No. Expungement requires the statutory petition process and a court order.
Can a conviction qualify? Yes. Alabama has separate provisions for qualifying misdemeanor convictions and certain pardoned felony convictions.
Is a pardon the same as expungement? No. A pardon and an expungement order are distinct legal actions.
Are all waiting periods identical? No. Timing requirements depend on the disposition and statutory pathway.
Does expungement eliminate every disclosure obligation? No. Statutory exceptions remain, including specified licensing and governmental contexts.

sources.label: Alabama Legislature — Code of Alabama, Title 15, Chapter 27
Alabama Administrative Office of Courts — Expungement Forms

criminal-law/alabama/juvenile-law.summary: Alabama juvenile courts generally handle delinquency allegations involving conduct committed before age 18, but state law sends certain serious charges against youths age 16 or older directly to adult criminal court. Prosecutors may also seek transfer of other qualifying cases involving children age 14 or older after a juvenile-court hearing. Juvenile proceedings provide rights to counsel and proof beyond a reasonable doubt, while available dispositions emphasize supervision, treatment, rehabilitation, and accountability rather than an adult criminal conviction.

sections.heading: Alabama juvenile jurisdiction and legal protections

facts.label: Court jurisdiction
facts.value: Juvenile courts have exclusive original jurisdiction over proceedings alleging that a child committed a delinquent act, subject to statutory exceptions and transfer provisions. A delinquent act generally means conduct that would constitute a criminal offense if committed by an adult. — Alabama Code §§ 12-15-102 and 12-15-114

facts.label: Age definition
facts.value: The statutory definition of a child generally covers individuals under 18. It also includes an individual under 21 who is before juvenile court for a delinquency matter arising before that individual's eighteenth birthday. — Alabama Code § 12-15-102(3)

facts.label: Questioning and counsel
facts.value: Before custodial questioning, a child must receive specified explanations of rights, including the right to counsel, the right to remain silent, and the right to communicate with a parent, legal guardian, or legal custodian. Counsel must be appointed when the statutory indigency requirements apply. — Alabama Code § 12-15-202

facts.label: Proof and adjudication
facts.value: The state must prove the alleged delinquent acts beyond a reasonable doubt. A juvenile delinquency adjudication is not a criminal conviction, although juvenile dispositions can have consequences in later proceedings expressly permitted by law. — Alabama Code §§ 12-15-212 and 12-15-220

rows: A prosecutor may seek adult prosecution for qualifying alleged crimes committed at age 14 or older. Transfer requires a hearing and statutory findings.
Specified offenses allegedly committed at age 16 or older fall outside juvenile jurisdiction, including capital offenses, Class A felonies, and felonies involving use of a deadly weapon.
The statute also covers specified felonies involving death, serious physical injury, dangerous instruments, or forcible compulsion.
A juvenile court may allow a child to remain with a parent or custodian under conditions, or place the child on probation.
Authorized delinquency dispositions include transfer of legal custody to the Department of Youth Services and restitution, subject to statutory requirements.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Alabama
bullets: Juvenile intake office: Juvenile intake officers receive complaints and determine whether allegations fall within juvenile jurisdiction and whether a petition should be filed. — Alabama Code § 12-15-118.

Juvenile court clerk: The clerk handles filings in existing juvenile cases. Alabama juvenile jurisdiction is exercised through district and circuit courts as provided by statute. — Alabama Code § 12-15-103.

Appeals: A written notice of appeal from an appealable juvenile order must be filed within 14 days. The appellate route depends on the record and other requirements of the rule. — Alabama Rules of Juvenile Procedure, Rule 28.

sections.heading: Common questions in Alabama
bullets: Does turning 18 automatically end a juvenile case? No. Alabama's definition of a child includes certain individuals under 21 facing delinquency proceedings for conduct occurring before age 18. — Alabama Code § 12-15-102(3).

Are juvenile records publicly available? Juvenile legal and social records are generally confidential, but the statute allows access and disclosure to specified people and entities. Confidentiality is not absolute. — Alabama Code § 12-15-133.

Is every 16-year-old charged in adult court? No. Automatic adult prosecution depends on the charged offense meeting the statutory categories; other cases may involve juvenile jurisdiction or a transfer hearing. — Alabama Code §§ 12-15-203 and 12-15-204.

What does a transfer judge consider? Factors include the alleged offense, prior delinquency record, earlier treatment efforts, demeanor, maturity, and the interests of the child and community. — Alabama Code § 12-15-203.

sources.label: Alabama Legislature — Code of Alabama, Title 12, Chapter 15

criminal-law/arizona/domestic-violence-c.summary: In Arizona, domestic violence generally means a specified criminal offense committed within a relationship covered by A.R.S. § 13-3601, rather than a separate charge with one fixed sentence. Qualifying relationships include spouses, former spouses, certain household members and relatives, people with a child together, and qualifying romantic or sexual partners. The underlying offense determines whether the case is a misdemeanor or felony; a misdemeanor domestic violence conviction also requires completion of a court-ordered domestic violence offender treatment program.

sections.heading: What makes an Arizona charge domestic violence

facts.label: Underlying criminal offense
facts.value: Arizona's definition covers enumerated offenses, including assault, specified aggravated assaults, threatening or intimidating, criminal damage, and specified disorderly conduct offenses. The qualifying relationship alone does not establish a crime; an underlying offense must also be proved. — A.R.S. § 13-3601(A)

facts.label: Covered relationships
facts.value: The statute includes current or former spouses, people residing or formerly residing in the same household, people with a child in common, and situations in which the victim or defendant is pregnant by the other party. It also covers specified family relationships. — A.R.S. § 13-3601(A)

facts.label: Dating relationships
facts.value: A current or previous romantic or sexual relationship can qualify. Statutory considerations include the relationship's type and length, frequency of interaction, and, if it ended, the time since termination. — A.R.S. § 13-3601(A)(6)

sections.heading: Assault classifications and misdemeanor jail limits

rows: Intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly causing physical injury
Class 1 misdemeanor assault; maximum jail term of six months.
Intentionally placing someone in reasonable apprehension of imminent physical injury
Class 2 misdemeanor assault; maximum jail term of four months.
Knowingly touching someone with intent to injure, insult, or provoke
Class 3 misdemeanor assault; maximum jail term of thirty days.
Does not establish one universal jail term. These misdemeanor limits do not describe felony aggravated assault penalties.

facts.label: Arrest without witnessing the offense
facts.value: An officer may arrest with or without a warrant when probable cause establishes domestic violence, even if the offense occurred outside the officer's presence. — A.R.S. § 13-3601(B)

facts.label: Required offender treatment
facts.value: A person convicted of a misdemeanor domestic violence offense must complete a domestic violence offender treatment program ordered by the court. — A.R.S. § 13-3601.01(A)

facts.label: Separate protective-order proceeding
facts.value: An order of protection is distinct from criminal prosecution. Available provisions include prohibiting contact and granting exclusive use of a shared residence. An order expires two years after service on the defendant. — A.R.S. § 13-3602

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Arizona
bullets: Local police departments and county sheriffs investigate reported domestic violence offenses. Prosecutors, rather than the complaining witness, pursue criminal charges.
Municipal and justice courts handle misdemeanor cases within their jurisdiction; Arizona Superior Court handles felony criminal trials.

Petitions for orders of protection may generally be filed in municipal, justice, or superior court. Superior Court has exclusive jurisdiction when a qualifying family-law action between the parties is pending. — A.R.S. § 13-3602
Arizona's judicial branch provides AZPOINT, an online protective-order interview and document-preparation system.

sections.heading: Common questions in Arizona
bullets: Must someone suffer a physical injury? No. Assault can involve reasonable apprehension of imminent injury or qualifying touching without physical injury. — A.R.S. § 13-1203
Can former partners qualify? Yes. Former spouses and qualifying former romantic or sexual partners are covered. — A.R.S. § 13-3601(A)
Is every domestic violence charge a felony? No. The underlying offense may be a misdemeanor or felony.
Does an order of protection establish a criminal conviction? No. It is a separate protective-order proceeding, not a criminal conviction. — A.R.S. § 13-3602

criminal-law/california/plea-bargaining.summary: California permits negotiated criminal pleas, but a prosecutor’s agreement does not by itself bind the sentencing judge, and state law restricts bargaining in specified serious-felony cases. Penal Code section 1192.5 governs qualifying negotiated pleas and generally protects defendants against punishment more severe than the approved agreement; separate statutes address withdrawing pleas, immigration warnings, and the procedural requirements for appealing a conviction entered after a guilty or no-contest plea.

sections.heading: How negotiated pleas work in California

facts.label: Court approval
facts.value: For negotiated pleas covered by section 1192.5, the prosecutor’s acceptance and the court’s approval are required. Once approved, the defendant generally cannot receive punishment more severe than the agreement specifies, unless the court withdraws its approval and provides the protections required by the statute. — California Penal Code § 1192.5

facts.label: Required judicial inquiry
facts.value: The court must inquire whether the plea is freely and voluntarily made and whether a factual basis exists. The court must also explain that its approval is not binding and may be withdrawn at sentencing after further consideration. — California Penal Code § 1192.5

facts.label: Limits in serious-felony cases
facts.value: Section 1192.7 restricts plea bargaining when an indictment or information charges a listed serious felony. Statutory exceptions include insufficient evidence to prove the prosecution’s case, inability to obtain a material witness’s testimony, or a reduction or dismissal that would not substantially change the sentence. — California Penal Code § 1192.7

rows: A defendant may apply to withdraw a guilty plea before judgment; good cause is required.
When probation is granted and entry of judgment is suspended, section 1018 permits an application within six months after the probation order.
Before accepting a guilty or no-contest plea, the court must warn that conviction may cause deportation, exclusion from admission, or denial of naturalization.
A no-contest plea has the same legal effect as a guilty plea for an offense punishable as a felony.
In a felony case, the notice of appeal generally must be filed within 60 days after rendition of judgment or the appealable order.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in California
bullets: Criminal prosecutions and plea proceedings take place in the California superior court handling the case. A section 1018 plea-withdrawal application belongs in that criminal proceeding.
A felony notice of appeal is filed with the superior court clerk, although the appeal is ordinarily heard by the California Court of Appeal. — California Rules of Court, rule 8.304(a)
Complaints about attorney misconduct are handled by the State Bar of California. A disciplinary complaint is separate from a court proceeding to withdraw or challenge a plea.

sections.heading: Common questions in California
bullets: Can the judge reject an agreement? Yes. Section 1192.5 requires court approval and allows the court to withdraw approval after further consideration.

Can a defendant withdraw a plea simply because of regret? Regret alone does not establish the good cause required under section 1018. A claim that the plea resulted from mistake, coercion, or another legally sufficient defect requires judicial evaluation.

Does a missing immigration warning automatically erase the conviction? No. Section 1016.5 requires additional statutory conditions, including a showing that conviction may produce one of the specified immigration consequences.

Can a defendant appeal after pleading guilty? Some appeals remain available. A challenge to the plea’s validity generally requires a sworn written statement and a trial-court certificate of probable cause; specified issues are exempt. — Penal Code § 1237.5; California Rules of Court, rule 8.304(b)

criminal-law/california/traffic-violatio.summary: California treats most ordinary traffic violations as infractions, not misdemeanors or felonies, but offenses such as reckless driving and driving under the influence can carry criminal penalties. Infractions do not authorize jail, while misdemeanor and felony traffic cases can involve incarceration, probation, fines, and separate driver’s license consequences. Traffic cases generally proceed in the superior court for the county where the violation occurred, while the California Department of Motor Vehicles handles license records and administrative actions under separate procedures.

facts.label: Infractions
facts.value: Vehicle Code violations are generally infractions unless another provision makes them misdemeanors or felonies. An infraction is not punishable by imprisonment, and defendants generally have no right to a jury trial or an appointed public defender in an infraction case. — California Vehicle Code § 40000.1; Penal Code § 19.6

facts.label: Misdemeanor and felony cases
facts.value: Reckless driving is a misdemeanor. DUI offenses can be misdemeanors or felonies depending on the applicable statute, prior convictions, and whether injury occurred; a traffic-related arrest is therefore not necessarily an infraction case. — California Vehicle Code §§ 23103, 23152, 23153, 23550, 23550.5

facts.label: Base fines versus total charges
facts.value: A statutory fine does not necessarily equal the total amount imposed. State and local penalty assessments and other authorized charges can increase the amount owed. — California Penal Code § 1464; Government Code § 76000

rows: Speed must be reasonable and prudent for conditions, including weather, visibility, traffic, and roadway conditions.
Failure to stop at a red light
A driver facing a steady circular red signal generally must stop and remain stopped, subject to authorized turns.
Driving with willful or wanton disregard for the safety of people or property.
For the basic offense, 5–90 days in county jail, a $145–$1,000 fine, or both — Vehicle Code § 23103
Driving under the influence of alcohol, drugs, or their combination is prohibited; driving with a blood-alcohol concentration of 0.08% or more is separately prohibited.
Criminal offense; penalties depend on the applicable circumstances and history — Vehicle Code §§ 23152, 23536, 23550

facts.label: Written trial option
facts.value: Eligible Vehicle Code and local traffic infraction cases may be tried by written declaration instead of an in-person trial. This procedure does not apply to misdemeanor charges. — California Vehicle Code § 40902; California Rules of Court, rule 4.210

facts.label: New trial after a written decision
facts.value: A defendant dissatisfied with a trial-by-declaration decision may request a trial de novo within 20 days after the clerk mails the decision. — California Rules of Court, rule 4.210(b)(7)

facts.label: Infraction appeal
facts.value: A notice of appeal generally must be filed within 30 days after rendition of the judgment or issuance of the appealable order. Infraction appeals go to the superior court’s appellate division. — California Rules of Court, rules 8.901–8.902

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in California
bullets: Superior court: The county superior court handles traffic citations and criminal traffic prosecutions; the citation identifies the court responsible for the case. — Vehicle Code § 40500

California DMV: Administrative license proceedings are separate from criminal court proceedings. An administrative-per-se suspension hearing generally must be requested within 10 days after receipt of the suspension or revocation notice. — Vehicle Code § 13558

sections.heading: Common questions in California
bullets: Can an ordinary traffic infraction result in jail? The infraction itself cannot be punished by imprisonment. — Penal Code § 19.6
Does paying a traffic fine remove DMV points? Payment does not itself erase a reportable conviction or its applicable point value. — Vehicle Code §§ 1803, 12810
Is driving below the posted limit always lawful? No. California’s basic speed law still prohibits speed that is unreasonable or unsafe for existing conditions. — Vehicle Code § 22350

criminal-law/arkansas/bail-and-bond.summary: Arkansas generally guarantees bail before conviction except in capital cases when the proof is evident or the presumption great, and its constitution prohibits excessive bail. Under the Arkansas Rules of Criminal Procedure, a judicial officer may require money bail only after determining that other conditions will not reasonably ensure the defendant’s appearance in court. Release can also include restrictions on travel, contact with specified people, or other activities, and posting a bond does not end the obligation to attend court.

sections.heading: Arkansas bail rights and release decisions

facts.label: Constitutional protection
facts.value: Before conviction, prisoners are entitled to bail by sufficient sureties except for capital offenses when the proof is evident or the presumption great. This constitutional guarantee concerns pretrial release, not an unrestricted right to release after conviction. — Arkansas Constitution, article 2, § 8

facts.label: Excessive bail
facts.value: The Arkansas Constitution expressly prohibits excessive bail. It does not establish a single statewide dollar amount for release on every criminal charge. — Arkansas Constitution, article 2, § 9

facts.label: When money bail is allowed
facts.value: A judicial officer must first determine that no other conditions will reasonably ensure the defendant’s appearance before setting money bail. — Arkansas Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 9.2(a)

facts.label: Factors affecting the amount
facts.value: Relevant considerations include residence, employment, financial condition, family relationships, reputation, the charge and likely sentence, criminal history, and past court appearances or flight. — Arkansas Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 9.2(c)

sections.heading: Forms of release and financial security

rows: Release based on the defendant’s promise to appear, subject to the judicial officer’s release determination. — Rule 9.1
The defendant and any additional obligated persons promise to pay a specified amount; money is not deposited as security at release. — Rule 9.2(b)(i)

The defendant executes an unsecured bond and deposits ten percent of its face amount with the court clerk. The rule provides for return of ninety percent of that deposit at the conclusion of proceedings if the defendant has not defaulted. — Rule 9.2(b)(ii)
Security can consist of the full amount in cash, property, or the obligation of qualified sureties. — Rule 9.2(b)(iii)
Conditions can restrict activities, associations, residence, travel, and contact with specified people. — Rules 9.1 and 9.3

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Arkansas
bullets: The court handling the criminal case addresses release conditions. Arkansas district courts conduct preliminary criminal proceedings, while circuit courts handle felony prosecutions; the responsible court depends on the case’s stage and jurisdiction.

The clerk of the court receiving a court-deposit bond maintains that deposit. A court deposit is distinct from a premium paid to a commercial bail bond company. — Arkansas Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 9.2(b)(ii)

The Arkansas Professional Bail Bondsman Licensing Board regulates licensed professional bail bond companies and bondsmen and handles complaints within its licensing authority. It does not replace the criminal court’s authority to set release conditions. — Arkansas Code, Title 17, Chapter 19

sections.heading: Common questions in Arkansas
bullets: Does every charge require cash bail? No. The rules permit nonfinancial release and require a finding that other conditions will not reasonably ensure appearance before money bail is imposed. — Rule 9.2(a)

Is a ten-percent court deposit the same as hiring a bondsman? No. The court-deposit option places money with the clerk under Rule 9.2(b)(ii); a professional bondsman operates under Arkansas’s separate licensing and bonding statutes.
Can release include a no-contact restriction? Yes. A judicial officer may prohibit approaching or communicating with particular people as a release condition. — Rule 9.3

Can missed court appearances cause forfeiture? Yes. Arkansas law provides procedures for forfeiting bail bonds when a defendant fails to appear, including notice and proceedings involving the surety. Circuit-court forfeiture procedures appear in Arkansas Code § 16-84-207.

criminal-law/arizona/traffic-violations.summary: Arizona treats many routine traffic violations as civil matters, but offenses such as reckless driving, criminal speeding, racing, and driving under the influence can lead to criminal prosecution. Criminal traffic cases can carry jail time, fines, and separate driver-license consequences; misdemeanor cases generally proceed in municipal or justice court, while felony cases proceed in superior court. The applicable charge, prior convictions, and statutory circumstances determine the possible penalties, so traffic offenses do not all follow the same rules.

sections.heading: Civil traffic violations versus criminal charges

facts.label: Civil classification
facts.value: Violations of Arizona’s vehicle-operation rules are civil traffic violations unless the law provides otherwise. Ordinary speeding under the reasonable-and-prudent-speed statute is distinct from criminal excessive speeding. — A.R.S. §§ 28-121, 28-701, 28-701.02

facts.label: Criminal speeding
facts.value: Excessive speed under Arizona’s criminal-speeding statute is a class 3 misdemeanor. The statute identifies particular speed and location circumstances; not every speeding allegation is criminal. — A.R.S. § 28-701.02

facts.label: Reckless driving
facts.value: Driving with reckless disregard for the safety of persons or property is reckless driving. The baseline offense is a class 2 misdemeanor, with enhanced treatment for qualifying prior convictions. — A.R.S. § 28-693

facts.label: Racing
facts.value: Arizona prohibits highway racing, speed competitions, drag racing, acceleration contests, and exhibitions of speed or acceleration. A first violation is a class 1 misdemeanor. — A.R.S. § 28-708

sections.heading: Misdemeanor classifications and general maximum penalties

facts.label: Impairment and alcohol concentration
facts.value: DUI includes driving or being in actual physical control while impaired to the slightest degree by alcohol, drugs, or a combination. A separate provision covers an alcohol concentration of 0.08 or more within two hours of driving when the statutory conditions are met. — A.R.S. § 28-1381(A)

facts.label: Extreme DUI
facts.value: Arizona separately addresses alcohol concentrations of at least 0.15 but below 0.20, and concentrations of 0.20 or more, under its extreme-DUI statute. These categories have different mandatory sentencing provisions. — A.R.S. § 28-1382

facts.label: Penalties beyond the table
facts.value: The table lists general misdemeanor ceilings, not complete sentencing packages. Offense-specific laws can require minimum incarceration, assessments, screening, treatment, or ignition interlock restrictions; statutory surcharges are separate from base fines. — A.R.S. §§ 28-1381, 28-1382, 12-116.01

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Arizona
bullets: Municipal courts hear misdemeanor traffic prosecutions within their statutory jurisdiction, including state-law offenses committed within city or town limits. — A.R.S. § 22-402

Justice courts hear misdemeanor traffic cases within their statutory jurisdiction. Superior courts handle felony prosecutions, including aggravated DUI cases. — A.R.S. §§ 22-301, 28-1383; Arizona Constitution, article VI, § 14

The Arizona Department of Transportation’s Motor Vehicle Division handles administrative driver-license matters. An implied-consent suspension hearing request must be submitted within 30 days after service of the suspension notice. — A.R.S. § 28-1321

sections.heading: Common questions in Arizona
bullets: Is every speeding ticket criminal? No. Arizona distinguishes ordinary civil speeding from criminal excessive speeding. — A.R.S. §§ 28-701, 28-701.02
Can DUI apply below 0.08? Yes. The slightest-degree impairment offense does not require an alcohol concentration of 0.08. — A.R.S. § 28-1381(A)(1)

Can reckless driving affect a license? Yes. Upon conviction, the judge may order a driving-privilege suspension of up to 90 days; qualifying repeat convictions have additional consequences. — A.R.S. § 28-693

Does paying a criminal fine resolve every consequence? No. Criminal sentencing and administrative license proceedings are distinct, and a case may involve both. Talk to a lawyer. — A.R.S. §§ 28-1321, 28-1381

criminal-law/arkansas/drug-charges.summary: Arkansas drug charges depend on the substance, its statutory schedule, the amount involved, and whether the allegation is possession, delivery, manufacture, or trafficking. Possession is not automatically a misdemeanor: Arkansas Code § 5-64-419 includes felony possession offenses, while separate statutes govern other drug crimes. The sentencing ranges below describe ordinary classifications, not a prediction of the sentence in a particular case; prior convictions, enhancements, and other sentencing laws can change the consequences.

facts.label: Possession
facts.value: Arkansas prohibits possessing a controlled substance unless it was obtained through a valid prescription or another legal authorization. The offense classification depends on the substance and amount, with additional rules for certain prior convictions. — Arkansas Code § 5-64-419.

facts.label: Different conduct means different charges
facts.value: Delivery, manufacture, possession with the purpose to deliver, and trafficking are distinct statutory offenses. Prosecutors must establish the elements of the particular offense charged; there is no single penalty covering every drug charge. — Arkansas Code, Title 5, Chapter 64, Subchapter 4.

facts.label: Drug paraphernalia
facts.value: Possession of drug paraphernalia can be a separate criminal charge. Section 5-64-443 distinguishes between intended uses and includes specific provisions concerning methamphetamine and cocaine. — Arkansas Code § 5-64-443.

sections.heading: Prior convictions and alternatives to conviction

facts.label: Habitual-offender sentencing
facts.value: Qualifying prior felony convictions can expose a defendant to extended imprisonment under Arkansas's habitual-offender statute. These rules are separate from the ordinary classification ranges listed above. — Arkansas Code § 5-4-501.

facts.label: First Offender Act
facts.value: For eligible defendants who have not previously been convicted of a felony, a court may defer adjudication and impose probation under the First Offender Act. Successful completion can result in discharge, dismissal, and expungement under the statute; this treatment is discretionary and subject to exclusions. — Arkansas Code §§ 16-93-301–16-93-303.

facts.label: Drug courts
facts.value: Arkansas law authorizes drug court programs combining judicial supervision with treatment. Participation is not an automatic entitlement for everyone charged with a drug offense. — Arkansas Drug Court Act, Arkansas Code §§ 16-98-301–16-98-309.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Arkansas
bullets: Circuit courts hear felony drug prosecutions. Criminal motions and other filings in an existing felony case belong in the court handling that case. — Arkansas Constitution, Amendment 80, § 6.

District courts have jurisdiction over misdemeanor criminal cases and conduct preliminary proceedings in felony matters. Their criminal jurisdiction does not include trying felony charges. — Arkansas Supreme Court Administrative Order 18.

The prosecuting attorney represents the State in criminal prosecutions. Drug prosecutions are criminal court proceedings, not consumer complaints handled through an administrative refund or compensation process. — Arkansas Code § 16-21-103.

sections.heading: Common questions in Arkansas
bullets: Is possession always a misdemeanor? No. Section 5-64-419 provides both misdemeanor and felony classifications, depending on the applicable statutory factors.
Does a first drug charge guarantee probation? No. First Offender Act treatment is discretionary, and eligibility restrictions apply. — Arkansas Code § 16-93-303.
Do the listed prison ranges determine time actually served? No. Release eligibility is governed by separate statutes and can depend on the offense and its date. — Arkansas Code, Title 16, Chapter 93.
Can paraphernalia produce a separate charge? Yes. Arkansas separately criminalizes specified conduct involving drug paraphernalia. — Arkansas Code § 5-64-443.

Arkansas Judiciary — District Courts

criminal-law/colorado/domestic-violence-.summary: In Colorado, domestic violence generally describes the relationship and circumstances surrounding an underlying criminal offense, rather than a separate standalone charge, and it can trigger mandatory arrest, protection orders, and treatment requirements. The definition covers violence against an intimate partner and certain other crimes used for coercion, control, punishment, intimidation, or revenge; the underlying offense determines the ordinary sentencing range, while domestic-violence provisions add specific procedures and consequences.

sections.heading: What qualifies as domestic violence in Colorado

facts.label: Statutory definition
facts.value: Domestic violence includes an act or threatened act of violence against someone with whom the accused has or had an intimate relationship. It also includes another crime against a person, property, or an animal when used to coerce, control, punish, intimidate, or take revenge against an intimate partner. — C.R.S. § 18-6-800.3(1)

facts.label: Covered relationships
facts.value: An intimate relationship includes spouses, former spouses, past or present unmarried couples, and parents of the same child, regardless of whether they married or lived together. Sharing a residence alone does not establish one of these relationships. — C.R.S. § 18-6-800.3(2)

facts.label: Underlying criminal charge
facts.value: The domestic-violence provisions operate alongside the underlying offense. Depending on the alleged conduct, that offense may be assault, harassment, criminal mischief, or another crime; the domestic-violence designation does not create one universal penalty range. — C.R.S. §§ 18-6-800.3 and 18-6-801

rows: A peace officer who determines that probable cause exists for a crime or offense involving domestic violence must arrest the suspected offender without undue delay.
When people accuse each other, officers must evaluate each complaint separately, including injuries, prior complaints, future-injury risk, and possible self-defense.
A person arrested under the domestic-violence arrest statute cannot be admitted to bail until appearing before a judge.
A mandatory protection order restrains the defendant from harassing, molesting, intimidating, retaliating against, or tampering with victims or witnesses. Additional conditions may restrict contact.
A conviction for a crime whose underlying factual basis includes domestic violence generally requires an evaluation and court-ordered treatment program, subject to statutory exceptions.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Colorado
bullets: Local police departments and county sheriffs investigate reported domestic-violence crimes. The arrest requirement depends on an officer's probable-cause determination. — C.R.S. § 18-6-803.6
District attorneys prosecute state criminal cases in their judicial districts; prosecution is not a private lawsuit controlled by the complaining witness. — C.R.S. § 20-1-102

County courts generally handle state misdemeanor cases, while district courts handle felony trials. County courts also conduct preliminary stages of felony proceedings. — C.R.S. §§ 13-6-106 and 16-5-301
Civil protection-order proceedings are separate from criminal prosecution. Colorado district and county courts have statutory authority to issue civil protection orders. — C.R.S. § 13-14-104.5

sections.heading: Common questions in Colorado
bullets: Must there be a physical injury? No. Threatened violence can qualify, and certain property or other crimes can qualify when committed for the purposes specified in the domestic-violence definition. — C.R.S. § 18-6-800.3

Can the alleged victim simply drop the charges? No. The prosecutor controls prosecution. Colorado also restricts dismissing domestic-violence charges solely because the victim does not want prosecution. — C.R.S. § 18-6-801(3)

Does permission to make contact cancel a protection order? No. The protected person's consent does not itself change the court's order. Prohibited contact can support a separate protection-order violation charge. — C.R.S. §§ 18-1-1001 and 18-6-803.5

Are firearms affected before conviction? Yes. In qualifying domestic-violence cases, the mandatory protection-order statute requires firearm and ammunition restrictions and relinquishment provisions. — C.R.S. § 18-1-1001(9)

Colorado General Assembly — Colorado Revised Statutes, Title 13
Colorado General Assembly — Colorado Revised Statutes, Title 16
Colorado General Assembly — Colorado Revised Statutes, Title 20

criminal-law/arizona/juvenile-law.summary: Arizona generally handles alleged crimes committed by people under 18 as juvenile delinquency matters in the juvenile division of superior court, but state law requires or permits adult prosecution for certain offenses and ages. Juvenile proceedings can involve appointed counsel, diversion, probation, restitution, or commitment to the Arizona Department of Juvenile Corrections; the available outcome depends on the offense and statutory requirements. A delinquency adjudication is generally not a criminal conviction, but it can still carry significant legal consequences.

sections.heading: Arizona juvenile jurisdiction and legal representation

facts.label: Age definition
facts.value: Arizona defines a juvenile or child as an individual who is under 18. A delinquent act generally means conduct that would be a criminal offense if committed by an adult, subject to statutory exceptions. — A.R.S. § 8-201

facts.label: Court handling the case
facts.value: The juvenile court is a division of Arizona superior court. It has original jurisdiction over delinquency proceedings, subject to exceptions that place certain cases in adult criminal court. — A.R.S. § 8-202

facts.label: Right to counsel
facts.value: A juvenile is entitled to representation by counsel in proceedings involving offenses, delinquency, or incorrigibility. When a juvenile is entitled to counsel and is indigent, the court must appoint an attorney unless representation is properly waived. — A.R.S. § 8-221

sections.heading: Major routes through an Arizona juvenile case

rows: Arizona authorizes diversion programs for eligible juveniles as an alternative to formal delinquency proceedings. Eligibility and program requirements are governed by statute.
An adjudication generally does not impose the civil disabilities ordinarily resulting from a conviction and is not deemed a criminal conviction, subject to statutory exceptions.
Authorized dispositions include probation and, when statutory requirements are met, commitment to the Arizona Department of Juvenile Corrections.
Juveniles ages 15, 16, or 17 accused of specified offenses, including first-degree murder, second-degree murder, forcible sexual assault, or armed robbery, must be prosecuted as adults.
For juveniles at least 14 years old, prosecutors may file adult charges for specified offenses, including class 1 and class 2 felonies.

facts.label: Victim restitution
facts.value: After a juvenile is adjudicated delinquent, the court must order full or partial restitution to the victim, considering the nature of the offense and the victim's economic loss. Restitution is distinct from a criminal fine. — A.R.S. § 8-344

facts.label: Record destruction
facts.value: Arizona provides a process for applying to destroy juvenile court records, but destruction is not automatic merely because a person turns 18. Eligibility depends on statutory conditions, and specified offenses are excluded from relief. — A.R.S. § 8-349

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Arizona
bullets: County superior court, juvenile division: delinquency proceedings, dispositions, and applications concerning eligible juvenile court records are handled in this court. — A.R.S. §§ 8-202, 8-341, 8-349
County attorney's office: the prosecutor has statutory responsibilities concerning juvenile diversion and decisions about eligible adult prosecutions. — A.R.S. §§ 8-321, 13-501

Adult criminal division of superior court: felony cases prosecuted against juveniles as adults proceed through the criminal court system rather than ordinary delinquency proceedings. — A.R.S. § 13-501

sections.heading: Common questions in Arizona
bullets: Does being under 18 guarantee juvenile court? No. Arizona requires adult prosecution for certain charges at ages 15 through 17 and permits it for specified offenses beginning at age 14. — A.R.S. § 13-501
Can a juvenile receive an appointed lawyer? Yes. Appointment is required when the juvenile is entitled to counsel and indigent, unless counsel is properly waived. — A.R.S. § 8-221
Is delinquency the same as a criminal conviction? Generally no, although statutory exceptions apply and an adjudication can still produce court-ordered consequences. — A.R.S. §§ 8-207, 8-341
Do juvenile records automatically disappear at 18? No. Arizona's record-destruction statute requires an application and satisfaction of its eligibility conditions. — A.R.S. § 8-349

sources.label: Arizona Legislature — Title 8, Child Safety

Arizona Legislature — A.R.S. § 13-501, Adult prosecution of juveniles

criminal-law/colorado/felony-vs-misdemea.summary: Colorado distinguishes felonies from misdemeanors primarily through statutory classification and authorized punishment: ordinary felonies have six classes, while misdemeanors committed on or after March 1, 2022, generally have two classes. Felony cases are generally tried in district court, and county courts generally handle misdemeanor cases; Colorado also uses separate classifications and sentencing rules for drug offenses. The offense date matters because older misdemeanor classifications and penalties differ, and special sentencing provisions can change the ordinary felony prison ranges.

facts.label: Felony classification
facts.value: Colorado classifies ordinary felonies from class 1, the most serious, through class 6. The sentencing statute establishes presumptive prison terms and fine ranges, but other provisions can increase or otherwise change the sentence. — C.R.S. § 18-1.3-401

facts.label: Misdemeanor classification
facts.value: For offenses committed on or after March 1, 2022, the ordinary misdemeanor scheme has classes 1 and 2. Earlier offenses remain subject to the classification and sentencing provisions applicable to their offense dates, including the former class 3 category. — C.R.S. § 18-1.3-501

facts.label: Drug offenses
facts.value: Drug felonies and drug misdemeanors have separate sentencing classifications. Their penalties cannot be determined from the ordinary felony and misdemeanor table alone. — C.R.S. §§ 18-1.3-401.5 and 18-1.3-501

facts.label: Below misdemeanors
facts.value: For offenses committed on or after March 1, 2022, an ordinary petty offense carries up to 10 days in jail, a fine up to $300, or both. A civil infraction carries a fine up to $100. — C.R.S. § 18-1.3-503

rows: C.R.S. § 18-1.3-501; up to $1,000 fine, jail, or both; offenses on or after March 1, 2022
C.R.S. § 18-1.3-501; up to $750 fine, jail, or both; offenses on or after March 1, 2022

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Colorado
bullets: Reports of suspected state-law crimes ordinarily go to local police or the county sheriff. District attorneys prosecute state criminal cases within their judicial districts; a private complaint does not itself establish criminal charges. — C.R.S. §§ 16-2.5-301, 16-2.5-103 and 20-1-102

District courts have jurisdiction over felony trials. County courts have jurisdiction over misdemeanors and conduct preliminary hearings in felony cases when authorized. — Colorado Constitution, article VI, § 9; C.R.S. § 13-6-106
Municipal ordinance prosecutions are distinct from state felony and misdemeanor prosecutions and are generally handled in municipal court. — C.R.S. § 13-10-104

sections.heading: Common questions in Colorado
bullets: Does a felony always mean prison? No. Probation may be available, but eligibility depends on the offense, criminal history and applicable sentencing restrictions. — C.R.S. § 18-1.3-201

Can a felony sentence exceed the table's range? Yes. Aggravated sentencing, crime-of-violence provisions and habitual-criminal provisions can change the ordinary range. The table also does not include mandatory parole. — C.R.S. §§ 18-1.3-401, 18-1.3-406 and 18-1.3-801

Are all misdemeanors punishable by less than a year? Not necessarily. Older offenses and separately classified drug misdemeanors can have different sentencing limits from the current ordinary misdemeanor classes. — C.R.S. § 18-1.3-501

What are the usual prosecution deadlines? The general limitation periods are three years for other felonies, eighteen months for misdemeanors and six months for petty offenses. Numerous offense-specific exceptions, extensions and tolling rules apply; some crimes have no limitation period. — C.R.S. § 16-5-401

Colorado General Assembly — Title 16, Criminal Proceedings
Colorado General Assembly — Title 13, Courts and Court Procedure
Colorado General Assembly — Title 20, District Attorneys

criminal-law/connecticut/drug-charges.summary: Connecticut drug charges depend on the substance, the conduct alleged, and the statute charged; possessing a controlled substance is different from selling it or possessing it with intent to sell. Under Connecticut General Statutes § 21a-279, unauthorized possession of a controlled substance other than cannabis is generally a class A misdemeanor, while sale and distribution offenses fall under separate statutes carrying more serious consequences. Cannabis has separate rules, and its legalization did not make every form of possession or sale lawful.

facts.label: Basic possession offense
facts.value: Section 21a-279(a)(1) covers possessing or controlling a controlled substance, other than cannabis, unless authorized by law. The basic offense is a class A misdemeanor. A lawful prescription can establish authorization; the substance's status as prescription medication does not by itself make possession lawful. — Conn. Gen. Stat. § 21a-279

facts.label: Class A misdemeanor sentencing limits
facts.value: The ordinary statutory maximum for a class A misdemeanor is one year of imprisonment and a $2,000 fine. These are maximums, not mandatory sentences for every possession conviction. — Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 53a-36, 53a-42

facts.label: Controlled-substance definitions
facts.value: Connecticut's drug laws distinguish controlled substances, narcotic substances, cannabis, and other defined categories. The applicable definition and statutory provision matter when identifying the offense and available punishment. — Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 21a-240, 21a-243

rows: Possession or control of a controlled substance other than cannabis is generally prosecuted under the basic possession statute.
Sale or possession with intent to sell
The statute reaches specified conduct including manufacturing, distributing, selling, and possessing with intent to sell; a completed sale is not required for every listed offense.
Certain trafficking offenses involving a person who is not drug-dependent
A separate statute addresses specified substances and conduct by a person who is not drug-dependent. Its sentencing provisions differ from ordinary possession.
Connecticut separately prohibits specified use, possession with intent to use, and delivery of drug paraphernalia. The statute contains exceptions, including cannabis-related exceptions.

facts.label: Search warrants
facts.value: Connecticut law authorizes search warrants upon a sworn application establishing probable cause. Whether a particular search required a warrant or qualified for an exception is a separate issue from whether the substance was illegal. — Conn. Gen. Stat. § 54-33a; U.S. Const. amend. IV

facts.label: Release before trial
facts.value: Connecticut's pretrial-release statute governs release conditions and bond determinations. An accusation alone is not a conviction, and a possession charge does not automatically require detention until trial. — Conn. Gen. Stat. § 54-64a

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Connecticut
bullets: Connecticut Superior Court handles state criminal drug prosecutions. Criminal matters are generally handled in Geographical Area courts, while Judicial District courts handle more serious criminal matters.
The Connecticut Division of Criminal Justice, through the appropriate State's Attorney's office, prosecutes state drug offenses.
The Connecticut Division of Public Defender Services provides representation to qualifying defendants in criminal cases. Eligibility depends on applicable financial and case requirements.

sections.heading: Common questions in Connecticut
bullets: Is ordinary drug possession always a felony? No. The basic non-cannabis possession offense under § 21a-279(a)(1) is a class A misdemeanor.
Does a sale charge require a completed transaction? No. Section 21a-277 also covers possession with intent to sell and other specified conduct.
Is cannabis treated exactly like other controlled substances? No. Section 21a-279 excludes cannabis from its basic possession provision, and separate laws govern cannabis.
Can a prescription matter? Yes. Section 21a-279 prohibits unauthorized possession; possession authorized by a valid prescription is legally different from unauthorized possession.
Who can assess a search or the exact sentencing exposure? Those issues depend on the charge and case facts. Talk to a lawyer.

sources.label: Connecticut General Assembly — Chapter 420b, Dependency-Producing Drugs
Connecticut General Assembly — Chapter 952, Penal Code
Connecticut General Assembly — Chapter 960, Information, Procedure and Bail
Connecticut Judicial Branch — Court Directory

criminal-law/connecticut/juvenile-law.summary: Connecticut generally handles alleged crimes committed before age 18 as juvenile delinquency matters in the Superior Court, although statutory age limits, offense exclusions, and transfer rules determine whether a particular case belongs there. Juvenile proceedings have different confidentiality rules and dispositions from adult criminal cases, and a delinquency adjudication is not a criminal conviction. Certain felony cases involving children age 15 or older can move to the regular criminal docket.

sections.heading: Connecticut juvenile jurisdiction and basic protections

facts.label: Court and governing law
facts.value: The Superior Court has jurisdiction over juvenile matters. Connecticut’s principal juvenile delinquency provisions appear in Chapter 815t of the General Statutes; juvenile matters are kept separate from other Superior Court business as the statute requires. — Connecticut General Statutes §§ 46b-121 and 46b-122.

facts.label: Age and offense definitions
facts.value: Section 46b-120 defines who is a child for delinquency proceedings and which violations constitute delinquent acts. Age when the alleged conduct occurred matters; motor vehicle offenses and certain other violations have specific exclusions, so not every offense involving someone under 18 is a delinquency case. — Connecticut General Statutes § 46b-120.

facts.label: Right to counsel
facts.value: At the commencement of a delinquency proceeding, the judge must inform the child and the child’s parent or guardian of the right to counsel. Counsel must be provided when the statutory financial-eligibility requirements are met. — Connecticut General Statutes § 46b-135.

sections.heading: How juvenile cases differ from adult cases

rows: An adjudication that a child is delinquent is not deemed a criminal conviction.
Juvenile delinquency records are generally confidential, but the statute authorizes access and disclosure to specified people and agencies.
Juvenile hearings are generally restricted to people whose presence is necessary, with statutory exceptions.
The juvenile court uses delinquency dispositions, including probation and authorized services or placement, rather than automatically imposing adult sentencing rules.
Specified felony cases involving children who were at least 15 when the alleged offense occurred are subject to mandatory or discretionary transfer rules.

sections.heading: Detention and transfer are separate decisions

facts.label: Detention before disposition
facts.value: Juvenile detention is governed by statutory custody, court-order, and detention criteria. An arrest or delinquency allegation does not by itself establish that a child must remain detained while the case proceeds. — Connecticut General Statutes § 46b-133.

facts.label: Transfer requirements
facts.value: Transfer depends on the child’s age, the charged felony, and the applicable statutory findings and procedures. Connecticut distinguishes automatic-transfer categories from cases requiring a prosecutor’s motion and judicial determination; return to juvenile court is available in specified circumstances. — Connecticut General Statutes § 46b-127.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Connecticut
bullets: Superior Court for Juvenile Matters: Connecticut’s Judicial Branch operates the juvenile court locations that handle delinquency proceedings. Case filings belong with the court handling the matter, subject to applicable jurisdiction and confidentiality rules.

Police and juvenile prosecutors: Police investigate alleged criminal conduct; juvenile prosecutors handle delinquency prosecutions. The juvenile court is not an administrative consumer-complaint agency.
Office of Chief Public Defender: Connecticut’s public defender system provides juvenile delinquency representation under the governing eligibility and appointment rules.

sections.heading: Common questions in Connecticut
bullets: Is a delinquency finding an adult conviction? No. Section 46b-145 expressly distinguishes a delinquency adjudication from a criminal conviction.
Are juvenile records completely secret? No. Section 46b-124 establishes confidentiality but also permits specified access and disclosures.
Can a child face adult prosecution? Yes. Section 46b-127 provides transfer procedures for specified felonies involving children age 15 or older.

Does turning 18 automatically make earlier conduct an adult case? No. The statutory definitions account for proceedings concerning conduct committed before age 18; transfer and offense-specific exclusions can still matter.

criminal-law/georgia/domestic-violence-c.summary: Georgia does not use one criminal charge for every domestic violence incident; prosecutors charge offenses such as battery, assault, stalking, or criminal trespass, with family-violence rules applying to qualifying relationships. Georgia’s Family Violence Act covers specified crimes between spouses, parents of the same child, certain family members, and people who live or formerly lived together. Criminal prosecution and a civil family violence protective order are separate proceedings with different purposes and procedures.

sections.heading: What counts as family violence in Georgia

facts.label: Covered conduct
facts.value: Family violence includes any felony, or battery, simple battery, simple assault, assault, stalking, criminal damage to property, unlawful restraint, or criminal trespass, when committed between people in a covered relationship. Not every argument or relationship conflict meets this definition. — O.C.G.A. § 19-13-1

facts.label: Covered relationships
facts.value: The statute covers past or present spouses; parents of the same child; parents and children; stepparents and stepchildren; foster parents and foster children; and other people living or formerly living in the same household. Dating alone is not a listed relationship under this definition. — O.C.G.A. § 19-13-1

facts.label: Parental discipline exclusion
facts.value: The definition excludes reasonable discipline administered by a parent to a child, including corporal punishment, restraint, or detention. This is not a blanket exemption for violence against children. — O.C.G.A. § 19-13-1

rows: Includes attempting a violent injury or committing an act that places another person in reasonable apprehension of immediately receiving a violent injury.
Includes intentionally making physical contact of an insulting or provoking nature, or intentionally causing physical harm.
Requires intentionally causing substantial physical harm or visible bodily harm; visible harm includes substantial bruising or swelling observable by someone other than the victim.
A second or subsequent conviction for family violence battery is a felony punishable by one to five years of imprisonment, whether the victim is the same person or someone else.
Generally permits a fine up to $1,000, confinement up to 12 months, or both; offense-specific enhancements can change the applicable classification or punishment.

facts.label: Temporary orders and hearing
facts.value: A superior court may issue temporary relief without first hearing from the respondent when the statutory requirements are met. A hearing must occur within 30 days after the petition is filed; otherwise, the petition stands dismissed unless the parties agree otherwise. — O.C.G.A. § 19-13-3

facts.label: Available relief and duration
facts.value: Relief can include prohibiting violence or contact, awarding possession of the residence, and temporary custody or support provisions. Protective orders may last up to 12 months and may be converted to a three-year or permanent order through the statutory process. — O.C.G.A. § 19-13-4

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Georgia
bullets: Local police departments and county sheriffs investigate alleged criminal conduct. Misdemeanor prosecutions generally proceed in state court where one exists; superior courts have exclusive jurisdiction over felony trials. — Georgia Constitution, Article VI, Section IV, Paragraph I; O.C.G.A. § 15-7-4
Civil family violence petitions belong in superior court, generally in the county where the respondent resides. Special venue provisions apply to nonresident respondents. — O.C.G.A. § 19-13-2

sections.heading: Common questions in Georgia
bullets: Must there be a visible injury? No. Simple assault and simple battery can apply without visible injury. — O.C.G.A. §§ 16-5-20, 16-5-23
Are former household members covered? Yes. The definition expressly includes people formerly living in the same household. — O.C.G.A. § 19-13-1
Does a protective order replace criminal charges? No. Civil protective relief and prosecution for a criminal offense are separate proceedings. — O.C.G.A. §§ 19-13-3, 19-13-4
Can repeat battery involve a different victim? Yes. The repeat-conviction provision expressly covers violence against the same or another victim. — O.C.G.A. § 16-5-23.1(f)

sources.label: Georgia General Assembly — Georgia Code access
Georgia.gov — Get a Protective Order
Georgia Commission on Family Violence

criminal-law/georgia/expungement.summary: Georgia generally calls expungement “record restriction”: qualifying criminal-history information is kept from most employment and licensing checks rather than physically destroyed, and criminal justice agencies retain access for authorized purposes. Under O.C.G.A. § 35-3-37, eligibility depends on how the case ended, the offense, and whether the request concerns an arrest without conviction or an eligible misdemeanor conviction. Restricting the Georgia criminal-history record does not automatically seal the court file; court-record sealing is a separate process.

facts.label: Restriction, not destruction
facts.value: Restricted information remains available to criminal justice agencies for law enforcement and criminal investigative purposes. Restriction limits its availability for noncriminal justice purposes; it does not erase the underlying event — O.C.G.A. § 35-3-37(a).

facts.label: Cases without convictions
facts.value: Qualifying dismissals, decisions not to prosecute, and acquittals can support restriction. Statutory exceptions apply, so a dismissed charge is not automatically eligible in every case — O.C.G.A. § 35-3-37(h)–(i).

facts.label: Court records
facts.value: A court file is distinct from the criminal-history information maintained through the Georgia Crime Information Center. Georgia provides a separate procedure for sealing qualifying court records — O.C.G.A. § 35-3-37(m).

rows: The administrative application process generally begins with the arresting agency and includes prosecuting-attorney review.
O.C.G.A. § 35-3-37; Georgia Bureau of Investigation guidance
Qualifying restriction is generally handled through the disposition-reporting process rather than the older arresting-agency application.
O.C.G.A. § 35-3-37; Georgia Bureau of Investigation guidance
A petition may be available after completion of the sentence and at least four conviction-free years, excluding nonserious traffic offenses, with no pending criminal charges.
The adult misdemeanor-conviction provision permits restriction of up to two misdemeanor convictions, or a series of misdemeanors arising from a single incident, during a lifetime.
The court considers whether the harm to the individual's privacy clearly outweighs the public interest in the information remaining publicly available.

facts.label: Not every misdemeanor qualifies
facts.value: The misdemeanor-conviction provision excludes specified offenses, including driving under the influence. Meeting the waiting period alone does not establish eligibility or require the court to grant restriction — O.C.G.A. § 35-3-37(j)(4).

facts.label: Successful First Offender discharge
facts.value: Georgia's First Offender Act allows qualifying defendants to receive deferred adjudication. Successful discharge exonerates the defendant, and the defendant is not considered to have a criminal conviction from that proceeding — O.C.G.A. §§ 42-8-60 and 42-8-62.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Georgia
bullets: Arresting law enforcement agency: the starting point for the administrative restriction application covering arrests before July 1, 2013.
Prosecuting attorney's office: reviews eligibility in the administrative process and handles qualifying restriction information through case-disposition reporting.
Court of conviction: receives petitions under the eligible misdemeanor-conviction provision, O.C.G.A. § 35-3-37(j)(4).
Court that handled the criminal case: considers applicable court-record sealing requests under O.C.G.A. § 35-3-37(m).
Georgia Bureau of Investigation, Georgia Crime Information Center: maintains statewide criminal-history information and publishes restriction procedures.

sections.heading: Common questions in Georgia
bullets: Does restriction delete the record? No. Authorized criminal justice access remains available.
Does a dismissal always qualify? No. The statute contains exceptions based on the circumstances and disposition of the case.
Can a misdemeanor conviction qualify? Some can, subject to offense exclusions, sentence completion, the four-year requirement, pending-charge restrictions, and judicial review.
Is the courthouse file automatically sealed? No. Criminal-history restriction and court-record sealing are separate procedures.

sources.label: Georgia.gov — Request Restriction of Your Arrest Record
Georgia Bureau of Investigation — Obtaining Criminal History Record Information

criminal-law/florida/juvenile-law.summary: Florida generally handles offenses committed before age 18 through its juvenile delinquency system, governed by Chapter 985, Florida Statutes, rather than through ordinary adult criminal proceedings. Circuit courts hear delinquency cases, and the Florida Department of Juvenile Justice administers detention, probation, and commitment programs. Juveniles have rights to counsel and an adjudicatory hearing, but qualifying cases can move to adult court, and juvenile records are not automatically confidential in every circumstance.

sections.heading: Florida juvenile jurisdiction and procedural rights

facts.label: Governing law and court
facts.value: Chapter 985, Florida Statutes, governs juvenile delinquency. Circuit courts have original jurisdiction over proceedings alleging that a child committed a delinquent act or violation of law. Jurisdiction can continue beyond the child's eighteenth birthday under statutory conditions; turning 18 does not automatically end an existing case. — Fla. Stat. §§ 985.01, 985.0301.

facts.label: Right to counsel
facts.value: A child is entitled to representation by legal counsel at all stages of delinquency proceedings. The court appoints counsel when the child and the child's parents or legal guardian are indigent under the applicable standards, subject to statutory rules governing waiver and payment. — Fla. Stat. § 985.033.

facts.label: Burden of proof and hearing
facts.value: An adjudicatory hearing determines whether the child committed the alleged delinquent act. The court conducts that hearing without a jury, and the allegations must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt. An adjudication of delinquency is not a criminal conviction. — Fla. Stat. § 985.35.

sections.heading: Key stages, deadlines, and possible outcomes

rows: A child detained under the statute receives a detention hearing within 24 hours after being taken into custody. Continued detention requires a judicial determination under the statutory criteria.

Florida law authorizes prearrest and postarrest diversion programs. Participation and eligibility depend on the applicable program and statutory requirements; diversion is not guaranteed in every case.
After the required findings and disposition process, the court may impose probation or commitment to the Department of Juvenile Justice, subject to statutory restrictions and required findings.
Juvenile probation involves supervision and court-imposed conditions. The statute authorizes requirements such as community service and restitution; the conditions depend on the disposition.

The state attorney may file adult charges against qualifying juveniles. For children aged 14 or 15, discretionary direct filing is limited to listed offenses; different criteria apply to those aged 16 or 17.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Florida
bullets: Circuit court, juvenile division: Delinquency petitions, detention decisions, adjudications, and dispositions are handled in circuit court under Chapter 985. The circuit court clerk maintains the court file, subject to access restrictions.
Office of the State Attorney: The state attorney for the judicial circuit makes delinquency charging decisions and exercises direct-filing authority where authorized. — Fla. Stat. §§ 985.15, 985.557.

Florida Department of Juvenile Justice: DJJ administers juvenile detention and supervises delinquency programs, including probation and residential commitment. Its Office of Inspector General receives complaints involving agency operations, employees, and providers.

Office of the Public Defender: Public defenders provide representation when appointed for eligible juveniles. Case-specific questions about detention, adult prosecution, or record access are matters to talk to a lawyer about.

sections.heading: Common questions in Florida
bullets: Does every juvenile case stay in juvenile court? No. Florida authorizes judicial waiver, direct filing by the state attorney, and indictment in specified circumstances. — Fla. Stat. §§ 985.556–985.558.

Are all juvenile records confidential? No. Section 985.04 protects many records but makes specified identifying information public for certain felony-related cases involving children aged 14 or older. Other statutory exceptions also apply.
Is a juvenile entitled to a jury? Not at a juvenile delinquency adjudicatory hearing; the judge decides the allegations. — Fla. Stat. § 985.35.

Does delinquency adjudication equal an adult conviction? No. Florida expressly distinguishes delinquency adjudications from criminal convictions, although other laws can still attach consequences to juvenile history. — Fla. Stat. § 985.35.

sources.label: Florida Legislature — Chapter 985, Juvenile Justice
Florida Legislature — Section 985.255, Detention criteria
Florida Legislature — Section 985.557, Direct filing
Florida Department of Juvenile Justice — Office of Inspector General

criminal-law/georgia/juvenile-law.summary: Georgia generally handles alleged criminal conduct committed before a person’s 17th birthday as a juvenile delinquency matter, although specified serious offenses committed at ages 13 through 16 fall within the superior court’s jurisdiction. The Georgia Juvenile Code provides procedures for detention, legal representation, adjudication, and disposition, with rehabilitation a central purpose. A delinquency adjudication is not an adult criminal conviction, but juvenile proceedings can still result in probation, placement outside the home, or commitment to the Department of Juvenile Justice.

facts.label: Controlling law
facts.value: The Georgia Juvenile Code is in Title 15, Chapter 11 of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated. Article 6 governs delinquency proceedings, including adjudication and disposition. — O.C.G.A. Title 15, Chapter 11, Article 6

facts.label: Age for delinquency jurisdiction
facts.value: For delinquency purposes, the definition of a child generally covers someone under 17. The definition also permits continued juvenile jurisdiction over certain people under 21 whose delinquent acts occurred before age 17; reaching 17 does not automatically end an existing juvenile case. — O.C.G.A. § 15-11-2

facts.label: Adult-court exceptions
facts.value: Superior court has exclusive original jurisdiction over specified offenses allegedly committed by children ages 13 through 16. Examples include murder, rape, and armed robbery committed with a firearm. These are statutory exceptions, not a rule that every felony allegation goes to adult court. — O.C.G.A. § 15-11-560

sections.heading: How different juvenile matters are handled

rows: Generally involves conduct that would be a crime if committed by an adult.
Certain conduct, including habitual truancy or running away, falls within a separate statutory category rather than ordinary delinquency.
The state must prove delinquency beyond a reasonable doubt; juvenile delinquency adjudications are heard without a jury.
Available orders include probation, restitution, and commitment to the Department of Juvenile Justice, subject to statutory conditions.
Special disposition rules apply, including provisions for restrictive custody; ordinary juvenile outcomes do not describe every designated-felony case.

facts.label: Legal representation
facts.value: Children have a right to legal representation in delinquency proceedings. Georgia law provides appointed counsel for children who qualify; a parent’s participation is not a substitute for the child’s lawyer. — O.C.G.A. Title 15, Chapter 11, Article 6

facts.label: Confidentiality is qualified
facts.value: Juvenile court and law-enforcement records are subject to special access restrictions, but juvenile confidentiality is not absolute. Statutory exceptions permit access or disclosure in specified circumstances, and sealing is governed by separate requirements. — O.C.G.A. Title 15, Chapter 11, Article 7

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Georgia
bullets: Juvenile delinquency proceedings are handled in the appropriate county juvenile court unless superior-court jurisdiction applies. The juvenile court clerk maintains that court’s filings and case records.
Superior court handles criminal cases falling within its jurisdiction under O.C.G.A. § 15-11-560.

The Georgia Department of Juvenile Justice administers state juvenile detention facilities and services for youth under its supervision. Facility or agency-service complaints fall within its administrative responsibilities.
The Georgia Public Defender Council and circuit public defender offices provide information about public defense, including juvenile representation.

sections.heading: Common questions in Georgia
bullets: Is a 17-year-old automatically treated as a juvenile? No. An offense committed at 17 generally falls outside ordinary juvenile delinquency jurisdiction.
Can a child face charges in adult court? Yes. Specified serious offenses and statutory transfer procedures can place a case in superior court.
Is delinquency the same as an adult conviction? No. A delinquency adjudication is legally distinct, although it can carry substantial consequences.
Are all juvenile records automatically erased at 18? No. Georgia has statutory sealing procedures, not a blanket rule erasing every juvenile record at adulthood.

criminal-law/delaware/domestic-violence-.summary: Delaware generally prosecutes domestic violence through offenses such as assault, reckless endangering, and unlawful imprisonment, rather than through one criminal charge called domestic violence. The applicable offense and its classification depend on the conduct, injury, mental state, and other statutory elements; the relationship between the people involved can also affect which court handles the case. A civil protection-from-abuse proceeding is separate from a criminal prosecution and does not itself establish criminal guilt.

sections.heading: How Delaware domestic violence cases are classified

facts.label: The underlying offense controls
facts.value: An allegation involving a spouse, partner, or other family member must satisfy the elements of a particular criminal offense. For example, third-degree assault includes intentionally or recklessly causing physical injury to another person. The domestic relationship does not automatically make every assault a felony. — 11 Del. C. § 611.

facts.label: Misdemeanor versus felony assault
facts.value: Third-degree assault is a class A misdemeanor. Second-degree assault is a class D felony, and first-degree assault is a class B felony. The felony provisions cover specifically defined circumstances involving injury, intent, weapons, or other statutory factors. — 11 Del. C. §§ 611–613.

facts.label: Civil protection is a separate process
facts.value: Delaware's protection-from-abuse law defines abuse for civil protective proceedings. That definition includes conduct beyond physical assault, but a civil finding of abuse is not a criminal conviction. — 10 Del. C. §§ 1041–1045.

sections.heading: Examples of charges and statutory imprisonment limits

rows: Reckless endangering in the second degree
Reckless endangering in the first degree

facts.label: Who is covered
facts.value: The statute covers specified family and household relationships, including former spouses, people living together as a couple, people with a child in common, and people in a current or former substantive dating relationship. Eligibility follows the statutory definitions. — 10 Del. C. § 1041.

facts.label: Available relief
facts.value: Family Court may prohibit abuse and contact, grant exclusive possession of a residence, and order other authorized relief. Its statutory powers also include firearm-related restrictions and temporary custody provisions. These are civil protective remedies, not the sentencing ranges for an assault conviction. — 10 Del. C. § 1045.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Delaware
bullets: Police agencies receive reports of suspected criminal conduct; the Delaware Department of Justice prosecutes state criminal cases. — 29 Del. C. § 2504.

Family Court hears protection-from-abuse petitions and has jurisdiction over specified adult misdemeanor offenses against family members. Its criminal jurisdiction is subject to statutory limits and exceptions. — 10 Del. C. §§ 922, 1042.
Superior Court handles adult felony prosecutions, including felony assault charges arising from domestic incidents. — 11 Del. C. § 2701.

sections.heading: Common questions in Delaware
bullets: Is domestic violence always a felony? No. Third-degree assault is a class A misdemeanor; more serious assault offenses are felonies. — 11 Del. C. §§ 611–613.

Can charges arise without an actual injury? Yes. Reckless endangering addresses conduct creating the specified substantial risk, without requiring that the threatened injury actually occur. — 11 Del. C. §§ 603–604.
Does a protection-from-abuse order equal a criminal conviction? No. It is relief issued through a separate civil proceeding. — 10 Del. C. §§ 1041–1045.

Are the table's imprisonment limits a prediction of the sentence? No. Sentencing depends on the conviction and applicable sentencing provisions, including any relevant enhancements. For an individual case, talk to a lawyer. — 11 Del. C. §§ 4205–4206.
