Delaware Code, Title 10, Chapter 9 — Family Court
Delaware Code, Title 11, Chapter 27 — Jurisdiction and Venue

criminal-law/georgia/traffic-violations.summary: Georgia generally treats violations of its traffic code as misdemeanors, although the punishment and licensing consequences depend on the offense and the driver’s record. A traffic case can involve court fines, possible jail time, and separate Department of Driver Services action, including points or license suspension. Georgia also imposes a $200 Super Speeder fee for qualifying speeding convictions, separate from the court’s fine; more serious conduct, including certain repeat DUI offenses, can carry felony consequences.

facts.label: General classification
facts.value: Unless another law provides otherwise, violating Georgia’s Uniform Rules of the Road is a misdemeanor. This means an ordinary traffic charge can be a criminal case rather than merely a civil ticket. — O.C.G.A. § 40-6-1(a).

facts.label: General misdemeanor ceiling
facts.value: The general misdemeanor punishment permits a fine of up to $1,000, confinement for up to 12 months, or both. Offense-specific provisions can establish different limits, and court costs and statutory assessments are separate from the base fine. — O.C.G.A. § 17-10-3.

facts.label: Reckless driving
facts.value: Driving with reckless disregard for the safety of persons or property is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $1,000, imprisonment for up to 12 months, or both. — O.C.G.A. § 40-6-390.

facts.label: Felony DUI
facts.value: A fourth or subsequent qualifying DUI conviction within the statutory 10-year period is a felony. The statute specifies how the period and qualifying convictions are counted. — O.C.G.A. § 40-6-391(c)(4).

rows: Speeding 34 mph or more above the limit

facts.label: Qualifying speeds
facts.value: The additional $200 state fee applies to a conviction for driving at least 75 mph on a two-lane road or at least 85 mph on any road or highway in Georgia. It is separate from the court fine. — O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189.

facts.label: Payment deadline
facts.value: Failure to pay the Super Speeder fee within 120 days after DDS notice results in suspension of the driver’s license or driving privilege. — O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189.

facts.label: Accumulated points
facts.value: Accumulating 15 or more points within 24 months triggers a points-based suspension. Separate suspension rules apply to certain offenses and younger drivers. — O.C.G.A. §§ 40-5-57 and 40-5-57.1.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Georgia
bullets: Traffic prosecutions are handled by courts with jurisdiction over the charge and location. Municipal, probate, and state courts commonly handle traffic misdemeanors; their jurisdiction is not identical. — O.C.G.A. §§ 36-32-1, 40-13-21, and 15-7-4.
Georgia superior courts handle felony prosecutions, including felony traffic offenses. — Georgia Constitution, Article VI, Section IV, Paragraph I.
The Georgia Department of Driver Services administers driver’s license records, points, suspensions, and Super Speeder fees. DDS does not decide guilt on the underlying traffic charge.

sections.heading: Common questions in Georgia
bullets: Is ordinary speeding a criminal offense? Generally yes: speeding under Georgia’s traffic code is ordinarily a misdemeanor. — O.C.G.A. §§ 40-6-1 and 40-6-181.
Does every speeding conviction carry points? No. DDS assigns no speeding points for convictions less than 15 mph above the limit; that does not eliminate the conviction or fine.
Does paying the court fine cover Super Speeder? No. The $200 DDS fee is an additional state assessment. — O.C.G.A. § 40-6-189.
Does Super Speeder itself add extra points? No. Points depend on the underlying speeding conviction, not the Super Speeder designation.

sources.label: Georgia General Assembly — Georgia Code
Georgia Department of Driver Services — Points and Points Reduction
Georgia Department of Driver Services — Super Speeder

criminal-law/hawaii/arrest-process.summary: In Hawaii, an arrest may occur under a warrant or, when statutory requirements are met, without one; an arrested person must be brought before a district judge without unnecessary delay. At the initial appearance, the court addresses the charge, counsel, and release conditions, while a felony case may require additional proceedings before prosecution in circuit court. Hawaii law also protects access to counsel and family during detention; an arrest does not itself establish guilt.

sections.heading: Authority to arrest and rights during detention

facts.label: Arrest without a warrant
facts.value: Police officers and other officers of justice may arrest without a warrant when they have probable cause to believe a person committed an offense, whether the offense occurred in their presence or otherwise. The statute connects probable cause to facts and circumstances supporting a reasonable suspicion that the person committed an offense. — Hawaii Revised Statutes § 803-5

facts.label: Access to counsel and family
facts.value: For an arrest for examination, Hawaii law prohibits denying the arrested person access to counsel or a family member at the detention location at reasonable intervals and for a reasonable time. — Hawaii Revised Statutes § 803-9

facts.label: Opportunity to consult counsel
facts.value: For an arrest for examination, examining the arrested person before providing a fair opportunity to see and consult counsel is prohibited. This statutory protection is separate from the court's later explanation of rights. — Hawaii Revised Statutes § 803-9

rows: An arrested person must be taken before a district judge without unnecessary delay.
Hawaii Rules of Penal Procedure, Rule 5
The judge informs the defendant of the charge, the right to counsel, and the right not to make a statement.
Hawaii Rules of Penal Procedure, Rule 5
The initial-appearance procedure includes addressing bail or release under applicable law.
Hawaii Rules of Penal Procedure, Rule 5
When applicable and not waived, a preliminary hearing determines whether probable cause supports holding the defendant to answer in circuit court; it is not a trial of guilt.
Hawaii Rules of Penal Procedure, Rule 5
An indigent defendant is entitled to assigned counsel unless that right is waived, subject to the rule's exception for petty misdemeanors when no imprisonment will be imposed.
Hawaii Rules of Penal Procedure, Rule 44

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Hawaii
bullets: District courts handle initial appearances for arrested defendants and preliminary hearings in felony cases. They also conduct trials for most misdemeanors, petty misdemeanors, and violations; jury-trial matters proceed in circuit court. — Hawaii Judiciary, District Courts; Hawaii Rules of Penal Procedure, Rule 5

Circuit courts handle felony prosecutions after the applicable charging and preliminary procedures. An initial district-court appearance does not mean the felony trial will occur there. — Hawaii Rules of Penal Procedure, Rules 5 and 7

Requests concerning release and appointment of counsel are matters for the court handling the criminal proceeding. The initial-appearance rules address these subjects. — Hawaii Rules of Penal Procedure, Rule 5

sections.heading: Common questions in Hawaii
bullets: Must an officer personally witness the offense? No. Hawaii's warrantless-arrest statute permits an arrest based on probable cause even when the offense occurred outside the officer's presence. — Hawaii Revised Statutes § 803-5
Does every arrest require a warrant? No. Section 803-5 expressly authorizes warrantless arrests when its probable-cause requirement is satisfied. — Hawaii Revised Statutes § 803-5

Is the first appearance a determination of guilt? No. It addresses the charge, rights, and release; a felony preliminary hearing addresses probable cause rather than guilt. — Hawaii Rules of Penal Procedure, Rule 5

Can police deny all contact with counsel during detention? Hawaii law prohibits denying reasonable access to counsel in an arrest for examination and prohibits examination before a fair opportunity to consult counsel. — Hawaii Revised Statutes § 803-9

Hawaii Legislature — HRS § 803-9

Hawaii Judiciary — District Courts

criminal-law/hawaii/expungement.summary: Hawaii allows qualifying arrest records to be expunged when an arrest or charge did not result in a conviction, subject to exceptions in Hawaii Revised Statutes § 831-3.2; it does not provide a general right to erase every criminal conviction. The Hawaii Criminal Justice Data Center handles arrest-record expungement, while court records involve the Judiciary’s separate procedures, so an expungement should not be understood as automatically eliminating every record of a criminal case.

facts.label: Main statute
facts.value: Hawaii Revised Statutes § 831-3.2 authorizes the attorney general or an authorized representative to issue an expungement order for qualifying arrest records. Its central category covers people arrested for or charged with a crime but not convicted. The statute contains exceptions, so a nonconviction outcome alone does not establish eligibility in every case. — HRS § 831-3.2

facts.label: Agency responsible
facts.value: The Hawaii Criminal Justice Data Center, part of the Department of the Attorney General, administers the state’s criminal-history expungement process. An application to that agency is distinct from a request concerning a court’s own records. — Hawaii Criminal Justice Data Center, Expungements

facts.label: Legal effect
facts.value: The statute provides that a person whose arrest record is expunged is treated as not having been arrested for the covered matter and may state that the person has no record of that arrest. That protection concerns the expunged arrest, not unrelated arrests or convictions. — HRS § 831-3.2

sections.heading: How common case outcomes are treated

rows: A not-guilty outcome falls within the statute’s nonconviction framework, subject to its exceptions.
Dismissal can support expungement eligibility, but the statutory exceptions and the case’s disposition still matter.
Deferred acceptance followed by discharge and dismissal
A one-year waiting period follows discharge and dismissal under the deferred-acceptance procedure.
The general nonconviction expungement provision does not authorize expungement while prosecution or disposition remains pending.
The general arrest-expungement provision is not a blanket remedy for convictions; a conviction requires a separately authorized legal basis.

facts.label: Deferred acceptance is not immediate dismissal
facts.value: Chapter 853 governs deferred acceptance of guilty and no-contest pleas. When the statutory conditions are satisfied, the court discharges the defendant and dismisses the charge without an adjudication of guilt. The discharge-and-dismissal date matters for the separate expungement waiting period. — HRS § 853-1

facts.label: Court-record distinction
facts.value: An HCJDC expungement addresses arrest records; court files and publicly accessible Judiciary information involve a separate court-record process. The Judiciary publishes instructions concerning expungement and sealing, and the statute addresses requests concerning court information associated with an expunged matter. — HRS § 831-3.2; Hawaii State Judiciary, Expungement

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Hawaii
bullets: Arrest-record expungement applications: Hawaii Criminal Justice Data Center, Department of the Attorney General. HCJDC publishes the application materials and eligibility information.
Court-record sealing matters: the Hawaii court where the underlying criminal case was filed. Judiciary procedures concern the court’s records rather than HCJDC’s criminal-history records.
Disputed eligibility or the consequences of an existing record: talk to a lawyer.

sections.heading: Common questions in Hawaii
bullets: Does a dismissal automatically erase the arrest? No. Dismissal and an expungement order are different events under HRS § 831-3.2.
Can a pending case be expunged under the general rule? No. Pending prosecution or disposition is a statutory exception.
Is a successfully completed deferred plea immediately eligible? No. The statute imposes a one-year period after discharge and dismissal.
Does expungement necessarily remove the court docket too? No. Arrest-record expungement and the handling of Judiciary records are separate processes.

sources.label: Hawaii Legislature — HRS § 831-3.2
Hawaii Legislature — HRS § 853-1
Hawaii Criminal Justice Data Center — Expungements
Hawaii State Judiciary — Expungement

criminal-law/idaho/domestic-violence-cha.summary: Idaho prosecutes domestic violence under Idaho Code § 18-918 when an assault or battery involves people who meet the statute’s definition of household members; the charge depends on the conduct, injury, and applicable enhancement provisions. A battery that inflicts a statutory traumatic injury is a felony, while qualifying domestic assaults and batteries without traumatic injury are generally misdemeanors. Criminal no-contact orders and civil protection orders are separate legal mechanisms, and violating either can create additional criminal exposure.

sections.heading: What Idaho domestic violence charges cover

facts.label: Qualifying relationships
facts.value: A household member includes a spouse, former spouse, a person with whom the accused has a child in common, or a person with whom the accused is cohabiting, whether or not they have married. A dating relationship alone does not automatically establish this statutory relationship — Idaho Code § 18-918(1).

facts.label: Traumatic injury
facts.value: The definition includes a bodily condition such as a wound or external or internal injury caused by physical force, whether the injury is minor or serious. It also includes injury of the nature described in Idaho’s attempted-strangulation statute. The felony distinction therefore does not require a severe or permanent injury — Idaho Code § 18-918(1).

facts.label: Battery versus assault
facts.value: Battery includes willful and unlawful force or violence, intentional and unlawful touching against another person’s will, or unlawfully and intentionally causing bodily harm. Assault includes an unlawful attempt, with apparent ability, to commit violent injury, or a qualifying intentional threat that creates a well-founded fear of imminent violence — Idaho Code §§ 18-901 and 18-903.

rows: A battery against a household member that inflicts traumatic injury is a felony punishable by up to ten years in prison.
Generally a misdemeanor; qualifying previous convictions can increase the punishment or change the classification.
An assault against a household member without traumatic injury is addressed by the domestic violence statute.
A court may prohibit contact in a criminal case. Violation of a qualifying order is a separate misdemeanor.
A petition for protection from domestic violence is a civil proceeding, distinct from prosecution of a criminal charge.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Idaho
bullets: Local police departments and county sheriffs receive reports of suspected domestic violence. Criminal charges are prosecuted on behalf of the state, rather than brought as a private civil claim by the alleged victim.
Idaho’s district courts handle felony prosecutions. Magistrate judges handle misdemeanor cases and preliminary proceedings in felony cases within the district court system.
A civil domestic violence protection-order petition is filed in district court under Idaho Code § 39-6304. That filing does not itself constitute a criminal charge or a criminal conviction.
A criminal no-contact order belongs to the criminal proceeding in which it was issued. The criminal court controls that order; it is not interchangeable with a civil protection order.

sections.heading: Common questions in Idaho
bullets: Does domestic battery always require a visible injury? No. Idaho’s battery definition includes intentional, unlawful touching against another person’s will, and § 18-918 separately addresses domestic battery without traumatic injury.
Can a minor injury support a felony charge? Yes. The statutory definition of traumatic injury expressly includes injuries that are minor or serious, provided the other elements are established.
Does an alleged victim’s agreement to contact cancel a criminal no-contact order? No. Private agreement does not amend or terminate a court order.
Are former spouses covered even if they no longer live together? Yes. Former spouses are expressly included in the household-member definition.
Is a civil protection order the same as a conviction? No. A protection order is civil relief; a criminal conviction requires a separate criminal proceeding.

sources.label: Idaho Legislature — Idaho Code § 18-918
Idaho Legislature — Idaho Code § 18-920
Idaho Legislature — Idaho Code § 39-6304
Idaho Legislature — Idaho Code § 18-903

criminal-law/idaho/drug-charges.summary: Idaho drug charges depend on the substance, amount, and alleged conduct: possession, delivery, manufacturing, and trafficking are separate offenses under the Idaho Uniform Controlled Substances Act. Possessing methamphetamine or cocaine is a felony, while possessing three ounces or less of marijuana is a misdemeanor; larger marijuana quantities can support felony charges. Drug paraphernalia can also produce a separate misdemeanor charge, and trafficking offenses carry mandatory minimum penalties that differ from ordinary possession penalties.

facts.label: Possession
facts.value: Idaho generally prohibits possession of a controlled substance unless it was obtained through a valid prescription or another statutory authorization. The substance and applicable schedule determine the offense classification — Idaho Code § 37-2732(c).

facts.label: Delivery and manufacturing
facts.value: Manufacturing, delivering, or possessing a controlled substance with intent to manufacture or deliver is prohibited. These are distinct from simple possession, and the prosecution must establish the conduct charged — Idaho Code § 37-2732(a).

facts.label: Trafficking
facts.value: Idaho's trafficking statute defines offenses using specified substances and quantity thresholds. Trafficking does not necessarily require proof of a completed sale: the statute also covers qualifying possession and manufacturing — Idaho Code § 37-2732B.

sections.heading: Maximum penalties for selected possession charges

facts.label: Paraphernalia possession
facts.value: Using, or possessing with intent to use, drug paraphernalia for prohibited controlled-substance activities is a misdemeanor punishable by up to one year in jail, a fine up to $1,000, or both — Idaho Code § 37-2734A(1).

facts.label: Initial appearance
facts.value: Idaho's initial-appearance rule addresses notice of the charge, the right to counsel, and conditions of release. An initial appearance is not a determination of guilt — Idaho Criminal Rule 5.

facts.label: Preliminary hearing
facts.value: For felony cases proceeding through a preliminary hearing, the magistrate determines whether probable cause supports holding the defendant to answer in district court. This differs from the proof beyond a reasonable doubt required for conviction — Idaho Criminal Rule 5.1.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Idaho
bullets: State misdemeanor drug cases are handled in the magistrate division of Idaho's district courts. Felony trials take place in district court; magistrates handle preliminary felony proceedings.
County prosecuting attorneys prosecute state drug offenses. Municipal prosecuting attorneys may handle misdemeanor cases within their jurisdiction.
Local police departments, county sheriffs, and the Idaho State Police investigate suspected drug crimes. Reporting suspected conduct does not itself establish a criminal charge or conviction.

sections.heading: Common questions in Idaho
bullets: Is a small amount of methamphetamine only a misdemeanor? No. Unlawful methamphetamine possession falls under the felony possession provision; a small quantity alone does not make it a misdemeanor — Idaho Code § 37-2732(c)(1).

Does exactly three ounces of marijuana trigger the larger-quantity felony? No. That felony provision applies to more than three ounces; exactly three ounces falls within the misdemeanor quantity category — Idaho Code § 37-2732(c)(3), (e).

Are the maximum penalties automatically imposed? No. A statutory maximum is a ceiling, not an automatic sentence. Trafficking provisions separately establish mandatory minimum penalties — Idaho Code §§ 37-2732, 37-2732B.
Can paraphernalia support its own charge? Yes. Idaho separately prohibits use or possession with intent to use drug paraphernalia for specified unlawful activities — Idaho Code § 37-2734A.

sources.label: Idaho Legislature — Idaho Code § 37-2732
Idaho Legislature — Idaho Code § 37-2732B
Idaho Legislature — Idaho Code § 37-2734A
Idaho Supreme Court — Idaho Criminal Rules

criminal-law/idaho/traffic-violations.summary: Idaho treats most routine traffic tickets as civil infractions, but reckless driving, inattentive driving and driving under the influence are criminal offenses that can carry jail time. The consequences depend on the charge, qualifying prior convictions and whether aggravating circumstances apply; a first ordinary DUI carries up to six months in jail and a $1,000 fine, plus license suspension. Infraction proceedings and criminal traffic prosecutions follow different court rules.

facts.label: Infraction classification
facts.value: Idaho's Infraction Rules govern civil public offenses classified as infractions. An infraction is not a crime, and an infraction judgment does not carry incarceration. Traffic offenses specifically classified as misdemeanors or felonies follow criminal procedures instead. — Idaho Infraction Rule 1.

facts.label: Reckless driving
facts.value: Driving carelessly and heedlessly, or without due caution, at a speed or in a manner likely to endanger a person or property constitutes reckless driving. The statute also covers passing when a line in the driver's lane indicates a sight-distance restriction. — Idaho Code § 49-1401(1).

facts.label: Inattentive driving
facts.value: This misdemeanor applies when driving is inattentive, careless or imprudent rather than heedless or wanton, or when the danger to people or property is slight. Idaho expressly identifies it as a lesser offense than reckless driving. — Idaho Code § 49-1401(3).

rows: Up to 6 months in county jail, a fine up to $1,000, or both.
Reckless driving with a qualifying prior conviction within 5 years
Up to 1 year in county jail, a fine up to $2,000, or both.
Up to 90 days in county jail, a fine up to $300, or both.
Up to 6 months in jail and a fine up to $1,000; statutory license suspension also applies.

facts.label: Alcohol concentration and impairment
facts.value: Idaho prohibits driving or actual physical control while under the influence of alcohol, drugs or other intoxicating substances, and separately prohibits an alcohol concentration of 0.08 or more. The law reaches highways, streets, bridges and public or private property open to the public. — Idaho Code § 18-8004(1)(a).

facts.label: Drivers under 21
facts.value: A person younger than 21 may not drive or be in actual physical control with an alcohol concentration of at least 0.02 but less than 0.08. Separate provisions address this offense. — Idaho Code § 18-8004(1)(d).

facts.label: First ordinary DUI suspension
facts.value: The court must impose a driver's license suspension of at least 90 days and no more than 180 days. The first 30 days are an absolute suspension without driving privileges. — Idaho Code § 18-8005(1).

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Idaho
bullets: Traffic infractions and misdemeanor traffic prosecutions are handled in the magistrate division of Idaho's district courts. Case filings go to the clerk of the court handling the citation or charge.
Felony traffic prosecutions are tried in district court; preliminary felony proceedings may occur before a magistrate.
The Idaho Transportation Department handles driver's license records and administrative licensing matters. Those proceedings are distinct from the court's determination of a criminal charge.

sections.heading: Common questions in Idaho
bullets: Can an ordinary traffic infraction result in jail? No. Idaho treats infractions as civil public offenses, not crimes.
Is inattentive driving merely a ticket? It is a misdemeanor, even when initiated by a citation, and carries possible jail time.
Does DUI always require a 0.08 test result? No. Idaho also prohibits driving while under the influence; the alcohol-concentration prohibition is a separate basis for liability.
Does paying an infraction resolve a separate criminal charge? No. An infraction disposition does not itself dispose of a separately charged misdemeanor or felony.

sources.label: Idaho Legislature — Idaho Code § 49-1401
Idaho Legislature — Idaho Code § 18-8004
Idaho Legislature — Idaho Code § 18-8005
Idaho Supreme Court — Idaho Infraction Rules

criminal-law/illinois/bail-and-bond.summary: Illinois no longer uses cash bail to determine release in criminal cases: monetary bail was abolished, and the statewide change took effect September 18, 2023. Courts instead decide whether a person should be released, released with conditions, or detained under statutory standards that require an individualized hearing. Detention is not automatic based on the charge alone, and the prosecution must establish the legal grounds for holding someone before trial.

sections.heading: Illinois bail and pretrial release rules

facts.label: Cash bail abolished
facts.value: Illinois abolished the requirement to post monetary bail. The governing provisions are in Article 110 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of 1963, as amended through the legislation commonly called the Pretrial Fairness Act. — 725 ILCS 5/110-1.5

facts.label: Presumption of release
facts.value: People charged with offenses are presumed eligible for pretrial release. Conditions must be the least restrictive necessary to reasonably ensure court appearances, protect people and the community, and prevent obstruction of the criminal justice process. — 725 ILCS 5/110-2

facts.label: Individual circumstances
facts.value: The court considers factors including the alleged offense, the evidence, the person's history and characteristics, and identified safety risks. Release decisions are individualized rather than determined by a cash-bail schedule. — 725 ILCS 5/110-5

facts.label: Detention standard
facts.value: A prosecutor must seek detention through a verified petition. The State bears a clear-and-convincing-evidence burden on the applicable statutory requirements, including why release conditions would not sufficiently address the identified threat or prevent willful flight. — 725 ILCS 5/110-6.1

rows: Release conditions include appearing as ordered, submitting to court orders, and not violating criminal statutes.
Depending on statutory findings and the circumstances, conditions may include no-contact requirements, geographic restrictions, or supervision.
Electronic monitoring is a possible release condition, not an automatic substitute for cash bail; statutory necessity requirements apply.
Detention is available only under specified statutory grounds, including qualifying safety-based cases or qualifying cases involving a high likelihood of willful flight.
The statute provides procedures for sanctions, modification of conditions, and revocation. A violation does not automatically require detention.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Illinois
bullets: The Illinois circuit court handling the criminal case decides pretrial release, conditions, detention, and requests to modify existing orders. These are criminal-case proceedings, not a separate civil bail complaint.
The county State's Attorney files a detention petition when seeking detention under Section 110-6.1. The judge, not the prosecutor or a commercial bond company, decides the petition.
The circuit court clerk maintains filings and orders in the criminal case. A person disputing a release or detention order can talk to a lawyer about the applicable court procedure.
Illinois Supreme Court Rule 604(h) governs appellate review of specified pretrial-release decisions. Review is through the Illinois Appellate Court, subject to the rule's procedural requirements.

sections.heading: Common questions in Illinois
bullets: Can someone pay a bondsman to obtain release? Illinois does not require monetary bail under its current pretrial-release system. Payment to a bondsman does not replace the court's release determination.
Does ending cash bail mean everyone is released? No. Section 110-6.1 permits detention when the State establishes the applicable statutory requirements at a hearing.
Does the accused have a lawyer at a detention hearing? Yes. Section 110-6.1 provides a right to counsel and appointed counsel when the accused is indigent.
Is inability to afford a release condition enough to justify detention? No. Section 110-5 prohibits detention solely because a person lacks the financial resources to comply with a release condition.

Can release conditions change? Yes. Article 110 permits modification of conditions and provides procedures for responding to alleged violations. The existing order remains a court order unless changed.

sources.label: Illinois General Assembly — Code of Criminal Procedure of 1963
Illinois General Assembly — 725 ILCS 5/110-6.1, denial of pretrial release
Illinois Courts — Illinois Supreme Court Rules

criminal-law/illinois/domestic-violence-.summary: Illinois prosecutes domestic battery when a person knowingly causes bodily harm to a family or household member, or makes insulting or provoking physical contact, without legal justification. A first offense is generally a Class A misdemeanor, but qualifying prior convictions can make it a felony; aggravated domestic battery covers great bodily harm, permanent disability or disfigurement, and strangulation. The charge and available punishment depend on the conduct, the relationship, and the defendant’s criminal history.

sections.heading: What Illinois domestic violence charges cover

facts.label: Domestic battery
facts.value: The prosecution must establish knowing conduct without legal justification: either bodily harm to a family or household member, or physical contact of an insulting or provoking nature with that person. Visible injury is not required for the physical-contact form of the offense. — 720 ILCS 5/12-3.2(a)

facts.label: Covered relationships
facts.value: Family or household members include spouses, former spouses, parents, children, relatives by blood or marriage, current or former co-residents, people with a child in common, and people who have or had a dating or engagement relationship. A casual acquaintance or ordinary social or business association is excluded from the dating category. — 720 ILCS 5/12-0.1

facts.label: Aggravated domestic battery
facts.value: A domestic battery becomes aggravated when the defendant knowingly causes great bodily harm, permanent disability, or permanent disfigurement, or strangles the victim. Strangulation means intentionally impeding normal breathing or blood circulation by pressure on the throat or neck, or by blocking the nose or mouth. — 720 ILCS 5/12-3.3(a), (a-5)

rows: Domestic battery without an applicable felony enhancement
Less than one year of imprisonment; fine up to $2,500. — 720 ILCS 5/12-3.2(b); 730 ILCS 5/5-4.5-55
Domestic battery with one or two prior domestic battery convictions
Ordinary prison range: 1–3 years. — 720 ILCS 5/12-3.2(b); 730 ILCS 5/5-4.5-45
Domestic battery with three prior domestic battery convictions
Ordinary prison range: 2–5 years. — 720 ILCS 5/12-3.2(b); 730 ILCS 5/5-4.5-40
Domestic battery with four or more prior domestic battery convictions
Ordinary prison range: 3–7 years. — 720 ILCS 5/12-3.2(b); 730 ILCS 5/5-4.5-35
Ordinary prison range: 3–7 years; probation or conditional discharge must include at least 60 consecutive days of imprisonment. — 720 ILCS 5/12-3.3(b); 730 ILCS 5/5-4.5-35

facts.label: Other qualifying convictions
facts.value: A prior domestic battery conviction is not the only route to a felony charge. Section 12-3.2 also lists other qualifying convictions, including specified violent offenses involving a family or household member. — 720 ILCS 5/12-3.2(b)

facts.label: Repeat aggravated domestic battery
facts.value: A second or subsequent aggravated domestic battery conviction requires imprisonment for 3–7 years, or an extended term of 7–14 years when the statutory extended-term requirements apply. — 720 ILCS 5/12-3.3(b)

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Illinois
bullets: Local police departments and county sheriffs receive reports of suspected domestic violence and investigate alleged criminal conduct.
The county State’s Attorney prosecutes Illinois criminal charges; the complaining witness does not independently control the prosecution. — 55 ILCS 5/3-9005

Illinois circuit courts hear domestic battery prosecutions. Circuit courts also handle petitions for orders of protection under the Illinois Domestic Violence Act of 1986. — Illinois Constitution, Article VI, Section 9; 750 ILCS 60/202

sections.heading: Common questions in Illinois
bullets: Must the alleged victim be a spouse? No. The statutory definition includes several other family, household, and dating relationships. — 720 ILCS 5/12-0.1
Does domestic battery require an injury? No. Insulting or provoking physical contact is a separate statutory basis. — 720 ILCS 5/12-3.2(a)
Is strangulation aggravated domestic battery? Yes, when committed in the course of a domestic battery as defined by the statute. — 720 ILCS 5/12-3.3(a-5)

Is a first domestic battery charge always a misdemeanor? No. Other qualifying prior convictions can trigger felony treatment, and aggravated conduct supports a separate felony charge. — 720 ILCS 5/12-3.2(b), 12-3.3

sources.label: Illinois General Assembly — Domestic battery, 720 ILCS 5/12-3.2
Illinois General Assembly — Aggravated domestic battery, 720 ILCS 5/12-3.3
Illinois General Assembly — Definitions, 720 ILCS 5/12-0.1
Illinois General Assembly — Unified Code of Corrections

criminal-law/illinois/drug-charges.summary: Illinois drug charges depend on the substance, its weight, and whether the allegation is possession, manufacture, or delivery; possession with intent to deliver is treated differently from possession alone. The Illinois Controlled Substances Act governs many non-cannabis drug offenses, while cannabis has separate statutes, and potential consequences range from misdemeanor penalties to lengthy felony prison terms. A charge’s classification does not by itself establish the sentence because offense-specific sentencing rules, criminal history, and eligibility for probation or other dispositions also matter.

sections.heading: Illinois drug offenses and important distinctions

facts.label: Possession
facts.value: Knowingly possessing a controlled substance without legal authorization is prohibited. Possession of less than 15 grams of a substance containing cocaine or heroin generally falls under the Class 4 felony provision; larger amounts trigger different classifications and sentencing provisions. — 720 ILCS 570/402.

facts.label: Delivery and intent to deliver
facts.value: Manufacturing, delivering, or possessing a controlled substance with intent to manufacture or deliver is prohibited unless authorized. The substance and quantity determine the applicable subsection and penalties. Delivery does not require a sale: the statutory definition includes an actual, constructive, or attempted transfer. — 720 ILCS 570/102(h), 401.

facts.label: Lawful adult cannabis possession
facts.value: For Illinois residents age 21 or older, the possession limits are 30 grams of cannabis flower, 500 milligrams of THC in cannabis-infused products, and 5 grams of cannabis concentrate. Nonresidents are limited to half those amounts. These limits do not authorize every form of possession, use, or distribution. — 410 ILCS 705/10-10, 10-35.

facts.label: Drug-specific sentences
facts.value: The table lists ordinary, nonextended prison ranges, not every possible drug sentence. Section 401(a) provides quantity-based prison ranges for specified offenses that can exceed the ordinary Class X range. A felony classification also does not necessarily mean imprisonment is mandatory. — 720 ILCS 570/401(a); 730 ILCS 5/5-5-3.

facts.label: First-offender probation
facts.value: Section 410 permits probation without entry of a judgment of conviction for qualifying possession defendants, with their consent. Successful completion results in discharge and dismissal; eligibility depends on statutory conditions, including prior drug convictions. — 720 ILCS 570/410.

facts.label: No monetary bail
facts.value: Illinois abolished monetary bail. Release conditions and any pretrial detention are governed by statutory procedures; detention requires an eligible charge and the findings required by law. — 725 ILCS 5/110-1.5, 110-6.1.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Illinois
bullets: Drug prosecutions are heard in Illinois circuit courts. Venue ordinarily lies in the county where the offense occurred. — Illinois Constitution, Article VI, Section 9; 725 ILCS 5/1-6.
Requests for appointed defense counsel are addressed to the criminal court. Illinois law provides for appointed counsel for qualifying defendants who cannot afford counsel. — 725 ILCS 5/113-3.
Motions challenging an unlawful search or seizure are filed in the criminal case and decided by the court. — 725 ILCS 5/114-12.

sections.heading: Common questions in Illinois
bullets: Is a small amount of cocaine merely a misdemeanor? Generally no. Possession of less than 15 grams falls under the Class 4 felony provision. — 720 ILCS 570/402(c).
Must money change hands for delivery? No. The statutory definition covers transfers without requiring payment. — 720 ILCS 570/102(h).

Does first-offender probation automatically erase the case? No. Section 410 discharge and dismissal is distinct from expungement, which has separate statutory requirements. — 720 ILCS 570/410; 20 ILCS 2630/5.2.
Does every drug charge require pretrial detention? No. Detention depends on statutory eligibility and judicial findings, not simply a drug allegation. — 725 ILCS 5/110-6.1.

Illinois General Assembly — Code of Criminal Procedure of 1963
Illinois General Assembly — Cannabis Regulation and Tax Act

criminal-law/iowa/bail-and-bond.summary: Iowa generally allows bail before conviction, but Iowa Code section 811.1 excludes defendants charged with a class “A” felony when the proof is evident or the presumption great. For eligible defendants, section 811.2 starts with release on personal recognizance or an unsecured appearance bond unless that would not reasonably assure appearance or would jeopardize another person’s physical safety; the court may then impose conditions, including financial security, while the Iowa Constitution prohibits excessive bail.

facts.label: Eligibility before conviction
facts.value: The statutory rule is that defendants are bailable before conviction. The class “A” felony exception depends on both the charge and the requirement that the proof be evident or the presumption great; it is not a general exclusion for every felony. — Iowa Code § 811.1

facts.label: Starting point for release
facts.value: For a bailable defendant, the court considers personal recognizance or an unsecured appearance bond. Additional conditions address the risks that the defendant will not appear or will jeopardize another person’s physical safety. — Iowa Code § 811.2

facts.label: Individual circumstances
facts.value: Release decisions consider matters including the nature and circumstances of the charge, the weight of the evidence, family ties, employment, financial resources, residence, criminal history, and the defendant’s record of appearing or failing to appear in court. — Iowa Code § 811.2

facts.label: Constitutional limit
facts.value: Iowa’s Constitution expressly prohibits excessive bail. That restriction is separate from the statutory rules governing eligibility and the conditions imposed in an individual case. — Iowa Constitution, article I, § 17

sections.heading: Forms of release available under Iowa law

rows: Release based on the defendant’s commitment to appear, without posting financial security.
A financial obligation without an upfront deposit securing that obligation.
Placement in the custody of a designated person or organization agreeing to supervise the defendant.
Conditions may limit travel, associations, or place of abode during release.
The court may authorize a specified bond with cash or securities deposited in an amount not exceeding ten percent of the bond.
A bail bond with sufficient solvent sureties, or a cash deposit in lieu of that bond.

facts.label: Failure to appear
facts.value: A defendant’s failure to appear when required can trigger forfeiture proceedings. Iowa law provides a process involving the defendant and any sureties before enforcement through judgment. Posting security does not eliminate the obligation to attend required proceedings. — Iowa Code § 811.6

facts.label: Financial security and other conditions
facts.value: The court may combine release conditions. A financial bond therefore does not necessarily replace supervision or restrictions on travel, associations, or residence. — Iowa Code § 811.2

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Iowa
bullets: Iowa District Court: Bail and release-condition issues belong in the criminal case before the judicial officer handling the matter. The court determines release conditions under Iowa Code § 811.2.

Clerk of District Court: The clerk maintains the criminal case record, including filed release orders and bond-related documents. The clerk’s administrative role is distinct from the judicial officer’s authority to set conditions.

sections.heading: Common questions in Iowa
bullets: Does every defendant have to pay money for release? No. Section 811.2 provides for personal recognizance and unsecured appearance bonds.
Can every Iowa bond be posted with ten percent? No. The percentage-deposit arrangement is an option the court may authorize, not an automatic payment method for every bond.
Does a felony charge automatically prevent bail? No. Section 811.1 identifies a specific class “A” felony exception with an additional evidentiary requirement.
Can bail include nonfinancial restrictions? Yes. Section 811.2 authorizes supervision and restrictions addressing travel, associations, and residence, among other conditions.

sources.label: Iowa Legislature — Iowa Code Chapter 811, Pretrial and Post-Trial Release
Iowa Legislature — Iowa Constitution

criminal-law/indiana/expungement.summary: Indiana permits expungement of qualifying arrests, dismissed cases, acquittals, and criminal convictions under Indiana Code Chapter 35-38-9, with eligibility depending on the outcome, offense, and time elapsed. Conviction waiting periods generally range from five to ten years, sometimes with an additional period measured from completion of the sentence, and certain felony petitions require written prosecutor consent. Expungement does not always seal the record: some felony records remain public but must be marked as expunged.

facts.label: Cases without a conviction
facts.value: Indiana provides a procedure for expunging qualifying arrest and charge records that did not result in a conviction, including dismissed charges and acquittals. The statute also addresses convictions vacated on appeal when the person is not being retried. — Indiana Code § 35-38-9-1

facts.label: Conviction categories
facts.value: Separate provisions govern misdemeanors, qualifying Class D and Level 6 felonies, other eligible felonies, and the more restrictive felony category requiring prosecutor consent. Eligibility is not determined by the offense level alone. — Indiana Code §§ 35-38-9-2 through 35-38-9-5

facts.label: Additional requirements
facts.value: Expiration of the waiting period does not automatically establish eligibility. The conviction provisions also address pending charges, intervening convictions, and payment of fines, fees, court costs, and restitution imposed as part of the sentence. — Indiana Code §§ 35-38-9-2 through 35-38-9-5

rows: Qualifying arrest or charge without a conviction
One year after the arrest; earlier filing is possible with prosecutor agreement
Misdemeanor, including a felony reduced to a misdemeanor
Qualifying Class D or Level 6 felony
Eight years after conviction or three years after completion of the sentence, whichever is later
Ten years after conviction or five years after completion of the sentence, whichever is later; written prosecutor consent is required

sections.heading: Sealing, public access, and legal effect

facts.label: Sealed conviction records
facts.value: Records expunged under the misdemeanor and qualifying Class D or Level 6 felony provisions are generally sealed from public access, subject to statutory exceptions. Expungement is not physical destruction of every government record. — Indiana Code § 35-38-9-6

facts.label: Felony records that remain public
facts.value: Records expunged under Sections 4 and 5 remain public, but the records must be clearly and visibly identified as expunged. — Indiana Code § 35-38-9-7

facts.label: Protection against discrimination
facts.value: Indiana prohibits specified discrimination based on expunged records, including refusal to employ or grant certain licenses because of an expunged arrest or conviction. The law also preserves specified criminal-justice uses of expunged convictions. — Indiana Code § 35-38-9-10

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Indiana
bullets: For conviction expungement, the petition is filed in a circuit or superior court in the county of conviction. Convictions in different counties require county-specific proceedings. — Indiana Code §§ 35-38-9-2 through 35-38-9-5

For a qualifying arrest without a conviction, Section 1 identifies the filing court, including a circuit or superior court in the county where the arrest occurred when no criminal case was filed. — Indiana Code § 35-38-9-1

The county prosecuting attorney participates in the court process. Indiana State Police maintains criminal-history records but does not replace the court as the authority deciding a conviction-expungement petition. — Indiana Code Chapter 35-38-9

sections.heading: Common questions in Indiana
bullets: Does expungement erase every record? No. Some records are sealed, while felony records expunged under Sections 4 and 5 remain public and marked as expunged.

Does every felony qualify? No. The felony provisions contain exclusions, including exclusions involving sex or violent offender status and specified offenses. — Indiana Code §§ 35-38-9-3 through 35-38-9-5
Is prosecutor consent always required? No. Written consent is expressly required for Section 5 relief; it is not a universal requirement for every expungement category.

Can conviction petitions be filed repeatedly? Indiana generally permits one lifetime conviction-expungement opportunity, with petitions in different counties filed within one year of the first petition, subject to statutory exceptions. — Indiana Code Chapter 35-38-9

sources.label: Indiana General Assembly — Indiana Code, Title 35, Chapter 35-38-9
Indiana Judicial Branch — Self-Service Legal Center

criminal-law/indiana/juvenile-law.summary: Indiana generally handles alleged law violations by children under 18 through juvenile delinquency proceedings, rather than ordinary adult criminal cases, although statutory exclusions and judicial waiver can place some cases in adult court. Indiana law distinguishes criminal acts from status offenses, provides rights to counsel and proof beyond a reasonable doubt, and authorizes dispositions ranging from supervision to placement outside the home. Confidentiality, continued jurisdiction, and possible record expungement depend on specific statutory rules.

facts.label: Criminal-act delinquency
facts.value: A child can commit a delinquent act by committing, before turning 18, conduct that would be an offense if committed by an adult, subject to statutory jurisdictional exceptions. — Indiana Code § 31-37-1-2

facts.label: Status offenses
facts.value: Indiana separately addresses conduct such as running away, habitual disobedience, and violations of compulsory school attendance requirements. These provisions have their own statutory elements; they are not interchangeable with ordinary criminal charges. — Indiana Code ch. 31-37-2

facts.label: Proof and procedural rights
facts.value: The child has rights to counsel, to refrain from self-incrimination, to confront and cross-examine witnesses, and to obtain witnesses or evidence through compulsory process. A delinquency finding requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt. — Indiana Code § 31-32-2-2

facts.label: Waiving rights
facts.value: Indiana specifies who may waive a child's constitutional or legal rights and the conditions for doing so. The parent-or-guardian route includes requirements concerning interests, meaningful consultation, and the child's knowing and voluntary agreement. — Indiana Code § 31-32-5-1

sections.heading: How a juvenile case can proceed

rows: Provides a statutory process for addressing a matter without proceeding through a formal delinquency adjudication.
Formal proceedings use a petition alleging delinquency, with filing governed by statutory authorization requirements.
The court determines whether the delinquency allegations have been proved.
Available orders include probation and other services or placements; eligibility and restrictions depend on the applicable disposition statute.
Certain charges are excluded from juvenile jurisdiction, while other cases may reach adult court through judicial waiver.

facts.label: Placement considerations
facts.value: When consistent with community safety and the child's best interests, a disposition must use the least restrictive, most family-like appropriate setting and satisfy statutory family-participation and restraint requirements. — Indiana Code § 31-37-18-6

facts.label: Confidentiality has exceptions
facts.value: Juvenile court records are subject to confidentiality and access rules, but specified records can be available to the public. Juvenile status does not guarantee that every record remains private. — Indiana Code ch. 31-39-2

facts.label: Expungement
facts.value: Indiana provides a petition-based process for expunging juvenile court and law-enforcement records. The court considers statutory factors; expungement is not simply an automatic consequence of reaching adulthood. — Indiana Code ch. 31-39-8

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Indiana
bullets: Delinquency proceedings are handled by the court exercising juvenile jurisdiction in the relevant county. Venue is governed by Indiana Code ch. 31-32-7.
The county prosecuting attorney has the statutory role in seeking authorization to file a delinquency petition. — Indiana Code ch. 31-37-10
A juvenile-record expungement petition goes to the juvenile court under Indiana Code ch. 31-39-8.

sections.heading: Common questions in Indiana
bullets: Does turning 18 always end juvenile jurisdiction? No. Indiana permits continued jurisdiction beyond that birthday in circumstances governed by Indiana Code ch. 31-30-2.
Can a juvenile case go to adult court? Yes. Statutory exclusions and judicial waiver are separate routes, with different requirements.
Does every delinquency finding require confinement? No. Indiana authorizes multiple dispositions, including probation, subject to the governing statutes.
Are juvenile records automatically erased at 18? No. Confidentiality and expungement are different legal concepts. Indiana provides a specific juvenile expungement process.

Indiana General Assembly — Title 31, Article 32: Juvenile Law General Procedural Provisions
Indiana General Assembly — Title 31, Article 37: Juvenile Law Delinquency
Indiana General Assembly — Title 31, Article 39: Juvenile Law Records

criminal-law/indiana/traffic-violations.summary: Indiana treats many routine traffic violations as civil infractions, but offenses such as operating while intoxicated and reckless driving can be crimes carrying jail time and fines. The charge depends on the conduct and statutory elements, not simply whether an officer issued a ticket; criminal penalties, court costs, and Bureau of Motor Vehicles license consequences are separate issues, and an offense’s classification determines the available criminal sentencing range.

sections.heading: Civil tickets versus criminal traffic charges

facts.label: Civil infractions
facts.value: Indiana generally uses civil proceedings to enforce traffic infractions. The government must prove an infraction by a preponderance of the evidence, rather than the criminal standard of proof beyond a reasonable doubt. An infraction alone does not authorize a jail sentence — Indiana Code § 34-28-5-1.

facts.label: Speeding
facts.value: Indiana prohibits driving faster than is reasonable and prudent under existing conditions. Compliance with a posted limit does not eliminate the statutory obligation to reduce speed when weather, visibility, pedestrians, or other hazards require it — Indiana Code § 9-21-5-1.

facts.label: Reckless driving
facts.value: Driving at an unreasonably high or low speed under the circumstances, so as to endanger others’ safety or property or block the proper flow of traffic, can constitute reckless driving. The statute also addresses specified passing and lane-related conduct — Indiana Code § 9-21-8-52.

facts.label: License consequences
facts.value: The Indiana Bureau of Motor Vehicles maintains driving records and assigns points to qualifying violations. Points remain active for two years from the conviction date; point consequences are distinct from the court’s fine or criminal sentence — Indiana BMV, Driver Record Points.

sections.heading: Common criminal charges and maximum misdemeanor penalties

rows: Operating with an alcohol concentration of at least 0.08 but below 0.15
Operating with an alcohol concentration of at least 0.15
Operating while intoxicated in a manner that endangers a person
Reckless driving under the statute’s basic offense

facts.label: Felony exposure
facts.value: Qualifying prior convictions and other aggravating circumstances can elevate operating-while-intoxicated charges to felonies. Separate provisions address offenses resulting in serious bodily injury or death; the misdemeanor ranges above do not describe those charges — Indiana Code §§ 9-30-5-3 through 9-30-5-5.

facts.label: Chemical-test refusal
facts.value: Indiana’s implied-consent law provides license-suspension consequences for refusing a qualifying chemical test. Refusal-related licensing proceedings are separate from whether the prosecution obtains an OWI conviction — Indiana Code §§ 9-30-6-1, 9-30-6-7, 9-30-6-9.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Indiana
bullets: Traffic infractions and criminal traffic cases are handled by courts with jurisdiction over the offense, including circuit, superior, and qualifying city or town courts. The court clerk maintains the case record — Indiana Code §§ 33-28-1-2, 33-29-1-1.5, 33-35-2-3.
County prosecuting attorneys prosecute state criminal traffic offenses — Indiana Code § 33-39-1-5.
The Indiana Bureau of Motor Vehicles handles driving records, points, and administrative license matters; it does not adjudicate criminal guilt.

sections.heading: Common questions in Indiana
bullets: Is every traffic ticket a crime? No. Many traffic offenses are civil infractions; OWI and reckless driving can be criminal offenses.
Does OWI require an alcohol concentration of 0.08? No. Operating while intoxicated is a separate offense from operating at a prohibited alcohol concentration — Indiana Code §§ 9-30-5-1 and 9-30-5-2.
Does paying a fine erase BMV points? No. Payment does not itself remove points associated with a conviction.
Are the listed fines the entire financial obligation? No. Court costs and authorized fees can be additional — Indiana Code § 33-37-4.

sources.label: Indiana General Assembly — Indiana Code Title 9, Motor Vehicles
Indiana General Assembly — Indiana Code Title 35, Criminal Law and Procedure
Indiana General Assembly — Indiana Code Title 34, Civil Law and Procedure
Indiana Bureau of Motor Vehicles — Driver Record Points

criminal-law/iowa/expungement.summary: Iowa allows expungement of qualifying dismissed or acquitted criminal cases, certain misdemeanor convictions, and records associated with successfully completed deferred judgments, but each route has different requirements. Under Iowa Code chapter 901C, expungement generally restricts public access rather than destroying records; misdemeanor-conviction relief ordinarily requires at least eight years after conviction, excludes numerous offenses, and is generally available only once in a person’s lifetime, subject to a same-transaction-or-occurrence exception.

facts.label: Dismissals and acquittals
facts.value: Section 901C.2 provides a route when all criminal charges in a case were dismissed or the defendant was acquitted of all charges. A dismissal of one count does not establish eligibility when another count in that case resulted in conviction. Additional statutory conditions apply. — Iowa Code § 901C.2

facts.label: Misdemeanor convictions
facts.value: Section 901C.3 allows expungement of qualifying misdemeanor convictions. It is not a general felony-expungement law, and its excluded-offense list makes some misdemeanors ineligible regardless of their age. — Iowa Code § 901C.3

facts.label: Deferred judgments
facts.value: Successful completion of probation and discharge following a deferred judgment provides a separate expungement route. A deferred judgment is distinct from a conviction followed by a suspended sentence. — Iowa Code §§ 907.3, 907.9

rows: Generally, at least 180 days must pass after acquittal or dismissal. The court may waive that period for good cause.
More than eight years must have passed since the conviction.
Misdemeanor-conviction expungement requires no pending criminal charges.
Misdemeanor-conviction expungement requires payment of court costs, fees, fines, restitution, and other court-ordered financial obligations.
An applicant for misdemeanor-conviction expungement must not have received more than two deferred judgments.
Relief under section 901C.3 is generally limited to once in a lifetime, but multiple misdemeanors arising from the same transaction or occurrence may be expunged.

sections.heading: Limits on relief and record access

facts.label: Excluded misdemeanor offenses
facts.value: The misdemeanor-conviction statute excludes specified offenses, including operating while intoxicated under section 321J.2 and domestic abuse assault under section 708.2A. Eligibility therefore depends on the precise conviction statute, not simply the misdemeanor classification. — Iowa Code § 901C.3

facts.label: Special dismissal and acquittal exclusions
facts.value: Section 901C.2 excludes a not-guilty verdict by reason of insanity and a finding that the defendant was incompetent to stand trial. These outcomes are not treated like ordinary acquittals or dismissals under that provision. — Iowa Code § 901C.2

facts.label: Confidentiality rather than destruction
facts.value: Expunged records become confidential under Iowa’s statutory framework. Expungement does not mean every government record is destroyed, and access remains possible as authorized by law. — Iowa Code §§ 901C.1–901C.3

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Iowa
bullets: For a dismissed or acquitted case, the application belongs in the Iowa district court where that criminal case was filed. — Iowa Code § 901C.2

For an eligible misdemeanor conviction, the application belongs in the district court where the conviction occurred. The court, rather than a records vendor, decides statutory eligibility. — Iowa Code § 901C.3
Deferred-judgment discharge and the associated expungement are handled through the criminal court supervising that disposition. — Iowa Code § 907.9

sections.heading: Common questions in Iowa
bullets: Does an old conviction disappear automatically? No. Section 901C.3 requires an application and satisfaction of its eligibility requirements.
Can a felony conviction use the eight-year rule? No. Section 901C.3 applies to eligible misdemeanor convictions, not felony convictions.
Does expungement destroy the court record? No. Chapter 901C uses confidentiality and restricted access rather than universal destruction.
Is completing probation enough to expunge any conviction? No. Deferred-judgment relief under section 907.9 is different from expungement of an ordinary conviction.

sources.label: Iowa Legislature — Iowa Code chapter 901C, Expungement of Criminal Records
Iowa Legislature — Iowa Code section 907.9, Discharge from Probation
Iowa Legislature — Iowa Code section 907.3, Deferred Judgment, Deferred Sentence, or Suspended Sentence

criminal-law/iowa/traffic-violations.summary: Iowa treats most violations of its traffic code as simple misdemeanors, but many routine offenses carry scheduled fines rather than the ordinary misdemeanor sentencing range. More serious driving conduct, including operating while intoxicated, has separate criminal penalties, and a conviction can also affect driving privileges. Criminal cases are handled in the Iowa District Court, while the Iowa Department of Transportation administers licensing actions; the applicable statute determines whether a particular charge carries possible jail time.

facts.label: Default classification
facts.value: Violating a provision of Iowa Code chapter 321 is a simple misdemeanor unless that provision or another Iowa law declares a different classification. The classification alone does not establish the fine because many traffic offenses have scheduled penalties. — Iowa Code § 321.482.

facts.label: Scheduled traffic fines
facts.value: Iowa's scheduled-violations law lists fines for numerous traffic offenses, including speeding and stop-sign violations. The amount depends on the particular offense and, for speeding, how far the driver exceeded the applicable limit. — Iowa Code § 805.8A.

facts.label: Ordinary simple-misdemeanor sentence
facts.value: Unless another penalty applies, a simple misdemeanor carries a fine of $105 to $855; imprisonment of up to 30 days may be imposed instead of or in addition to the fine. These are not the default amounts for offenses governed by a scheduled fine. — Iowa Code § 903.1(1)(a).

rows: Speed must be reasonable and proper under existing conditions, and statutory or applicable posted limits also govern.
A driver must maintain control and reduce speed to a reasonable and proper rate in specified circumstances, including approaching an intersection.
Drivers must obey the stopping and right-of-way requirements applicable to stop and yield signs.
Driving with willful or wanton disregard for the safety of persons or property is a simple misdemeanor.
A first OWI offense is a serious misdemeanor with offense-specific sentencing requirements.

sections.heading: Criminal penalties and driving privileges are separate

facts.label: OWI sentencing
facts.value: First-offense OWI generally requires at least 48 hours of imprisonment and permits up to one year, subject to the statute's sentencing provisions. OWI is not simply another scheduled traffic fine. — Iowa Code § 321J.2(2)(a), (3).

facts.label: Habitual-offender consequences
facts.value: Iowa's habitual-offender law identifies qualifying conviction patterns and provides a separate process affecting driving privileges. Not every traffic conviction counts in the same way under that law. — Iowa Code §§ 321.555–321.560.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Iowa
bullets: Iowa District Court: The district court handles state traffic prosecutions. Magistrates handle simple-misdemeanor matters, and district associate judges also have criminal jurisdiction within statutory limits. — Iowa Code §§ 602.6405, 602.6306.
Clerk of District Court: Traffic-case filings and court records are handled through the clerk's office for the court where the case is pending.

Iowa Department of Transportation: Driver-licensing matters, including administrative suspensions and revocations, are separate from the court's determination of criminal charges. — Iowa Code chapters 321 and 321J.

sections.heading: Common questions in Iowa
bullets: Is an ordinary traffic ticket a criminal charge? Most chapter 321 violations are simple misdemeanors unless another classification applies, although many use scheduled fines. — Iowa Code §§ 321.482, 805.8A.
Does every traffic misdemeanor permit the ordinary misdemeanor sentence? No. A specific scheduled penalty or offense-specific sentencing provision can control instead. — Iowa Code §§ 805.8A, 903.1.
Is reckless driving the same as speeding? No. Reckless driving requires willful or wanton disregard for safety; speeding has separate statutory requirements. — Iowa Code §§ 321.277, 321.285.

Can an OWI matter affect a license separately from the criminal case? Yes. Iowa provides administrative revocation procedures for chemical-test refusal and qualifying test results. — Iowa Code §§ 321J.9, 321J.12.

sources.label: Iowa Legislature — Chapter 321, Motor Vehicles and Law of the Road
Iowa Legislature — Section 805.8A, Motor Vehicle and Transportation Scheduled Violations
Iowa Legislature — Chapter 321J, Operating While Intoxicated
Iowa Legislature — Section 903.1, Maximum Sentence for Misdemeanants

criminal-law/kansas/felony-vs-misdemeano.summary: Kansas distinguishes felonies from misdemeanors primarily by the punishment the law authorizes: a felony can be punished by death or imprisonment in a state correctional institution, while misdemeanors generally carry county-jail exposure rather than a state-prison sentence. Kansas divides classified misdemeanors into Classes A, B, and C, but sentences most felonies through sentencing grids that consider offense severity and criminal history; the classification alone does not establish the sentence a particular defendant will receive.

facts.label: Felony definition
facts.value: A felony is a crime punishable by death or imprisonment in a state correctional institution. The authorized punishment, rather than whether a particular defendant actually goes to prison, determines this classification — K.S.A. 21-5102(a).

facts.label: Misdemeanors and infractions
facts.value: Kansas separately recognizes misdemeanors, traffic infractions, and cigarette or tobacco infractions. An offense that is not a felony is therefore not necessarily a misdemeanor — K.S.A. 21-5102.

facts.label: Separate sentencing structures
facts.value: Kansas uses separate sentencing grids for most nondrug and drug felonies. Each grid considers both the crime's severity level and the defendant's criminal-history category — K.S.A. 21-6804 and 21-6805.

sections.heading: Kansas misdemeanor jail and fine limits

columns: General maximum fine for an individual
rows: Term specified in the law defining the offense
Fine specified in the law defining the offense

facts.label: Felony severity and criminal history
facts.value: The nondrug grid has ten severity levels and nine criminal-history categories. Grid blocks provide sentencing ranges and generally designate presumptive imprisonment, presumptive nonprison sentences, or border-box treatment; statutory exceptions can change the applicable rules — K.S.A. 21-6804.

facts.label: No single felony maximum
facts.value: Kansas does not impose one universal maximum prison term for all felonies. The applicable offense, sentencing grid, and any special sentencing provisions control; off-grid offenses are governed by separate rules — K.S.A. 21-6804 and 21-6805.

facts.label: Limits of the misdemeanor table
facts.value: The listed fines are the general class-based limits for individuals. Kansas also authorizes an alternative fine tied to pecuniary gain, and unclassified misdemeanors use offense-specific provisions — K.S.A. 21-6611(b), (e).

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Kansas
bullets: Kansas district courts hear prosecutions for state-law felonies and misdemeanors under their general original jurisdiction — K.S.A. 20-301.
Municipal courts hear cases involving violations of their city's ordinances. A municipal ordinance prosecution is distinct from a state-law felony prosecution — K.S.A. 12-4104.
County or district attorneys prosecute state criminal cases within their statutory authority; municipal prosecutors handle city ordinance prosecutions — K.S.A. 19-702, 22a-104, and 12-4110.

sections.heading: Common questions in Kansas
bullets: Does every felony conviction mean prison? No. Kansas sentencing grids include presumptive nonprison sentences, although offense-specific rules and criminal history matter — K.S.A. 21-6804 and 21-6805.
Is a Class A misdemeanor more serious than Class C? Under the general sentencing limits, yes: Class A authorizes up to one year in jail, while Class C authorizes up to one month — K.S.A. 21-6602.
Are drug and nondrug felonies sentenced on the same grid? No. Kansas has separate grids for these categories — K.S.A. 21-6804 and 21-6805.
Is a traffic infraction a misdemeanor? Not under Kansas's classification statute, which treats traffic infractions as a separate category — K.S.A. 21-5102.

criminal-law/kansas/juvenile-law.summary: Kansas handles most qualifying offenses committed by children ages 10 through 17 under the Revised Kansas Juvenile Justice Code, with juvenile cases heard in district court rather than a separate statewide juvenile court system. A juvenile adjudication is different from an adult criminal conviction, but the court can impose supervision, restitution and other dispositions; some cases can proceed as adult prosecutions or extended-jurisdiction juvenile prosecutions under statutory procedures.

sections.heading: Who Kansas juvenile criminal law covers

facts.label: Governing law
facts.value: The Revised Kansas Juvenile Justice Code governs juvenile-offender proceedings. These proceedings are distinct from child-in-need-of-care cases, which address matters such as abuse, neglect and lack of parental care. — K.S.A. 38-2301; K.S.A. 38-2201.

facts.label: Age at the offense
facts.value: The definition of a juvenile generally covers someone who was at least 10 but younger than 18 when the alleged act occurred. The statute contains exclusions, so age alone does not establish that every offense belongs in juvenile proceedings. — K.S.A. 38-2302.

facts.label: Traffic and other exclusions
facts.value: The juvenile-offender definition excludes specified traffic offenses committed by children age 14 or older. It also excludes certain other statutory categories, including specified fish-and-game and boating violations. Not every charge against a minor is therefore a juvenile-offender case. — K.S.A. 38-2302.

facts.label: Possible adult prosecution
facts.value: The prosecutor may request adult prosecution under the statutory transfer process. The court considers statutory factors at a hearing, including the alleged offense, the child's history and the prospects for rehabilitation through available juvenile services. Transfer is not simply the prosecutor's unilateral decision. — K.S.A. 38-2347.

sections.heading: Potential outcomes in Kansas juvenile cases

rows: The court may impose probation with conditions as an authorized juvenile disposition.
Community or public service is among the available disposition options.
The court may require restitution for damage or injury caused by the offense.
Commitment to a juvenile correctional facility is subject to statutory eligibility and sentencing restrictions; it is not available merely because any juvenile offense occurred.
This designation combines a juvenile sentence with a stayed adult sentence, subject to statutory procedures and conditions.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Kansas
bullets: Kansas district courts hear juvenile-offender proceedings. The district court clerk maintains the court's filings; the clerk does not decide whether to prosecute or what disposition to impose.

County or district attorneys prosecute juvenile-offender cases. A police report and a prosecutor's juvenile complaint are different documents, and reporting an allegation does not itself establish an adjudication.
Local police departments and county sheriffs receive reports of alleged criminal conduct and investigate incidents involving juveniles.
The Kansas Department of Corrections, Juvenile Services, administers state juvenile corrections functions. It is not a substitute for the district court or the prosecuting attorney.

sections.heading: Common questions in Kansas
bullets: Does turning 18 automatically erase a juvenile case? No. The statutory definition generally looks to age when the act occurred, and a birthday does not itself erase the proceeding or its records.
Is a juvenile adjudication the same as an adult conviction? No. They are distinct legal outcomes, although juvenile adjudications can have later legal consequences.
Can a Kansas juvenile receive an adult sentence? Yes. Adult prosecution is possible through statutory procedures, and extended-jurisdiction juvenile cases can include a stayed adult sentence.

Does every juvenile offense lead to confinement? No. Kansas authorizes several dispositions, including probation, community service and restitution, while correctional placement has additional statutory restrictions.

criminal-law/kansas/traffic-violations.summary: Kansas distinguishes traffic infractions, such as ordinary speeding, from criminal traffic offenses, including driving under the influence, reckless driving, and fleeing a police officer. The applicable charge and consequences depend on the conduct, prior convictions, and whether prosecutors allege circumstances that elevate the offense; some traffic offenses can be felonies rather than misdemeanors. State-law cases generally proceed in district court, while municipal courts handle violations of city traffic ordinances.

facts.label: Reckless driving
facts.value: Kansas defines reckless driving as driving a vehicle in willful or wanton disregard for the safety of persons or property. The statute expressly classifies the offense as a misdemeanor; it is distinct from an ordinary speeding violation. — K.S.A. 8-1566.

facts.label: Driving under the influence
facts.value: Kansas DUI law covers operating or attempting to operate a vehicle under specified alcohol or drug conditions. These include an alcohol concentration of 0.08 or more and impairment by alcohol, drugs, or a combination that makes the person incapable of safely driving. — K.S.A. 8-1567.

facts.label: Fleeing or attempting to elude
facts.value: Willfully failing or refusing to stop, or fleeing or attempting to elude a pursuing police vehicle after the required signal, can constitute a criminal offense. The statute includes requirements concerning the officer, police vehicle, and signal. — K.S.A. 8-1568.

rows: Maximum-speed violations are generally traffic infractions. The applicable limit depends on the roadway and legally established speed restrictions.
Imprisonment from 5 to 90 days, a fine from $25 to $500, or both.
Imprisonment from 10 days to 6 months, a fine from $50 to $500, or both.
Class B nonperson misdemeanor. The statute also provides specific sentencing and alcohol-related requirements.
The basic offense is a class B nonperson misdemeanor for a first conviction. Repeat convictions and specified aggravating circumstances can increase the classification.

facts.label: Separate proceedings
facts.value: An alcohol-related incident can produce both a criminal DUI prosecution and a separate administrative driver's-license proceeding. A license suspension is not itself a criminal conviction. — K.S.A. 8-1567; 8-1002.

facts.label: Prior convictions
facts.value: Kansas DUI law contains specific rules for counting prior convictions, including qualifying municipal and out-of-state convictions. The classification cannot reliably be determined solely from the number of prior Kansas district-court cases. — K.S.A. 8-1567.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Kansas
bullets: Kansas district courts handle prosecutions for state traffic offenses, including state-law misdemeanors and felonies. — K.S.A. 20-301.

Municipal courts handle alleged violations of city ordinances, including municipal traffic ordinances. Their jurisdiction is different from district-court jurisdiction over state criminal charges. — K.S.A. 12-4104.

The Kansas Department of Revenue, Division of Vehicles, administers driver's-license actions, including the administrative process associated with alcohol-related testing incidents. These matters are separate from the traffic prosecution. — K.S.A. 8-1002.

sections.heading: Common questions in Kansas
bullets: Is every traffic ticket a criminal misdemeanor? No. Kansas distinguishes traffic infractions from misdemeanor and felony traffic offenses. Ordinary speeding is generally an infraction.
Does reckless driving require a collision? No. The statutory definition focuses on willful or wanton disregard for safety, not whether a collision occurred. — K.S.A. 8-1566.
Can DUI involve prescription drugs? Yes. Kansas DUI law reaches drug impairment, and lawful entitlement to use a drug is not a defense to the prohibited conduct. — K.S.A. 8-1567.
Can fleeing police be a felony? Yes. Kansas law provides felony classifications for specified aggravating conduct and certain repeat offenses. — K.S.A. 8-1568.

Kansas Office of Revisor of Statutes: K.S.A. 8-1566, Reckless driving
Kansas Office of Revisor of Statutes: K.S.A. 8-1567, Driving under the influence
