criminal-law/kentucky/traffic-violations.summary: Kentucky traffic cases can involve violations, misdemeanors, or felonies, depending on the offense and circumstances; a traffic citation does not necessarily charge a misdemeanor or felony. State law separately regulates speeding, careless driving, licensing, and driving under the influence, while the Kentucky Transportation Cabinet administers license points and suspensions. District Court handles traffic violations and misdemeanor prosecutions, but felony traffic charges generally proceed to Circuit Court after preliminary proceedings in District Court.

facts.label: Violations versus crimes
facts.value: Kentucky distinguishes a violation from a misdemeanor or felony. Under the Penal Code definitions, a violation is an offense for which imprisonment cannot be imposed; misdemeanors and felonies are crimes. The particular traffic statute determines the applicable punishment — KRS 500.080.

facts.label: Trial court
facts.value: District Court has jurisdiction over violations and misdemeanors, except where the charge is joined with an indicted felony. District Court also conducts preliminary proceedings in felony cases — KRS 24A.110.

facts.label: Careless driving
facts.value: Kentucky requires drivers to operate carefully, with regard for the safety and convenience of pedestrians and other vehicles. The statute also prohibits operating in a manner that is likely to endanger people or property — KRS 189.290.

facts.label: DUI escalation
facts.value: A fourth or subsequent DUI offense within ten years is a Class D felony. The DUI statute provides separate penalties for first, second, and third offenses within that period, with increased mandatory confinement when specified aggravating circumstances apply — KRS 189A.010.

sections.heading: Common traffic charges and their governing laws

rows: Drivers must obey applicable speed limits and may not drive faster than is reasonable and prudent for conditions.
Drivers generally must obey official traffic-control devices, subject to statutory exceptions.
Operating a motor vehicle on a highway generally requires a valid operator's license, subject to statutory exemptions.
Prohibited conduct includes driving under the influence of alcohol or an impairing substance; an alcohol concentration of 0.08 or more is a separate statutory basis.
Kentucky has a separate offense for driving while a license is suspended or revoked for specified DUI-related reasons.

facts.label: Point thresholds
facts.value: Accumulating 12 or more points within two years for drivers age 18 or older, or seven or more points within two years for drivers under 18, can lead to suspension proceedings. The Transportation Cabinet schedules a hearing to review driving privileges — Kentucky Transportation Cabinet, Kentucky Point System.

facts.label: Points are not the entire consequence
facts.value: The point system is separate from court fines and criminal punishment. Certain offenses can result in license action without reaching the ordinary point threshold — Kentucky Transportation Cabinet, Kentucky Point System; KRS 189A.070.

facts.label: Prepayable tickets
facts.value: Kentucky permits prepayment of eligible traffic citations, but not every charge is prepayable. Prepayment constitutes a guilty plea and waiver of trial — Kentucky Court of Justice, District Court.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Kentucky
bullets: Traffic prosecutions are ordinarily handled in the District Court for the county where the alleged offense occurred. The county's Office of Circuit Court Clerk maintains the court case records and handles court payments.

The Kentucky Transportation Cabinet's Division of Driver Licensing administers driver records, points, and licensing actions. Those administrative matters are distinct from deciding guilt in a traffic prosecution.
Felony traffic prosecutions are tried in Circuit Court, although preliminary proceedings generally occur in District Court — KRS 24A.110.

sections.heading: Common questions in Kentucky
bullets: Is every traffic ticket a criminal charge? No. Kentucky distinguishes violations from misdemeanor and felony crimes — KRS 500.080.
Can a traffic offense become a felony? Yes. A fourth or subsequent DUI within ten years is a Class D felony — KRS 189A.010.
Does paying an eligible ticket avoid a guilty plea? No. Prepayment constitutes a guilty plea and waives trial.
Do younger drivers have a lower point threshold? Yes. Drivers under 18 face suspension proceedings at seven points within two years, compared with 12 points for adults.

sources.label: Kentucky General Assembly — Kentucky Revised Statutes
Kentucky Transportation Cabinet — Kentucky Point System
Kentucky Court of Justice — District Court

criminal-law/louisiana/arrest-process.summary: In Louisiana, an arrest places a person in custody through actual restraint or submission to authority; officers may arrest under a warrant or under circumstances authorized for warrantless arrests. After arrest, separate rules govern booking, access to counsel, judicial review of probable cause, and bail, including a 48-hour probable-cause deadline for warrantless arrests and a separate 72-hour deadline, excluding legal holidays, for appearance before a judge for appointment of counsel.

facts.label: What counts as an arrest
facts.value: An arrest is taking a person into custody. Actual restraint is necessary, but it may result either from physical force or from submission to the arresting person's authority. Handcuffs are not part of the statutory definition — Louisiana Code of Criminal Procedure art. 201.

facts.label: Arrests without a warrant
facts.value: An officer may make a warrantless arrest in circumstances listed by statute, including reasonable cause to believe the person committed an offense outside the officer's presence. Louisiana's statutory authority is not limited exclusively to felonies — Louisiana Code of Criminal Procedure art. 213.

facts.label: Notice and questioning
facts.value: Louisiana's Constitution requires a person arrested or detained in connection with an offense investigation to be advised fully of the reason, the right to remain silent, the privilege against self-incrimination, the right to counsel, and the right to appointed counsel if indigent — Louisiana Constitution art. I, §13.

facts.label: Force during arrest
facts.value: An arresting person may use reasonable force to effect an arrest and detention and to overcome resistance or threatened resistance. The statute does not authorize unlimited force — Louisiana Code of Criminal Procedure art. 220.

sections.heading: Louisiana arrest deadlines and procedural steps

rows: The person making the arrest must promptly conduct the arrested person to the nearest jail or police station and cause the person to be booked.
Louisiana Code of Criminal Procedure art. 228
The booked person must be allowed to communicate with counsel, friends, or relatives.
Louisiana Code of Criminal Procedure art. 229
For an arrest without a warrant, a judge must determine probable cause within 48 hours of arrest.
Louisiana Code of Criminal Procedure art. 230.2
A person in custody must be brought before a judge within 72 hours of arrest, excluding legal holidays, for appointment of counsel.
Louisiana Code of Criminal Procedure art. 230.1

facts.label: Missing the counsel-appearance deadline
facts.value: Failure to bring the person before a judge as required by Article 230.1 results in release forthwith. That failure does not invalidate later proceedings against the defendant — Louisiana Code of Criminal Procedure art. 230.1.

facts.label: Bail is a separate question
facts.value: Louisiana's Constitution generally provides for bail before and during trial, but contains exceptions. It also prohibits excessive bail; arrest alone does not establish either an automatic right to release without conditions or a particular bond amount — Louisiana Constitution art. I, §18.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Louisiana
bullets: Criminal-case requests concerning detention, counsel, or bail belong before the court exercising criminal jurisdiction over the matter. Louisiana district courts have original criminal jurisdiction, subject to constitutional exceptions — Louisiana Constitution art. V, §16.

An allegation of officer misconduct may be submitted to the arresting police department or sheriff's office through its complaint process. An administrative complaint is separate from the criminal case and does not itself order release.

Public-defender representation is handled through the district public defender system and court appointment procedures. Eligibility and representation in a particular case are matters to talk to a lawyer about.

sections.heading: Common questions in Louisiana
bullets: Does every arrest require a warrant? No. Article 213 authorizes warrantless arrests in specified circumstances.
Are the 48-hour and 72-hour deadlines interchangeable? No. Article 230.2 addresses probable cause after warrantless arrest; Article 230.1 addresses appearance for appointment of counsel.
Does release for a missed Article 230.1 deadline dismiss the charge? No. The article expressly preserves subsequent proceedings.
Must an officer always put someone in handcuffs to arrest them? No. Submission to authority can establish the restraint required by Article 201.

sources.label: Louisiana Legislature — Louisiana Laws, Code of Criminal Procedure
Louisiana Senate — Constitution, Article I
Louisiana Senate — Constitution, Article V

criminal-law/louisiana/bail-and-bond.summary: Louisiana generally allows bail before and during trial, but the state constitution recognizes exceptions and prohibits excessive bail. Courts consider the charge, the evidence, the defendant’s circumstances, and public-safety concerns when setting an amount; bail is not simply a fixed price attached to an offense. The rules change after conviction, when eligibility depends partly on the possible or imposed sentence and the stage of the case.

facts.label: Constitutional protection
facts.value: Excessive bail is prohibited. Before and during trial, the general rule is release on sufficient surety, subject to the constitution’s exceptions; this is not an unconditional right to release in every prosecution. — Louisiana Constitution, Article I, §18.

facts.label: Capital charges
facts.value: The general constitutional right to bail does not extend to a person charged with a capital offense when the proof is evident and the presumption of guilt is great. The charge alone does not state the full constitutional test. — Louisiana Constitution, Article I, §18.

facts.label: Other detention exceptions
facts.value: The constitution also permits denial of bail in specified noncapital circumstances involving crimes of violence or controlled dangerous substances, subject to its hearing and evidentiary requirements. — Louisiana Constitution, Article I, §18.

facts.label: Meaning of bail
facts.value: Bail is security given to assure a person’s appearance before the proper court whenever required. It concerns release and appearance obligations, not a determination of guilt or innocence. — Louisiana Code of Criminal Procedure, Article 311.

sections.heading: What affects the amount of bail?

rows: The court considers the seriousness of the offense, including whether it is a crime of violence or involves a controlled dangerous substance. — Code of Criminal Procedure, Article 316.
The weight of the evidence against the defendant is a bail-setting consideration. — Article 316.
The defendant’s previous criminal record is a relevant factor. — Article 316.
The court considers the defendant’s ability to give bail; financial ability is not the only factor. — Article 316.
The nature and seriousness of the danger posed by release are relevant considerations. — Article 316.

facts.label: Before sentencing
facts.value: After conviction but before sentencing, the constitution provides bail when the maximum sentence that may be imposed is imprisonment for five years or less. For a greater maximum sentence, the judge may grant bail. — Louisiana Constitution, Article I, §18.

facts.label: After sentencing
facts.value: After sentencing and until final judgment, the constitution provides bail when the sentence actually imposed is imprisonment for five years or less. For a greater sentence, the judge may grant bail. — Louisiana Constitution, Article I, §18.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Louisiana
bullets: Bail requests and disputes are judicial matters handled in the criminal proceeding by a court with authority over bail. Louisiana Code of Criminal Procedure, Article 314, governs authority to fix bail.
Louisiana district courts have exclusive original jurisdiction over felony cases, subject to the constitution’s juvenile-jurisdiction exception. — Louisiana Constitution, Article V, §16.

The clerk of the court handling the prosecution maintains that court’s case filings; the clerk does not replace the judge as the decision-maker on bail. For case-specific legal questions, talk to a lawyer.

sections.heading: Common questions in Louisiana
bullets: Is everyone entitled to bail? No. Article I, §18 contains exceptions to the general pretrial right.
Does inability to pay alone determine bail? No. Financial ability is one of the factors listed in Code of Criminal Procedure Article 316.
Does posting bail resolve the charge? No. Bail secures required court appearances; it does not dispose of the prosecution.
Is bail automatically unavailable after conviction? No. Article I, §18 establishes separate rules before and after sentencing.

sources.label: Louisiana Senate — Constitution, Article I
Louisiana Legislature — Code of Criminal Procedure
Louisiana Senate — Constitution, Article V

criminal-law/louisiana/drug-charges.summary: Louisiana drug charges depend on the substance’s controlled-substance schedule, the alleged conduct, the quantity involved, and any qualifying prior convictions; there is no single penalty for all drug offenses. The Uniform Controlled Dangerous Substances Law separately addresses possession and manufacturing or distribution offenses, while marijuana possession has specific penalty rules. State felony prosecutions generally proceed in district court, and a qualifying prior felony can affect sentencing under Louisiana’s habitual-offender law.

facts.label: Controlling law
facts.value: Louisiana’s Uniform Controlled Dangerous Substances Law regulates controlled drugs. Louisiana Revised Statutes 40:964 lists substances in Schedules I through V; the applicable offense and penalty provisions depend on the schedule and substance. — La. R.S. 40:961–40:995; 40:964

facts.label: Possession versus distribution
facts.value: The principal drug statutes distinguish knowing or intentional possession from conduct such as manufacture, distribution, dispensing, and possession with intent to distribute. A distribution-related charge is legally distinct from simple possession. — La. R.S. 40:966–40:970

facts.label: Lawfully obtained medication
facts.value: The possession provisions recognize exceptions for controlled substances obtained directly from a practitioner or through a valid prescription or order in professional practice, as well as possession otherwise authorized by law. — La. R.S. 40:966(C)–40:970(C)

facts.label: Prior felony convictions
facts.value: Louisiana’s habitual-offender statute can increase the sentencing exposure of a person convicted of a subsequent felony. Its application depends on the convictions and statutory requirements, rather than merely whether the person has previously been arrested. — La. R.S. 15:529.1

rows: Heroin; marijuana, which also has specific rules

facts.label: Small-quantity marijuana possession
facts.value: Possession of 14 grams or less of marijuana is punishable by a fine of no more than $100, without imprisonment. This provision applies to a first or subsequent conviction; it does not legalize possession or cover distribution. — La. R.S. 40:966(C)

facts.label: Searches and seizures
facts.value: Louisiana’s constitution protects against unreasonable searches and seizures. A defendant may seek suppression of evidence on constitutional grounds through a motion to suppress; whether suppression is warranted depends on the facts and governing law. — La. Const. art. I, §5; La. Code Crim. Proc. art. 703

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Louisiana
bullets: State felony drug prosecutions generally belong in Louisiana district courts, which have original felony jurisdiction, subject to constitutional exceptions. — La. Const. art. V, §16.
Motions challenging evidence are filed in the court handling the criminal prosecution. A motion to suppress is a court filing, not an administrative complaint. — La. Code Crim. Proc. art. 703.

The district attorney has charge and control of criminal prosecutions instituted or pending in the district and determines whom, when, and how to prosecute, subject to applicable law. — La. Code Crim. Proc. art. 61.

sections.heading: Common questions in Louisiana
bullets: Is possessing a small amount of marijuana legal? No. The fine-only rule for 14 grams or less changes the punishment, not the prohibition. — La. R.S. 40:966(C).
Does every drug possession charge carry the same sentence? No. Louisiana uses different provisions based on the substance, quantity, and other statutory factors. — La. R.S. 40:966–40:970.

Does a previous arrest automatically trigger habitual-offender sentencing? No. The statute concerns qualifying felony convictions and requires the applicable statutory conditions. — La. R.S. 15:529.1.
Can a drug charge involve prescription medication? Yes. Controlled prescription drugs remain regulated, although lawful prescription possession is recognized. — La. R.S. 40:966(C)–40:970(C).

sources.label: Louisiana State Legislature — Louisiana Laws, including the Revised Statutes, Constitution, and Code of Criminal Procedure
Louisiana Supreme Court — official court information and opinions

criminal-law/louisiana/domestic-violence.summary: Louisiana prosecutes domestic violence through several criminal offenses, including domestic abuse battery, dating partner battery, and domestic abuse aggravated assault; the applicable charge depends on the relationship and alleged conduct. Prior convictions and circumstances such as strangulation, burning, or a child’s presence can trigger special penalty provisions under the domestic abuse battery statute. Criminal charges are separate from civil protective-order proceedings, and violating a qualifying protective order can itself be a crime.

sections.heading: How Louisiana classifies domestic violence charges

facts.label: Domestic abuse battery
facts.value: Domestic abuse battery is the intentional use of force or violence by one household member or family member against another. The statute supplies its own relationship definitions; the ordinary meaning of “domestic violence” does not determine the charge. — La. R.S. 14:35.3(A)–(B)

facts.label: Dating relationships
facts.value: Louisiana separately defines dating partner battery. Its dating-partner definition addresses an intimate or romantic relationship and excludes a casual relationship or ordinary association in a business or social context. — La. R.S. 14:34.9

facts.label: Assault versus battery
facts.value: Battery includes the intentional use of force or violence against another person. Assault includes an attempt to commit a battery or intentionally placing another person in reasonable apprehension of receiving a battery, so physical contact is not necessary for every assault charge. — La. R.S. 14:33 and 14:36

rows: The basic penalty is a $300–$1,000 fine and imprisonment for 30 days to six months. The statute also imposes mandatory custody and conditions affecting suspension of sentence.
Separate sentencing provisions apply to second, third, and fourth or subsequent convictions; the statute governs which prior convictions count.
Domestic abuse battery involving strangulation or burning is subject to specific enhanced penalty provisions.
This offense addresses an assault with a dangerous weapon by one household member or family member against another.
Willful disobedience of qualifying protective restrictions can constitute a separate criminal offense.

facts.label: Separate civil remedy
facts.value: The Domestic Abuse Assistance Act authorizes civil protective relief. A protective-order proceeding does not itself decide criminal guilt or replace a prosecution. — La. R.S. 46:2131–2143

facts.label: Prosecution control
facts.value: Subject to the attorney general’s supervision as provided by law, the district attorney has charge and control of criminal prosecutions in the district and determines whom, when, and how to prosecute. A complaining witness does not independently dismiss a prosecution. — La. Code Crim. Proc. art. 61

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Louisiana
bullets: Alleged criminal conduct is investigated by local law enforcement, including municipal police departments and parish sheriffs’ offices; prosecution ordinarily falls to the district attorney.

Civil petitions under the Domestic Abuse Assistance Act fall within district-court jurisdiction, with additional jurisdiction where another court is legally empowered to hear family or juvenile matters. — La. R.S. 46:2133

The Louisiana Protective Order Registry, administered through the Louisiana Supreme Court’s Judicial Administrator’s Office, maintains protective-order information; it is not a prosecutor or a court that independently grants orders. — La. R.S. 46:2136.2

sections.heading: Common questions in Louisiana
bullets: Must the parties be married? No. The domestic abuse battery statute covers defined household and family relationships, and Louisiana separately criminalizes dating partner battery. — La. R.S. 14:35.3 and 14:34.9
Can the complaining witness drop the charges? The witness does not control dismissal; the district attorney controls the prosecution. — La. Code Crim. Proc. art. 61
Is every domestic abuse battery charge a felony? No. Louisiana has a basic first-conviction penalty and separate repeat-offense and enhancement provisions. — La. R.S. 14:35.3
Does an assault require an injury? No. Intentionally placing someone in reasonable apprehension of receiving a battery can qualify as assault. — La. R.S. 14:36

sources.label: Louisiana State Legislature — Louisiana Laws, Revised Statutes and Code of Criminal Procedure
Louisiana Supreme Court — Louisiana Protective Order Registry

criminal-law/louisiana/traffic-violation.summary: Louisiana traffic violations can be criminal offenses, including speeding, careless operation, reckless operation, and driving while intoxicated; the applicable statute determines what prosecutors must prove and what punishment is available. A citation does not necessarily mean a felony charge, but some traffic offenses carry possible jail time, and impaired-driving cases can also involve separate driver’s-license proceedings. Cases may be handled in district, parish, city, or qualifying mayor’s courts, depending on location and jurisdiction.

sections.heading: Louisiana traffic offenses and criminal exposure

facts.label: Speeding and unsafe speed
facts.value: Louisiana prohibits driving faster than is reasonable and prudent under existing conditions and hazards. Compliance with a posted maximum does not eliminate the separate duty to reduce speed when conditions require it. — La. R.S. 32:64.

facts.label: Careless operation
facts.value: Drivers must operate vehicles carefully and prudently, without endangering another person’s life, limb, or property. This is a separate offense from reckless operation. — La. R.S. 32:58.

facts.label: Reckless operation
facts.value: Reckless operation involves operating a vehicle, aircraft, vessel, or other conveyance in a criminally negligent or reckless manner. A first conviction carries a fine of up to $200, imprisonment for up to 90 days, or both. — La. R.S. 14:99.

sections.heading: Common charges and their legal requirements

rows: Speed must satisfy posted limits and the reasonable-and-prudent standard for actual conditions.
Traffic-control signals establish when vehicles must stop and when movement is permitted, subject to statutory exceptions.
Driving must not endanger another person’s life, limb, or property.
The prosecution must establish criminally negligent or reckless operation.
Operating a covered conveyance while under the influence of alcohol is prohibited; a blood-alcohol concentration of 0.08 percent or more is also a statutory basis.

sections.heading: Impaired driving and separate license consequences

facts.label: Alcohol is not the only basis
facts.value: Louisiana’s DWI statute also covers specified drug-related impairment and combinations of alcohol and drugs. The offense is not limited to driving a passenger car. — La. R.S. 14:98.

facts.label: First-offense DWI punishment
facts.value: The statutory sentencing range includes a $300–$1,000 fine and imprisonment from 10 days to six months. Suspension of imprisonment and probation are governed by additional statutory conditions. — La. R.S. 14:98.1.

facts.label: Administrative proceedings
facts.value: Chemical-test refusal or qualifying test results can trigger driver’s-license action under Louisiana’s implied-consent laws, separate from prosecution of the criminal charge. — La. R.S. 32:661–668.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Louisiana
bullets: Traffic prosecutions are handled by the court with jurisdiction over the charge and location. Louisiana district courts have criminal jurisdiction, while statutes establish the jurisdiction of parish, city, and mayor’s courts. — Louisiana Constitution, Article V, Section 16; La. R.S. 13:1446, 13:1894, and 33:441.

The Louisiana Department of Public Safety and Corrections, through the Office of Motor Vehicles, administers driver’s-license matters. Criminal sentencing and administrative license action are distinct processes. — La. R.S. 32:402 and 32:667–668.

sections.heading: Common questions in Louisiana
bullets: Can reckless driving result in jail? Yes. A first reckless-operation conviction permits imprisonment for up to 90 days. — La. R.S. 14:99.
Is careless operation the same as reckless operation? No. Louisiana defines them in separate statutes with different language describing the prohibited conduct. — La. R.S. 32:58 and 14:99.
Does driving below the posted limit always prevent a speeding charge? No. Speed must also be reasonable and prudent for the conditions. — La. R.S. 32:64.
Must a DWI prosecution depend on a 0.08 percent test result? No. Operating under the influence of alcoholic beverages is a separate statutory basis. — La. R.S. 14:98.

Louisiana Supreme Court — Louisiana court system

criminal-law/louisiana/juvenile-law.summary: Louisiana generally handles offenses committed before a person’s seventeenth birthday as juvenile delinquency matters, although specified serious charges can place some younger teenagers in adult criminal court. The Louisiana Children’s Code governs delinquency proceedings, including constitutional protections, adjudication, and disposition; it expressly excludes a constitutional right to a jury trial in juvenile adjudications. The age at the alleged offense, the offense charged, and the applicable jurisdictional provisions determine whether a case proceeds under juvenile or adult criminal law.

sections.heading: Louisiana juvenile jurisdiction and basic protections

facts.label: Age boundary
facts.value: For delinquency proceedings, the Children’s Code generally defines a child as a person under seventeen and includes someone accused of committing a delinquent act before turning seventeen. Turning seventeen after an alleged offense does not, by itself, make that earlier offense an adult criminal case. Historical cases can involve earlier versions of Louisiana’s age rules. — Louisiana Children’s Code art. 804.

facts.label: What delinquency means
facts.value: A delinquent act generally means conduct by a child that would constitute an offense under state law, another state’s law, federal law, or a local ordinance. Juvenile delinquency is distinct from child-protection proceedings and families-in-need-of-services proceedings. — Louisiana Children’s Code art. 804; Titles VI and VII.

facts.label: Constitutional protections
facts.value: Rights guaranteed to criminal defendants by the United States Constitution or Louisiana Constitution apply in delinquency proceedings, except the right to trial by jury. A juvenile adjudication therefore does not use the same jury-trial framework as an adult criminal prosecution. — Louisiana Children’s Code art. 808.

rows: A delinquency proceeding is commenced by a petition, and the district attorney has authority to file it.
The state must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the child committed the delinquent act alleged in the petition.
The court’s disposition must reflect the statutory guidelines, including the child’s needs and society’s best interests; removal from parental custody is subject to statutory limits.

Article 305 provides adult criminal jurisdiction for specified charges involving children who were at least fifteen when the alleged act occurred, subject to the article’s charging and procedural requirements.
Separate transfer provisions permit a juvenile court to consider transferring qualifying cases for adult prosecution after the required proceedings.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Louisiana
bullets: Juvenile delinquency matters belong in the court exercising juvenile jurisdiction for the locality. Depending on the jurisdiction, that can be a specialized juvenile court or another court assigned juvenile jurisdiction by law. — Louisiana Children’s Code art. 302.

The district attorney is the prosecuting office responsible for filing a delinquency petition. A private complaint is not itself the petition that commences the court proceeding. — Louisiana Children’s Code art. 842.

The Louisiana Office of Juvenile Justice administers juvenile services, including supervision and secure-care responsibilities within its authority. It is not the court that decides whether the state has proved a delinquency allegation. — Louisiana Office of Juvenile Justice; Louisiana Children’s Code art. 881.

sections.heading: Common questions in Louisiana
bullets: Are seventeen-year-olds automatically handled as juveniles? No. Under the current general delinquency definition, the relevant cutoff is the seventeenth birthday. Earlier offenses and historical statutory changes can require a different analysis. — Louisiana Children’s Code art. 804.
Can a juvenile demand a jury? Not in a juvenile delinquency adjudication under the Children’s Code. Article 808 expressly excepts jury trial from its constitutional-rights provision.
Is the burden of proof lower because the defendant is a child? No. The state must prove the alleged delinquent act beyond a reasonable doubt. — Louisiana Children’s Code art. 881.

Can someone younger than seventeen face adult prosecution? Yes. Louisiana has both offense-specific adult-jurisdiction provisions and judicial-transfer procedures. Adult prosecution is not authorized merely because any delinquency allegation is serious. — Louisiana Children’s Code arts. 305 and 857–864.

Louisiana Supreme Court — Louisiana judicial system

criminal-law/maine/juvenile-law.summary: Maine generally handles offenses committed before age 18 under the Maine Juvenile Code, with the District Court acting as the Juvenile Court rather than treating the case as an ordinary adult prosecution. The law provides for investigation, possible informal resolution, adjudication and dispositions that can include probation or commitment to the Department of Corrections; certain cases may be transferred for adult prosecution after a bind-over hearing.

facts.label: Governing law
facts.value: The Maine Juvenile Code is in Title 15, Part 6 of the Maine Revised Statutes. Its stated purposes include providing care and guidance, protecting the public and holding juveniles accountable for their conduct. — 15 M.R.S. §§ 3001–3002

facts.label: Age definition
facts.value: The code defines a juvenile as a person who had not attained 18 years of age when the juvenile crime was committed. The age at the alleged offense therefore matters, not simply the person’s age when proceedings begin. — 15 M.R.S. § 3003

facts.label: Court with jurisdiction
facts.value: Maine’s District Court exercises the jurisdiction and powers of the Juvenile Court. The code separately addresses the court’s authority over juvenile crimes and the circumstances permitting adult prosecution. — 15 M.R.S. § 3101

facts.label: What constitutes a juvenile crime
facts.value: The statutory definition includes conduct that would constitute a crime if committed by an adult, subject to listed exceptions, and certain additional conduct expressly identified by the Legislature. Not every legal violation by a minor is processed as a juvenile crime. — 15 M.R.S. § 3103

rows: A juvenile community corrections officer investigates qualifying referrals and considers whether further action or an informal adjustment is appropriate.
The code permits qualifying matters to be addressed through an agreed informal adjustment rather than immediately proceeding through a contested adjudication.
The Juvenile Court may bind over an eligible case after a hearing and the findings required by statute; transfer is not automatic merely because an allegation is serious.
Probation is an authorized juvenile disposition and may include court-ordered conditions.
Statutory alternatives include restitution, community service and, when authorized, commitment to the Department of Corrections.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Maine
bullets: Juvenile proceedings are handled through the Maine District Court acting as the Juvenile Court. The court clerk maintains filings in the court case. — 15 M.R.S. § 3101

The Maine Department of Corrections’ juvenile community corrections officers perform statutory intake and preliminary-investigation functions. Their role is distinct from the judge’s adjudicatory role. — 15 M.R.S. § 3301

The district attorney represents the State in juvenile prosecution. A juvenile petition is the formal charging document governed by the Juvenile Code, rather than a private civil complaint. — 15 M.R.S. § 3305

sections.heading: Common questions in Maine
bullets: Does turning 18 automatically make an earlier offense an adult case? No. The juvenile definition looks to age when the alleged juvenile crime occurred; jurisdiction and any adult transfer are governed separately. — 15 M.R.S. §§ 3003, 3101

Can a juvenile face adult prosecution? Yes. Maine permits bind-over in statutorily eligible cases after a hearing and required findings. The court considers statutory factors concerning the offense and the juvenile. — 15 M.R.S. § 3101(4)

Does every referral require a formal court case? No. The preliminary-investigation process allows qualifying referrals to be resolved without a formal adjudication, including through informal adjustment. — 15 M.R.S. § 3301

Is confinement mandatory for every adjudication? No. The disposition statute authorizes several alternatives, including probation, restitution and community service, as well as commitment where legally authorized. — 15 M.R.S. § 3314

criminal-law/maryland/traffic-violations.summary: Maryland distinguishes payable traffic citations from offenses that require a court appearance, including driving under the influence and driving while impaired. Many Transportation Article violations are misdemeanors, but the consequences depend on the specific offense: some carry fines and license points, while others can carry incarceration and separate administrative license sanctions. Most traffic cases begin in the District Court of Maryland, and paying a payable citation constitutes a guilty plea rather than a contested resolution.

sections.heading: Maryland traffic offenses and court procedures

facts.label: Criminal classification
facts.value: A violation of the Maryland Vehicle Law is a misdemeanor unless the violation is designated a felony or civil offense. A traffic charge therefore is not necessarily a civil matter merely because it involves driving. — Maryland Code, Transportation § 27-101(a).

facts.label: Payable citations
facts.value: For a payable citation, the listed options generally are paying the fine, requesting a waiver hearing, or requesting a trial. The response deadline is 30 days after receipt of the citation. — District Court of Maryland, Traffic.

facts.label: Waiver hearing versus trial
facts.value: At a waiver hearing, the defendant pleads guilty with an explanation and may ask for a reduced fine or probation instead of a conviction. A trial allows the defendant to contest the charge. Neither procedure guarantees a particular result. — District Court of Maryland, Traffic.

facts.label: Must-appear charges
facts.value: A citation marked 'must appear' cannot be resolved simply by paying the scheduled fine. The court sends notice of the trial date. — District Court of Maryland, Traffic.

rows: Drivers may not exceed applicable maximum limits or drive faster than is reasonable and prudent under existing conditions.
Includes driving with wanton or willful disregard for the safety of persons or property, or in a manner indicating that disregard.
Driving carelessly or imprudently in a manner that endangers any property or the life or person of any individual.
Maryland separately prohibits driving under the influence of alcohol, under the influence of alcohol per se, and while impaired by alcohol.
Separate provisions cover impairment by drugs or drugs combined with alcohol, and specified impairment involving controlled dangerous substances.

facts.label: Point accumulation
facts.value: For points accumulated within two years, MVA identifies these action levels: 3–4 points, warning letter; 5–7, Driver Improvement Program; 8–11, suspension; and 12 or more, revocation. — Transportation § 16-404; Maryland MVA, Point Accumulation.

facts.label: Separate consequences
facts.value: A court fine and MVA licensing action are distinct consequences. Paying a citation does not prevent points from being assessed when the conviction is for a point-bearing offense. — District Court of Maryland, Traffic; Maryland MVA, Point Accumulation.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Maryland
bullets: District Court of Maryland: Processes traffic citations, waiver hearings, and trials; the citation and court notices identify the relevant case and court.
Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration: Maintains driver records and administers point-related licensing actions and Driver Improvement Program requirements.

sections.heading: Common questions in Maryland
bullets: Does paying a ticket admit guilt? Yes. For a payable citation, payment constitutes a guilty plea.
Can every traffic charge be paid without appearing? No. Charges designated 'must appear' require a court appearance.
Are reckless and negligent driving the same? No. Maryland defines them separately in Transportation § 21-901.1.
Does a fine replace license points? No. A conviction may produce both a court fine and MVA points.

sources.label: District Court of Maryland — Traffic
Maryland MVA — Point Accumulation
Maryland General Assembly — Transportation § 21-901.1
Maryland General Assembly — Transportation § 21-902

criminal-law/massachusetts/arrest-proces.summary: In Massachusetts, arrest can lead to booking, a bail decision, and arraignment in court, where the charge is formally presented and a plea is entered. State law provides a specific telephone-access right at the place of detention, while Massachusetts criminal procedure requires an arrested defendant who remains in custody to be brought before a court without unnecessary delay. Release may be on personal recognizance or subject to bail or conditions; qualifying cases can involve a separate dangerousness hearing.

sections.heading: After arrest: telephone access and court appearance

facts.label: Telephone access
facts.value: The official in charge of a station or other place of detention must permit an arrested person to use a telephone, at that person's expense, to communicate with family or friends, arrange release on bail, or engage an attorney. — Massachusetts General Laws, chapter 276, § 33A

facts.label: One-hour deadline
facts.value: The arrested person must be informed of the telephone right immediately upon arrival, and telephone use must be permitted within one hour thereafter. This deadline concerns telephone access, not release from custody. — Massachusetts General Laws, chapter 276, § 33A

facts.label: Initial court appearance
facts.value: An arrested defendant who has not been released must be brought before a court without unnecessary delay. At the initial appearance, the court addresses the charge and applicable rights, including representation by counsel. — Massachusetts Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 7

rows: The ordinary bail statute favors release on personal recognizance without surety unless that release will not reasonably assure appearance.
Relevant considerations include the charge, possible penalty, family ties, employment, financial resources, criminal record, and history of court appearances.
The court must consider financial resources. Bail exceeding what a defendant can afford requires specific findings under the statute.
For qualifying charges, the Commonwealth may request detention or release conditions through a separate statutory proceeding.
Detention requires clear and convincing evidence that no release conditions will reasonably assure the safety of another person or the community.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Massachusetts
bullets: District Court or Boston Municipal Court: These courts handle initial appearances and arraignments in criminal cases within their jurisdiction. The court addresses counsel and release at the initial-appearance stage. — Massachusetts Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 7
Superior Court: A defendant aggrieved by a District Court bail decision has a statutory route to petition the Superior Court for review. — G.L. c. 276, § 58
The court conducting a dangerousness hearing: The defendant has rights to counsel, to testify, to present witnesses and information, and to cross-examine witnesses who appear. — G.L. c. 276, § 58A

sections.heading: Common questions in Massachusetts
bullets: Does an arrest establish guilt? No. Arraignment is an early court proceeding, not a finding of guilt. A not-guilty plea leaves the charge to be resolved through later proceedings. — Massachusetts Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 7

Must everyone arrested pay cash to leave custody? No. Massachusetts law provides for release on personal recognizance without surety, subject to statutory exceptions and the court's findings. — G.L. c. 276, § 58

Can someone be detained because of alleged dangerousness? Yes, but § 58A requires an eligible case and the prescribed hearing and findings; an accusation alone does not satisfy the detention standard. — G.L. c. 276, § 58A

Is arraignment the same as a dangerousness hearing? No. Arraignment addresses the charge and plea; a dangerousness hearing determines whether conditions can reasonably assure safety. — Massachusetts Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 7; G.L. c. 276, § 58A

criminal-law/maine/traffic-violations.summary: Maine distinguishes civil traffic infractions from criminal motor-vehicle offenses: an ordinary traffic ticket does not necessarily charge a crime, but criminal speeding, operating under the influence, and driving to endanger do. Criminal charges can carry imprisonment and fines, while licensing consequences may arise separately through the Secretary of State. The offense charged, its statutory classification, and any qualifying prior convictions determine which criminal penalties and license sanctions apply.

sections.heading: Civil traffic tickets versus criminal charges

facts.label: Traffic infractions
facts.value: A Maine traffic infraction is a civil violation rather than a crime. Its punishment does not include imprisonment; traffic-infraction proceedings are handled in the District Court system. — 29-A M.R.S. § 103

facts.label: Criminal speeding
facts.value: Operating a motor vehicle at a speed exceeding the maximum lawful speed by 30 miles per hour or more is a Class E crime. The threshold is measured against the applicable lawful speed limit, not a single statewide driving speed. — 29-A M.R.S. § 2074

facts.label: Operating under the influence
facts.value: Maine calls the offense operating under the influence, or OUI. The statute covers operating while under the influence of intoxicants or with an alcohol level of 0.08 grams or more per 100 milliliters of blood or 210 liters of breath. — 29-A M.R.S. § 2411(1-A)

rows: Civil violation; no imprisonment as punishment
Exceeding the lawful speed limit by at least 30 mph
Class E crime; license suspension also applies
Generally Class D; qualifying circumstances can produce a higher classification

facts.label: General sentencing ceilings
facts.value: The general maximum imprisonment is six months for a Class E crime and 364 days for a Class D crime. The general maximum fine for an individual is $1,000 for Class E and $2,000 for Class D. Offense-specific sentencing provisions also matter. — 17-A M.R.S. §§ 1604, 1704

facts.label: Driving to endanger
facts.value: This offense requires criminal negligence in driving that endangers another person's property or any person, including the operator or a passenger. It carries a mandatory minimum $575 fine and a court-ordered license suspension of at least 30 days and no more than 180 days. — 29-A M.R.S. § 2413

facts.label: Separate licensing action
facts.value: The Secretary of State has statutory authority to impose an administrative suspension for operating with an excessive alcohol level. That licensing process is separate from the criminal OUI prosecution. — 29-A M.R.S. § 2453

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Maine
bullets: Maine Judicial Branch Violations Bureau: processes civil traffic-infraction cases within the District Court system; it does not handle criminal motor-vehicle prosecutions as ordinary traffic tickets.
Maine trial courts: criminal traffic charges proceed through the criminal court system, with cases administered through the Unified Criminal Docket.
Maine Secretary of State, Bureau of Motor Vehicles: administers driver-license records, suspensions, and applicable administrative hearing processes.

sections.heading: Common questions in Maine
bullets: Is every speeding ticket criminal? No. Maine specifically makes speeding by 30 mph or more above the lawful limit a Class E crime. — 29-A M.R.S. § 2074
Can OUI apply without an alcohol reading of 0.08? Yes. Operating while under the influence of intoxicants is an alternative statutory basis for the offense. — 29-A M.R.S. § 2411
Does driving to endanger require an actual collision? No. The statute requires criminally negligent driving that endangers property or people, not a completed collision. — 29-A M.R.S. § 2413

Can a traffic incident affect both a criminal case and a license? Yes. Maine provides criminal penalties and separate administrative licensing procedures, including alcohol-related suspensions. — 29-A M.R.S. §§ 2411, 2453

Maine Legislature — Title 17-A, Maine Criminal Code
