criminal-law/massachusetts/expungement.summary: Massachusetts allows criminal-record expungement in limited circumstances, including certain offenses committed before age 21 and cases involving specified errors, identity misuse, or fraud on the court. Expungement permanently erases a record rather than merely restricting public access, which is generally what sealing does. Eligibility depends on the legal route, the offense, and the record’s history; completing a sentence or obtaining a dismissal does not automatically entitle someone to expungement.

facts.label: Meaning of expungement
facts.value: Massachusetts defines expungement as permanent erasure or destruction so that the record is no longer accessible to or maintained by the court, criminal justice agencies, or law enforcement agencies. This is different from sealing, which preserves records while restricting access. — Massachusetts General Laws, chapter 276, § 100E; Massachusetts Court System, Expunge your criminal record.

facts.label: Time-based eligibility
facts.value: The time-based process covers qualifying offenses committed before the person’s 21st birthday. Eligibility also depends on limits concerning the person’s criminal records, the type of offense, pending proceedings, and other statutory conditions; age alone is insufficient. — Massachusetts General Laws, chapter 276, §§ 100F–100J; Massachusetts Court System, Expunge your criminal record.

facts.label: Excluded offenses
facts.value: The time-based process excludes specified offenses, including sex offenses, offenses resulting in death or serious bodily injury, and certain offenses involving dangerous weapons. These exclusions are separate from the special grounds for expungement based on errors or fraud. — Massachusetts Court System, Expunge your criminal record; Massachusetts General Laws, chapter 276, § 100K.

facts.label: Error-based judicial findings
facts.value: Under § 100K, the court must find clear and convincing evidence that the record was created because of a listed statutory ground. The court must also determine that expungement is in the best interests of justice and include written findings supporting its decision. — Massachusetts General Laws, chapter 276, § 100K.

sections.heading: Routes, waiting periods, and qualifying grounds

rows: At least three years must have elapsed after completion of the sentence, including probation; additional eligibility requirements apply.
Massachusetts Court System, Expunge your criminal record
At least seven years must have elapsed after completion of the sentence, including probation; additional eligibility requirements apply.
Massachusetts Court System, Expunge your criminal record
False identification and unauthorized use or theft of identity are expressly listed grounds.
The statute covers demonstrable errors by law enforcement, civilian or expert witnesses, and court employees.
Demonstrable fraud perpetrated upon the court is a listed ground; this route does not require the three- or seven-year waiting period.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Massachusetts
bullets: The Commissioner of Probation receives time-based expungement requests and reviews statutory eligibility before an eligible request proceeds to the court.
A petition relying on § 100K grounds is filed in the court where the criminal case was handled, rather than through the Commissioner’s time-based screening process.
The Massachusetts Court System publishes separate forms for time-based and non-time-based expungement. Expungement is a statutory records proceeding, not an administrative misconduct complaint.

sections.heading: Common questions in Massachusetts
bullets: Is expungement the same as sealing? No. Expungement permanently erases or destroys covered records; sealing generally restricts access without destroying them.
Does a dismissal automatically qualify? No. A dismissal alone does not establish eligibility under either expungement route.
Does the offense have to predate age 21? That requirement applies to time-based expungement, not to the separate grounds listed in § 100K.
Is there always a waiting period? No. Petitions based on the special grounds in § 100K are not subject to the time-based route’s three- and seven-year periods.

sources.label: Massachusetts Legislature — General Laws, chapter 276, section 100E
Massachusetts Legislature — General Laws, chapter 276, section 100F
Massachusetts Legislature — General Laws, chapter 276, section 100K
Massachusetts Court System — Expunge your criminal record

criminal-law/maine/expungement.summary: Maine does not provide a general process that erases every eligible criminal conviction; its record-clearing rules distinguish limited adult record relief, juvenile sealing, and restrictions on disclosure of confidential criminal history information. Whether information remains available depends on the record, the applicable statute, and who requests it. A dismissal, an acquittal, a sealing order, and a governor’s pardon have different legal effects, and none should automatically be treated as destruction of every related record.

sections.heading: What record clearing means in Maine

facts.label: Adult conviction relief
facts.value: Maine has a statutory procedure for restricting dissemination of certain adult conviction information. It is not a general entitlement to erase any conviction after a waiting period; eligibility is governed by the specific statutory requirements. — 15 M.R.S. § 2251.

facts.label: Confidential is not destroyed
facts.value: Maine distinguishes public criminal history record information from confidential criminal history record information. Confidential information remains subject to authorized disclosure, including disclosure for criminal justice purposes. — 16 M.R.S. §§ 703, 705.

facts.label: Different record systems
facts.value: Maine’s criminal history information law does not make every document concerning a criminal case part of the same disclosure system. Court records and juvenile records have separate access rules. — 16 M.R.S. § 703; 15 M.R.S. § 3308.

rows: Limited statutory relief exists; passage of time alone does not establish eligibility.
These dispositions fall within the statutory framework for confidential criminal history information, rather than automatic destruction of every record.
Juvenile records have special confidentiality rules, and qualifying records may be sealed by court order.
Executive clemency is a separate process from judicial sealing; the governor has constitutional authority to grant pardons after conviction, except in impeachment cases.

facts.label: Waiting period
facts.value: A person may petition to seal juvenile records when at least three years have elapsed since discharge from the disposition. The statute also requires no subsequent juvenile adjudication or criminal conviction and no pending proceeding seeking an adjudication or conviction. — 15 M.R.S. § 3308(8).

facts.label: Court decision
facts.value: Satisfying the threshold conditions does not make sealing automatic. The Juvenile Court considers whether the person’s rehabilitation has been attained to a satisfactory degree. — 15 M.R.S. § 3308(8).

facts.label: Effect of sealing
facts.value: After sealing, the person may deny the existence of the juvenile record. The statute nevertheless permits specified court-authorized inspection; sealing is not the same as physical destruction. — 15 M.R.S. § 3308(8).

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Maine
bullets: Adult statutory record relief is handled through the court, rather than through a general administrative expungement application to the police. The governing adult-record statute controls the application.
A juvenile sealing petition goes to the Juvenile Court under 15 M.R.S. § 3308(8). Maine District Court exercises juvenile jurisdiction.

The Maine State Police State Bureau of Identification maintains Maine’s central criminal history records. Questions about that repository concern a different record system from the court’s own case file.

sections.heading: Common questions in Maine
bullets: Does a dismissed charge disappear everywhere? No. Confidential criminal history treatment does not itself destroy court files or every agency record.
Are all juvenile cases public? No. Maine has special juvenile confidentiality rules, although statutory exceptions allow public access in specified cases.
Does juvenile sealing happen automatically after three years? No. The statute requires a petition, additional eligibility conditions, and a court determination.
Is a pardon the same as expungement? No. A pardon is executive clemency, not a judicial order destroying records. Questions about an individual record’s eligibility require talking to a lawyer.

sources.label: Maine Legislature — 15 M.R.S. § 2251
Maine Legislature — Juvenile records, 15 M.R.S. § 3308
Maine Legislature — Criminal history information definitions, 16 M.R.S. § 703
Maine Legislature — Constitution of Maine

criminal-law/massachusetts/traffic-viola.summary: Massachusetts separates ordinary traffic tickets, called civil motor vehicle infractions, from criminal motor vehicle offenses such as operating under the influence and negligent operation. Civil tickets generally proceed through payment or a requested court hearing, while criminal charges can involve arraignment, prosecution, fines, incarceration, and license consequences under Massachusetts General Laws Chapters 90 and 90C. The procedure depends on the specific charge: a citation can identify civil infractions, criminal offenses, or both, and criminal allegations are not resolved simply by paying a ticket.

facts.label: Civil classification
facts.value: A civil motor vehicle infraction is a motor vehicle law violation for which the prescribed penalty does not include imprisonment, subject to statutory exclusions. It is not prosecuted as a criminal offense merely because it involves driving. — Massachusetts General Laws, Chapter 90C, § 1.

facts.label: Criminal classification
facts.value: Operating under the influence, reckless or negligent operation, and specified leaving-the-scene offenses are criminal motor vehicle offenses. The prosecution must prove a criminal charge beyond a reasonable doubt. — Massachusetts General Laws, Chapter 90, § 24.

facts.label: Separate licensing consequences
facts.value: Court penalties and Registry of Motor Vehicles licensing actions are distinct. Section 24 provides license consequences for specified offenses in addition to criminal punishment. — Massachusetts General Laws, Chapter 90, § 24.

rows: Generally a civil infraction; speed must be reasonable and proper for conditions, not merely below a posted limit.
Criminal offense covering operation on specified public-access locations while impaired by alcohol or specified drugs, or with a blood alcohol percentage of 0.08 or greater.
Criminal offense when a vehicle is operated recklessly, or negligently so that the lives or safety of the public might be endangered.
Criminal offense when an operator knowingly causes damage to another vehicle or property and leaves without stopping and providing required identifying information.

facts.label: Civil citation response
facts.value: The ordinary deadline to pay or request a hearing on a civil motor vehicle citation is 20 days from issuance. Failure to respond can result in additional charges and license or registration consequences. — Massachusetts General Laws, Chapter 90C, § 3; Massachusetts RMV civil citation guidance.

facts.label: Civil hearing standard
facts.value: Civil responsibility is decided under a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard, rather than the criminal beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard. The statutory process includes a hearing before a clerk-magistrate and an avenue for appeal to a judge. — Massachusetts General Laws, Chapter 90C, § 3.

facts.label: Basic OUI penalty range
facts.value: The basic OUI provision authorizes a fine of $500 to $5,000, imprisonment for up to two and one-half years, or both. Repeat offenses and specified circumstances carry different consequences; the statute also provides alternative dispositions for eligible defendants. — Massachusetts General Laws, Chapter 90, § 24(1)(a)(1).

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Massachusetts
bullets: Registry of Motor Vehicles: processes civil citation payments and hearing requests through the citation-response system. It also administers driver licensing actions.
District Court or Boston Municipal Court: handles civil motor vehicle infraction hearings and criminal motor vehicle cases within the court’s jurisdiction.
Issuing police department: handles complaints about an officer’s conduct. An administrative complaint is separate from the statutory process for contesting a citation.

sections.heading: Common questions in Massachusetts
bullets: Is every traffic ticket a criminal charge? No. Ordinary civil motor vehicle infractions are distinct from offenses carrying criminal penalties.
Can a civil ticket be contested? Yes. Massachusetts provides a hearing process, ordinarily requested within 20 days of issuance.
Does negligent operation require an actual collision? No. Section 24 addresses operation that might endanger the lives or safety of the public.
Does paying a civil fine resolve a separate criminal charge? No. Civil payment procedures do not dispose of criminal allegations.

sources.label: Massachusetts General Laws, Chapter 90C, § 3
Massachusetts General Laws, Chapter 90, § 24
Massachusetts General Laws, Chapter 90, § 17
Massachusetts RMV: Appeal your traffic ticket

criminal-law/michigan/domestic-violence-.summary: Michigan prosecutes domestic violence through assault statutes that apply to specified family, household, and dating relationships; the charge does not require marriage or a current shared home. A first domestic assault is generally a misdemeanor punishable by up to 93 days in jail, while aggravated domestic assault and qualifying repeat offenses carry greater penalties, including possible felony charges. Certain eligible defendants may receive deferred proceedings, but dismissal is not automatic.

sections.heading: What Michigan domestic assault charges cover

facts.label: Covered relationships
facts.value: The domestic assault provision covers a spouse or former spouse, someone with whom the defendant has or previously had a dating relationship, someone with whom the defendant has a child in common, and a current or former resident of the same household. — MCL 750.81(2)

facts.label: Dating relationship
facts.value: Michigan defines this as frequent, intimate associations primarily characterized by an expectation of affectional involvement. A casual relationship or ordinary fraternization in a business or social context does not qualify. — MCL 750.81(6)

facts.label: Injury and aggravated assault
facts.value: Ordinary domestic assault does not require a serious or aggravated injury. Aggravated domestic assault involves an assault without a weapon that causes serious or aggravated injury, without intent to commit murder or inflict great bodily harm less than murder. — MCL 750.81(2); MCL 750.81a(2)

rows: Domestic assault, no qualifying prior conviction
93 days in jail, $500 fine, or both
Domestic assault, one qualifying prior conviction
1 year in jail, $1,000 fine, or both
Domestic assault, two or more qualifying prior convictions
5 years in prison, $5,000 fine, or both
Aggravated domestic assault, no qualifying prior conviction
1 year in jail, $1,000 fine, or both
Aggravated domestic assault, qualifying prior conviction
5 years in prison, $5,000 fine, or both

facts.label: Eligibility and consent
facts.value: For an eligible defendant who pleads guilty to or is found guilty of covered misdemeanor domestic assault, the court may defer proceedings without entering a judgment of guilt and impose probation. Both the defendant and prosecutor must consent; the prosecutor must consult the victim. Statutory criminal-history restrictions apply. — MCL 769.4a(1)

facts.label: Completion and violations
facts.value: Successful fulfillment of probation leads to discharge and dismissal without an adjudication of guilt. Violations can result in entry of a judgment of guilt and sentencing. This disposition is available only once, and the statute provides for a nonpublic record rather than destruction of every record. — MCL 769.4a

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Michigan
bullets: Reports of suspected domestic assault are handled by law enforcement, including municipal police, county sheriffs, and the Michigan State Police. Michigan permits warrantless arrest for covered domestic assaults based on reasonable cause even when the officer did not witness the conduct. — MCL 764.15a
District courts generally handle misdemeanor domestic assault cases and preliminary examinations in felony prosecutions; circuit courts handle felony trials. — MCL 600.8311; MCL 600.601
A domestic relationship personal protection order is a separate civil proceeding in circuit court, not a criminal assault charge. — MCL 600.2950

sections.heading: Common questions in Michigan
bullets: Must the people be married? No. Dating partners, former household residents, and people with a child in common can fall within the statute. — MCL 750.81(2)

Does every second offense become a felony? No. Ordinary domestic assault with one qualifying prior conviction is a misdemeanor; aggravated domestic assault with a qualifying prior conviction is a felony. — MCL 750.81(3); MCL 750.81a(3)
Is deferred dismissal guaranteed for a first offense? No. Eligibility, required consent, and the court’s exercise of discretion govern deferred proceedings. — MCL 769.4a
Does deferred dismissal erase the case entirely? No. Michigan retains a nonpublic record, and the disposition can matter in later proceedings specified by law. — MCL 769.4a

sources.label: Michigan Legislature — MCL 750.81
Michigan Legislature — MCL 750.81a
Michigan Legislature — MCL 769.4a
Michigan Legislature — MCL 764.15a

criminal-law/michigan/bail-and-bond.summary: Michigan generally permits release on bail before conviction, but its Constitution allows detention without bail in specified categories when the required findings are made. Michigan Court Rule 6.106 governs release decisions, including personal recognizance, conditional release, and money bail, with attention to court appearance and public safety. There is no single statewide dollar amount for criminal bail; the court makes an individualized decision under the governing constitutional and court-rule standards.

sections.heading: Michigan’s right to bail and release standards

facts.label: Constitutional starting point
facts.value: Before conviction, people generally have a right to bail by sufficient sureties. The Michigan Constitution identifies exceptions, including murder and treason when the proof is evident or the presumption great; additional exceptions have their own eligibility requirements and findings. — Michigan Constitution, Article I, § 15

facts.label: Excessive bail
facts.value: Michigan’s Constitution expressly prohibits excessive bail. This protection is separate from the question of whether a defendant qualifies for release before trial. — Michigan Constitution, Article I, § 16

facts.label: Personal recognizance
facts.value: Unless detention is authorized, the court must order release on personal recognizance or an unsecured appearance bond unless it determines that release will not reasonably ensure the defendant’s appearance or will present a danger to the public. — MCR 6.106(C)

facts.label: Individual circumstances
facts.value: Release decisions consider information such as the defendant’s criminal record, prior court appearances, family and community ties, employment, financial history, the seriousness of the charge, and potential danger. — MCR 6.106(F)

rows: Release based on the defendant’s promise to appear, without an upfront bail payment. — MCR 6.106(C)
A bond obligation that does not require an upfront deposit as a condition of release. — MCR 6.106(C)
Conditions may include travel restrictions, reporting requirements, restrictions on contact with specified people, or other authorized supervision. — MCR 6.106(D)
Authorized forms include a cash or surety bond and, when ordered, a bond secured by a 10 percent cash deposit. Money bail may accompany nonfinancial conditions. — MCR 6.106(E)
Available only under the applicable constitutional and procedural requirements, not simply because a charge is a felony. — Michigan Constitution, Article I, § 15; MCR 6.106(B)

facts.label: Conditions of release
facts.value: Release requires the defendant to appear as ordered, remain within the court’s authority, and comply with applicable conditions. Conditions can restrict conduct even when no money deposit is required. — MCR 6.106(C)–(E)

facts.label: Changing the order
facts.value: Michigan’s criminal rules provide procedures for modifying and reviewing custody and release decisions. A release order is not necessarily fixed for the entire case. — MCR 6.106

facts.label: Violations
facts.value: Violating release conditions can result in modification or revocation of release under the rule’s procedures. Money-bond forfeiture is a separate potential consequence involving the bond obligation. — MCR 6.106

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Michigan
bullets: The criminal court handling the case is the forum for requests concerning the defendant’s release order. District courts generally handle initial felony proceedings and misdemeanor cases; circuit courts handle felony cases after bindover. — MCR 6.104; MCR 6.110
Court clerks maintain case records and process filings; a judge makes the custody or release decision. Review of that decision follows the applicable court procedures. — MCR 6.106

sections.heading: Common questions in Michigan
bullets: Does every defendant have to pay money? No. Michigan expressly provides for personal recognizance and unsecured appearance bonds. — MCR 6.106(C)
Is a 10 percent deposit automatic? No. A deposit bond is one authorized option when the court orders that form of money bail. — MCR 6.106(E)
Can a felony defendant receive bail? Yes. A felony charge alone does not establish a constitutional exception to bail. — Michigan Constitution, Article I, § 15
Can release include a no-contact restriction? Yes. The court may impose restrictions on contact with specified people as a condition of release. — MCR 6.106(D)

sources.label: Michigan Legislature — Constitution, Article I, § 15
Michigan Legislature — Constitution, Article I, § 16
Michigan Courts — Current Court Rules

criminal-law/michigan/juvenile-law.summary: Michigan generally handles alleged crimes committed before a person’s 18th birthday in the family division of circuit court under the Juvenile Code, although certain cases can proceed under adult criminal procedures. Juvenile cases emphasize rehabilitation, but available outcomes include probation, restitution, placement outside the home, and commitment to state supervision. The route a case takes depends on the person’s age, the alleged offense, and whether prosecutors seek a waiver, a designated proceeding, or adult-court jurisdiction authorized by statute.

sections.heading: Michigan juvenile jurisdiction and legal protections

facts.label: Court and age limit
facts.value: The family division of circuit court generally has jurisdiction over a juvenile under 18 alleged to have violated a criminal law or municipal ordinance. Michigan’s Juvenile Code is Chapter XIIA of the Probate Code of 1939. — MCL 712A.2(a)(1)

facts.label: Right to counsel
facts.value: In delinquency proceedings, the court must advise the juvenile of the right to an attorney at each stage. The statute requires appointment in specified circumstances, including when a responsible parent or guardian refuses to retain counsel and the juvenile does not waive counsel. — MCL 712A.17c

facts.label: Trial protections
facts.value: A delinquency charge must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt. Michigan also provides a jury-trial right in juvenile proceedings, subject to statutory exceptions; a juvenile jury consists of six people. — MCR 3.942(C); MCL 712A.17(2)

sections.heading: Routes through the Michigan juvenile system

rows: The family division determines whether the juvenile committed the alleged offense and, if responsibility is established, enters a disposition.

For a juvenile age 14 or older accused of conduct that would be a felony if committed by an adult, the prosecutor may request waiver to a court of general criminal jurisdiction. Waiver requires judicial findings.
A case may remain in the family division but proceed with the juvenile tried in the same manner as an adult. Designation requirements depend on the offense.
Circuit court has criminal jurisdiction over specified juvenile violations committed by a person age 14 or older but under 18. This route is distinct from traditional judicial waiver.
Jurisdiction can continue beyond the 18th birthday. Statutory provisions allow retention to age 19 and, in specified circumstances, age 21.

facts.label: Available dispositions
facts.value: The family division may warn and dismiss, impose probation or supervision, order placement with an authorized custodian or institution, or commit the juvenile to the responsible state agency, depending on statutory requirements. — MCL 712A.18

facts.label: Restitution
facts.value: Michigan law requires restitution for victims in covered juvenile cases. Restitution addresses losses caused by the offense and is separate from the court’s rehabilitative disposition. — MCL 712A.30; MCL 780.794

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Michigan
bullets: Family division of circuit court: Juvenile delinquency petitions and related proceedings are handled under the Juvenile Code; court authorization of a petition is governed by MCL 712A.11.

County prosecuting attorney: Prosecutors represent the people in juvenile proceedings when required by the Juvenile Code and pursue applicable waiver or designation requests. — MCL 712A.17; MCL 712A.4; MCL 712A.2d

sections.heading: Common questions in Michigan
bullets: Are 17-year-olds generally included in juvenile court? Yes. Ordinary delinquency jurisdiction covers alleged offenses committed before age 18, subject to adult-prosecution exceptions. — MCL 712A.2
Does turning 18 automatically end a juvenile case? No. Michigan permits continued jurisdiction under statutory age and case requirements. — MCL 712A.2a

Can a juvenile face adult criminal proceedings? Yes. Michigan has traditional waiver, designated proceedings, and statutory criminal jurisdiction for specified juvenile violations. — MCL 712A.4; MCL 712A.2d; MCL 600.606

sources.label: Michigan Legislature — Probate Code of 1939, including the Juvenile Code
Michigan Legislature — MCL 600.606, specified juvenile violations
Michigan Courts — Michigan Court Rules
Michigan Legislature — MCL 780.794, juvenile restitution

criminal-law/michigan/plea-bargaining.summary: Michigan permits criminal cases to be resolved through negotiated guilty or no-contest pleas, but the prosecutor’s agreement alone does not establish a valid plea or guarantee a particular sentence. Under Michigan Court Rule 6.302, the court must determine that a plea is understanding, voluntary, and accurate, and sentencing promises receive separate scrutiny. Withdrawal rights depend on when withdrawal is requested, whether the court accepted a sentencing agreement, and whether the defendant identifies a legally sufficient problem with the plea.

facts.label: Available pleas
facts.value: Michigan recognizes guilty, not guilty, and no-contest pleas. A no-contest plea requires the court’s consent; it is not simply an option the defendant can demand. — MCR 6.301(A)-(B)

facts.label: Agreement on the record
facts.value: When a plea results from an agreement with the prosecutor, the agreement must be stated on the record or reduced to writing and signed by the parties. The court must confirm its terms with the prosecutor and defendant’s lawyer. — MCR 6.302(C)(2)

facts.label: Required disclosures
facts.value: Before accepting the plea, the court must explain the offense, the maximum possible prison sentence, any mandatory minimum prison sentence, and specified rights surrendered by pleading. These include trial rights and the right to an appeal as of right. — MCR 6.302(B)

facts.label: Voluntariness
facts.value: The court must examine whether promises outside the disclosed agreement, threats, or other improper pressures produced the plea. A negotiated disposition does not eliminate the court’s duty to determine voluntariness. — MCR 6.302(C)

sections.heading: Different plea arrangements and their consequences

rows: The court questions the defendant to establish support for a finding of guilt. — MCR 6.302(D)(1)
The court obtains support for guilt without questioning the defendant about participation in the crime and states why a no-contest plea is appropriate. — MCR 6.302(D)(2)
When the agreement concerns a specific sentence or disposition, the court may accept it, reject it, or defer its decision pending the presentence report. — MCR 6.302(C)(3)
A prosecutor’s sentencing recommendation is distinct from a binding sentence agreement. The court must explain the applicable consequences if it does not follow the recommendation. — MCR 6.302(C)(3)
With court approval and prosecutor consent, a defendant may preserve appellate review of a specified pretrial ruling. A successful appeal permits withdrawal of the plea. — MCR 6.301(C)

facts.label: Before acceptance
facts.value: A defendant may withdraw a plea as of right before the court accepts it on the record. — MCR 6.310(A)

facts.label: After acceptance, before sentencing
facts.value: Withdrawal generally requires the court’s permission. The rule addresses the interests of justice, substantial prejudice to the prosecution, and separate circumstances involving sentencing agreements or judicial sentencing evaluations. — MCR 6.310(B)

facts.label: After sentencing
facts.value: Plea withdrawal is not automatic. Michigan provides a motion procedure for challenging an error in the plea proceeding, with different remedies depending on the defect. — MCR 6.310(C)

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Michigan
bullets: A plea-withdrawal motion belongs in the criminal case before the trial court that handled the plea. — MCR 6.310
Michigan district courts handle most misdemeanor prosecutions; circuit courts handle felony prosecutions and sentencing. — MCL 600.8311; MCL 600.601

An appeal from a circuit-court conviction based on a guilty or no-contest plea generally requires an application for leave to appeal in the Michigan Court of Appeals, rather than an appeal as of right. — MCR 7.203(A)-(B)

sections.heading: Common questions in Michigan
bullets: Does no contest prevent a conviction? No. The court can enter a conviction after accepting the plea. — MCR 6.301; MCR 6.302.
Must the judge follow every prosecutor recommendation? No. A recommendation is not necessarily a binding sentencing agreement. — MCR 6.302(C)(3).
Can a defendant withdraw merely because the sentence is disappointing? Not automatically; withdrawal depends on the governing rule and circumstances. — MCR 6.310.
Can a plea preserve a pretrial issue? Yes, through an approved conditional plea with prosecutor consent. — MCR 6.301(C).

sources.label: Michigan Courts — Court Rules, including Chapters 6 and 7
Michigan Legislature — MCL 600.8311
Michigan Legislature — MCL 600.601

criminal-law/mississippi/domestic-violen.summary: Mississippi prosecutes domestic violence primarily as simple domestic violence or aggravated domestic violence under Mississippi Code Section 97-3-7, depending on the conduct, injury, weapon use, and relationship between the people involved. Ordinary simple domestic violence carries up to six months in county jail, a fine of up to $500, or both; aggravated domestic violence generally carries two to twenty years in prison, while qualifying prior convictions can trigger separate felony provisions and higher penalties.

sections.heading: What makes an assault domestic violence

facts.label: Relationship requirement
facts.value: The domestic-violence provisions cover specified relationships, including spouses, former spouses, people who live or formerly lived together as spouses, current or former dating partners, and people who share a biological or legally adopted child. The statute also covers specified children within these relationships. — Miss. Code Ann. § 97-3-7(3)-(4)

facts.label: Simple domestic violence
facts.value: Covered conduct includes attempting to cause bodily injury; purposely, knowingly, or recklessly causing bodily injury; negligently causing bodily injury with a deadly weapon or other means likely to cause death or serious bodily harm; and using physical menace to put someone in fear of imminent serious bodily harm. — Miss. Code Ann. § 97-3-7(3)

facts.label: Aggravated domestic violence
facts.value: Covered conduct includes attempting to cause serious bodily injury, causing serious bodily injury under the circumstances specified by the statute, certain assaults involving deadly weapons or dangerous means, and strangulation or attempted strangulation. — Miss. Code Ann. § 97-3-7(4)

rows: Up to six months in county jail, a fine up to $500, or both.
The general imprisonment range is two to twenty years in the custody of the Mississippi Department of Corrections.
Qualifying prior convictions can trigger separate felony sentencing provisions; the number, timing, and type of convictions matter.
Strangulation and attempted strangulation are expressly included in aggravated domestic violence; a completed serious injury is not required for the attempt alternative.

sections.heading: Criminal cases and protective orders are different

facts.label: Separate proceedings
facts.value: Mississippi's Protection from Domestic Abuse Law provides a civil protective-order process separate from prosecution for assault or domestic violence. A protective-order petition is not itself a criminal charge. — Miss. Code Ann. §§ 93-21-1 through 93-21-33

facts.label: Order violations
facts.value: Violating a domestic-abuse protective order can create separate criminal liability. Whether an assault also occurred is a different question from whether the order was violated. — Miss. Code Ann. § 93-21-21

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Mississippi
bullets: Municipal police departments and county sheriffs investigate reported domestic violence. Criminal arrest authority is governed in part by Mississippi Code Section 99-3-7.
Justice courts and municipal courts handle misdemeanor cases within their respective jurisdiction. Circuit courts handle felony prosecutions. — Miss. Code Ann. §§ 9-11-9, 21-23-7, 9-7-81.
Civil domestic-abuse protective-order petitions fall under the jurisdiction provisions of Mississippi Code Section 93-21-7, which identify chancery, county, justice, and municipal courts.

sections.heading: Common questions in Mississippi
bullets: Must the people be married? No. Section 97-3-7 includes other specified relationships, including dating partners and people who share a child.
Must there be a visible injury? No. Simple domestic violence includes attempted injury and physical menace causing fear of imminent serious bodily harm.
Is every domestic-violence charge a felony? No. Ordinary simple domestic violence is a misdemeanor; aggravated domestic violence and qualifying repeat-offender offenses carry felony penalties.
Can the complaining witness dismiss the charge? Not unilaterally. A criminal prosecution is brought by the State, and the witness's wishes do not themselves terminate it.

sources.label: Mississippi Legislature — Mississippi Code
Mississippi Judiciary — Justice Courts
Mississippi Judiciary — Circuit Courts

criminal-law/minnesota/bail-and-bond.summary: Minnesota generally allows people charged with crimes to seek pretrial release, with the court deciding whether release requires money, other conditions, or both. Minnesota’s Constitution prohibits excessive bail, and Rule 6 of the Minnesota Rules of Criminal Procedure governs release decisions, including consideration of court appearance and public safety. Domestic-abuse cases have additional statutory requirements, and a domestic abuse no-contact order can remain legally distinct from the conditions attached to bail or bond.

sections.heading: Minnesota’s right to bail and release standards

facts.label: Constitutional protection
facts.value: Minnesota’s Constitution says excessive bail must not be required and that people are bailable by sufficient sureties, except in capital cases when the proof is evident or the presumption great. Minnesota does not currently authorize the death penalty. — Minnesota Constitution, article I, section 7

facts.label: Starting point for release
facts.value: The court must order release on personal recognizance or an unsecured appearance bond unless it determines that release will endanger public safety or will not reasonably assure the defendant’s appearance. If that standard is not met, the court may impose release conditions. — Minnesota Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 6.02

facts.label: Individual circumstances
facts.value: Relevant considerations include the charged offense, weight of the evidence, family ties, employment, financial resources, residence, criminal history, court-appearance record, and safety concerns. The release decision is not based solely on the name of the charge. — Minnesota Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 6.02

sections.heading: Types of pretrial release in Minnesota

rows: Release based on the defendant’s promise to appear, without posting monetary security. — Rule 6.02
A bond obligation without an advance deposit of money or other security. — Rule 6.02
Release subject to court-ordered restrictions, which may address travel, association, residence, supervision, or public safety. — Rule 6.02
Release requiring financial security in the form and amount authorized by the court. — Rule 6.02

When imposing release conditions, the court must also set a money-bail amount under which release may occur without the other conditions imposed under Rule 6.02. Separate statutory orders may still apply. — Rule 6.02; Minnesota Statutes, section 629.75

facts.label: Additional safety assessment
facts.value: For covered domestic-abuse arrests, the judge must assess threats to the alleged victim or another person, threats to public safety, and the likelihood of court appearance when deciding release. The statute authorizes protective release conditions. — Minnesota Statutes, section 629.72

facts.label: Separate no-contact order
facts.value: A domestic abuse no-contact order is independent of a proceeding’s bail or conditional-release orders. Posting bail therefore does not, by itself, terminate that order. — Minnesota Statutes, section 629.75

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Minnesota
bullets: Minnesota district courts handle bail and release conditions in criminal cases. Requests to review release conditions belong in the court handling the criminal proceeding. — Minnesota Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 6.02
The Minnesota Judicial Branch’s Bail Bond Program maintains approval information for bail bond agents and bonding companies and provides a complaint process concerning program participants.
The district court administrator maintains the criminal case file, including filed release orders; the custodial jail administers release under the applicable court order.

sections.heading: Common questions in Minnesota
bullets: Is cash always required? No. Rule 6.02 expressly permits personal recognizance and unsecured appearance bonds.
Can release conditions change? Yes. Rule 6.02 provides for judicial review of release conditions.
Does paying bail cancel a domestic abuse no-contact order? No. That order is independent of bail and conditional release under section 629.75.
Does bail decide guilt? No. Bail concerns release while criminal proceedings are pending, not a determination of guilt.

sources.label: Minnesota Constitution, article I
Minnesota Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 6
Minnesota Statutes, section 629.72
Minnesota Statutes, section 629.75

criminal-law/missouri/bail-and-bond.summary: Missouri generally guarantees bail before conviction, except in capital cases when the proof is evident or the presumption of guilt is great; the Missouri Constitution also prohibits excessive bail. Missouri Supreme Court Rule 33.01 directs courts to begin with personal recognizance or an unsecured appearance bond and, when additional restrictions are necessary, to use the least restrictive conditions that reasonably assure appearance and protect others, with attention to the defendant’s ability to pay.

facts.label: Constitutional right
facts.value: Before conviction, people accused of crimes are entitled to bail by sufficient sureties, except for capital offenses when the proof is evident or the presumption great. This constitutional guarantee expressly concerns release before conviction, not an automatic right to release after a guilty verdict. — Missouri Constitution, Article I, § 20

facts.label: Excessive bail
facts.value: Missouri’s Constitution separately prohibits requiring excessive bail. That prohibition does not establish a fixed statewide dollar maximum for every criminal charge. — Missouri Constitution, Article I, § 21

facts.label: Starting point for release
facts.value: The court must order personal recognizance or an unsecured appearance bond unless it determines that this release will not reasonably assure appearance or that the defendant poses a danger to a crime victim, the community, or another person. — Missouri Supreme Court Rule 33.01

facts.label: Individualized conditions
facts.value: When additional conditions are necessary, the court must impose the least restrictive condition or combination that reasonably addresses appearance and safety. Monetary conditions require consideration of ability to pay; conditions cannot be used to detain someone solely because of inability to pay. — Missouri Supreme Court Rule 33.01

rows: Release based on the defendant’s undertaking to appear, without an upfront monetary security requirement.
A bond obligation that does not require depositing the stated amount as a prerequisite to release.
Release may include supervision by a designated person or organization.
The court may restrict travel or place of abode as part of the release order.
Money or other security may be required when justified under the rule’s appearance, safety, and financial-condition standards.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Missouri
bullets: Criminal release decisions belong to the court handling the prosecution. In a Missouri circuit-court case, bond-related filings are part of that criminal case; the circuit clerk maintains the case record, while the judge decides release conditions.

Complaints about licensed bail bond agents or general bail bond agents fall within the regulatory responsibilities of the Missouri Department of Commerce and Insurance. Missouri’s bail-agent licensing provisions are in Chapter 374, RSMo.
A licensing complaint against an agent does not itself change a criminal court’s bond order. Court-ordered release conditions and professional licensing enforcement are separate matters.

sections.heading: Common questions in Missouri
bullets: Does every charge have a fixed bond price? Rule 33.01 requires an individualized release decision, rather than making the charge alone the complete basis for the conditions.
Can a court consider whether the defendant can afford bond? Yes. Rule 33.01 expressly addresses financial resources and ability to pay when monetary release conditions are considered.
Does release on recognizance mean the case is dismissed? No. It is a form of pretrial release, and the defendant remains obligated to appear and comply with the release order.
Is cash payment always required for release? No. Rule 33.01 provides for recognizance, unsecured bonds, and nonmonetary conditions, as well as monetary conditions when warranted.

sources.label: Missouri Secretary of State — Missouri Constitution
Missouri Courts — Supreme Court Rules
Missouri Revisor of Statutes — Chapter 374

criminal-law/mississippi/expungement.summary: Mississippi permits expungement of certain misdemeanor convictions, eligible felony convictions, and arrests that did not result in a conviction under Mississippi Code Section 99-19-71. Eligibility depends on the offense and case outcome; qualifying felony convictions generally carry a five-year waiting period after successful completion of all terms and conditions of the sentence. Expungement requires a court order, and Mississippi law preserves limited access to expunged information rather than guaranteeing that every trace of a case disappears.

facts.label: First-offense misdemeanors
facts.value: A person convicted of a misdemeanor, other than a traffic violation, who is a first offender may petition the justice, county, circuit, or municipal court in which the conviction occurred to expunge the conviction from public records. — Miss. Code Ann. § 99-19-71(1)

facts.label: Eligible felony convictions
facts.value: Mississippi allows expungement of qualifying felony convictions, but the statute excludes specified offenses. The waiting period is five years after successful completion of all terms and conditions of the sentence, not simply five years after conviction or release from incarceration. — Miss. Code Ann. § 99-19-71(2)

facts.label: Excluded felonies
facts.value: Excluded categories include crimes of violence as defined in Section 97-3-2 and offenses requiring sex-offender registration. These are not the only exclusions; eligibility depends on the statutory offense, not merely whether a sentence involved prison. — Miss. Code Ann. §§ 99-19-71(2), 97-3-2

facts.label: Arrests without a conviction
facts.value: A person arrested and released whose case was dismissed, whose charges were dropped, or whose case had no disposition may petition for expungement of the arrest record. This is a separate statutory basis from expungement of a conviction. — Miss. Code Ann. § 99-19-71

sections.heading: How the type of record affects eligibility

rows: Potentially eligible through the court of conviction; the general provision excludes traffic violations.
Five years must pass after successful completion of all sentence terms and conditions.
Excluded from the general felony-expungement provision.
The arrest record may be the subject of an expungement petition.
DUI has a separate expungement provision with its own restrictions; the ordinary misdemeanor rule does not establish eligibility.

facts.label: Public record and legal status
facts.value: The statute provides for removal of an eligible conviction from public records and restoration of the person to the legal status occupied before the arrest or indictment. That relief remains subject to statutory exceptions. — Miss. Code Ann. § 99-19-71

facts.label: Nonpublic records remain
facts.value: The Mississippi Criminal Information Center retains a nonpublic record of an expunged conviction. The statute allows specified criminal-justice uses, including determining eligibility for first-offender treatment and use in determining habitual-offender status. Expungement therefore does not mean complete destruction of all government information. — Miss. Code Ann. § 99-19-71

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Mississippi
bullets: For a misdemeanor conviction, the petition belongs in the justice, county, circuit, or municipal court where the conviction occurred. — Miss. Code Ann. § 99-19-71(1)
For an eligible felony conviction, the petition belongs in the court where the conviction occurred. — Miss. Code Ann. § 99-19-71(2)

Expungement is judicial relief: a complaint to a records agency does not replace the required court order. Questions about eligibility or an order's scope are matters to talk to a lawyer about. — Miss. Code Ann. § 99-19-71

sections.heading: Common questions in Mississippi
bullets: Does dismissal automatically erase an arrest? No. Section 99-19-71 authorizes a petition for expungement after qualifying nonconviction outcomes.
Does the felony waiting period start at sentencing? Not ordinarily. The five-year period runs after successful completion of all sentence terms and conditions.
Can every felony be expunged? No. Section 99-19-71 excludes specified offenses, including statutorily defined crimes of violence.
Does expungement eliminate every government record? No. Mississippi preserves a nonpublic record for specified criminal-justice purposes.

sources.label: Mississippi Legislature — Mississippi Code, including Sections 99-19-71, 97-3-2, and 63-11-30
State of Mississippi Judiciary — Court information

criminal-law/missouri/domestic-violence-.summary: Missouri prosecutes domestic assault in four degrees, with charges depending on the alleged conduct, mental state, injuries, and relationship between the people involved. First-, second-, and third-degree domestic assault are felonies; fourth-degree domestic assault is generally a misdemeanor, although qualifying prior offenses can make it a felony. These criminal charges are separate from civil orders of protection, and violating an order can create an additional criminal offense.

sections.heading: What makes an assault a domestic assault in Missouri

facts.label: Covered relationships
facts.value: The domestic-assault statutes require a domestic victim. This includes qualifying family or household members, such as spouses, former spouses, relatives by blood or marriage, people who live or previously lived together, people in a continuing romantic or intimate relationship, and people who have a child together. The definition also includes children who are members of the household or family. — Mo. Rev. Stat. §§ 565.002, 455.010

facts.label: Injury is not always required
facts.value: Some domestic-assault offenses cover attempts or threats rather than completed injuries. Fourth-degree domestic assault includes purposely placing a domestic victim in apprehension of immediate physical injury and knowingly making physical contact that the victim would regard as offensive. — Mo. Rev. Stat. § 565.076

facts.label: Serious physical injury
facts.value: This means physical injury creating a substantial risk of death or causing serious disfigurement or protracted loss or impairment of the function of any part of the body. — Mo. Rev. Stat. § 565.002

rows: Attempting to kill, or knowingly causing or attempting to cause serious physical injury to a domestic victim.
Class B felony: 5–15 years. Class A felony if serious physical injury is inflicted: 10–30 years or life. §§ 565.072, 558.011.
Includes knowingly causing physical injury, recklessly causing serious physical injury, or recklessly causing physical injury using a deadly weapon.
Class D felony: up to 7 years. §§ 565.073, 558.011.
Attempting to cause physical injury, or knowingly causing physical pain or illness to a domestic victim.
Class E felony: up to 4 years. §§ 565.074, 558.011.
Includes certain reckless injuries, threats of immediate injury, offensive contact, and conduct creating a substantial risk of death or serious physical injury.
Generally a class A misdemeanor: up to 1 year. Qualifying prior offenses can elevate it to a class E felony. §§ 565.076, 558.011.

sections.heading: Protective orders and separate criminal liability

facts.label: Civil proceedings
facts.value: Missouri's Adult Abuse Act authorizes orders of protection through a civil court proceeding. A protection-order petition and a criminal domestic-assault prosecution are distinct proceedings. — Mo. Rev. Stat. §§ 455.010–455.085

facts.label: Violating an order
facts.value: Violating specified provisions of an order of protection can constitute a separate criminal offense when the statutory requirements, including notice, are met. Not every provision of a civil order carries the same criminal enforcement consequences. — Mo. Rev. Stat. § 455.085

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Missouri
bullets: Local police departments and county sheriffs receive reports of alleged domestic assaults; criminal prosecution is handled by the prosecutor with jurisdiction.
Missouri circuit courts hear state domestic-assault criminal cases. — Mo. Rev. Stat. § 478.070

Civil adult protection-order petitions may be filed in circuit court in the county where the petitioner resides, where the alleged abuse occurred, or where the respondent may be served. — Mo. Rev. Stat. § 455.015

sections.heading: Common questions in Missouri
bullets: Is every domestic-assault charge a felony? No. Fourth-degree domestic assault is generally a class A misdemeanor. — § 565.076
Must the people involved be married? No. Several other family, household, parenting, and intimate relationships qualify. — §§ 565.002, 455.010
Does no visible injury mean no charge? No. Attempts, certain threats, and offensive contact can satisfy particular domestic-assault provisions. — §§ 565.072–565.076
Is a protection order a criminal conviction? No. A civil protection order is distinct from a conviction, although violating specified provisions can be a crime. — § 455.085

sources.label: Missouri Revisor of Statutes — Chapter 565, Offenses Against the Person
Missouri Revisor of Statutes — Chapter 558, Imprisonment
Missouri Revisor of Statutes — Chapter 455, Abuse — Adults and Children
Missouri Revisor of Statutes — Circuit court jurisdiction, Section 478.070

criminal-law/missouri/arrest-process.summary: In Missouri, an arrest occurs when an officer actually restrains a person or the person submits to the officer’s custody; officers may arrest under a warrant or under statutory authority for a warrantless arrest. Arrest is not a conviction, and later proceedings address the charge, release conditions, counsel, and any trial. Missouri statutes, Supreme Court rules, and constitutional protections govern different stages, with state criminal charges generally handled in circuit court.

facts.label: What counts as an arrest
facts.value: An arrest is made by actual restraint of the defendant or by the defendant’s submission to the officer’s custody. The statute also states that the defendant must not be subjected to more restraint than necessary for arrest and detention. — Mo. Rev. Stat. § 544.180

facts.label: Arrest without a warrant
facts.value: Missouri law authorizes specified law enforcement officers to make warrantless arrests when they have reasonable grounds to believe a person violated state law, including a felony. An arrest warrant is therefore not required for every lawful arrest. — Mo. Rev. Stat. § 544.216

facts.label: Search and seizure protections
facts.value: The Missouri Constitution protects people, homes, papers, and effects against unreasonable searches and seizures. Warrants require probable cause supported by a written oath or affirmation and must describe the place to be searched or the person or thing to be seized as nearly as possible. — Missouri Constitution, art. I, § 15

facts.label: Rights in a criminal prosecution
facts.value: An accused person has constitutional rights to appear and defend personally and through counsel, to know the nature and cause of the accusation, and to a speedy public trial by an impartial jury, subject to applicable constitutional provisions. — Missouri Constitution, art. I, § 18(a)

rows: A complaint is a written statement of the essential facts constituting the charged offense. Missouri Supreme Court Rule 22.02 governs its requirements.
Rule 33.01 governs release in bailable cases, including recognizance, unsecured bonds, and conditions intended to address appearance and safety.
Under Rule 33.01, a court must not impose a financial release condition that results in detention solely because the defendant cannot pay.
Rule 31.02 governs the right to counsel, including advising an unrepresented defendant and appointment of counsel when its requirements are met.
Under Rule 24.01, arraignment occurs in open court and includes stating the substance of the charge and calling on the defendant to plead.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Missouri
bullets: State criminal proceedings are handled in Missouri circuit courts. The circuit clerk maintains the court’s criminal case filings and records; the judge decides release conditions and contested legal issues. — Missouri Constitution, art. V, § 14; Missouri Supreme Court Rule 33.01

Municipal ordinance prosecutions are handled in municipal divisions of circuit courts. They are distinct from state criminal prosecutions, even when a municipal police officer made the arrest. — Missouri Constitution, art. V, § 27; Missouri Supreme Court Rule 37

The Missouri State Public Defender System provides representation to eligible indigent defendants in cases covered by its governing statute. Its coverage does not extend automatically to every matter involving an arrest. — Mo. Rev. Stat. § 600.042

sections.heading: Common questions in Missouri
bullets: Does an officer always need an arrest warrant? No. Section 544.216 authorizes warrantless arrests in specified circumstances.
Is cash bail automatic after arrest? No. Rule 33.01 provides for recognizance, unsecured bonds, and other release conditions in bailable cases.
Does arrest mean the person is guilty? No. Missouri places the burden of proving guilt beyond a reasonable doubt on the state. — Mo. Rev. Stat. § 556.046

Can an arrested person have a lawyer? The Missouri Constitution protects the right to counsel in criminal prosecutions, and Rule 31.02 addresses representation and appointment. Questions about a particular arrest are matters to talk to a lawyer about.

Missouri Revisor of Statutes — Section 544.216
Missouri Courts — Supreme Court Rules
Missouri Revisor — Revised Statutes and Constitution

criminal-law/montana/bail-and-bond.summary: Montana’s Constitution makes criminal defendants eligible for bail through sufficient sureties, except in capital cases when the proof is evident or the presumption great, and separately prohibits excessive bail. Montana’s criminal bail procedures appear in Title 46, chapter 9 of the Montana Code Annotated; release can involve personal recognizance, financial security, and court-imposed conditions, so eligibility for bail does not itself guarantee release without restrictions or payment.

facts.label: Constitutional right
facts.value: All persons are bailable by sufficient sureties except for capital offenses when the proof is evident or the presumption great. The exception concerns capital offenses, not every felony or every allegation of violence. — Montana Constitution, Article II, § 21

facts.label: Excessive bail
facts.value: Montana expressly prohibits excessive bail. That protection is separate from the constitutional rule identifying offenses for which bail may be denied. The Constitution does not establish a statewide dollar amount for individual charges. — Montana Constitution, Article II, §§ 21–22

facts.label: Criminal bail statutes
facts.value: Title 46, chapter 9 governs bail, including release decisions, conditions, security, and proceedings involving bail after a defendant fails to appear. A release order remains distinct from a determination of guilt or innocence. — Montana Code Annotated, Title 46, chapter 9

facts.label: Release conditions
facts.value: Release may carry conditions in addition to any financial requirement. Posting the required security does not cancel the defendant’s obligation to appear or comply with the court’s release order. — Montana Code Annotated, Title 46, chapter 9

rows: Release based on the defendant’s promise to appear rather than a required cash deposit; court-ordered conditions may still apply.
Money deposited as security for the defendant’s obligations. The court controls its disposition under applicable law.
A surety undertakes a financial obligation securing the defendant’s appearance. A commercial bond arrangement is separate from the court’s release decision.
Restrictions or obligations imposed by the court remain enforceable while the defendant is released.
Failure to appear can trigger proceedings against the money or bond securing release; it does not resolve the underlying criminal charge.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Montana
bullets: Criminal court: Bail and release requests are addressed in the criminal proceeding by the court with authority over release. Montana district courts handle felony prosecutions; justice, city, and municipal courts handle criminal matters within their jurisdiction.
Court clerk: The clerk maintains the criminal case’s filings and court orders. A clerk’s administrative role does not include independently changing the judge’s bail amount or release conditions.

Montana Commissioner of Securities and Insurance: The State Auditor’s office regulates insurance and insurance producers, including insurance-related licensing and complaints involving commercial surety business. It does not replace the criminal court or modify a release order.

sections.heading: Common questions in Montana
bullets: Is everyone constitutionally entitled to bail? The Montana Constitution has an exception for capital offenses when the proof is evident or the presumption great. It also separately prohibits excessive bail.
Does release mean the charge has been dismissed? No. Bail concerns release while proceedings continue, not whether the prosecution has proved the charge.
Does paying bail eliminate other restrictions? No. Financial security and nonfinancial release conditions are separate obligations under the court’s order.

Is a bondsman’s fee the same as cash deposited with the court? No. A commercial bond premium pays for the surety arrangement; cash bail is security held under court authority. Their treatment is not interchangeable.

sources.label: Montana Constitution, Article II, § 21 — Bail

criminal-law/montana/domestic-violence-c.summary: Montana’s principal domestic violence charge is partner or family member assault, commonly called PFMA, under Montana Code Annotated § 45-5-206. It covers specified conduct causing bodily injury or reasonable apprehension of bodily injury when the accused and alleged victim have a qualifying relationship; visible injury is not required for every form of the offense. Prior qualifying convictions and the circumstances of the alleged conduct can affect the charge and punishment.

facts.label: Bodily injury
facts.value: PFMA includes purposely or knowingly causing bodily injury to a partner or family member. The relationship is an element of this particular offense, not merely background information about an ordinary assault. — Montana Code Annotated § 45-5-206(1)(a)

facts.label: Injury involving a weapon
facts.value: The statute separately covers negligently causing bodily injury to a partner or family member with a weapon. This provision uses a different mental-state requirement from the purposeful-or-knowing injury provision. — Montana Code Annotated § 45-5-206(1)(b)

facts.label: Apprehension without physical injury
facts.value: Purposely or knowingly causing reasonable apprehension of bodily injury to a partner or family member also constitutes PFMA. This alternative does not require proof that bodily injury actually occurred. — Montana Code Annotated § 45-5-206(1)(c)

facts.label: Qualifying relationships
facts.value: The statute defines both partners and family members. Covered relationships include spouses, former spouses, people who have a child together, and people who have been or are currently in a dating or ongoing intimate relationship. Family coverage includes specified parental, child, sibling, and other family relationships. — Montana Code Annotated § 45-5-206(2)

rows: The PFMA statute provides a first-conviction sentencing tier with imprisonment and a fine.
Separate sentencing tiers apply to a second conviction and to a third or subsequent conviction.
The statute addresses when convictions under similar laws in other jurisdictions count as prior convictions.
PFMA sentencing provisions include counseling assessment and treatment requirements, not merely incarceration and fines.

Montana separately criminalizes purposely or knowingly impeding a partner’s or family member’s normal breathing or blood circulation by pressure on the throat or neck or by blocking the nose and mouth.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Montana
bullets: Local police departments and county sheriffs receive reports of suspected domestic violence and investigate alleged criminal conduct. A criminal prosecution is brought by the government rather than filed as a private civil lawsuit.
County attorneys and city attorneys prosecute criminal cases within their respective authority. The responsible prosecuting office depends on the charge and the court handling the case.

Montana district courts handle felony criminal cases. Justice, city, and municipal courts handle misdemeanor matters within their statutory jurisdiction; the Montana Judicial Branch publishes information about these courts.

Civil protection-order proceedings are separate from criminal prosecution. A protection-order petition is not itself a PFMA criminal charge, and the two types of proceedings can exist alongside one another.

sections.heading: Common questions in Montana
bullets: Does PFMA require a visible injury? No. The reasonable-apprehension alternative addresses fear of bodily injury without requiring an actual bodily injury. — Montana Code Annotated § 45-5-206(1)(c)

Must the people involved currently live together? No. The statutory definition includes former spouses and people with a child in common; current cohabitation is not a universal requirement. — Montana Code Annotated § 45-5-206(2)
Can prior convictions change the punishment? Yes. Montana provides escalating PFMA sentencing tiers and rules addressing qualifying prior convictions. — Montana Code Annotated § 45-5-206
Is strangulation addressed separately? Yes. Strangulation of a partner or family member is a separate statutory offense, rather than simply another name for PFMA. — Montana Code Annotated § 45-5-215

sources.label: Montana Legislature — Partner or family member assault, § 45-5-206
Montana Legislature — Strangulation of partner or family member, § 45-5-215

criminal-law/nebraska/dui-consequences.summary: Nebraska DUI can result in jail or prison, fines, license revocation, and court-ordered treatment, with consequences depending on prior convictions, alcohol concentration, and whether someone was injured or killed. A first DUI is generally a Class W misdemeanor, while repeat offenses can become felonies; Nebraska also has an administrative license-revocation process separate from the criminal prosecution, so a single arrest can produce both court proceedings and Department of Motor Vehicles action.

facts.label: Impairment and alcohol concentration
facts.value: Nebraska prohibits operating or being in actual physical control of a motor vehicle while under the influence of alcohol or drugs. It also prohibits driving with an alcohol concentration of at least 0.08 grams per 100 milliliters of blood or per 210 liters of breath. Proof of the prohibited concentration is not required for an impairment-based prosecution. — Neb. Rev. Stat. § 60-6,196

facts.label: Higher alcohol concentration
facts.value: An alcohol concentration of 0.15 or more places a conviction in an enhanced penalty category. Nebraska's sentencing statute distinguishes these cases from lower-concentration DUI cases. — Neb. Rev. Stat. § 60-6,197.03

facts.label: Prior convictions
facts.value: Nebraska generally uses a 15-year lookback for qualifying prior DUI and refusal convictions, measured between the prior violation and the current violation. Qualifying convictions from other jurisdictions can count. — Neb. Rev. Stat. § 60-6,197.02

rows: Class W misdemeanor. The ordinary nonprobation sentence includes 7–60 days in jail, a $500 fine, and six months of license revocation.
Class W misdemeanor with enhanced requirements, including a one-year license-revocation period.
A felony rather than a misdemeanor; the applicable sentencing category depends on alcohol concentration and refusal circumstances.
Probation has its own mandatory conditions. It does not automatically eliminate confinement, community service, license restrictions, or ignition-interlock requirements.
Causing serious bodily injury while driving under the influence can support a separate felony charge.

facts.label: Separate DMV proceeding
facts.value: The Nebraska Department of Motor Vehicles administers license revocation following qualifying chemical-test failures or refusals. This administrative process is distinct from the criminal court's determination of guilt and sentencing. — Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 60-498.01 and 60-498.02

facts.label: Hearing deadline
facts.value: A petition requesting an administrative license-revocation hearing must be delivered to or postmarked to the DMV within 10 days after service of the notice of revocation. This deadline concerns the administrative hearing, not the criminal case. — Neb. Rev. Stat. § 60-498.01

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Nebraska
bullets: Nebraska county courts handle misdemeanor DUI prosecutions. Felony prosecutions proceed in district court after the applicable preliminary proceedings. — Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 24-302 and 24-517

The Nebraska Department of Motor Vehicles receives petitions for administrative license-revocation hearings; those petitions are separate from filings in the criminal prosecution. — Neb. Rev. Stat. § 60-498.01

sections.heading: Common questions in Nebraska
bullets: Can DUI involve drugs rather than alcohol? Yes. Nebraska's DUI prohibition covers impairment by any drug. — Neb. Rev. Stat. § 60-6,196
Does refusing a chemical test avoid criminal consequences? No. Nebraska separately criminalizes refusal of a required chemical test under its implied-consent law. — Neb. Rev. Stat. § 60-6,197
Can an out-of-state DUI increase the penalty? Yes, when it satisfies Nebraska's statutory definition of a prior conviction. — Neb. Rev. Stat. § 60-6,197.02
Does a first DUI always mean the same sentence? No. Alcohol concentration and whether probation is imposed affect the statutory requirements. — Neb. Rev. Stat. § 60-6,197.03

Nebraska Legislature — DUI penalties, § 60-6,197.03
Nebraska Legislature — Prior convictions, § 60-6,197.02
Nebraska Legislature — Administrative revocation procedure, § 60-498.01

criminal-law/nebraska/expungement.summary: Nebraska does not offer a general procedure that erases every criminal conviction; its principal forms of relief are conviction set-asides, restrictions on public access to certain criminal records, juvenile record sealing, and pardons. A set-aside under Nebraska Revised Statute § 29-2264 does not itself seal or destroy the conviction record. The available remedy depends on the outcome of the case, the sentence, and whether the record concerns an adult criminal case or a juvenile proceeding.

facts.label: Statutory procedure
facts.value: Nebraska’s conviction set-aside procedure is established by Nebraska Revised Statute § 29-2264. Eligible defendants include people sentenced to probation who successfully complete it and people sentenced to a fine only who satisfy the statutory conditions. Relief is not automatic. — Neb. Rev. Stat. § 29-2264

facts.label: Court consideration
facts.value: The sentencing court considers the defendant’s behavior after sentencing, the likelihood of further criminal activity, and other relevant information. The statute calls for a determination that setting aside the conviction is in the defendant’s best interest and consistent with public welfare. — Neb. Rev. Stat. § 29-2264

facts.label: Legal effect and limits
facts.value: A set-aside nullifies the conviction and removes resulting civil disabilities and disqualifications, subject to statutory exceptions. It does not erase the historical record, and the conviction can still have consequences in later criminal proceedings. — Neb. Rev. Stat. § 29-2264

rows: Changes the conviction’s legal effect but does not itself seal the record.
Arrest that does not lead to prosecution
Statutory conditions depend on the disposition; arrest alone is not a conviction.
Criminal charge dismissed or resulting in acquittal
The statute addresses court records and criminal history records.
A pardon and a judicial sealing order are separate forms of relief.
Separate procedures apply; sealing does not mean physical destruction.

facts.label: Restricted access is not destruction
facts.value: Nebraska law limits public dissemination of qualifying criminal history information while permitting specified access and uses. A sealed record is therefore not necessarily inaccessible to every government agency or for every legal purpose. — Neb. Rev. Stat. § 29-3523

facts.label: Juvenile proceedings
facts.value: Nebraska provides sealing procedures for qualifying juvenile records, including court-initiated sealing in specified circumstances. Eligibility and procedure depend on the case’s disposition and the statutory requirements. — Neb. Rev. Stat. § 43-2,108.01

facts.label: Pardon authority
facts.value: The Nebraska Board of Pardons consists of the Governor, Attorney General, and Secretary of State. Its constitutional clemency authority is separate from a court’s authority to set aside a conviction. — Nebraska Constitution, Article IV, § 13

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Nebraska
bullets: The sentencing court handles conviction set-aside petitions under § 29-2264.
The court with jurisdiction over the criminal case handles applicable judicial sealing proceedings under § 29-3523.
The court responsible for the juvenile matter handles sealing under § 43-2,108.01.
The Nebraska Board of Pardons handles pardon applications, not judicial set-aside petitions.

sections.heading: Common questions in Nebraska
bullets: Does a set-aside remove the case from public court records? No. A set-aside under § 29-2264 is not itself a sealing order.
Is a dismissed charge treated like a conviction? No. Section 29-3523 separately addresses records of charges ending in dismissal or acquittal.
Does a pardon automatically destroy the record? No. Nebraska provides a separate judicial sealing procedure for pardoned convictions under § 29-3523.
Are juvenile records covered by the adult set-aside law? Juvenile sealing has its own statutory framework under § 43-2,108.01.

Nebraska Legislature — § 43-2,108.01

criminal-law/nebraska/drug-charges.summary: Nebraska drug charges depend on the substance, amount, and whether the allegation is possession or manufacturing, delivery, or possession with intent to deliver under Nebraska Revised Statute § 28-416. Unauthorized possession of a controlled substance other than marijuana generally is a Class IV felony, while marijuana possession has separate quantity-based rules. Nebraska also has voter-approved medical cannabis protections, so the ordinary marijuana possession penalties do not describe every legally protected medical use.

sections.heading: What determines a Nebraska drug charge

facts.label: Possession versus distribution
facts.value: Nebraska separately prohibits knowingly or intentionally possessing a controlled substance and manufacturing, distributing, delivering, dispensing, or possessing a controlled substance with intent to do those acts. A lawful prescription or other statutory authorization can change whether possession is prohibited. — Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-416(1), (3)

facts.label: Drug classification and quantity
facts.value: The applicable penalty can depend on the controlled substance's schedule and, for specified trafficking offenses, its weight. Cocaine, heroin, and methamphetamine offenses have additional quantity-based provisions; the ordinary possession penalty is not the sentencing rule for every drug case. — Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-416

facts.label: Medical cannabis exception
facts.value: Nebraska voters approved the Nebraska Medical Cannabis Patient Protection Act in 2024. It protects qualifying medical cannabis conduct involving an allowable amount of up to five ounces, subject to the Act's practitioner-recommendation and other requirements; it does not establish unrestricted adult-use legalization. — Nebraska Initiative Measure 437 (2024)

rows: Controlled substance other than marijuana, under the general possession provision
Up to two years' imprisonment, a $10,000 fine, or both; post-release supervision rules also apply. §§ 28-416(3), 28-105
Marijuana: one ounce or less, first offense
$300 fine and a citation; a drug education course may also be assigned. § 28-416(13)
Marijuana: more than one ounce but not more than one pound
Up to three months' imprisonment, a $500 fine, or both. §§ 28-416(12), 28-106
Up to two years' imprisonment, a $10,000 fine, or both; post-release supervision rules also apply. §§ 28-416(11), 28-105

sections.heading: Sentencing details that affect the result

facts.label: Class IV felony supervision
facts.value: Section 28-105 lists a maximum of twelve months' post-release supervision for a Class IV felony and a minimum of nine months when imprisonment is imposed, subject to statutory exceptions. A prison maximum alone therefore does not describe the entire potential sentence. — Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-105

facts.label: Repeat small-quantity marijuana cases
facts.value: The first-offense infraction rule is not the rule for every case involving one ounce or less. Section 28-416 establishes separate misdemeanor treatment for second and third or subsequent offenses. — Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-416(13)

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Nebraska
bullets: County courts generally handle misdemeanor and infraction drug prosecutions and preliminary proceedings in felony cases. District courts handle felony trials.
The county attorney ordinarily prosecutes state drug charges. Reports of suspected criminal activity are handled by local police, county sheriffs, or the Nebraska State Patrol.
A challenge to a criminal charge, search, or sentence belongs in the criminal court process rather than a consumer complaint proceeding.

sections.heading: Common questions in Nebraska
bullets: Is simple possession always a misdemeanor? No. Unauthorized possession of a controlled substance other than marijuana generally is a Class IV felony under § 28-416(3).
Is possessing exactly one ounce treated like possessing more than one ounce? No. The small-quantity provision includes one ounce; the next quantity category requires more than one ounce.
Does medical cannabis legalization eliminate marijuana charges? No. Medical protections depend on statutory eligibility and requirements, and unauthorized possession remains subject to criminal law.
Does every Class IV felony result in the maximum prison sentence? No. The statutory maximum is not an automatic sentence; sentencing depends on applicable law and the case. Talk to a lawyer.
