criminal-law/nevada/domestic-violence-ch.summary: Nevada’s principal domestic battery statute is NRS 200.485, which applies when a battery involves a relationship covered by NRS 33.018. A first or second qualifying offense within seven years ordinarily carries misdemeanor penalties, including mandatory jail time, community service, fines, and counseling; a third qualifying offense is a felony. Strangulation, substantial bodily harm, deadly weapons, and certain prior felony convictions can change the charge or punishment, so the ordinary misdemeanor ranges do not cover every case.

sections.heading: What Nevada domestic violence charges cover

facts.label: Domestic battery
facts.value: Battery means a willful and unlawful use of force or violence against another person. NRS 200.485 supplies special penalties when the battery constitutes domestic violence under NRS 33.018. — NRS 200.481(1)(a); NRS 200.485

facts.label: Covered relationships
facts.value: Covered relationships include spouses, former spouses, people related by blood or marriage, people in current or former dating relationships, and people who have a child together. The statute also covers specified children and guardianship relationships. Merely sharing a residence does not, by itself, establish a covered relationship. — NRS 33.018(1)

facts.label: Conduct beyond battery
facts.value: Nevada’s domestic violence definition also includes assault, coercion, sexual assault, false imprisonment, and certain other conduct. The criminal charge and sentence depend on the particular offense; not every domestic violence allegation is prosecuted as battery. — NRS 33.018

facts.label: Arrest and self-defense
facts.value: Nevada has a mandatory-arrest framework for qualifying domestic battery cases, subject to statutory conditions and exceptions. When an officer believes both people committed battery, the officer must assess the primary physical aggressor, including whether someone acted in self-defense. — NRS 171.137

rows: First offense within seven years, ordinary case
Misdemeanor: 2 days to 6 months in jail, 48 to 120 hours of community service, and a $200 to $1,000 fine. — NRS 200.485(1)(a)
Second offense within seven years, ordinary case
Misdemeanor: 10 days to 6 months in jail, 100 to 200 hours of community service, and a $500 to $1,000 fine. — NRS 200.485(1)(b)
Category B felony: 1 to 6 years in state prison and a $1,000 to $5,000 fine. — NRS 200.485(1)(c)
Category B felony: 1 to 6 years in state prison and a fine of up to $5,000, unless a greater penalty applies under the statute. — NRS 200.485

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Nevada
bullets: Local police departments and county sheriffs investigate reported domestic violence crimes. Arrest authority and domestic battery arrest duties are governed by NRS 171.137.
County district attorneys and, for applicable municipal cases, city attorneys prosecute criminal charges. A reporting person does not personally control the prosecution.

Justice courts and municipal courts handle misdemeanor matters within their jurisdiction. District courts handle felony trials; justice courts generally conduct felony preliminary proceedings. — NRS 4.370; NRS 5.050; NRS 171.196.

Domestic violence protection orders are separate civil proceedings under NRS Chapter 33. Nevada’s judiciary publishes protection-order information and court forms through its official self-help website.

sections.heading: Common questions in Nevada
bullets: Can the reporting person drop the charges? Not unilaterally. Charging decisions belong to the prosecutor, and NRS 200.485 restricts dismissal or reduction of domestic battery charges unless the prosecutor knows, or it is obvious, that probable cause is lacking or the charge cannot be proved at trial.
Does a first conviction require counseling? Yes. NRS 200.485 requires counseling for first and second offenses in addition to the listed criminal penalties.
Can an out-of-state conviction count? Yes. A conviction under another jurisdiction’s law can qualify if that law prohibits the same or similar conduct. — NRS 200.485.

Is a protection order the same as a criminal conviction? No. Protection orders are civil remedies under NRS Chapter 33, although violating an order can result in a separate criminal charge. — NRS 33.100.

Nevada Legislature — NRS Chapter 33, Injunctions and Protection Orders
Nevada Legislature — NRS Chapter 171, Criminal Proceedings
Supreme Court of Nevada — Self-Help Center

criminal-law/nevada/felony-vs-misdemeano.summary: Nevada divides crimes into felonies, gross misdemeanors, and misdemeanors, based on the punishment authorized by law rather than the sentence a person actually receives. Felonies can carry state-prison sentences and are divided into categories A through E; ordinary misdemeanors generally carry no more than six months in county jail, while gross misdemeanors generally carry up to 364 days. The classification also affects which court handles the trial and whether a felony preliminary examination is available.

facts.label: Felony definition
facts.value: A felony is a crime punishable by death or imprisonment in state prison. A suspended prison sentence or a grant of probation does not, by itself, turn a felony conviction into a misdemeanor — NRS 193.120.

facts.label: Misdemeanor definition
facts.value: A misdemeanor is a crime punishable by a fine of no more than $1,000, imprisonment in county jail for no more than six months, or both — NRS 193.120.

facts.label: Gross misdemeanor definition
facts.value: Nevada treats a crime that is neither a felony nor a misdemeanor as a gross misdemeanor. This is a separate classification, not one of the five felony categories — NRS 193.120.

facts.label: Offense-specific penalties
facts.value: The general punishment provisions contain exceptions for offenses governed by different statutory penalties. The statute defining a particular offense therefore matters as well as its classification — NRS 193.130–193.150.

rows: Death or life imprisonment, with or without parole eligibility, as the offense statute specifies.
Penalties are specified in the offense statute — NRS 193.130(2)(a).
A minimum term of at least 1 year and a maximum term of no more than 20 years; the offense statute supplies the particular range.
Any fine depends on the applicable offense statute — NRS 193.130(2)(b).
Up to $10,000, unless a greater fine is authorized or required — NRS 193.130(2)(c).
Up to $5,000, unless a greater fine is authorized or required — NRS 193.130(2)(d).
1–4 years in state prison; suspension and probation generally apply, subject to statutory exceptions.
Up to $5,000, unless a greater fine is authorized or required — NRS 193.130(2)(e).
Up to 364 days in county jail.
Up to $2,000, or both jail and a fine, unless another penalty applies — NRS 193.140.
Up to 6 months in county jail.
Up to $1,000, or both jail and a fine, unless another penalty applies — NRS 193.150.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Nevada
bullets: Justice courts have jurisdiction over misdemeanor criminal cases, subject to statutory jurisdictional exceptions — NRS 4.370.
Municipal courts handle criminal violations of their cities’ municipal ordinances. The municipal-court statute also addresses jurisdiction shared with justice courts — NRS 5.050.

District courts handle felony and gross-misdemeanor trials. Justice courts conduct preliminary examinations in cases that may proceed to district court — Nevada Constitution, Article 6, Section 6; NRS 171.196.
A criminal complaint is a written statement of the essential facts constituting the charged public offense, made under oath before a magistrate or another authorized person — NRS 171.102.

sections.heading: Common questions in Nevada
bullets: Is a gross misdemeanor a felony? No. Nevada expressly separates gross misdemeanors from both felonies and misdemeanors — NRS 193.120.
Does every felony conviction require time in prison? No. Category E sentencing generally requires suspension of the prison sentence and probation, but statutory exceptions apply — NRS 193.130(2)(e).
Is every category B felony punishable by 20 years? No. Twenty years is the category’s general outer limit; the particular offense statute establishes its sentencing range — NRS 193.130(2)(b).
Does every felony case have a preliminary examination? No. A defendant can waive the examination, and an indictment can provide a separate route to district court — NRS 171.196.
Are the listed fines the entire financial consequence? Not necessarily. For example, a felony sentence may also include restitution when appropriate — NRS 176.033.

sources.label: Nevada Legislature — NRS Chapter 193: General Provisions on Crimes and Punishments
Nevada Legislature — NRS Chapter 171: Proceedings to Commitment
Nevada Legislature — NRS Chapter 4: Justice Courts
Nevada Legislature — NRS Chapter 5: Municipal Courts

criminal-law/nevada/expungement.summary: Nevada generally uses record sealing, not expungement, to limit access to adult criminal records; sealing does not physically destroy the records. Under NRS 179.245, eligible convictions have waiting periods based on the offense, while NRS 179.255 allows petitions following an acquittal or dismissal without the conviction waiting period. Some convictions cannot be sealed under the ordinary conviction-sealing statute, and a sealing order does not restore firearm rights or prevent every form of authorized access.

facts.label: Legal effect
facts.value: After records are sealed, the proceedings generally are deemed never to have occurred, and the person generally may answer inquiries accordingly. Nevada law preserves specific exceptions for access to sealed records. — NRS 179.285 and 179.295

facts.label: Excluded convictions
facts.value: The ordinary conviction-sealing process excludes sexual offenses and crimes against a child as defined in the statute, as well as specified felony impaired-driving offenses. The statutory definitions, rather than an offense's informal description, control eligibility. — NRS 179.245

facts.label: Acquittals and dismissals
facts.value: A person whose charges were dismissed or who was acquitted may petition the court where the charges were dismissed or the acquittal occurred. These cases do not carry the waiting periods applicable to convictions. — NRS 179.255

rows: Category A felony, crime of violence, or residential burglary
Category B, C, or D felony not governed by a longer period or exclusion
Other misdemeanors not assigned a special waiting period

facts.label: Starting the clock
facts.value: Waiting periods do not necessarily begin on the conviction date. NRS 179.245 measures time using release from actual custody, discharge from parole or probation, or the end of a suspended sentence, depending on the conviction category and the applicable statutory language. — NRS 179.245

facts.label: Petition materials
facts.value: A conviction-sealing petition must include a current, verified criminal-history record from Nevada's Central Repository for Nevada Records of Criminal History and identify relevant agencies possessing the records. Additional criminal-history materials may be required under the statute. — NRS 179.245

facts.label: Prosecutor participation
facts.value: The prosecuting attorney receives notice and an opportunity to participate. A prosecutor's stipulation can allow a petition to be granted without a hearing; the court still issues the sealing order. — NRS 179.245 and 179.255

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Nevada
bullets: For an eligible conviction, the ordinary filing court is the court where the conviction occurred. Depending on the case, that can be a district, justice, or municipal court. — NRS 179.245
For an acquittal or dismissal, the petition goes to the court where that disposition occurred. — NRS 179.255

The Nevada Department of Public Safety's Central Repository maintains statewide criminal-history information. It supplies records used in the process but does not replace the court as the decision-maker on a sealing petition. — NRS 179.245

sections.heading: Common questions in Nevada
bullets: Is sealing automatic when the waiting period ends? No. The ordinary conviction-sealing process requires a petition and court order; expiration of the waiting period alone does not seal records. — NRS 179.245
Does sealing restore gun rights? No. A sealing order does not restore the right to bear arms. — NRS 179.285
Can sealed records ever be inspected? Yes. Nevada authorizes inspection in specified circumstances, including certain proceedings involving the person whose records were sealed. — NRS 179.295

Does sealing restore other civil rights? Nevada's sealing statute restores voting, public-office, and jury-service rights lost because of the conviction. Separate laws may restore particular rights earlier. — NRS 179.285

sources.label: Nevada Legislature — NRS Chapter 179, sealing criminal records
Nevada Legislature — NRS 202.360, firearm restrictions

criminal-law/nevada/drug-charges.summary: Nevada drug charges depend on the substance, quantity, alleged conduct and prior convictions; possession, sale and trafficking are separate offenses under Nevada Revised Statutes Chapter 453. Adult cannabis possession is lawful within statutory limits, but that does not legalize public consumption, unauthorized sales or possession of other controlled substances. Potential outcomes range from probation to prison, and the applicable offense statute—not simply the description “drug charge”—determines the felony category, sentencing range and available exceptions.

sections.heading: What determines a Nevada drug charge

facts.label: Possession
facts.value: Nevada prohibits knowing or intentional possession of a controlled substance unless it was lawfully obtained or otherwise authorized. The statute distinguishes substances, quantities and prior offenses rather than assigning every possession case the same penalty. — NRS 453.336

facts.label: Sale and related conduct
facts.value: Selling, manufacturing, delivering or transporting controlled substances can constitute separate prohibited conduct. Possession for the purpose of sale is also a distinct offense; the prosecution does not have to allege a completed sale to charge possession for sale. — NRS 453.321 and 453.337–453.338

facts.label: Trafficking
facts.value: Nevada has separate trafficking provisions tied to specified substances and quantities. For substances covered by NRS 453.3385, the statute expressly includes the weight of a mixture containing the controlled substance, not just its pure drug content. — NRS 453.3385

sections.heading: Nevada penalty categories and cannabis limits

rows: State prison term of 1–5 years; a fine up to $10,000 may also apply unless a greater fine is authorized or required.
State prison term of 1–4 years; a fine up to $5,000 may also apply unless a greater fine is authorized or required.
State prison term of 1–4 years, generally suspended with probation, subject to statutory exceptions; a fine up to $5,000 may also apply.
For adults 21 or older, possession of up to 2.5 ounces of usable cannabis or one-quarter ounce of concentrated cannabis is protected within the statute’s conditions.
Adult-use legalization does not generally authorize consumption in public places; licensed cannabis consumption lounges have a statutory exception.

facts.label: Deferred proceedings
facts.value: For qualifying possession defendants without specified prior drug convictions, the court may defer proceedings with the defendant’s consent and impose probation without entering a judgment of conviction. Successful completion results in discharge and dismissal under this provision. — NRS 453.3363

facts.label: Probation is not automatic in every case
facts.value: The general category E rule favors suspended sentencing and probation, but statutory exceptions matter. A sale or trafficking charge does not acquire that treatment merely because the case involves drugs. — NRS 193.130 and 453.3405

facts.label: Sealing records
facts.value: Nevada provides different record-sealing procedures for convictions and for cases ending in dismissal or acquittal. Eligibility and timing depend on the disposition and applicable statute; dismissal does not itself mean every record has been sealed. — NRS 179.245 and 179.255

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Nevada
bullets: Justice courts conduct preliminary examinations in felony cases and generally handle misdemeanor criminal proceedings within their jurisdiction. — NRS 4.370
Nevada district courts adjudicate felony drug prosecutions. Criminal motions and requests for relief belong in the court handling the prosecution. — NRS 3.220
Record-sealing petitions are court proceedings governed by Nevada’s sealing statutes, not administrative complaints to a cannabis regulator. — NRS 179.245 and 179.255

sections.heading: Common questions in Nevada
bullets: Is all personal-use drug possession legal? No. Nevada’s adult-use cannabis protections do not legalize possession of other controlled substances. — NRS 453.336 and 678D.200
Does a small quantity automatically make possession a misdemeanor? No. Nevada can classify unlawful controlled-substance possession as a felony even when the allegation is personal use. — NRS 453.336
Can a possession case end without a conviction? Yes. Qualifying defendants may receive deferred proceedings and dismissal after successfully completing probation. — NRS 453.3363
Does a lawful cannabis amount permit unlicensed sales? No. Personal possession protections do not authorize commercial sales outside Nevada’s licensing framework. — NRS 678D.200

sources.label: Nevada Legislature — Chapter 453, Controlled Substances
Nevada Legislature — Chapter 193, General Provisions on Crimes and Punishments
Nevada Legislature — Chapter 179, Criminal Procedure and Record Sealing
Nevada Legislature — Chapter 678D, Adult Use of Cannabis

criminal-law/nevada/traffic-violations.summary: Nevada treats many routine traffic violations as civil infractions rather than crimes, but DUI, reckless driving, and certain other driving offenses remain criminal. The statewide change took effect January 1, 2023, under Assembly Bill 116; it did not eliminate traffic fines or license consequences. Whether a case is civil, a misdemeanor, or a felony depends on the charged statute and circumstances, including prior offenses and whether another person suffered death or substantial bodily harm.

sections.heading: Civil infractions versus criminal traffic offenses

facts.label: Decriminalization
facts.value: Assembly Bill 116 changed many minor traffic offenses from misdemeanors to civil infractions effective January 1, 2023. Nevada's traffic laws now distinguish civil-infraction proceedings from criminal prosecutions. Not every offense arising from driving was decriminalized. — Nevada Legislature, AB 116 (2021); NRS Chapter 484A

facts.label: Ordinary speeding
facts.value: Ordinary violations of Nevada's basic speed restrictions are civil infractions. The law prohibits driving faster than is reasonable or proper for conditions, as well as exceeding applicable speed limits. Separate criminal charges can apply when conduct satisfies another offense's elements. — NRS 484B.600

facts.label: General misdemeanor ceiling
facts.value: Unless a statute provides a different punishment, a Nevada misdemeanor is punishable by up to six months in county jail, a fine of up to $1,000, or both. Traffic statutes may impose their own minimum penalties or additional requirements. — NRS 193.150

rows: Driving or being in actual physical control while impaired, or with a prohibited alcohol concentration, remains criminal.
Generally a misdemeanor; penalties include a $400–$1,000 fine and two days to six months in jail, with community service available as a statutory alternative.
Generally a category B felony carrying one to six years in prison and a $2,000–$5,000 fine.
DUI causing death or substantial bodily harm
Category B felony carrying two to twenty years in prison and a $2,000–$5,000 fine.
Driving in willful or wanton disregard for safety is criminal; death or substantial bodily harm can elevate the offense to a felony.

facts.label: Alcohol concentration
facts.value: For the ordinary adult DUI prohibition, Nevada uses an alcohol concentration of 0.08 or more. Impairment can support a DUI charge independently of that numerical threshold. — NRS 484C.110

facts.label: Administrative consequences
facts.value: Driver's-license revocation proceedings are separate from criminal prosecution. Nevada law provides for administrative review of specified revocation orders, so the criminal court is not the only body involved in a DUI matter. — NRS 484C.220–484C.230

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Nevada
bullets: Justice courts and municipal courts handle traffic civil infractions within their statutory jurisdiction; the citation identifies the court handling the case. — NRS Chapter 484A

Criminal traffic misdemeanors generally proceed in justice or municipal court, depending on jurisdiction. Felony trials proceed in district court, although preliminary proceedings may occur in justice court. — NRS 4.370; NRS 5.050; Nevada Constitution, Article 6, Section 6

The Nevada Department of Motor Vehicles handles driver's-license administrative actions and related administrative hearings. Those proceedings are distinct from contesting the criminal charge. — NRS 484C.220–484C.230

sections.heading: Common questions in Nevada
bullets: Is every traffic ticket a criminal charge? No. Many routine violations are civil infractions, while DUI and reckless driving remain criminal.
Can a first DUI lead to jail? Yes. Nevada's first-offense DUI statute includes jail, while allowing community service as a statutory alternative. — NRS 484C.400
Can someone face DUI below 0.08? Yes. The impairment prohibition is separate from the alcohol-concentration prohibition. — NRS 484C.110
Does paying a traffic penalty necessarily end a license proceeding? No. Administrative license proceedings are separate from the court case. — NRS 484C.220–484C.230

sources.label: Nevada Legislature — NRS Chapter 484A: Traffic Laws Generally
Nevada Legislature — NRS Chapter 484B: Rules of the Road
Nevada Legislature — NRS Chapter 484C: Driving Under the Influence
Nevada Legislature — NRS Chapter 193: General Provisions on Crimes and Punishments

criminal-law/new-jersey/plea-bargaining.summary: New Jersey permits negotiated guilty pleas, but a prosecutor’s agreement does not itself determine the sentence: the judge must accept the plea and impose a lawful sentence. Under New Jersey Court Rule 3:9-2, the court generally must establish a factual basis and determine that the plea is voluntary and informed before accepting it. Court Rule 3:9-3 governs Superior Court plea agreements, including disclosure of their terms and protections when the court rejects the contemplated disposition.

sections.heading: How plea bargaining works in New Jersey

facts.label: Negotiated terms
facts.value: The prosecutor and defense may negotiate a guilty plea involving dismissal of other charges, a recommendation for a particular sentence, or an agreement not to oppose a requested sentence. The agreement must be disclosed to the court when the plea is entered. — N.J. Court Rule 3:9-3

facts.label: Acceptance of the plea
facts.value: The judge must personally question the defendant and determine that there is a factual basis for the plea, that it is voluntary, and that the defendant understands the charge and the plea’s consequences. New Jersey does not permit a plea of nolo contendere, or no contest. — N.J. Court Rule 3:9-2

facts.label: Judge’s role
facts.value: The judge may not participate in plea negotiations. The rules nevertheless allow a judge, following the prescribed procedure, to indicate the maximum sentence the judge would impose on a guilty plea based on the information then available. — N.J. Court Rule 3:9-3

facts.label: Written plea form
facts.value: A defendant entering a guilty plea must complete and sign the prescribed plea form. The form supplements, rather than replaces, the judge’s questioning in court. — N.J. Court Rule 3:9-2

rows: The parties disclose the plea agreement on the record in open court when the plea is offered. — Rule 3:9-3
If the court determines at sentencing that the interests of justice would not be served by the agreement, the defendant must have an opportunity to withdraw the plea. — Rule 3:9-3(e)
A motion to withdraw a guilty plea ordinarily must be made before sentencing. Filing the motion does not automatically entitle the defendant to withdraw the plea. — Rule 3:21-1
The court may permit withdrawal after sentencing to correct a manifest injustice. — Rule 3:21-1
Municipal guilty pleas and plea agreements are governed by the separate municipal court rule and the Supreme Court’s accompanying plea-agreement guidelines. — Rule 7:6-2

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in New Jersey
bullets: Superior Court, Law Division, Criminal Part: This is the trial-level forum for indictable criminal prosecutions and related plea proceedings. A plea-withdrawal motion is addressed to the court handling the criminal case. — N.J. Court Rules 3:1-1 and 3:21-1

Municipal court: Municipal plea proceedings generally involve disorderly persons offenses, petty disorderly persons offenses, municipal ordinance violations, and traffic matters within that court’s jurisdiction. — N.J. Court Rule 7:1

Superior Court, Appellate Division: Appeals from Superior Court final criminal judgments generally go here. Municipal court criminal judgments instead ordinarily receive initial appellate review in the Superior Court, Law Division. — N.J. Court Rules 2:2-3 and 3:23-1

sections.heading: Common questions in New Jersey
bullets: Does the prosecutor control the sentence? No. The judge imposes sentence, and the plea agreement remains subject to judicial review under Rule 3:9-3.
Can a defendant plead no contest? No. Rule 3:9-2 expressly prohibits nolo contendere pleas.
Can a guilty plea be withdrawn after sentencing? Yes, but Rule 3:21-1 requires correction of a manifest injustice; withdrawal is not automatic.
Is a signed plea form enough by itself? No. Rule 3:9-2 also requires the judge to question the defendant personally before accepting the plea.

sources.label: New Jersey Courts — Rules of Court, Parts II, III, and VII
New Jersey Courts — Criminal Division

criminal-law/new-hampshire/plea-bargaini.summary: New Hampshire permits criminal cases to be resolved through negotiated guilty pleas, but the prosecutor’s agreement does not itself establish a conviction or sentence: the court must accept the plea and impose sentence. New Hampshire Rule of Criminal Procedure 11 governs pleas and plea agreements, including the court’s inquiry into voluntariness and the defendant’s understanding of the rights surrendered; sentencing remains subject to applicable statutes.

facts.label: Governing rule
facts.value: New Hampshire Rule of Criminal Procedure 11 governs pleas, including guilty pleas, pleas of nolo contendere, and plea agreements. A negotiated disposition still requires judicial action; an agreement between the parties is not itself a court judgment. — N.H. R. Crim. P. 11

facts.label: Knowing and voluntary plea
facts.value: Before accepting a guilty plea, the court must determine that the defendant understands the charge and the consequences of pleading guilty and that the plea is voluntary. The plea process includes addressing the trial rights the defendant gives up. — N.H. R. Crim. P. 11

facts.label: Factual basis
facts.value: The court must satisfy itself that there is a factual basis for a guilty plea before entering judgment on it. A negotiated agreement does not eliminate this requirement. — N.H. R. Crim. P. 11

facts.label: Appointed counsel
facts.value: New Hampshire provides appointed counsel for eligible indigent defendants under its criminal-defense appointment statute. Eligibility depends on the charge and statutory conditions; the existence of plea negotiations does not independently determine eligibility. — RSA 604-A:2

sections.heading: What a New Hampshire plea agreement can address

rows: Negotiations can concern dismissal of charges or a plea to a different charge. The resulting plea remains subject to the court’s acceptance process. — N.H. R. Crim. P. 11
Negotiations can address the proposed sentence, but the court imposes punishment within the governing statutory framework. — N.H. R. Crim. P. 11; RSA 651:2
The court must not participate in plea discussions between the prosecution and defense. Its role includes considering the agreement and conducting the plea inquiry. — N.H. R. Crim. P. 11
A plea agreement must be disclosed to the court when the plea is offered. The judge’s consideration is not replaced by an undisclosed understanding between the parties. — N.H. R. Crim. P. 11
A plea of nolo contendere requires the court’s consent. It is a plea option, not a guarantee that the court will approve a negotiated resolution. — N.H. R. Crim. P. 11

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in New Hampshire
bullets: Court filings concerning a proposed plea, sentencing, or withdrawal belong in the criminal case before the court handling it. A complaint to an administrative office does not substitute for a judicial ruling. — N.H. R. Crim. P. 11
Plea discussions occur with the prosecutor handling the case, ordinarily through defense counsel. The judge is not a negotiating party. — N.H. R. Crim. P. 11
Requests for appointed defense counsel are determined through the court under New Hampshire’s indigent-defense appointment provisions. — RSA 604-A:2

sections.heading: Common questions in New Hampshire
bullets: Does signing an agreement finish the case? No. The court must conduct the required plea process, accept the plea, and enter the appropriate judgment and sentence. — N.H. R. Crim. P. 11
Can the judge negotiate the deal? No. Rule 11 prohibits judicial participation in plea discussions. — N.H. R. Crim. P. 11
Does a guilty plea waive trial rights? Yes. The plea inquiry addresses rights surrendered by pleading guilty, including the rights associated with a trial. — N.H. R. Crim. P. 11
Can an agreement authorize an otherwise unlawful sentence? No. A negotiated sentence remains subject to the applicable sentencing statutes. — RSA 651:2

sources.label: New Hampshire Judicial Branch — Rules of Criminal Procedure
New Hampshire General Court — RSA 604-A:2, Representation
New Hampshire General Court — RSA 651:2, Sentences and Limitations

criminal-law/new-hampshire/domestic-viol.summary: New Hampshire prosecutes domestic violence under RSA 631:2-b and may also charge offenses such as assault when the statutory elements are met; the relationship between the accused and the alleged victim matters to the domestic violence designation. The charge and potential punishment depend on the conduct, injury, mental state, and other statutory circumstances, rather than the domestic relationship alone. Criminal prosecution is separate from a civil protective-order case under RSA chapter 173-B, although knowingly violating a qualifying protective order is itself a crime.

sections.heading: What counts as a domestic violence charge

facts.label: Domestic violence statute
facts.value: RSA 631:2-b establishes the criminal offense of domestic violence involving a family or household member or an intimate partner. It covers specified conduct, not merely an argument or an accusation that a relationship is abusive. — RSA 631:2-b

facts.label: Conduct beyond physical injury
facts.value: The statute reaches specified threatening conduct, unlawful confinement, harassment, and property damage, as well as bodily injury. Physical injury therefore is not required for every form of the offense. Each charged form has its own statutory elements. — RSA 631:2-b

facts.label: Relationship requirement
facts.value: The domestic violence statute uses defined relationship categories. Dating relationships can qualify as intimate partnerships; marriage and shared residence are not universal requirements. — RSA 631:2-b; RSA 173-B:1

facts.label: Separate civil proceeding
facts.value: A domestic violence protective-order petition is a civil proceeding. Issuance of a protective order is not itself a criminal conviction, and a criminal conviction is not a prerequisite to obtaining civil protection. — RSA 173-B:3–5

sections.heading: Related offenses and general sentencing limits

rows: Generally a misdemeanor; specified circumstances can change the classification.
Class B felony; the general maximum is 7 years of imprisonment and a $4,000 fine.
Class A felony; the general maximum is 15 years of imprisonment and a $4,000 fine.
A class A misdemeanor under RSA 173-B:9; the general maximum is 1 year of imprisonment and a $2,000 fine.

facts.label: Temporary protection
facts.value: Courts may issue temporary relief without advance notice when the statutory immediate-and-present-danger standard is met. Emergency relief is also available through the procedures in the statute when court is closed. — RSA 173-B:4

facts.label: Final-order duration
facts.value: Final protective relief may last up to one year. The statute provides procedures for extensions; an extension is not automatic. — RSA 173-B:5

facts.label: Permission from the protected person
facts.value: A protective order remains enforceable despite the protected person's invitation or apparent permission to violate it. Private agreement does not amend the court's order. — RSA 173-B:5

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in New Hampshire
bullets: Local police departments and the New Hampshire State Police receive reports of suspected domestic violence; criminal charges proceed through law enforcement and prosecutors.
Circuit Court District Division handles misdemeanor criminal cases. Superior Court handles felony prosecutions.

Civil domestic violence protective-order petitions are filed in Circuit Court. RSA 173-B:3 governs petitions and permits filing where either party resides; its temporary-residence provision addresses a petitioner who has fled abuse.

sections.heading: Common questions in New Hampshire
bullets: Is every domestic violence charge a felony? No. Classification depends on the charged statutory conduct and applicable circumstances. — RSA 631:2-b
Can an unmarried dating partner qualify? Yes. The statutory intimate-partner category includes qualifying dating relationships. — RSA 173-B:1
Must there be a visible injury? No. Some prohibited conduct does not require bodily injury, including specified threats and harassment. — RSA 631:2-b
Does a civil protective order replace a criminal case? No. Civil protective relief and criminal prosecution are distinct proceedings. — RSA chapter 173-B; RSA 631:2-b

sources.label: New Hampshire General Court — RSA chapter 631, Assault and Related Offenses
New Hampshire General Court — RSA chapter 173-B, Protection of Persons from Domestic Abuse
New Hampshire General Court — RSA 651:2, Sentences and Limitations

criminal-law/new-york/drug-charges.summary: New York drug charges depend on the substance, its weight, and whether prosecutors allege possession, intent to sell, or a sale; offenses under Penal Law Article 220 range from misdemeanors to serious felonies. Cannabis is governed separately by Article 222, which permits limited possession by adults 21 and older but retains offenses for unlawful possession and sale. Sentencing depends on the conviction, prior record, and statutory eligibility for alternatives such as judicial diversion.

sections.heading: What New York drug laws cover

facts.label: Controlled substances
facts.value: Article 220 defines controlled substances by reference to New York’s public-health schedules, with exclusions that include cannabis. The prosecution must establish the elements of the particular possession or sale offense charged. — N.Y. Penal Law § 220.00; N.Y. Public Health Law § 3306

facts.label: Sale does not require payment
facts.value: The statutory definition of “sell” includes selling, exchanging, giving, disposing of a substance to another person, or offering or agreeing to do so. A money transaction is not required. — N.Y. Penal Law § 220.00(1)

facts.label: Weight rules vary
facts.value: Some offenses use the aggregate weight of a preparation, compound, mixture, or substance containing a drug; others use different measurements. The applicable threshold depends on the specific drug and statutory subdivision. — N.Y. Penal Law §§ 220.06–220.21

sections.heading: Examples of New York drug charges

rows: Knowingly and unlawfully possessing a controlled substance, subject to statutory exceptions
Possessing a controlled substance with intent to sell
Possessing a narcotic drug with intent to sell
Knowingly and unlawfully selling a controlled substance
Knowingly and unlawfully selling a narcotic drug

facts.label: Misdemeanor maximum
facts.value: A class A misdemeanor carries a maximum jail term of 364 days. — N.Y. Penal Law § 70.15(1)

facts.label: Felony sentencing
facts.value: New York has specific sentencing provisions for felony drug offenders. Offense classification and prior felony history affect the applicable sentence; many felony drug prison sentences also include post-release supervision. — N.Y. Penal Law §§ 70.70, 70.71, 70.45

facts.label: Lawful adult cannabis possession
facts.value: Adults 21 or older may possess up to three ounces of cannabis and up to 24 grams of concentrated cannabis under the general adult-use possession provision. This does not authorize unlicensed commercial sales. — N.Y. Penal Law § 222.05

facts.label: Judicial diversion
facts.value: Eligible defendants charged with specified felonies may enter court-supervised substance-use treatment through judicial diversion. Eligibility and admission depend on statutory criteria and judicial findings; diversion is not automatic. — N.Y. Criminal Procedure Law §§ 216.00, 216.05

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in New York
bullets: Criminal drug prosecutions are brought by prosecutors, ordinarily the county district attorney; a private complainant does not file an Article 220 prosecution directly.

Outside New York City, local criminal courts handle misdemeanor cases and initial felony proceedings; County Court or Supreme Court handles felony prosecutions. In New York City, Criminal Court handles misdemeanors and initial felony proceedings, while Supreme Court handles felonies. — N.Y. Criminal Procedure Law §§ 10.10, 10.20, 10.30
The New York State Unified Court System’s court locator identifies courts by county and court type.

sections.heading: Common questions in New York
bullets: Is every possession charge a felony? No. Seventh-degree controlled-substance possession is a class A misdemeanor. — Penal Law § 220.03
Can giving drugs away count as selling? Yes. New York’s definition of selling includes giving a controlled substance to another person. — Penal Law § 220.00(1)
Does legal cannabis mean all cannabis possession is lawful? No. Age, quantity, and other statutory restrictions still matter. — Penal Law Article 222

Is treatment available instead of ordinary prosecution? Judicial diversion is available in qualifying felony cases, subject to statutory eligibility and court approval. Talk to a lawyer. — Criminal Procedure Law Article 216

sources.label: New York Senate — Penal Law Article 220
New York Senate — Penal Law § 222.05
New York Senate — Criminal Procedure Law Article 216
New York State Unified Court System — Court Locator

criminal-law/new-jersey/traffic-violatio.summary: New Jersey generally treats ordinary traffic violations, including driving while intoxicated, as motor-vehicle offenses rather than indictable crimes, but municipal courts can impose fines, license consequences, and jail where a statute authorizes it. Charges usually proceed in the municipal court serving the place of the alleged violation, while related indictable charges belong in Superior Court; the consequences depend on the particular statute, prior offenses, and whether the case involves injury, intoxication, or a suspended license.

sections.heading: How New Jersey classifies traffic cases

facts.label: Municipal-court jurisdiction
facts.value: Municipal courts have jurisdiction over violations of motor-vehicle and traffic laws. An offense does not become an indictable crime simply because it carries possible jail time. — N.J.S.A. 2B:12-17; Title 39.

facts.label: DWI classification
facts.value: New Jersey prosecutes driving while intoxicated under its motor-vehicle code, not as an ordinary Criminal Code offense. Nevertheless, DWI can carry substantial sanctions, including ignition-interlock requirements and, depending on the circumstances, imprisonment. — N.J.S.A. 39:4-50.

facts.label: Separate criminal charges
facts.value: Driving conduct can also support Criminal Code charges. Assault by auto and death by auto are separate offenses from ordinary traffic violations and require proof of their statutory elements. — N.J.S.A. 2C:12-1(c); 2C:11-5.

sections.heading: Common violations and their legal basis

rows: Speed limits and the obligation to drive at an appropriate reduced speed under specified conditions.
Driving carelessly or without due caution in a manner that endangers, or is likely to endanger, people or property.
Driving heedlessly in willful or wanton disregard of others' rights or safety. A first conviction can carry up to 60 days in jail, a $50–$200 fine, or both.
Failure to obey an applicable official traffic-control device, subject to statutory exceptions.
Operating a motor vehicle while driving privileges are suspended or revoked; sanctions vary with the circumstances and prior violations.

facts.label: MVC points
facts.value: The New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission assigns points for specified moving violations. MVC states that accumulating 12 or more points on a current driving record results in suspension; points are separate from the court's fine. — New Jersey MVC, Points and Schedule of Point Values.

facts.label: Municipal appeal deadline
facts.value: An appeal from a municipal-court judgment must be taken within 20 days after entry of judgment. The appeal goes to the Superior Court, Law Division, and ordinarily proceeds on the municipal-court record. — New Jersey Court Rules 3:23-2 and 3:23-8.

facts.label: Expungement exclusion
facts.value: The Criminal Code's expungement chapter does not apply to Title 39 motor-vehicle offenses. — N.J.S.A. 2C:52-28.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in New Jersey
bullets: Municipal court: The court identified on the summons handles the traffic charge, plea, trial, and sentencing within its jurisdiction. — N.J.S.A. 2B:12-17.

Superior Court, Law Division: This court hears municipal-court appeals. The notice of appeal is filed with the municipal-court administrator, with additional service and filing requirements under the court rules. — Rules 3:23-2 and 3:23-3.

New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission: MVC administers driver records, points, and administrative license actions; it does not replace the municipal court as the forum deciding the traffic charge. — New Jersey MVC, Points.

sections.heading: Common questions in New Jersey
bullets: Can a traffic ticket lead to jail? Yes. Some Title 39 offenses authorize imprisonment, including reckless driving and DWI. — N.J.S.A. 39:4-96; 39:4-50.
Does paying a payable ticket count as a guilty plea? Yes. Payment through the violations bureau constitutes a guilty plea and waiver of trial. — Rule 7:12-3.
Can every ticket be resolved by payment without court? No. Only eligible matters can be handled through the violations bureau; some charges require a court appearance. — Rule 7:12-3.
Can a Title 39 conviction be expunged under New Jersey's criminal expungement law? No. That chapter expressly excludes Title 39 offenses. — N.J.S.A. 2C:52-28.

sources.label: New Jersey Legislature — Statutes
New Jersey Courts — Municipal Court
New Jersey Courts — Rules of Court
New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission — Points

criminal-law/new-york/expungement.summary: New York generally uses sealing rather than expungement: records become restricted, not destroyed, and remain accessible for purposes authorized by law. Its Clean Slate Act provides automatic sealing of eligible convictions after statutory waiting periods, while a separate application process permits discretionary sealing of a limited number of convictions after ten years. Certain cannabis convictions qualify for expungement, and cases ending favorably to the accused generally qualify for sealing under separate rules.

facts.label: Application-based sealing
facts.value: A court may seal up to two eligible convictions, only one of which may be a felony. Multiple convictions arising from the same criminal transaction can count as one conviction. Sealing is discretionary, not guaranteed. — N.Y. Criminal Procedure Law § 160.59.

facts.label: Ten-year waiting period
facts.value: The application-based waiting period runs from sentencing or release from incarceration, whichever is later. Time incarcerated after the conviction is excluded from the calculation. A pending criminal charge or a subsequent criminal conviction can prevent eligibility. — N.Y. Criminal Procedure Law § 160.59(5).

facts.label: Clean Slate rollout
facts.value: The Clean Slate Act took effect November 16, 2024. The statute gives the court system three years to complete the initial identification and sealing process, so eligibility does not mean every qualifying record was already sealed in 2026. — N.Y. Criminal Procedure Law § 160.57; Laws of 2023, chapter 631.

rows: Generally three years from sentencing or release from incarceration, whichever is later; other conditions apply.
Generally eight years from sentencing or release from incarceration, whichever is later; other conditions apply.
Generally ten years; up to two eligible convictions, including no more than one felony.
Cases ending favorably to the accused
Generally follows a qualifying dismissal, acquittal, or other favorable termination.
Sealing under CPL § 160.50, subject to statutory exceptions.
Eligibility depends on the offense covered by the statute.
Expungement under CPL § 160.50(5), rather than ordinary conviction sealing.

facts.label: Clean Slate restrictions
facts.value: Sealing requires that the person have no pending New York criminal charge and not be under probation or parole supervision. Sex offenses and sexually violent offenses are excluded, as are class A felonies other than those defined in Penal Law article 220. — N.Y. Criminal Procedure Law § 160.57.

facts.label: Different exclusions for applications
facts.value: The application-based law excludes violent felony offenses, class A felonies, specified sex offenses, and other listed offenses. Eligibility under Clean Slate and eligibility under the application process are not identical. — N.Y. Criminal Procedure Law § 160.59(1).

facts.label: Sealed does not mean erased
facts.value: Authorized access remains available for specified purposes. For example, Clean Slate permits access in criminal proceedings and for certain legally required employment-related background checks. — N.Y. Criminal Procedure Law § 160.57.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in New York
bullets: Applications under CPL § 160.59 go to the court of conviction. When an application covers convictions from different courts, the statute designates the court that handled the most serious conviction; equally serious convictions are handled by the court of the most recent conviction.
The district attorney for the county where the conviction occurred receives the application and may oppose sealing. — CPL § 160.59.
Clean Slate is an automatic court-system process, not the discretionary application procedure under CPL § 160.59.

sections.heading: Common questions in New York
bullets: Does New York offer expungement? Yes, for specified cannabis convictions; ordinary conviction relief generally involves sealing.
Are violent felonies always excluded? They are excluded from CPL § 160.59, but Clean Slate does not categorically exclude every violent felony.
Is sealing guaranteed after ten years? No. CPL § 160.59 requires eligibility and a discretionary court decision.
Can New York seal a federal conviction? These New York procedures do not seal federal convictions.

New York Senate: Criminal Procedure Law § 160.59

criminal-law/north-carolina/traffic-viol.summary: North Carolina treats many traffic violations as infractions, but offenses such as reckless driving, impaired driving, and certain speeding violations are crimes. The charge determines whether the case involves an infraction penalty or criminal sentencing, while license consequences are handled under separate motor vehicle laws. Traffic cases generally begin in District Court, and paying a citation that is eligible for waiver resolves the charge rather than merely paying an administrative fee.

sections.heading: How North Carolina classifies traffic violations

facts.label: Infractions versus crimes
facts.value: An infraction is a noncriminal violation of law. Under the general motor vehicle penalty provision, violations of Article 3 of Chapter 20 are infractions unless another classification applies. The particular offense statute matters because some traffic offenses expressly carry misdemeanor or felony classifications. — N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 14-3.1, 20-176.

facts.label: Criminal speeding threshold
facts.value: Driving more than 15 mph over the applicable limit while traveling more than 55 mph, or driving more than 80 mph, is a Class 3 misdemeanor. Speeding below those criminal thresholds can still be an infraction. — N.C. Gen. Stat. § 20-141(j1).

facts.label: Reckless driving
facts.value: Driving carelessly and heedlessly in willful or wanton disregard of others’ rights or safety is reckless driving. The statute also covers driving without due caution at a speed or in a manner that endangers or is likely to endanger a person or property. Reckless driving is a Class 2 misdemeanor. — N.C. Gen. Stat. § 20-140.

rows: Generally an infraction when no criminal classification applies.
Class 3 misdemeanor under the speed thresholds described above.
Class 2 misdemeanor; the statute addresses dangerous conduct, not just a particular speed.
Misdemeanor sentenced under the separate impaired-driving sentencing statute.
Generally an infraction carrying a $100 fine and court costs; a school bus driver’s violation is a Class 2 misdemeanor.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in North Carolina
bullets: District Court hears traffic infractions and generally has original jurisdiction over misdemeanors. The county clerk of superior court maintains the court file and processes filings for District Court cases. — N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 7A-253, 7A-272; North Carolina Judicial Branch, Traffic Violations.
The district attorney’s office prosecutes criminal traffic charges. It is separate from the clerk’s office, which handles court records and administrative processing. — N.C. Gen. Stat. § 7A-61.

The North Carolina Division of Motor Vehicles administers driver-license records and statutory suspensions or revocations. A court case and a DMV licensing action are distinct processes. — N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 20-16, 20-17.

sections.heading: Common questions in North Carolina
bullets: Does every traffic ticket create a criminal conviction? No. An infraction is noncriminal, although it can still have financial and licensing consequences. Misdemeanor traffic charges are criminal cases. — N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 14-3.1, 20-176.

Does paying a ticket contest the charge? No. For a waivable offense, payment constitutes a waiver of trial and an admission of responsibility or guilty plea, depending on the charge. Not every charge is waivable. — North Carolina Judicial Branch, Traffic Violations.
Are court costs the same as a fine? No. Court costs are separate statutory charges and can be imposed in addition to a fine. — N.C. Gen. Stat. § 7A-304.

Does a texting conviction add license points? The texting statute prohibits driver-license points and insurance surcharge assessments for its violations. It nevertheless imposes a fine and court costs for the ordinary infraction. — N.C. Gen. Stat. § 20-137.4A(c).

sources.label: North Carolina General Assembly — Chapter 20, Motor Vehicles

North Carolina General Assembly — Section 14-3.1, Infraction defined
North Carolina Judicial Branch — Traffic Violations

criminal-law/north-carolina/drug-charges.summary: North Carolina drug charges depend on the substance, amount, and alleged conduct, with penalties ranging from misdemeanors to felonies carrying mandatory prison terms. Under the North Carolina Controlled Substances Act, cocaine possession is a felony, and possessing enough of certain drugs can support a trafficking charge without proof of a sale. Prior convictions, the offense date, and eligibility for statutory exceptions can affect the outcome; limited first-offender dismissal and overdose-related immunity provisions also exist.

sections.heading: How North Carolina classifies drug charges

facts.label: Governing law
facts.value: The North Carolina Controlled Substances Act prohibits unauthorized possession, manufacture, sale, delivery, and possession with intent to manufacture, sell, or deliver controlled substances. Separate statutory schedules identify the regulated substances. — N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 90-86 through 90-113.8; § 90-95(a).

facts.label: Possession versus distribution
facts.value: Simple possession and possession with intent to sell or deliver are different offenses. A completed sale is not required for a possession-with-intent charge, but the State must establish the additional intent element. — N.C. Gen. Stat. § 90-95(a)(1), (3).

facts.label: Trafficking does not require a sale
facts.value: Trafficking provisions cover specified quantities possessed, transported, manufactured, sold, or delivered. For cocaine, the threshold is 28 grams, and the statute includes mixtures containing cocaine. — N.C. Gen. Stat. § 90-95(h)(3).

rows: Structured sentencing; no single prison term applies to every defendant.
Possession of cocaine with intent to sell or deliver
Trafficking: 28 grams to less than 200 grams
35–51 months imprisonment and a fine of at least $50,000.
Trafficking: 200 grams to less than 400 grams
70–93 months imprisonment and a fine of at least $100,000.
175–222 months imprisonment and a fine of at least $250,000.

facts.label: Penalty-table authority
facts.value: The cocaine classifications and trafficking penalties above come from § 90-95. Ordinary felony sentencing accounts for offense class and prior-record level; trafficking has its own sentencing rules. — N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 90-95(b)(1), (d)(2), (h)(3); 15A-1340.13.

facts.label: Substantial assistance
facts.value: The trafficking statute permits specified sentencing departures when the court finds substantial assistance in identifying, arresting, or convicting accomplices, accessories, co-conspirators, or principals. This exception is not automatic. — N.C. Gen. Stat. § 90-95(h)(5).

facts.label: Conditional discharge
facts.value: Section 90-96 provides conditional-discharge procedures for eligible possession and paraphernalia cases. Successful completion can result in discharge and dismissal without an adjudication of guilt; eligibility restrictions and probation conditions apply. — N.C. Gen. Stat. § 90-96.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in North Carolina
bullets: District Court generally handles misdemeanor criminal trials and preliminary proceedings in felony cases. Superior Court generally handles felony trials and misdemeanor appeals for trial anew. — N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 7A-271, 7A-272.

The district attorney prosecutes State criminal cases. Criminal motions and other case filings belong in the court handling the prosecution; the clerk of superior court maintains court records. — N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 7A-61, 7A-109.

sections.heading: Common questions in North Carolina
bullets: Is every drug-possession charge a misdemeanor? No. Cocaine possession is a Class I felony, even below the cocaine trafficking threshold. — § 90-95(d)(2).
Does trafficking require proof of dealing? No. Possession of a statutory trafficking quantity can itself qualify. — § 90-95(h).
Does seeking overdose help prevent all drug charges? No. Section 90-96.2 provides limited immunity for specified offenses when statutory conditions are met, not blanket immunity from prosecution.
Does conditional discharge automatically erase the record? No. Discharge and dismissal under § 90-96 are distinct from expunction procedures. Talk to a lawyer.

criminal-law/north-carolina/expungement.summary: North Carolina calls expungement “expunction,” and eligibility depends on the charge’s outcome, the offense, the person’s criminal history, and the statute used. Dismissed charges and not-guilty findings have a different statutory route from convictions, while qualifying nonviolent convictions generally require a waiting period and additional eligibility findings. An expunction generally restores the person’s legal status before the proceeding, but it does not eliminate every government record or every legally permitted use of the information.

facts.label: Dismissals and acquittals
facts.value: G.S. 15A-146 provides for expunction of qualifying charges dismissed by the court or prosecutor and charges resulting in a finding of not guilty or not responsible. These outcomes are governed separately from conviction-expunction rules. — N.C. Gen. Stat. § 15A-146

facts.label: Nonviolent convictions
facts.value: G.S. 15A-145.5 permits expunction of qualifying nonviolent misdemeanor and felony convictions. Its definition excludes specified offenses, including Class A through G felonies and offenses containing assault as an essential element; an offense’s everyday description as “nonviolent” does not establish eligibility. — N.C. Gen. Stat. § 15A-145.5

facts.label: Offenses committed before age 18
facts.value: A separate statute covers certain first-offender misdemeanor convictions for offenses committed before age 18, other than traffic violations, and certain misdemeanor possession-of-alcohol convictions committed before age 21. — N.C. Gen. Stat. § 15A-145

rows: Generally five years after conviction or completion of any active sentence, probation, and post-release supervision, whichever occurs later.
Generally ten years after conviction or completion of any active sentence, probation, and post-release supervision, whichever occurs later.
At least two years after conviction or completion of probation, whichever occurs later.
The conviction waiting periods above do not apply to petitions under the dismissal-and-acquittal statute.
$175; the statute provides an exception for an indigent petitioner.

sections.heading: What an expunction does—and does not do

facts.label: Legal effect
facts.value: An order under G.S. 15A-145.5 generally restores the person to the status occupied before the arrest, indictment, or information. The statute generally protects the person from perjury or false-statement liability for failing to acknowledge expunged proceedings, subject to statutory exceptions. — N.C. Gen. Stat. § 15A-145.5

facts.label: Continuing government access
facts.value: The Administrative Office of the Courts maintains confidential expunction records. State law authorizes access and use in specified circumstances, including access by prosecutors for purposes permitted by statute; expunction is not a promise that every government trace disappears. — N.C. Gen. Stat. § 15A-151

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in North Carolina
bullets: Conviction petitions under G.S. 15A-145.5 are filed in the court of the county where the conviction occurred.
Dismissal and acquittal petitions under G.S. 15A-146 belong in the court of the county where the charge was brought.

The county clerk of superior court handles court filings. The North Carolina Judicial Branch publishes statute-specific expunction forms; a judge determines whether statutory requirements are satisfied.

sections.heading: Common questions in North Carolina
bullets: Does finishing the waiting period guarantee expunction? No. Offense exclusions, criminal-history restrictions, and other statutory findings also matter under G.S. 15A-145.5.
Can a dismissed charge be expunged even though there was no conviction? Yes. G.S. 15A-146 expressly addresses qualifying dismissals and not-guilty findings.
Are all misdemeanor convictions eligible? No. G.S. 15A-145.5 excludes specified misdemeanor offenses as well as specified felonies.
Are expunged records unavailable to everyone? No. G.S. 15A-151 preserves confidential records and authorizes specified access.

criminal-law/north-dakota/arrest-process.summary: In North Dakota, an arrest brings a person into criminal custody but does not establish guilt; the next court proceedings address the accusation, legal representation, and release or detention. North Dakota Rule of Criminal Procedure 5 requires an arrested person to be brought before a magistrate without unnecessary delay, while separate rules govern arrest warrants, appointed counsel, and release conditions. The process differs depending on whether the charge is a felony, misdemeanor, or municipal ordinance violation.

sections.heading: Arrest and the first court appearance

facts.label: Arrest warrants
facts.value: A court may issue an arrest warrant when the complaint and supporting materials establish probable cause that an offense occurred and the defendant committed it. Rule 4 also provides for a summons instead of an arrest warrant in appropriate circumstances. — N.D.R.Crim.P. 4

facts.label: Appearance after arrest
facts.value: An officer making an arrest under a warrant, or a person making an arrest without a warrant, must bring the arrested person before the nearest available magistrate without unnecessary delay. — N.D.R.Crim.P. 5(a)

facts.label: Information at the initial appearance
facts.value: The initial appearance includes information about the charge, the right to counsel, and the right to remain silent. The magistrate also addresses release under Rule 46. An initial appearance is not a trial or a determination of guilt. — N.D.R.Crim.P. 5

facts.label: Counsel
facts.value: An indigent defendant facing a felony charge is entitled to assigned counsel. For a nonfelony charge, the rule links appointed representation to the possibility of imprisonment; it permits proceedings without appointed counsel when the court determines imprisonment will not be imposed if the defendant is convicted. — N.D.R.Crim.P. 44

rows: Determines whether the complaint and supporting materials establish probable cause for an arrest warrant. — N.D.R.Crim.P. 4
Addresses the accusation, procedural rights, counsel, and release following arrest. — N.D.R.Crim.P. 5
Formally presents the indictment, information, or complaint and calls on the defendant to enter a plea. — N.D.R.Crim.P. 10
Addresses release pending trial and conditions intended to reasonably assure appearance and community safety. — N.D.R.Crim.P. 46
Addresses eligibility for assigned counsel and any waiver of counsel. — N.D.R.Crim.P. 44

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in North Dakota
bullets: North Dakota district courts handle state criminal prosecutions, including felony and misdemeanor cases. Criminal motions are filed in the court handling the prosecution.
Municipal courts handle prosecutions for violations of municipal ordinances. They are not the trial courts for state felony prosecutions.
The North Dakota Commission on Legal Counsel for Indigents administers the state indigent-defense system. Appointment of counsel is a court determination under the applicable eligibility rules.

Complaints about officer conduct may be received by the employing police department or sheriff’s office. An administrative complaint does not itself dismiss a criminal charge or change a court’s release order.

sections.heading: Common questions in North Dakota
bullets: Does every arrest require a warrant? No. North Dakota law authorizes warrantless arrests in specified circumstances. — N.D.C.C. § 29-06-15.

Must the officer have the warrant in hand? No. Rule 4 permits execution without physical possession, but requires notice of the charged offense and the existence of the warrant; requested access to the warrant must follow as soon as possible. — N.D.R.Crim.P. 4.
Is release always unconditional? No. The court may impose release conditions under Rule 46; an arrest does not establish a universal cash-bail amount. — N.D.R.Crim.P. 46.
Can a defendant give up counsel? Yes, but waiver must satisfy the governing legal requirements. Rule 44 governs the right to counsel and waiver. — N.D.R.Crim.P. 44.

North Dakota Supreme Court — Criminal Rule 5: Initial Appearance
North Dakota Supreme Court — Criminal Rule 44: Right to and Assignment of Counsel

criminal-law/north-dakota/domestic-viole.summary: North Dakota has a specific domestic violence crime, and conduct involving a family or household member can also support charges such as assault, aggravated assault, or terrorizing when the statutory elements are met. The applicable charge and punishment depend on the conduct, injury, relationship, and any qualifying prior convictions, rather than the domestic label alone. Criminal prosecution is separate from a civil domestic violence protection order, although knowingly violating such an order can itself be criminal.

facts.label: Specific criminal offense
facts.value: North Dakota's domestic violence statute addresses willfully causing bodily injury, substantial bodily injury, or serious bodily injury to a family or household member. Its grading provisions distinguish injury levels and qualifying prior offenses. — N.D.C.C. § 12.1-17-01.2

facts.label: Covered relationships
facts.value: The family-or-household-member definition includes spouses, former spouses, parents, children, relatives by blood or marriage, people living together or who previously lived together, people in a dating relationship, and people who have a child together. Sharing a current address is therefore not required for every covered relationship. — N.D.C.C. §§ 12.1-17-01.2 and 14-07.1-01

facts.label: Other possible charges
facts.value: Simple assault, assault, aggravated assault, and terrorizing are separate statutory offenses. A domestic relationship does not replace the prosecution's obligation to establish the elements of the particular offense charged. — N.D.C.C. §§ 12.1-17-01, 12.1-17-01.1, 12.1-17-02, and 12.1-17-04

facts.label: Separate proceedings
facts.value: A district court may issue a civil domestic violence protection order under Chapter 14-07.1. This proceeding is distinct from determining criminal guilt under Chapter 12.1-17; the penalty table lists classification ceilings, not automatic sentences for every domestic incident. — N.D.C.C. §§ 14-07.1-02 and 12.1-32-01

facts.label: Available protective restrictions
facts.value: Protection orders can restrain contact and further domestic violence and can exclude a respondent from a dwelling. The statute also authorizes other specified relief, including temporary custody and visitation provisions. — N.D.C.C. § 14-07.1-02

facts.label: Violating an order
facts.value: Violating a covered domestic violence protection order after actual notice of the order's provisions is a separate criminal offense. A new physical injury is not necessary when the violation consists of prohibited contact. — N.D.C.C. § 14-07.1-06

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in North Dakota
bullets: Local police departments and county sheriffs receive reports and investigate alleged domestic violence crimes.
The county state's attorney handles prosecution of state criminal offenses; North Dakota district courts hear state criminal cases.
Civil domestic violence protection-order petitions are filed in district court. The North Dakota Courts Legal Self Help Center publishes the relevant forms and procedural information.

sections.heading: Common questions in North Dakota
bullets: Must the parties be married? No. The statutory definition includes several unmarried relationships, including dating partners and people who have a child together. — N.D.C.C. § 14-07.1-01
Is every domestic violence charge a felony? No. Section 12.1-17-01.2 includes misdemeanor and felony classifications, depending on the statutory circumstances.
Does a protection order establish a criminal conviction? No. A civil protection-order proceeding and a criminal prosecution are separate proceedings. — N.D.C.C. Chapters 14-07.1 and 12.1-17

Can prior offenses affect the charge? Yes. The domestic violence statute contains enhanced classifications involving qualifying prior offenses; the precise statutory requirements matter. — N.D.C.C. § 12.1-17-01.2

North Dakota Legislative Branch — Chapter 12.1-32, Penalties and Sentencing
