North Dakota Courts — Domestic Violence Protection Order

criminal-law/north-dakota/expungement.summary: North Dakota provides a court process for sealing eligible criminal records under North Dakota Century Code chapter 12-60.1, rather than a general right to erase every criminal case through expungement. Sealing restricts public access but does not mean the underlying records are physically destroyed or unavailable for every official purpose. Eligibility depends on the offense and the statutory requirements, and a petition does not guarantee relief; the court decides whether sealing is justified in the particular case.

sections.heading: What criminal-record sealing means in North Dakota

facts.label: Governing law
facts.value: North Dakota Century Code chapter 12-60.1, Sealing Criminal Records, establishes the petition-based process for sealing eligible criminal records. Section 12-60.1-02 addresses petitions to seal criminal records. — N.D.C.C. ch. 12-60.1; § 12-60.1-02

facts.label: Sealing versus destruction
facts.value: Sealing limits access to records; it is not the same as destroying them. A sealed record remains subject to the access rules and exceptions established by North Dakota law. — N.D.C.C. ch. 12-60.1

facts.label: Court approval
facts.value: Relief under the general sealing procedure requires a court order. Finishing a sentence does not, by itself, establish that the conviction record has been sealed through this procedure. — N.D.C.C. § 12-60.1-02

rows: The statute establishes eligibility requirements and exclusions; not every conviction qualifies.
The petition is directed to the court in which the criminal record was established.
The prosecuting attorney receives notice and has an opportunity to respond to the request.
The court evaluates the request under the statutory standards rather than granting relief solely because a petition was filed.
Public access is restricted, while access authorized by law can remain available.

facts.label: Public access and official access differ
facts.value: A record being unavailable to the general public does not establish that it is unavailable to criminal justice agencies. The statutory access provisions continue to govern sealed records. — N.D.C.C. ch. 12-60.1

facts.label: Separate from overturning a conviction
facts.value: A sealing petition concerns access to the criminal record. It is not an appeal or a determination that the conviction was legally invalid. — N.D.C.C. ch. 12-60.1

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in North Dakota
bullets: Court where the record was established: The statutory sealing request is a court petition, not an administrative complaint submitted to a statewide records agency. — N.D.C.C. § 12-60.1-02

North Dakota Legal Self Help Center: The North Dakota Court System provides self-help information about court procedures. The center provides legal information, not representation or an eligibility ruling. — North Dakota Court System, Legal Self Help Center
Disputed eligibility or consequences: Questions about how a particular conviction fits the statute require an individualized legal assessment; talk to a lawyer.

sections.heading: Common questions in North Dakota
bullets: Does sealing erase the conviction? No. Sealing restricts access to the record rather than invalidating the conviction or physically destroying every record. — N.D.C.C. ch. 12-60.1

Is every criminal conviction eligible? No. The statute contains eligibility requirements and exclusions, so the existence of a criminal record alone does not establish eligibility. — N.D.C.C. § 12-60.1-02
Does completing probation automatically seal the case? Not through the general petition-based sealing procedure. That procedure requires a request and a court order. — N.D.C.C. § 12-60.1-02
Can officials still access a sealed record? Sealing is not an absolute prohibition on access. North Dakota law preserves access in specified circumstances. — N.D.C.C. ch. 12-60.1

sources.label: North Dakota Legislative Branch — Century Code chapter 12-60.1, Sealing Criminal Records
North Dakota Court System — Legal Self Help Center

criminal-law/ohio/traffic-violations.summary: Ohio traffic violations range from minor misdemeanors, which carry no jail sentence, to offenses that can result in incarceration, license suspension, and criminal records. The consequences depend on the statute charged, prior convictions, and circumstances such as impaired driving or injury; a ticket’s monetary charge is not necessarily the entire financial consequence. Ohio also maintains a separate driver-license points system, under which accumulating 12 points within two years triggers a six-month suspension.

facts.label: Minor misdemeanors
facts.value: A minor misdemeanor is a criminal offense, but Ohio does not authorize a jail sentence for that classification. The maximum fine for an individual is $150; court costs can be additional. Not every traffic offense qualifies as a minor misdemeanor. — Ohio Revised Code §§ 2929.24, 2929.28.

facts.label: Citations instead of arrest
facts.value: For a minor misdemeanor, an officer generally must issue a citation rather than arrest the person. Statutory exceptions include a person’s inability to provide satisfactory evidence of identity or refusal to sign the citation. — Ohio Revised Code § 2935.26.

facts.label: Impaired driving
facts.value: Ohio calls its principal impaired-driving offense operating a vehicle under the influence, or OVI. The statute covers impairment by alcohol, a drug of abuse, or both, and also prohibits operating with specified concentrations of alcohol or certain drugs. Penalties depend on the applicable statutory category and prior offenses. — Ohio Revised Code § 4511.19.

facts.label: Limits of the sentencing table
facts.value: The table states general misdemeanor limits, not the complete punishment for every traffic offense. OVI has offense-specific sentencing provisions, including mandatory sanctions in applicable cases, and repeat OVI can be a felony. — Ohio Revised Code §§ 2929.24, 2929.28, 4511.19.

facts.label: Twelve-point suspension
facts.value: The registrar imposes a six-month suspension when a driver accumulates 12 or more points within two years. The statute provides notice and an opportunity to appeal in the municipal or county court with jurisdiction over the person’s residence. — Ohio Revised Code § 4510.037.

facts.label: Points vary
facts.value: Ohio assigns six points for OVI and four points for operating a vehicle in willful or wanton disregard of the safety of persons or property. Speeding points depend on the statutory speed thresholds rather than a single uniform point value. — Ohio Revised Code § 4510.036.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Ohio
bullets: Municipal and county courts handle misdemeanor traffic prosecutions within their jurisdiction; authorized mayor’s courts also handle certain traffic cases. — R.C. §§ 1901.20, 1907.02, 1905.01.
Courts of common pleas handle felony traffic prosecutions, including felony OVI cases. — R.C. § 2931.03.
The Ohio Bureau of Motor Vehicles administers license records and points suspensions. It does not decide guilt on a traffic charge. — R.C. §§ 4510.036–4510.037.

sections.heading: Common questions in Ohio
bullets: Can a minor-misdemeanor ticket mean jail? Not as the sentence for that classification; higher misdemeanor classifications permit jail. — R.C. § 2929.24.
Is the listed maximum fine the total bill? No. Court costs and other authorized sanctions can be separate. — R.C. §§ 2929.28, 2947.23.
Does every speeding conviction carry the same points? No. Ohio uses statutory speed thresholds to determine speeding points. — R.C. § 4510.036.
Is OVI always a misdemeanor? No. Certain repeat-offense categories are felonies. — R.C. § 4511.19.

sources.label: Ohio Revised Code § 2929.24 — Misdemeanor jail terms
Ohio Revised Code § 2929.28 — Financial sanctions
Ohio Revised Code § 4511.19 — OVI
Ohio Revised Code § 4510.037 — Points suspension

criminal-law/north-dakota/traffic-violat.summary: North Dakota treats many routine traffic violations as noncriminal offenses, but conduct such as reckless driving and driving under the influence can result in criminal prosecution. The consequences depend on the offense: a noncriminal violation generally carries a statutory fee, while a misdemeanor can carry jail time and a fine, and certain violations also affect driving privileges. Criminal penalties, traffic-point consequences, and administrative license proceedings operate under separate provisions of the North Dakota Century Code.

sections.heading: Noncriminal tickets and criminal traffic charges

facts.label: Noncriminal framework
facts.value: Chapter 39-06.1 establishes North Dakota’s procedures for noncriminal traffic offenses. Its exceptions identify traffic conduct that remains subject to criminal prosecution, including driving under the influence and reckless driving. A traffic citation therefore does not necessarily mean the driver faces a criminal charge. — N.D.C.C. §§ 39-06.1-02 and 39-06.1-05

facts.label: Fees are offense-specific
facts.value: North Dakota sets statutory fees for noncriminal traffic violations. Speeding fees depend on the applicable statutory category and the amount by which the driver exceeded the speed limit; there is no single fee covering every speeding violation. — N.D.C.C. § 39-06.1-06

facts.label: Points and suspension
facts.value: The Department of Transportation maintains a traffic-point system. Accumulating twelve or more points triggers suspension under the statutory schedule; the monetary fee and the licensing consequence are distinct parts of the traffic-enforcement system. — N.D.C.C. § 39-06.1-10

facts.label: Separate DUI license proceedings
facts.value: An alcohol-related driving incident can produce an administrative license proceeding separate from the criminal case. Chapter 39-20 governs chemical testing and related license consequences, including administrative hearing procedures. — N.D.C.C. §§ 39-20-04.1 and 39-20-05

rows: Handled through the noncriminal statutory framework; the applicable fee depends on the violation.
A class B misdemeanor, covering specified reckless driving or driving without due caution at a speed or in a manner likely to endanger a person or property.
Generally a class B misdemeanor. DUI has offense-specific sentencing requirements in addition to its criminal classification.
Up to thirty days of imprisonment, a $1,500 fine, or both.
Up to 360 days of imprisonment, a $3,000 fine, or both. This is a classification ceiling, not the penalty for every traffic crime.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in North Dakota
bullets: District courts handle prosecutions under state criminal traffic statutes. Municipal courts handle violations of municipal ordinances, including municipal traffic ordinances. — N.D.C.C. §§ 27-05-06 and 40-18-01
The court with jurisdiction over a noncriminal traffic citation handles a request to contest that citation under the statutory hearing process. — N.D.C.C. § 39-06.1-02

The North Dakota Department of Transportation handles driver-license records, traffic points, and administrative license proceedings. These licensing matters are separate from a court’s determination of a criminal charge. — N.D.C.C. § 39-06.1-10 and ch. 39-20

sections.heading: Common questions in North Dakota
bullets: Is every traffic ticket a criminal charge? No. Chapter 39-06.1 provides a noncriminal process for many traffic violations while expressly excluding specified offenses from that treatment.
Can reckless driving lead to jail? Yes. Reckless driving is a class B misdemeanor, whose general maximum includes thirty days of imprisonment. — N.D.C.C. §§ 39-08-03 and 12.1-32-01
Does paying a traffic fee prevent points? No. Payment does not itself exempt a point-bearing violation from the statutory point system. — N.D.C.C. § 39-06.1-10
Does a DUI involve only the criminal court? No. Administrative license proceedings under chapter 39-20 can accompany the criminal prosecution under section 39-08-01.

North Dakota Legislative Branch — Chapter 39-08, Regulations Governing Operators
North Dakota Legislative Branch — Chapter 12.1-32, Penalties and Sentencing
North Dakota Legislative Branch — Chapter 39-20, Chemical Test for Intoxication

criminal-law/oklahoma/expungement.summary: Oklahoma allows qualifying criminal records to be sealed through a district-court expungement under Title 22, Sections 18 and 19, but eligibility depends on the disposition and criminal history rather than simply how old the case is. A separate deferred-sentence procedure under Section 991c is narrower and does not itself erase the arrest record maintained by the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation (OSBI). Sealing also does not necessarily eliminate access by law enforcement.

facts.label: Full-record expungement framework
facts.value: Section 18 identifies people authorized to seek expungement; Section 19 supplies the court procedure. For these provisions, expungement means sealing criminal records, not physically destroying them. Eligibility alone does not guarantee that the court will grant relief. — 22 O.S. §§ 18–19

facts.label: Deferred-sentence relief
facts.value: After successful completion of a deferred judgment, Section 991c provides for discharge without a judgment of guilt, expungement of the guilty or nolo contendere plea, and dismissal of the charge. This is distinct from sealing arrest and criminal-history records under Sections 18 and 19. — 22 O.S. § 991c

facts.label: Court’s balancing test
facts.value: At the expungement hearing, the court considers whether harm to privacy or other dangers to the person outweigh the public interest in retaining the records. The statute permits sealing all or part of the record. — 22 O.S. § 19

rows: A person acquitted of the charge is within an expressly authorized category.
The conviction must have been reversed with instructions to dismiss by an appellate court of competent jurisdiction, followed by dismissal.
Factual innocence established through DNA evidence subsequent to conviction is an eligibility category.
The person must have received a full gubernatorial pardon based on a written finding of actual innocence.
Section 18 also contains conditional categories involving dismissals, deferred sentences, misdemeanors, and certain nonviolent felonies; these are not blanket eligibility rules.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Oklahoma
bullets: A Section 18 expungement petition is filed in the district court for the district where the arrest occurred. The district court, rather than OSBI, decides the petition. — 22 O.S. § 19(A)

The court must set a hearing and provide at least 30 days’ notice to the prosecuting agency, the arresting agency, OSBI, and any other person or agency the court believes may have relevant information. — 22 O.S. § 19(B)

OSBI maintains Oklahoma’s statewide criminal-history repository and processes expungement orders affecting its records. Its administrative role is separate from the district court’s authority to order sealing. — Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation; 22 O.S. § 19

sections.heading: Common questions in Oklahoma
bullets: Does a dismissal automatically seal everything? No. Dismissal and record sealing are different legal events; Section 18 eligibility and Section 19 procedures govern broader sealing.

Does completing a deferred sentence remove my OSBI arrest record? Not by itself. Section 991c relief concerns the plea and deferred criminal proceeding; broader criminal-history sealing is a separate matter.
Are sealed records destroyed? No. Oklahoma defines this expungement as sealing, and Section 19 preserves specified law-enforcement access. — 22 O.S. §§ 18(B), 19

Can an ordinary pardon establish the actual-innocence category? No. That particular category requires a full pardon based on a written finding of actual innocence. Other eligibility categories have separate requirements. — 22 O.S. § 18(A)(4)

sources.label: Oklahoma State Courts Network — Title 22, Criminal Procedure, Sections 18, 19, and 991c
Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation — criminal-history and expungement information

criminal-law/oklahoma/bail-and-bond.summary: Oklahoma’s Constitution generally guarantees release before trial on sufficient sureties, but it permits denial of bail for specified categories of charges when constitutional requirements are met. Excessive bail is prohibited, and a court’s release decision is separate from a commercial bondsman’s agreement to provide a bond. Oklahoma district courts handle criminal bail proceedings, while the Oklahoma Insurance Department regulates licensed bail bondsmen; bond forfeiture is governed by statutory procedures distinct from the prosecution of the underlying charge.

facts.label: General right to bail
facts.value: All persons are generally bailable by sufficient sureties. The Constitution identifies exceptions rather than making pretrial release unconditional for every criminal charge. — Oklahoma Constitution, Article II, § 8

facts.label: Capital charges
facts.value: The constitutional exception for capital offenses applies when the proof of guilt is evident or the presumption of guilt is great. A capital charge therefore falls under a different constitutional bail rule from an ordinary bailable offense. — Oklahoma Constitution, Article II, § 8

facts.label: Other categories permitting denial
facts.value: The Constitution also identifies violent offenses, offenses carrying a maximum sentence of life imprisonment or life without parole, certain felony charges involving prior felony convictions, and specified controlled-dangerous-substances offenses. For these noncapital categories, denial requires the prescribed showing concerning guilt and a determination that no release conditions would assure the safety of another person or the community. — Oklahoma Constitution, Article II, § 8

facts.label: Excessive bail
facts.value: Oklahoma expressly prohibits excessive bail. This protection is separate from the constitutional provisions identifying when bail may be denied altogether. — Oklahoma Constitution, Article II, § 9

sections.heading: Key distinctions in Oklahoma bail proceedings

rows: The constitutional starting point is bail by sufficient sureties, subject to enumerated exceptions.
The Constitution prohibits an excessive bail requirement.
The Insurance Commissioner administers Oklahoma’s statutory bail-bondsman licensing framework.
Appearance-bond forfeiture follows statutory procedures governing the court and bondsman; forfeiture is not a conviction of the charged offense.
District courts have general original jurisdiction, including criminal proceedings.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Oklahoma
bullets: Criminal bail proceedings: The district court handling the criminal case is the forum for the case’s bail and release determinations. District courts’ general jurisdiction is established by Oklahoma Constitution, Article VII, § 7.

Bondsman licensing or regulatory complaints: The Oklahoma Insurance Department regulates bail bondsmen under the Insurance Commissioner’s authority. An administrative complaint concerns the regulated bondsman, not appellate review of a judge’s bail ruling. — 59 O.S. § 1302.

Bond-forfeiture proceedings: The court administering the appearance bond handles forfeiture under the statutory process. This is distinct from the Insurance Department’s licensing role. — 59 O.S. § 1332.

sections.heading: Common questions in Oklahoma
bullets: Is everyone entitled to bail? No. Article II, § 8 establishes a general right but includes capital and specified noncapital exceptions.

Does a violent charge automatically require detention without bail? No. The noncapital exception requires the constitutional findings concerning guilt and whether release conditions can assure another person’s or the community’s safety.
Can Oklahoma require excessive bail? No. Article II, § 9 expressly prohibits excessive bail.
Does the Insurance Department decide whether a defendant gets released? No. It regulates bondsmen; judicial bail decisions belong to the courts.

sources.label: Oklahoma State Courts Network — Oklahoma Constitution
Oklahoma State Courts Network — Title 59, Professions and Occupations
Oklahoma Insurance Department

criminal-law/oklahoma/traffic-violations.summary: Oklahoma traffic cases can involve state criminal charges or municipal ordinance violations, depending on the conduct and where the case is filed; there is no single statewide penalty for every ticket. Title 47 governs major offenses such as speeding, reckless driving, and driving under the influence, while local ordinances govern municipal charges. A conviction can also have driver-license consequences separate from the court’s sentence, and commercial drivers face additional statutory rules.

sections.heading: How Oklahoma traffic charges are classified

facts.label: State-law violations
facts.value: Violations of Title 47 are generally misdemeanors unless the law declares the particular violation a felony. The charging statute matters because individual offenses can have their own penalties and repeat-offender provisions. — 47 O.S. § 17-101.

facts.label: Reckless driving
facts.value: Driving carelessly or wantonly without regard for the safety of persons or property can constitute reckless driving. For a first conviction, the statute authorizes five to 90 days in jail, a $100 to $500 fine, or both. — 47 O.S. § 11-901.

facts.label: DUI is not limited to alcohol
facts.value: Oklahoma’s DUI statute covers specified alcohol concentrations and driving under the influence of alcohol, intoxicating substances, or a combination. It applies to driving, operating, or being in actual physical control of a motor vehicle under the circumstances specified in the statute. — 47 O.S. § 11-902.

rows: Speed must be reasonable and proper for traffic, road conditions, and other existing conditions; compliance with a posted limit does not replace that duty.
The statute specifies the duties associated with green, yellow, and red traffic-control signals.
Drivers approaching stop or yield signs must comply with the stopping and right-of-way requirements applicable to the intersection.
Careless or wanton driving without regard for safety is a distinct offense, not merely another name for speeding.
The statute includes an alcohol concentration of 0.08 or more measured within its specified testing period, as well as separate impairment-based grounds.

facts.label: Separate consequences
facts.value: A criminal traffic case and a driver-license action are different proceedings. Oklahoma law provides for license revocation upon specified convictions and for administrative revocation in circumstances governed by the implied-consent laws. — 47 O.S. §§ 6-205, 753–754.

facts.label: Commercial driving privileges
facts.value: Commercial drivers can face disqualification under rules distinct from ordinary license sanctions, including rules addressing serious traffic violations and specified major offenses. — 47 O.S. § 6-205.2.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Oklahoma
bullets: District courts hear prosecutions under Oklahoma criminal law, including state traffic charges. Their general jurisdiction comes from Article VII, § 7 of the Oklahoma Constitution.

Municipal courts hear municipal ordinance cases within their statutory jurisdiction. Municipal courts not of record have jurisdiction over violations of their municipality’s ordinances. — 11 O.S. § 27-103.

The Oklahoma Department of Public Safety administers driver-license revocation proceedings under the implied-consent statutes; that administrative process is separate from the criminal prosecution. — 47 O.S. §§ 753–754.

sections.heading: Common questions in Oklahoma
bullets: Is every traffic violation a felony? No. Title 47 generally classifies violations as misdemeanors unless a felony classification is specified. — 47 O.S. § 17-101.
Can reckless driving result in jail? Yes. A first conviction permits five to 90 days in jail, a fine, or both. — 47 O.S. § 11-901.
Can driving below the posted limit still violate the speed law? Yes. Speed must also be reasonable and proper for existing conditions. — 47 O.S. § 11-801.
Does DUI require an alcohol test result of 0.08 or more? No. The statute also contains impairment-based grounds involving alcohol or other intoxicating substances. — 47 O.S. § 11-902.

sources.label: Oklahoma Legislature — Title 47, Motor Vehicles
Oklahoma Legislature — Title 11, Cities and Towns
Oklahoma Department of Public Safety

criminal-law/oregon/bail-and-bond.summary: Oregon uses a court-supervised pretrial release system that includes release on recognizance, conditional release, and security release; commercial bail bonds are not the state's standard release mechanism. When a court orders security release, Oregon law generally requires a deposit of 10 percent of the security amount rather than payment of the entire amount. Release decisions address court appearances and safety, and some defendants may be held without release under the Oregon Constitution's exceptions and applicable statutory procedures.

facts.label: Release decisions
facts.value: Oregon law directs the release decision toward the least onerous conditions reasonably likely to ensure the person's later appearance and the safety of the victim, the public, and the person. Courts apply statutory release criteria rather than treating payment as the only consideration. — ORS 135.230 and 135.245

facts.label: Release before an individual hearing
facts.value: Circuit court presiding judges must issue standing pretrial release orders consistent with guidelines established by the Chief Justice. These orders identify circumstances for recognizance release, conditional release, or detention pending a release decision. — ORS 135.233

facts.label: Constitutional limits
facts.value: The Oregon Constitution generally protects bail before conviction but includes exceptions for murder and treason when the proof is evident or the presumption strong. It also permits detention for qualifying violent felonies upon constitutionally required findings concerning danger and the likelihood of release-condition violations. — Oregon Constitution, Article I, sections 14 and 43

rows: Release based on a promise to appear, without a security deposit.
Nonfinancial restrictions may include supervision, limits on travel or associations, and other conditions addressing appearance and safety.
The defendant executes a security release agreement and deposits 10 percent of the court-set security amount with the clerk.
The statute also permits specified full-value security alternatives, including cash, stocks, bonds, or qualifying real property.
Discharge of the release obligations allows return of the deposit subject to statutory retention and other legally authorized dispositions; the full deposit is not necessarily refunded.

facts.label: Written obligations
facts.value: A release agreement requires the defendant to appear as ordered, submit to the court's orders and process, and comply with applicable restrictions. Leaving Oregon requires the court's permission under the statutory release conditions. — ORS 135.250 and 135.255

facts.label: Failure to appear
facts.value: A breach of the release agreement can lead to forfeiture proceedings involving security. Failure to appear can also constitute a separate crime when the elements of Oregon's failure-to-appear statutes are met. — ORS 135.280, 162.195 and 162.205

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Oregon
bullets: Release decisions and requests to change release conditions belong in the court handling the criminal case. Circuit courts handle felony prosecutions and many misdemeanor prosecutions; municipal and justice courts also handle criminal matters within their jurisdiction.

Security deposits are made through the court clerk under ORS 135.265. County jail release operations implement applicable court orders but do not replace the court's authority to determine release conditions.

sections.heading: Common questions in Oregon
bullets: Does every arrested person have to pay bail? No. Oregon authorizes recognizance and conditional release without a security deposit.
Does a $20,000 security amount normally require $20,000 upfront? No. The statutory 10 percent deposit would be $2,000 under the deposit procedure in ORS 135.265.
Does paying security end the criminal case? No. Security concerns release while the case proceeds; it does not resolve the charge or eliminate appearance requirements.
Can release conditions change? Yes. Oregon law permits modification of release decisions and sanctions for violations. For case-specific questions, talk to a lawyer. — ORS 135.285

sources.label: Oregon Legislature — ORS Chapter 135, pretrial procedure and release
Oregon Legislature — Oregon Constitution
Oregon Legislature — ORS Chapter 162, failure to appear

criminal-law/oregon/drug-charges.summary: Oregon again treats possession of many controlled substances as a crime, following changes effective September 1, 2024, under House Bill 4002. Possession of smaller amounts of drugs such as heroin, cocaine, and methamphetamine can be a drug enforcement misdemeanor, while specified quantities and other statutory circumstances can support felony charges. Manufacturing and delivery are separate offenses, and the applicable charge depends on the substance, quantity, alleged conduct, and the requirements of the particular Oregon statute.

sections.heading: Oregon possession, delivery, and manufacturing charges

facts.label: Possession after Measure 110
facts.value: House Bill 4002 replaced the Class E violation treatment for specified controlled-substance possession with a drug enforcement misdemeanor, effective September 1, 2024. The former civil-violation framework is not the current rule for those offenses — Oregon Laws 2024, chapter 70.

facts.label: Substance-specific possession statutes
facts.value: Unlawful possession of heroin is addressed in ORS 475.854; cocaine in ORS 475.884; and methamphetamine in ORS 475.894. Each statute distinguishes the basic possession offense from circumstances supporting felony treatment — ORS 475.854, 475.884, and 475.894.

facts.label: Delivery and manufacture
facts.value: Oregon separately prohibits unlawful manufacture and delivery. Heroin offenses appear in ORS 475.846 and 475.850; cocaine offenses in ORS 475.876 and 475.880; and methamphetamine offenses in ORS 475.886 and 475.890 — ORS chapter 475.

facts.label: Meaning of delivery
facts.value: Delivery includes an actual, constructive, or attempted transfer of a controlled substance from one person to another. The statutory definition does not require a sale or payment — ORS 475.005.

rows: Oregon Laws 2024, chapter 70; special sentencing provisions apply.
ORS 161.615; this is not the classification assigned to every possession offense.
ORS 161.605; the specific drug statute determines classification.
ORS 161.605; the specific drug statute determines classification.
ORS 161.605; the specific drug statute determines classification.

sections.heading: Sentencing and deflection are different processes

facts.label: Maximum does not mean mandatory
facts.value: A felony classification's statutory maximum is not automatically the sentence imposed. Oregon felony sentencing generally operates under sentencing guidelines, including rules governing presumptive sentences and departures — ORS 161.605 and 137.669.

facts.label: Drug enforcement misdemeanor sentencing
facts.value: The 2024 legislation established special sentencing provisions for drug enforcement misdemeanors. Their 180-day maximum should not be treated as an automatic jail sentence for every conviction — Oregon Laws 2024, chapter 70.

facts.label: County deflection programs
facts.value: House Bill 4002 established a state-supported framework for local deflection programs connecting people with substance-use treatment and other services as an alternative to criminal justice involvement. Availability and program operation vary locally; deflection is not automatic statewide dismissal — Oregon Laws 2024, chapter 70.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Oregon
bullets: State criminal drug prosecutions ordinarily proceed in the Oregon circuit court for the relevant county. Circuit courts are Oregon's general-jurisdiction trial courts.
County district attorneys prosecute state criminal charges. A treatment provider or deflection program does not itself exercise the prosecutor's charging authority.
The Oregon Criminal Justice Commission administers the state's deflection grant program; participating counties operate local programs under the statutory framework.
Questions about a particular charge, defense, or sentencing exposure: talk to a lawyer.

sections.heading: Common questions in Oregon
bullets: Is possession still only a ticket under Measure 110? No. Specified possession offenses became drug enforcement misdemeanors on September 1, 2024.
Is every possession case a misdemeanor? No. Substance-specific statutes retain felony classifications for specified quantities or circumstances.
Must money change hands for delivery? No. Oregon's definition includes transfers and attempted transfers without requiring payment.
Does a felony maximum predict the sentence? No. Guidelines, offense-specific provisions, and the case's circumstances affect sentencing.

Oregon Legislature — ORS chapter 161
Oregon Legislature — 2024 HB 4002 enrolled
Oregon Judicial Department — Circuit Courts

criminal-law/oregon/expungement.summary: Oregon generally calls adult criminal expungement a “set aside” under ORS 137.225: a court order setting aside an eligible conviction or arrest-related record and sealing the associated official records. Eligibility depends on the offense, the outcome of the case, the applicable waiting period, completion of the sentence, and other criminal history or pending charges. Not every conviction qualifies, and Oregon has separate procedures for juvenile records rather than one expungement rule covering every case.

sections.heading: What an Oregon set-aside order does

facts.label: Legal effect
facts.value: After entry of a qualifying order, the applicant is deemed, for purposes of law, not to have been previously convicted, arrested, cited, or charged as covered by the order. The statute permits answers to questions about that history accordingly, subject to statutory exceptions. — ORS 137.225

facts.label: Sealing rather than physical destruction
facts.value: The court orders the relevant official records sealed, including records held by law enforcement agencies. This is not a guarantee that privately collected information, news coverage, or every independently maintained record disappears. — ORS 137.225

facts.label: Sentence completion
facts.value: For a conviction set aside, the applicant must have fully complied with and performed the court’s sentence. Passage of the waiting period alone does not establish eligibility. — ORS 137.225

rows: Conviction or release from imprisonment for that conviction, whichever is later — ORS 137.225
Conviction or release from imprisonment for that conviction, whichever is later — ORS 137.225
Conviction or release from imprisonment for that conviction, whichever is later — ORS 137.225
Eligible Class B or Class C misdemeanor, or violation
Conviction or release from imprisonment for that conviction, whichever is later — ORS 137.225

facts.label: Excluded offenses
facts.value: Convictions for driving under the influence of intoxicants are excluded. Most sex-crime convictions are also excluded, although the statute contains limited exceptions. An offense’s classification alone does not establish eligibility. — ORS 137.225

facts.label: Other criminal proceedings
facts.value: Pending criminal charges and other convictions can prevent a set aside. The statute contains criminal-history restrictions and exceptions, so the waiting-period table is not a complete eligibility test. — ORS 137.225

facts.label: Cases without a conviction
facts.value: The statute separately addresses arrests, citations, and charges that did not result in conviction, including acquittals and dismissals. Those applications do not use the conviction waiting-period table. — ORS 137.225

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Oregon
bullets: A conviction set-aside motion is filed in the court that entered the conviction. The prosecuting attorney receives a copy. — ORS 137.225

The Oregon Judicial Department publishes adult set-aside forms and instructions. A set aside requires court action; it is not obtained by submitting a general complaint to a state agency. — Oregon Judicial Department, Set Aside forms

For conviction applications, fingerprint-based criminal-history review through the Oregon State Police is part of the statutory process. No court filing fee is charged for a motion under ORS 137.225. — ORS 137.225

sections.heading: Common questions in Oregon
bullets: Does eligibility automatically seal the record? No. An eligible person must obtain a court order under ORS 137.225.
Can an Oregon DUII conviction be set aside? No. DUII convictions are excluded under ORS 137.225.
Can a dismissed charge qualify? Yes. ORS 137.225 provides a route for qualifying dismissed charges, subject to its conditions and exclusions.
Does finishing probation erase a conviction? No. Sentence completion and a set-aside order are different legal events. For an individual eligibility assessment, talk to a lawyer.

sources.label: Oregon Legislature — ORS Chapter 137, including ORS 137.225
Oregon Judicial Department — Set Aside forms

criminal-law/oregon/juvenile-law.summary: Oregon generally handles allegations that a person committed a crime before turning 18 in juvenile court under ORS chapter 419C, rather than through an ordinary adult criminal prosecution. Juvenile proceedings provide rights to counsel and proof beyond a reasonable doubt, but adjudication is by a judge rather than a jury. Possible outcomes include probation, restitution, and commitment to the Oregon Youth Authority; specified cases can be transferred to adult court through statutory waiver proceedings.

sections.heading: Oregon juvenile jurisdiction and procedural rights

facts.label: Which cases belong in juvenile court
facts.value: The juvenile court has exclusive original jurisdiction over a person under 18 who commits an act violating federal, state, or local law, subject to statutory exceptions. Jurisdiction can continue beyond the eighteenth birthday, but the ordinary statutory ceiling is age 25. — ORS 419C.005

facts.label: Right to a lawyer
facts.value: A youth has the right to counsel in proceedings under ORS chapter 419C. Court-appointed representation is governed by the statute's eligibility and appointment provisions; representation is not limited to the adjudication hearing itself. — ORS 419C.200

facts.label: Judge and burden of proof
facts.value: The court conducts the adjudication hearing without a jury. Facts establishing juvenile court jurisdiction must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt; allegations in a petition alone do not establish responsibility. — ORS 419C.400

facts.label: Adult-court transfer
facts.value: Oregon permits waiver to adult court for qualifying allegations involving youths age 15 or older. Transfer requires the findings specified by statute, including findings addressing the youth's sophistication and maturity and whether retaining juvenile jurisdiction serves the relevant interests. — ORS 419C.349

rows: A juvenile adjudication is not a criminal conviction. That distinction does not eliminate every possible legal consequence.
The juvenile court may place an adjudicated youth on probation under court-imposed conditions.
A disposition may include restitution for economic damages resulting from the adjudicated conduct, under the statutory restitution process.
The court may commit an adjudicated youth to the Oregon Youth Authority when the statutory requirements are satisfied.
Access and disclosure depend on the type of juvenile record and the statutory exception involved; juvenile records are not uniformly public or uniformly secret.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Oregon
bullets: Juvenile court: Oregon circuit courts exercise juvenile jurisdiction. Delinquency petitions and court proceedings fall within that jurisdiction, rather than a separate statewide juvenile tribunal. — ORS 419B.100; ORS 419C.005

County juvenile department: County juvenile departments perform statutory juvenile-justice functions, including work connected with referrals, supervision, and juvenile court proceedings. Their role is distinct from the judge's authority to adjudicate a petition. — ORS 419A.010; ORS 419A.020

Oregon Youth Authority: OYA is the state agency responsible for youths committed to its legal custody. It is not the court that determines whether the allegations in a delinquency petition are proved. — ORS 419C.478; ORS chapter 420A

sections.heading: Common questions in Oregon
bullets: Does turning 18 automatically end a juvenile case? No. Oregon law allows juvenile jurisdiction to continue into adulthood, subject to statutory termination rules and the age ceiling. — ORS 419C.005
Does a youth receive a jury trial in juvenile court? No. The judge hears the adjudication, although the state must establish jurisdictional facts beyond a reasonable doubt. — ORS 419C.400
Can a juvenile case become an adult prosecution? Yes. Oregon provides statutory waiver procedures; age alone does not establish that the requirements for waiver are met. — ORS 419C.349

Are juvenile records automatically confidential forever? No. Oregon distinguishes among records and permits specified disclosures. Expunction is a separate statutory process with eligibility rules and exclusions. — ORS 419A.255; ORS 419A.262

sources.label: Oregon Legislature — ORS chapter 419C, Juvenile Code: Delinquency
Oregon Legislature — ORS chapter 419A, Juvenile Code: General Provisions
Oregon Legislature — ORS chapter 419B, Juvenile Code: Dependency
Oregon Legislature — ORS chapter 420A, Oregon Youth Authority

criminal-law/oregon/traffic-violations.summary: Oregon treats many traffic offenses as violations, but conduct such as driving under the influence of intoxicants (DUII), reckless driving, and leaving a property-damage crash without fulfilling statutory duties can be criminal. The distinction matters because violations do not authorize jail, while criminal traffic offenses can bring incarceration, probation, fines, and license consequences. The charge, prior convictions, and circumstances determine the applicable penalties; court proceedings and Oregon Driver and Motor Vehicle Services (DMV) licensing actions can involve separate processes.

facts.label: Noncriminal violations
facts.value: An offense designated as a violation does not authorize imprisonment. Oregon's traffic statutes classify many ordinary driving offenses this way rather than as misdemeanors or felonies. — ORS 153.008

facts.label: Violation trials
facts.value: A traffic-violation case is tried to the court without a jury. The prosecution must prove the violation by a preponderance of the evidence, and the defendant has no right to appointed counsel at public expense for that proceeding. — ORS 153.076

facts.label: Criminal cases
facts.value: For a criminal traffic charge, the prosecution must prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. A criminal conviction is distinct from a DMV administrative licensing action arising from the same driving incident. — ORS 136.415; ORS 813.410

rows: Generally a Class B traffic violation; it becomes a Class A traffic violation when it contributes to an accident.
Class A misdemeanor for recklessly driving on a highway or premises open to the public in a manner that endangers persons or property.
Generally a Class A misdemeanor; specified repeat-offense circumstances make it a Class C felony. The statute covers alcohol and other intoxicants.
Failure to perform duties of a driver when property is damaged
Class A misdemeanor. Duties depend on the circumstances and include stopping and providing required identifying information.

facts.label: Class A misdemeanor limits
facts.value: The ordinary maximum sentence is 364 days of imprisonment and a $6,250 fine. These are maximums, not the automatic sentence for every criminal traffic conviction. Offense-specific requirements can also apply. — ORS 161.615; ORS 161.635

facts.label: DUII diversion
facts.value: Oregon has a court-supervised DUII diversion process for defendants who meet statutory eligibility requirements. Successful completion can result in dismissal of the DUII charge; diversion is not available automatically to every person charged. — ORS 813.200–813.255

facts.label: Separate license proceedings
facts.value: An implied-consent suspension involving a chemical-test failure or refusal has an administrative process separate from the prosecution. A DUII conviction also carries statutory license consequences. — ORS 813.100; ORS 813.400; ORS 813.410

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Oregon
bullets: Traffic citations identify the court handling the case. Depending on location and jurisdiction, traffic matters may be heard in a circuit court, justice court, or municipal court. — ORS 153.036; ORS 153.045

Oregon DMV handles driver records and administrative licensing matters, including the implied-consent hearing process. A court challenge to an administrative decision is governed by separate statutory review provisions. — ORS 813.410; ORS 813.450

Criminal traffic prosecutions proceed in a court with criminal jurisdiction. Circuit courts have general jurisdiction; municipal and justice court criminal authority is limited by law. — Oregon Constitution, Article VII (Original), section 9; ORS 51.050; ORS 221.339

sections.heading: Common questions in Oregon
bullets: Can a traffic violation itself result in jail? No. An offense classified as a violation does not authorize imprisonment. Criminal traffic offenses are different. — ORS 153.008

Are careless driving and reckless driving the same? No. Careless driving is a traffic violation, while reckless driving is a Class A misdemeanor with a different statutory standard. — ORS 811.135; ORS 811.140
Is every DUII a misdemeanor? No. Oregon classifies DUII as a felony in specified repeat-offense circumstances. — ORS 813.010
Does resolving the criminal case automatically resolve a DMV suspension? No. Implied-consent licensing proceedings and criminal proceedings are separate. — ORS 813.410

sources.label: Oregon Legislature — ORS Chapter 811
Oregon Legislature — ORS Chapter 813
Oregon Legislature — ORS Chapter 153
Oregon Legislature — ORS Chapter 161

criminal-law/oregon/plea-bargaining.summary: Oregon law expressly permits plea discussions between prosecutors and represented defendants through defense counsel, or directly with defendants who do not have counsel. A negotiated resolution can involve charges or sentencing recommendations, but the court must independently determine that a guilty or no-contest plea is voluntary and intelligently made before accepting it. Oregon also permits certain conditional pleas that preserve specified pretrial issues for appeal, with the required written reservation and approvals.

facts.label: Statutory authority
facts.value: Oregon’s plea-discussion statutes authorize prosecutors to negotiate with defense counsel, or with an unrepresented defendant, toward an agreement involving a guilty or no-contest plea. Negotiations can concern other charges and the prosecutor’s sentencing position. — ORS 135.405

facts.label: Defense counsel’s responsibilities
facts.value: Defense counsel may not conclude a plea agreement without the defendant’s consent and must advise the defendant of plea offers and developments in plea discussions. The decision to accept a negotiated plea belongs to the defendant. — ORS 135.425

facts.label: Court review
facts.value: The court must determine that a guilty or no-contest plea is voluntary and intelligently made. An agreement between the prosecution and defense does not eliminate this requirement. — ORS 135.390

rows: A defendant may plead guilty, not guilty, or, with the court’s consent, no contest.
With the court’s and state’s consent, a defendant may plead guilty or no contest while reserving in writing appellate review of an adverse determination of a specified pretrial motion.
A defendant who prevails on the reserved appeal may withdraw the plea.
Before entering judgment on a guilty plea, the court must make an inquiry sufficient to satisfy itself that a factual basis exists.
Before judgment, the court may permit withdrawal of a guilty or no-contest plea and substitution of a not-guilty plea. Permission is discretionary under this provision.

facts.label: Personal explanation by the judge
facts.value: Before accepting a guilty or no-contest plea, the court must personally address the defendant and explain specified consequences, including waiver of jury trial, confrontation, and the privilege against self-incrimination, along with the maximum possible sentence and any mandatory minimum sentence. — ORS 135.385

facts.label: Immigration warning
facts.value: The required plea advisement includes notice that a conviction may result in deportation, exclusion from admission to the United States, or denial of naturalization under federal law for a defendant who is not a United States citizen. — ORS 135.385

facts.label: Limits on appeal
facts.value: A guilty or no-contest plea restricts appellate review of the conviction. Conditional pleas provide a statutory route for preserving specified pretrial issues; review of sentencing issues is separately governed by Oregon’s criminal-appeal statutes. — ORS 135.335(3); ORS 138.105

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Oregon
bullets: A plea is entered in the trial court handling the criminal case. Oregon circuit courts handle felony prosecutions and also hear misdemeanor cases; some misdemeanors are handled in municipal or justice courts.
Plea negotiations involve the prosecuting office responsible for the case and defense counsel, or the defendant if unrepresented. Court clerks do not negotiate plea agreements.

The Oregon Judicial Department’s circuit-court directory identifies state trial courts. A challenge to a plea or resulting judgment is a court matter, not an administrative complaint that automatically changes the conviction.

sections.heading: Common questions in Oregon
bullets: Is a plea agreement required? No. ORS 135.405 authorizes plea discussions but does not guarantee an agreement.
Can a defendant plead no contest? Yes, with the court’s consent. ORS 135.335(1).
Can a defendant undo a plea before judgment? The court may allow withdrawal; ORS 135.365 does not make withdrawal automatic.
Can an appeal issue survive a plea? Yes. A qualifying conditional plea requires a written reservation and consent from both the court and the state. ORS 135.335(3).

sources.label: Oregon Legislature — ORS Chapter 135, Arraignment and Pretrial Provisions
Oregon Legislature — ORS Chapter 138, Appeals and Post-Conviction Relief
Oregon Judicial Department — Oregon Circuit Courts

criminal-law/pennsylvania/bail-and-bond.summary: Pennsylvania generally permits release on bail before conviction, but the state constitution allows detention in specified cases, including capital charges, offenses carrying a maximum sentence of life imprisonment, and cases where no release conditions can reasonably assure safety, when the constitutional evidentiary standard is met. Pennsylvania’s criminal rules recognize five types of release, and the bail authority must consider individual circumstances rather than treat the charge alone as controlling; monetary bail is not required in every case.

sections.heading: Eligibility and the initial bail decision

facts.label: Constitutional exceptions
facts.value: Article I, Section 14 permits denial of bail for capital offenses, offenses whose maximum sentence is life imprisonment, or cases where no condition or combination of conditions other than imprisonment will reasonably assure the safety of any person and the community, when the proof is evident or presumption great. Excessive bail is prohibited. — Pennsylvania Constitution, Article I, §§ 13–14

facts.label: Individual assessment
facts.value: The bail authority considers relevant information about the charge, employment and finances, family relationships, residence, age, character, mental condition, criminal record, previous court appearances, and other factors bearing on appearance and compliance. — Pa.R.Crim.P. 523

facts.label: Release conditions
facts.value: Every bail bond includes obligations to appear as required, obey further orders, notify the bail authority of an address change, and refrain from criminal activity and witness or victim intimidation. Additional conditions may be imposed under the bail rules. — Pa.R.Crim.P. 526–527

sections.heading: Types of bail available in Pennsylvania

rows: Release on the defendant’s agreement to comply with the bond’s conditions, without monetary security. — Pa.R.Crim.P. 524(C)(1)
Release subject to additional conditions considered necessary to reasonably ensure appearance and compliance. — Pa.R.Crim.P. 524(C)(2)
No money is deposited initially; the defendant agrees to liability for a fixed sum upon failure to appear or comply. — Pa.R.Crim.P. 524(C)(3)
Release requires nominal cash security and a designated person, organization, or bail agency serving as surety. — Pa.R.Crim.P. 524(C)(4)
Release depends on compliance with an imposed monetary condition. The amount must be reasonably necessary to ensure appearance and compliance. — Pa.R.Crim.P. 524(C)(5), 528

facts.label: Changing bail
facts.value: Bail conditions can be modified through the procedures governing issuing authorities and courts. Authority to change an existing order depends on which judicial officer imposed it and the case’s procedural stage. — Pa.R.Crim.P. 529

facts.label: Violations
facts.value: Violating release conditions can lead to an arrest warrant, modification of conditions, or revocation of release. Monetary bail may also be forfeited under the rule’s procedures; forfeiture concerns the security pledged for the bond. — Pa.R.Crim.P. 536

facts.label: Duration
facts.value: Unless revoked, a bail bond generally remains effective through final disposition, including direct appeals to Pennsylvania appellate courts. The rules separately govern eligibility for release after a finding of guilt. — Pa.R.Crim.P. 521, 534

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Pennsylvania
bullets: Initial bail ordinarily is set by the issuing authority at the preliminary arraignment, commonly a magisterial district judge; Philadelphia uses its Municipal Court procedures. — Pa.R.Crim.P. 540, 1003

Requests to modify bail are judicial matters handled under Rule 529, including proceedings in the Court of Common Pleas. A complaint to an administrative agency does not itself change a bail order. — Pa.R.Crim.P. 529

sections.heading: Common questions in Pennsylvania
bullets: Does every defendant have to pay cash? No. Recognizance, nonmonetary conditions, and unsecured bonds are recognized alternatives. — Pa.R.Crim.P. 524

Is there a statewide fixed price for each charge? The rules require consideration of individual factors, and monetary bail must be reasonably necessary for appearance and compliance. — Pa.R.Crim.P. 523, 528
Can bail change after release? Yes. Conditions may be modified, and violations can result in revocation. — Pa.R.Crim.P. 529, 536
Does bail automatically end at sentencing? No. The bond generally continues through final disposition, but post-conviction release is subject to separate rules. — Pa.R.Crim.P. 521, 534

Pennsylvania Code: Rule 523, Release Criteria
Pennsylvania Code: Rule 524, Types of Release on Bail
Pennsylvania Code: Rule 536, Procedures Upon Violation of Conditions

criminal-law/pennsylvania/juvenile-law.summary: Pennsylvania generally handles alleged crimes committed by children age 10 or older and under 18 through delinquency proceedings under the Juvenile Act, rather than ordinary criminal prosecution. The Court of Common Pleas hears these cases, where the central questions are whether the child committed a delinquent act and needs treatment, supervision, or rehabilitation. Some offenses fall outside the Act’s definition of a delinquent act, and other cases can be transferred to criminal court under statutory procedures.

facts.label: Governing law and court
facts.value: The Juvenile Act governs delinquency proceedings in the Court of Common Pleas. Its purposes include accountability, community protection, and developing competencies that help children become responsible community members. — 42 Pa.C.S. §§ 6301–6303.

facts.label: Age limits
facts.value: A delinquent act generally means a qualifying offense committed by a child age 10 or older. The Act generally defines a child as someone under 18, but also includes someone under 21 who committed a delinquent act before turning 18. — 42 Pa.C.S. § 6302.

facts.label: Criminal-court exceptions
facts.value: Murder is excluded from the definition of a delinquent act. Certain other serious offenses are also excluded when statutory age, weapon, or prior-adjudication conditions apply. Separate provisions govern transfers between juvenile and criminal proceedings. — 42 Pa.C.S. §§ 6302, 6322, 6355.

rows: When a child is not released, an informal hearing must occur no later than 72 hours after placement in detention or shelter care.
For a detained child, the hearing generally must be held no later than 10 days after the petition is filed, subject to statutory exceptions.
A party is entitled to counsel at all stages of proceedings under the Act, with appointed counsel when financially unable to employ counsel.
The court must find beyond a reasonable doubt that the child committed the alleged delinquent acts.
Juvenile Act hearings are conducted by the court without a jury.

facts.label: Disposition options
facts.value: Available orders include probation, restitution, fines within statutory conditions, and placement. The disposition must address the child’s needs and public protection; placement is not automatic after every adjudication. — 42 Pa.C.S. § 6352.

facts.label: Not an ordinary criminal conviction
facts.value: A juvenile disposition is not a criminal conviction and does not impose the civil disabilities ordinarily resulting from conviction. However, the statute permits specified later uses of juvenile adjudications, including certain sentencing uses. — 42 Pa.C.S. § 6354.

facts.label: Privacy and expungement
facts.value: Juvenile records have restricted access, but statutory exceptions permit disclosure. Expungement is a separate statutory process; turning 18 alone does not establish entitlement to erase every juvenile record. — 42 Pa.C.S. § 6307; 18 Pa.C.S. § 9123.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Pennsylvania
bullets: Delinquency proceedings: the county Court of Common Pleas exercises juvenile jurisdiction. Statutory venue rules determine the proper county. — 42 Pa.C.S. §§ 6302, 6321.
Informal adjustment: an authorized probation officer may adjust a complaint without a petition when statutory conditions are met. — 42 Pa.C.S. § 6323.
Expungement: juvenile-record expungement requires a court order under the applicable statutory grounds. — 18 Pa.C.S. § 9123.

sections.heading: Common questions in Pennsylvania
bullets: Does every juvenile case stay in juvenile court? No. Offense exclusions and transfer provisions can place a case in criminal court. — 42 Pa.C.S. §§ 6302, 6322, 6355.
Does jurisdiction always end at 18? No. The statutory definition can cover a person under 21 for conduct committed before 18. — 42 Pa.C.S. § 6302.
Are all hearings private? No. The Act permits public access in specified circumstances. — 42 Pa.C.S. § 6336.
Does proof of an offense automatically establish delinquency? No. The court also determines whether the child needs treatment, supervision, or rehabilitation. — 42 Pa.C.S. § 6341(b).

sources.label: Pennsylvania General Assembly — Juvenile Act, Title 42, Chapter 63
Pennsylvania General Assembly — Juvenile Records Expungement, 18 Pa.C.S. § 9123

criminal-law/south-carolina/bail-and-bon.summary: South Carolina generally provides for release on personal recognizance without a secured bond for people charged with noncapital offenses, unless that release would not reasonably assure their appearance or would create an unreasonable danger to the community. Courts may impose financial and nonfinancial release conditions, while the state constitution allows bail to be denied in specified circumstances. The initial bond proceeding concerns pretrial release, not whether the accused is guilty.

sections.heading: South Carolina’s rules for pretrial release

facts.label: Constitutional protection
facts.value: The South Carolina Constitution prohibits excessive bail. It permits denial of bail for capital offenses, offenses punishable by life imprisonment, and legislatively defined violent offenses when the proof is evident or the presumption great. — South Carolina Constitution, Article I, § 15

facts.label: Personal recognizance
facts.value: For a noncapital offense, the statutory starting point is release on personal recognizance without surety and with an unsecured appearance bond, subject to the court’s assessment of appearance and community safety. This is not an automatic entitlement to release without conditions. — S.C. Code § 17-15-10

facts.label: Individual circumstances
facts.value: The court considers available information about the accused’s circumstances, including family ties, employment, financial resources, character and mental condition, residence in the community, convictions, and history of appearing in court or fleeing prosecution. — S.C. Code § 17-15-30

rows: An arrested person must be brought before a magistrate or municipal judge without unnecessary delay and no later than 24 hours after arrest.
South Carolina Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 2
Release may place the accused in the custody of a designated person or organization agreeing to provide supervision.
The court may restrict travel, association, or place of abode during release.
The court may require an appearance bond secured by a cash deposit or acceptable sureties.
Electronic monitoring is among the conditions the court may impose when reasonably necessary under the release statute.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in South Carolina
bullets: Initial bond proceedings ordinarily occur in magistrate or municipal court. Rule 2 governs the initial appearance; a particular judge’s authority to grant bail remains subject to statutory limits.

Bond conditions are judicial orders. South Carolina’s release statutes authorize courts to impose and amend conditions; an insurance regulator does not decide whether a criminal defendant should be released. — S.C. Code §§ 17-15-20 and 17-15-40

The South Carolina Department of Insurance regulates licensed bail bondsmen and runners under Title 38, Chapter 53. Complaints about a licensed bondsman’s business conduct fall within that regulatory framework, rather than the criminal court’s determination of bail.

sections.heading: Common questions in South Carolina
bullets: Does everyone qualify for recognizance release? No. Section 17-15-10 allows a different release arrangement when recognizance would not reasonably assure appearance or would create an unreasonable danger to the community.

Must every defendant hire a commercial bondsman? No. South Carolina law provides for recognizance release and other arrangements, including a cash-secured appearance bond. — S.C. Code §§ 17-15-10 and 17-15-20
Can release include restrictions beyond money? Yes. Supervision, travel and association restrictions, and electronic monitoring are statutory possibilities. — S.C. Code § 17-15-20

Does the 24-hour rule guarantee release within 24 hours? No. Rule 2 establishes the deadline for the initial appearance, not a guarantee that bail will be granted or that release conditions will be satisfied.

South Carolina Legislature — Constitution, Article I
South Carolina Judicial Branch — Court rules

criminal-law/south-carolina/drug-charges.summary: South Carolina drug charges depend on the substance, quantity, alleged conduct, and prior convictions; simple possession, distribution, and trafficking are different offenses under the South Carolina Controlled Substances Act. First-offense possession of one ounce or less of marijuana is a misdemeanor, while specified quantities can support trafficking charges even without an alleged sale. Penalties and eligibility for alternatives to conviction vary by the particular statutory charge.

facts.label: Possession versus distribution
facts.value: The law separately prohibits unauthorized possession and manufacturing, distributing, delivering, purchasing, or possessing with intent to distribute controlled substances. An alleged sale is not necessary for every distribution-related offense — S.C. Code § 44-53-370(a), (c).

facts.label: First-offense marijuana possession
facts.value: Possession of one ounce or less of marijuana is a misdemeanor. For a first offense, the statutory punishment is a fine of $100–$200 or imprisonment for no more than 30 days. These are statutory amounts, not a statement of the total financial obligation after applicable assessments — S.C. Code § 44-53-370(d)(4).

facts.label: Subsequent marijuana possession
facts.value: For a second or subsequent offense involving one ounce or less of marijuana, the statute provides a fine of $200–$1,000, imprisonment for no more than one year, or both — S.C. Code § 44-53-370(d)(4).

facts.label: Conditional discharge
facts.value: For qualifying possession offenses, an eligible person without a prior drug conviction may receive probation without entry of a judgment of guilt, with the person's consent. This is discretionary, not automatic; successful completion results in discharge and dismissal, and the provision may be used only once — S.C. Code § 44-53-450.

rows: 10 grams of cocaine or a mixture containing cocaine
4 grams of heroin or a mixture containing heroin
10 grams of methamphetamine or a mixture containing methamphetamine

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in South Carolina
bullets: Criminal prosecutions are brought by the State, not initiated as private civil claims for punishment. Local police departments and county sheriffs investigate drug offenses; the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division also has statewide controlled-substance enforcement responsibilities.

Magistrates and municipal courts handle qualifying lower-level offenses within their criminal jurisdiction, including first-offense simple marijuana possession. Their general criminal sentencing jurisdiction includes offenses punishable by no more than 30 days or the applicable statutory fine limit — S.C. Code §§ 22-3-550 and 14-25-65.

The Court of General Sessions is the criminal branch of South Carolina's circuit court and handles felony drug prosecutions. The county clerk of court maintains circuit-court filings, and the circuit solicitor's office prosecutes criminal cases for the State.

sections.heading: Common questions in South Carolina
bullets: Does trafficking require proof of selling drugs? No. The trafficking statutes also cover knowing actual or constructive possession of the specified quantities — S.C. Code §§ 44-53-370(e) and 44-53-375(C).

Do the listed trafficking weights mean pure drugs only? Not necessarily. The cocaine, heroin, and methamphetamine provisions expressly include mixtures containing the named substance; the statutory wording is not limited to the weight of the pure drug.

Is first-offense marijuana possession legal or merely a ticket? It remains a criminal misdemeanor. A first offense involving one ounce or less carries the statutory fine or jail exposure described above — S.C. Code § 44-53-370(d)(4).

Does conditional discharge automatically erase records? No. Discharge and dismissal are distinct from expungement. Section 44-53-450 separately provides an application process for an expungement order.

criminal-law/south-carolina/felony-vs-mi.summary: South Carolina does not use a simple one-year dividing line between felonies and misdemeanors: some misdemeanors carry as much as three years in prison, while classified felonies have maximum terms ranging from five to thirty years. The state’s classification statutes and the statute defining the particular offense determine its classification and authorized punishment. Some offenses fall outside the classification system, and the charge also affects whether proceedings belong in summary court or the Court of General Sessions.

sections.heading: How South Carolina classifies criminal offenses

facts.label: Classification system
facts.value: South Carolina establishes six felony classes, A through F, and three misdemeanor classes, A through C. The classification provisions also recognize offenses exempt from that system. — S.C. Code §§ 16-1-10, 16-1-20

facts.label: Offense lists
facts.value: The code separately lists classified felonies and misdemeanors. A charge’s statutory designation matters; a possible sentence longer than one year does not automatically make a South Carolina offense a felony. — S.C. Code §§ 16-1-90, 16-1-100

facts.label: Exempt offenses
facts.value: The classification table is not a complete sentencing guide. Exempt offenses are governed by their own penalty provisions, and offense-specific statutes may contain additional sentencing requirements. — S.C. Code §§ 16-1-10, 16-1-20

sections.heading: Maximum imprisonment by class under S.C. Code § 16-1-20

facts.label: First degree
facts.value: Assault and battery in the first degree is a felony punishable by imprisonment for not more than ten years. — S.C. Code § 16-3-600(C)

facts.label: Second degree
facts.value: Assault and battery in the second degree is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of not more than $2,500, imprisonment for not more than three years, or both. This illustrates why sentence length alone does not establish felony status. — S.C. Code § 16-3-600(D)

facts.label: Third degree
facts.value: Assault and battery in the third degree is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of not more than $500, imprisonment for not more than thirty days, or both. — S.C. Code § 16-3-600(E)

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in South Carolina
bullets: Court of General Sessions: This is the circuit court’s criminal court. Its criminal jurisdiction includes cases not assigned exclusively to an inferior court; it handles felony prosecutions and misdemeanors beyond summary-court jurisdiction. — S.C. Code § 14-5-340

Magistrates court: The general criminal trial jurisdiction covers offenses punishable by a fine or forfeiture not exceeding $500, imprisonment not exceeding thirty days, or both, subject to statutory exceptions. — S.C. Code § 22-3-550

Preliminary hearings: Magistrates have authority to conduct preliminary examinations in criminal cases beyond their trial jurisdiction. A magistrate’s involvement therefore does not establish that the charge is a misdemeanor. — S.C. Code § 22-3-540

sections.heading: Common questions in South Carolina
bullets: Can a misdemeanor carry three years? Yes. Class A misdemeanors have a three-year maximum under the classification statute. — S.C. Code § 16-1-20
Does every felony have a maximum of thirty years or less? No. The classification chart does not cover every offense; exempt offenses have separate punishment provisions. — S.C. Code § 16-1-10
Are all misdemeanors tried in magistrates court? No. General magistrates-court jurisdiction has punishment limits, and some misdemeanors exceed those limits. — S.C. Code §§ 22-3-550, 14-5-340
Is a class maximum a mandatory sentence? No. A maximum is a ceiling, not itself a mandatory minimum. The offense’s separate sentencing provisions also matter. — S.C. Code § 16-1-20

South Carolina Legislature — Title 16, Chapter 3: Offenses Against the Person
South Carolina Legislature — Title 22, Chapter 3: Jurisdiction and Procedure in Magistrates' Courts

criminal-law/south-carolina/expungement.summary: South Carolina allows expungement for qualifying dismissed charges, acquittals, completed diversion cases, and certain convictions, but eligibility depends on the disposition and the statute covering the offense. There is no general right to erase every misdemeanor or felony: conviction-based relief can depend on the offense’s maximum penalty, the time since conviction or completion of a sentence, and later convictions. Adult expungement applications generally go through the circuit solicitor, while juvenile record destruction is handled by the Family Court.

facts.label: Charges that did not result in conviction
facts.value: South Carolina provides for destruction of qualifying arrest records when a charge is discharged, proceedings are dismissed, or the defendant is found not guilty. The statute contains exceptions, including for certain dismissals connected to plea agreements involving another offense; a dismissal alone does not establish eligibility in every case. — S.C. Code § 17-1-40

facts.label: Limited first-offense conviction relief
facts.value: A first offense carrying a maximum punishment of 30 days’ imprisonment, a $1,000 fine, or both may qualify after three years from conviction if the statutory conditions are met, including no additional conviction during that period. The maximum authorized punishment—not merely the sentence actually imposed—matters. — S.C. Code § 22-5-910

facts.label: Excluded offenses and a longer waiting period
facts.value: Section 22-5-910 excludes specified categories, including motor vehicle offenses and offenses involving operation of a motor vehicle. First-offense domestic violence in the third degree has a five-year waiting period rather than the ordinary three-year period. — S.C. Code § 22-5-910

facts.label: Limits on record destruction
facts.value: Expungement does not necessarily eliminate every record held by every agency. South Carolina permits specified retention and restricted use of records, including records needed to determine eligibility for certain statutory benefits. — S.C. Code §§ 17-1-40, 17-22-150, 44-53-450

rows: Qualifying arrest records are subject to destruction, with statutory exceptions.
Certain offenses punishable by no more than 30 days, a $1,000 fine, or both can qualify after the applicable waiting period.
Successful completion provides a route to an order destroying qualifying official arrest records.
Qualifying proceedings discharged and dismissed under this section can support an application for expungement.
Family Court may order destruction of eligible juvenile records under separate statutory conditions.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in South Carolina
bullets: Circuit solicitor: The solicitor’s office in the judicial circuit where the charge originated generally processes adult expungement applications under the Uniform Expungement of Criminal Records Act. — S.C. Code Title 17, Chapter 22, Article 9.

Magistrates and municipal courts: These courts have responsibility for expungement of qualifying dismissals and acquittals in cases within their jurisdiction, subject to statutory exceptions. — S.C. Code § 17-22-950.
Family Court: Applications to destroy eligible juvenile records fall under the juvenile expungement statute, rather than the ordinary adult conviction process. — S.C. Code § 63-19-2050.

sections.heading: Common questions in South Carolina
bullets: Does every dismissal qualify? No. Section 17-1-40 contains exceptions, including certain charges dismissed through a plea agreement involving another charge.
Does a small fine make a conviction eligible? Not by itself. Section 22-5-910 looks at the offense’s authorized maximum punishment and other statutory conditions, not just the punishment imposed.
Is the ordinary waiting period measured from release? Under § 22-5-910, the ordinary three-year period runs from conviction. Other expungement statutes use different eligibility rules.
Does completing pretrial intervention automatically erase the records? Section 17-22-150 provides an application-and-order process for destruction of qualifying records after successful completion.
Are juvenile records governed by the same rules? No. Section 63-19-2050 provides a separate Family Court process with its own eligibility requirements.
