criminal-law/south-carolina/domestic-vio.summary: South Carolina criminalizes domestic violence against a household member under S.C. Code § 16-25-20, with three degrees carrying different penalties; a separate statute covers domestic violence of a high and aggravated nature. The applicable charge depends on statutory factors, including injury, prior convictions, and aggravating circumstances, rather than injury alone. Third-degree domestic violence is a misdemeanor, while first-degree domestic violence and domestic violence of a high and aggravated nature are felonies.

sections.heading: What South Carolina domestic violence charges cover

facts.label: Basic offense
facts.value: The statute prohibits causing physical harm or injury to a household member. It also prohibits offering or attempting to cause physical harm or injury, with apparent present ability, under circumstances reasonably creating fear of imminent peril. A completed physical injury is therefore not required for every charge. — S.C. Code § 16-25-20(A)

facts.label: Household relationship
facts.value: The statutory definition includes spouses, former spouses, and people who have a child in common. It also addresses cohabiting and formerly cohabiting partners. The required household relationship distinguishes this offense from other assault charges. — S.C. Code § 16-25-10(3)

facts.label: Factors affecting the degree
facts.value: The statute identifies aggravating factors involving injury, qualifying prior convictions, protection-order violations, and specified circumstances surrounding the offense. An offense committed in a minor's presence can support an elevated degree when the statutory requirements are met. — S.C. Code § 16-25-20(B)–(D)

facts.label: High and aggravated nature
facts.value: This separate felony includes specified conduct manifesting extreme indifference to human life, as well as certain protection-order violations committed while committing first-degree domestic violence. The statute lists examples of extreme-indifference circumstances. — S.C. Code § 16-25-65

rows: $1,000–$2,500 fine, imprisonment up to 90 days, or both
$2,500–$5,000 fine, imprisonment up to three years, or both
Domestic violence of a high and aggravated nature

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in South Carolina
bullets: Local police departments and county sheriffs investigate reported domestic violence. South Carolina authorizes warrantless arrests under specified probable-cause circumstances, including some offenses committed outside an officer's presence. — S.C. Code § 16-25-70.

Magistrates and municipal courts have express jurisdiction over third-degree domestic violence. Second-degree, first-degree, and high-and-aggravated-nature charges are handled in the Court of General Sessions. — S.C. Code § 16-25-20; South Carolina Judicial Branch.

A civil order-of-protection proceeding is separate from criminal prosecution. Family court has jurisdiction over petitions under the Protection from Domestic Abuse Act; magistrates have limited emergency jurisdiction when family court is not in session. — S.C. Code § 20-4-30.

sections.heading: Common questions in South Carolina
bullets: Must there be a visible injury? No. The basic offense also covers qualifying offers or attempts to cause physical harm, with apparent present ability and circumstances reasonably creating fear of imminent peril. — S.C. Code § 16-25-20(A).

Is every domestic violence charge a felony? No. Second- and third-degree offenses are misdemeanors. First-degree domestic violence and domestic violence of a high and aggravated nature are felonies. — S.C. Code §§ 16-25-20, 16-25-65.

Can a prior conviction affect the degree? Yes. The degree provisions include qualifying prior domestic violence convictions within the preceding 10 years. The required number differs by degree. — S.C. Code § 16-25-20(B)–(C).

Does a protection order replace a criminal case? No. Civil protection proceedings and criminal charges are separate. A protection-order violation can also affect the criminal charge when the statutory conditions are satisfied. — S.C. Code §§ 20-4-30, 16-25-20, 16-25-65.

sources.label: South Carolina Legislature — Title 16, Chapter 25: Domestic Violence
South Carolina Legislature — Title 20, Chapter 4: Protection from Domestic Abuse
South Carolina Judicial Branch

criminal-law/south-carolina/juvenile-law.summary: South Carolina generally handles juvenile delinquency cases in family court under the South Carolina Juvenile Justice Code, although statutory exceptions allow some cases involving young people to proceed in adult criminal court. The process can include intake, detention decisions, adjudication, and a disposition such as probation or commitment to the Department of Juvenile Justice; the available outcome depends on the offense, the child's circumstances, and the applicable statutory requirements.

facts.label: Governing law
facts.value: The South Carolina Juvenile Justice Code is Title 63, Chapter 19 of the South Carolina Code of Laws. It governs juvenile justice administration, custody, court proceedings, dispositions, and juvenile records. — S.C. Code Ann. § 63-19-10 and Title 63, Chapter 19

facts.label: Family court jurisdiction
facts.value: Family court has exclusive original jurisdiction over proceedings concerning children alleged to have violated state law or a municipal ordinance, subject to statutory exceptions. A juvenile case is not necessarily an adult criminal prosecution. — S.C. Code Ann. § 63-3-510

facts.label: Age and adult prosecution
facts.value: The statutory definition of a child uses an under-eighteen threshold but includes exceptions. Separate provisions govern when family court may transfer a case for adult criminal proceedings; age alone does not resolve jurisdiction in every case. — S.C. Code Ann. §§ 63-19-20, 63-19-1210

rows: The code distinguishes taking a child into custody from an arrest and provides for notification of a parent, guardian, or custodian.
Secure detention is subject to statutory eligibility restrictions; it is not an automatic result of every delinquency allegation.
Family court can transfer qualifying cases under statutory procedures and offense- and age-related criteria.
Authorized dispositions include probation, restitution, and community service, subject to the statute's conditions.
Commitment to the Department of Juvenile Justice is a possible disposition, with statutory limits and restrictions.

facts.label: Restricted records
facts.value: Juvenile court records have statutory confidentiality protections. Access and disclosure are governed by specific exceptions, so confidentiality does not mean that no government agency or other authorized person can obtain information. — S.C. Code Ann. § 63-19-2010

facts.label: Expungement
facts.value: South Carolina provides a statutory process for expunging qualifying juvenile records. Eligibility depends on the statutory conditions and exclusions; confidentiality and expungement are different legal protections. — S.C. Code Ann. § 63-19-2050

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in South Carolina
bullets: Family court: The county clerk of court handles family court filings and court records. Juvenile proceedings fall within family court jurisdiction unless an applicable exception places the matter elsewhere. — S.C. Code Ann. § 63-3-510

South Carolina Department of Juvenile Justice: DJJ administers state juvenile justice services, including community services and juvenile facilities. Its county offices handle local juvenile justice functions; DJJ is not the court that adjudicates delinquency. — S.C. Code Ann., Title 63, Chapter 19

Expungement proceedings: The juvenile expungement statute provides for an application to the court, rather than treating records as automatically erased when a person becomes an adult. — S.C. Code Ann. § 63-19-2050

sections.heading: Common questions in South Carolina
bullets: Does every case involving someone under eighteen stay in juvenile court? No. Statutory definitions, exceptions, and transfer provisions can place a case in adult criminal court. — §§ 63-19-20, 63-19-1210
Is detention required whenever a child is accused of an offense? No. South Carolina restricts when a child may be held in secure detention. — § 63-19-820
Can family court order restitution? Yes. Restitution is among the dispositions authorized by the Juvenile Justice Code. — § 63-19-1410

Are juvenile records automatically erased at adulthood? No. Statutory confidentiality is separate from expungement, which has its own eligibility requirements and court process. — §§ 63-19-2010, 63-19-2050

criminal-law/south-dakota/traffic-violat.summary: South Dakota treats driving under the influence and reckless driving as criminal offenses, with possible jail time, fines, and consequences for driving privileges. A first DUI is a Class 1 misdemeanor, while a qualifying third DUI is a Class 6 felony; the classification depends on the applicable prior-conviction rules, not simply the number of traffic stops. Criminal sentencing and driver-license proceedings are separate parts of the state's traffic-law system.

sections.heading: Criminal traffic offenses in South Dakota

facts.label: Driving under the influence
facts.value: South Dakota prohibits driving or being in actual physical control of a vehicle with a blood-alcohol concentration of 0.08 percent or more, or while under the influence of alcohol, marijuana, or a controlled drug or substance. The statute also addresses other impairing substances and combined impairment — SDCL § 32-23-1.

facts.label: A result below 0.08 is not an automatic defense
facts.value: The DUI statute contains separate grounds based on alcohol concentration and being under the influence. A prosecution therefore does not always require proof of an alcohol concentration of at least 0.08 percent — SDCL § 32-23-1.

facts.label: Reckless driving
facts.value: Driving carelessly and heedlessly in willful or wanton disregard of others' rights or safety, or without due caution at a speed or in a manner that endangers or is likely to endanger a person or property, constitutes reckless driving — SDCL § 32-24-1.

sections.heading: Offense classifications and maximum criminal penalties

rows: 1 year in county jail; $2,000 fine; or both
1 year in county jail; $2,000 fine; or both
Third DUI under applicable repeat-offender rules
2 years in the state penitentiary; a $4,000 fine may also be imposed
1 year in county jail; $2,000 fine; or both
Class 2 misdemeanor, where the charged traffic statute specifies this class
30 days in county jail; $500 fine; or both

facts.label: Maximum penalties are not standard ticket amounts
facts.value: The general sentencing statutes establish maximum incarceration and fines for offense classes. They do not mean every conviction receives the maximum, and the listed fines do not represent a complete total of court costs or other consequences — SDCL §§ 22-6-1 and 22-6-2.

facts.label: Prior convictions matter
facts.value: South Dakota has distinct provisions for first, second, and third DUI convictions. Rules governing which earlier convictions count must be applied before assigning a repeat-offender classification — SDCL §§ 32-23-2 through 32-23-4 and 32-23-4.1.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in South Dakota
bullets: Criminal traffic cases are handled within South Dakota's Unified Judicial System. Circuit courts have general trial jurisdiction; magistrate courts handle matters within their statutory jurisdiction.
The clerk of the court handling a traffic case maintains its filings and court record. The Unified Judicial System publishes courthouse and clerk contact information.
The South Dakota Department of Public Safety's Driver Licensing Program handles driver-license administration. It is not the court deciding guilt on a criminal traffic charge.

sections.heading: Common questions in South Dakota
bullets: Is a first DUI a felony? No. A first violation of SDCL § 32-23-1 is a Class 1 misdemeanor under § 32-23-2.
Can reckless driving result in jail? Yes. It is a Class 1 misdemeanor, carrying a maximum of one year in county jail.
Must the vehicle be moving for DUI? No. Section 32-23-1 also covers actual physical control of a vehicle.
Does every traffic violation carry the same penalty? No. The charged statute determines the offense and classification. For questions about a particular charge or prior conviction, talk to a lawyer.

South Dakota Legislature — SDCL Chapter 22-6, Authorized Punishments
South Dakota Legislature — SDCL Chapter 32-24, Reckless Driving

criminal-law/tennessee/expungement.summary: Tennessee permits expungement of qualifying criminal records, including many dismissed charges, acquittals, successfully completed judicial-diversion cases, and certain convictions under Tennessee Code § 40-32-101. Eligibility depends on the outcome, offense, criminal history, and applicable statutory conditions; completing a sentence does not automatically erase a conviction. Expungement generally requires a court order and removes qualifying public records, but it does not necessarily eliminate confidential government records or copies held by private organizations.

facts.label: Dismissals and acquittals
facts.value: Tennessee authorizes expungement for qualifying cases involving dismissal, a grand jury returning no true bill, a verdict of not guilty, and certain arrests that did not result in charges. The statute contains exceptions, so the disposition of each charge matters. — Tenn. Code Ann. § 40-32-101(a)

facts.label: Convictions
facts.value: Some convictions qualify under separate statutory provisions. Not every misdemeanor qualifies, and felony eligibility is limited. The offense, sentence, prior record, completion of sentence requirements, and applicable waiting period can determine eligibility. — Tenn. Code Ann. § 40-32-101(g), (k)

facts.label: Judicial diversion
facts.value: Successful completion of judicial diversion can lead to discharge and dismissal without an adjudication of guilt. Expungement is a separate court process authorized after qualifying discharge and dismissal; it is not simply the same thing as finishing probation. — Tenn. Code Ann. § 40-35-313(a), (b)

facts.label: Limits on destruction
facts.value: The statute distinguishes public records from certain confidential law-enforcement and other government records. An expungement order therefore does not mean that every government-held reference to the case must disappear. — Tenn. Code Ann. § 40-32-101(b)

sections.heading: How the case outcome changes the process

rows: A qualifying dismissal supports removal of public records upon petition; statutory exceptions apply.
The statute provides an expungement route for a charge ending in acquittal.
Grand jury returns no true bill
This is an expressly recognized basis for qualifying expungement.
Qualifying discharge and dismissal can be followed by an application for expungement.
Only convictions meeting the applicable statutory eligibility rules qualify.

facts.label: Court action
facts.value: For qualifying nonconviction records, the statute provides for a petition in the court having jurisdiction over the previous action. A dismissal and an order expunging the resulting records are distinct procedural events. — Tenn. Code Ann. § 40-32-101(a)

facts.label: Nonconviction costs
facts.value: The qualifying nonconviction-expungement provision directs removal and destruction of public records without cost to the person. That rule should not be treated as a universal statement about every diversion or conviction proceeding. — Tenn. Code Ann. § 40-32-101(a)(1)(A)

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Tennessee
bullets: The court with jurisdiction over the original criminal action handles the applicable expungement request. Depending on the case, this may be a General Sessions, Criminal, or Circuit Court.

The clerk of that court maintains the case filings and processes entered orders. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation handles state criminal-history records but does not replace the court as the authority granting expungement.
Eligibility disputes and questions about an order’s scope are legal questions; talk to a lawyer.

sections.heading: Common questions in Tennessee
bullets: Does a dismissed charge automatically vanish? No. Dismissal establishes a case outcome; expungement is the separate statutory process for removing qualifying records.
Can every misdemeanor be expunged? No. Tennessee excludes certain misdemeanor convictions from conviction-expungement eligibility.
Does completing probation erase a conviction? No. Sentence completion alone is not an expungement order.
Will every background-check copy disappear? Not necessarily. Court-ordered expungement does not guarantee deletion of copies previously obtained by private organizations.

sources.label: Tennessee Administrative Office of the Courts — Expungements
Tennessee Bureau of Investigation — Expungements

criminal-law/south-carolina/traffic-viol.summary: South Carolina generally treats violations of its Uniform Act Regulating Traffic on Highways as misdemeanors unless a law expressly makes the offense a felony, so a traffic charge can be a criminal matter rather than merely an administrative ticket. Consequences depend on the specific offense and can include fines, jail, driver’s license points, and suspension; ordinary traffic misdemeanors are commonly handled in magistrates or municipal courts, while felony charges proceed in circuit court.

sections.heading: How South Carolina classifies traffic offenses

facts.label: Default criminal classification
facts.value: A violation of the Uniform Act Regulating Traffic on Highways is a misdemeanor unless that chapter or another South Carolina law declares it a felony. The classification and available punishment therefore depend on the particular statute charged. — S.C. Code § 56-5-6190

facts.label: Reckless driving
facts.value: Driving with wilful or wanton disregard for the safety of persons or property is reckless driving. The statutory punishment is a $25–$200 fine or imprisonment for up to 30 days; this fine range does not represent the total after applicable court assessments. — S.C. Code § 56-5-2920

facts.label: DUI and unlawful alcohol concentration
facts.value: DUI covers driving while alcohol, drugs, or their combination materially and appreciably impair driving faculties. A separate statute prohibits driving with an alcohol concentration of 0.08 percent or more, subject to that statute’s requirements. — S.C. Code §§ 56-5-2930, 56-5-2933

rows: Speeding no more than 10 mph above the posted limit
Speeding more than 10 but less than 25 mph above the posted limit
Speeding 25 mph or more above the posted limit
Disobeying an official traffic control device

facts.label: Point-based suspension
facts.value: South Carolina’s point system provides for license suspension when a driver accumulates 12 or more points, subject to the statutory calculation and procedures. License consequences are separate from the criminal court’s punishment. — S.C. Code §§ 56-1-740, 56-1-750

facts.label: Repeat reckless driving
facts.value: The Department of Motor Vehicles must suspend a driver’s license for three months upon receiving satisfactory evidence of two reckless-driving convictions within five years. — S.C. Code § 56-5-2920

facts.label: Felony DUI
facts.value: Driving under the influence can become felony DUI when the driver also commits an act forbidden by law or neglects a legal driving duty and that conduct proximately causes great bodily injury or death to another person. — S.C. Code § 56-5-2945

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in South Carolina
bullets: Magistrates courts handle traffic prosecutions within their criminal jurisdiction. Their ordinary jurisdiction includes offenses punishable by a fine not exceeding $500 or imprisonment not exceeding 30 days, with statutory exceptions. — S.C. Code § 22-3-550
Municipal courts handle municipal ordinance prosecutions and exercise specified criminal jurisdiction over state-law offenses occurring within the municipality. — S.C. Code § 14-25-65

The South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles administers driver’s license points and point-related suspensions; it does not decide criminal guilt on the underlying traffic charge. — S.C. Code §§ 56-1-720, 56-1-740

sections.heading: Common questions in South Carolina
bullets: Is an ordinary traffic violation necessarily a civil infraction? No. The traffic chapter generally classifies violations as misdemeanors unless expressly designated felonies. — S.C. Code § 56-5-6190
Does speeding automatically constitute reckless driving? The statutes define separate offenses. Reckless driving requires wilful or wanton disregard for safety. — S.C. Code §§ 56-5-1520, 56-5-2920
Can DUI involve prescription medication? Yes. The DUI statute covers impairment by drugs without limiting its application to illegal substances. — S.C. Code § 56-5-2930
Are points the same as a fine? No. Points concern licensing consequences; fines are criminal penalties imposed under the applicable offense statute. — S.C. Code §§ 56-1-720, 56-5-6190

South Carolina Legislature — Title 56, Chapter 1: Driver’s License
South Carolina Legislature — Title 22, Chapter 3: Jurisdiction and Procedure in Magistrates’ Courts

criminal-law/texas/juvenile-law.summary: Texas generally handles alleged criminal conduct committed at ages 10 through 16 in juvenile court under Title 3 of the Texas Family Code, although the court can retain authority over some people after they turn 17. Juvenile proceedings distinguish delinquent conduct from conduct indicating a need for supervision, and outcomes can include probation, placement, or commitment to the Texas Juvenile Justice Department. Certain felony allegations can lead to transfer to adult criminal court, while juvenile records are subject to confidentiality and sealing rules rather than guaranteed erasure.

facts.label: Age at the alleged conduct
facts.value: The ordinary definition of a child covers someone at least 10 and under 17. It also includes someone 17 or older but under 18 accused or found to have engaged in qualifying conduct before turning 17; separate provisions address continuing jurisdiction. — Texas Family Code §§ 51.02(2), 51.041–51.042.

facts.label: Two categories of conduct
facts.value: Delinquent conduct generally includes violations punishable by imprisonment or confinement in jail, excluding traffic offenses, together with other specifically listed conduct. Conduct indicating a need for supervision includes certain fine-only offenses and specified noncriminal behavior, such as qualifying runaway conduct. — Texas Family Code § 51.03.

facts.label: Juvenile courts
facts.value: Texas uses designated juvenile courts rather than one statewide juvenile trial court. A district court, criminal district court, county court at law, or constitutional county court may be designated as a juvenile court. — Texas Family Code § 51.04.

rows: The state must prove delinquent conduct or conduct indicating a need for supervision beyond a reasonable doubt at adjudication. — Family Code § 54.03(f).

A child has a right to counsel at specified stages, including detention, adjudication, disposition, and transfer hearings. Appointment requirements are governed separately. — Family Code §§ 51.10, 51.101.
An adjudication hearing is by jury unless the child waives that right in accordance with the statutory waiver requirements. — Family Code §§ 51.09, 54.03(c).
Special admissibility requirements apply to a child's statements, including statutory conditions for written statements and recorded custodial statements. — Family Code § 51.095.

For a child not released, the hearing generally must occur promptly and no later than the second working day after custody begins; additional rules govern certain weekend custody. — Family Code § 54.01(a).

sections.heading: Dispositions and transfer to adult court

facts.label: Disposition is a separate decision
facts.value: After adjudication, the court separately determines whether a disposition is needed. Available outcomes depend on statutory findings and eligibility; they can include probation, out-of-home placement, or commitment to the Texas Juvenile Justice Department. — Texas Family Code § 54.04.

facts.label: Adult criminal prosecution
facts.value: Transfer is not automatic because an allegation is serious. For an ordinary discretionary transfer, the child must have been at least 14 for specified serious felonies or at least 15 for other eligible felonies, and the court must make required findings after investigation and a hearing. — Texas Family Code § 54.02(a).

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Texas
bullets: County juvenile probation departments perform intake functions, including preliminary inquiries into juvenile-court jurisdiction and whether further proceedings are warranted. — Texas Family Code § 53.01.
The prosecuting attorney files a juvenile petition when statutory requirements are met; adjudication occurs in the designated juvenile court. — Texas Family Code §§ 51.04, 53.04.

Juvenile probation services are subject to complaint procedures established by the local juvenile board. — Texas Family Code §  juvenile-board complaint procedures are not specified here; talk to a lawyer.

sections.heading: Common questions in Texas
bullets: Is a juvenile adjudication an adult criminal conviction? Generally no, although statutes provide exceptions and collateral consequences. — Texas Family Code § 51.13.
Does turning 17 automatically end an existing juvenile case? No. Continuing jurisdiction depends on the proceeding and applicable statutory conditions. — Texas Family Code §§ 51.041–51.042.
Can parents waive all of a child's rights? No. The general waiver rule requires agreement by the child and the child's attorney, along with other safeguards. — Texas Family Code § 51.09.

sources.label: Texas Legislature — Family Code Chapter 51
Texas Legislature — Family Code Chapter 53
Texas Legislature — Family Code Chapter 54

criminal-law/utah/arrest-process.summary: In Utah, an arrest may be based on a warrant or on statutory authority to arrest without one; an arrest does not establish guilt. After a warrantless arrest, Utah’s criminal rules require judicial review of probable cause, while the initial appearance addresses the accusation, counsel, and release or detention. The next steps depend on the charge: justice courts generally handle misdemeanors within their jurisdiction, while district courts handle felonies, including any required preliminary hearing.

facts.label: Arrest under a warrant
facts.value: A peace officer may arrest someone under a warrant. The warrant is authority to take the person into custody, not a finding that the person is guilty. — Utah Code § 77-7-2; Utah Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 6.

facts.label: Warrantless felony arrest
facts.value: Utah permits a peace officer to arrest without a warrant when the officer has reasonable cause to believe a felony has been committed and reasonable cause to believe the person arrested committed it. — Utah Code § 77-7-2(2).

facts.label: Offenses committed in the officer’s presence
facts.value: An officer may arrest for a public offense committed or attempted in the officer’s presence. Utah also authorizes warrantless arrests in additional circumstances specified by statute; the presence requirement is not universal. — Utah Code § 77-7-2.

rows: A warrantless arrest is subject to a magistrate’s determination of probable cause. This review is distinct from a trial on guilt.
Utah Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 9
The court informs the defendant of the charge and applicable rights, including the right to counsel.
Utah Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 7
The initial-appearance process addresses representation and appointed counsel for defendants who qualify.
Utah Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 7
The court addresses whether the defendant will be released and the conditions of any release. Arrest does not automatically require detention through trial.
Utah Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rules 7 and 9
For charges carrying a preliminary-examination right, the court considers whether probable cause supports further proceedings, unless that examination is waived.
Utah Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 7

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Utah
bullets: Criminal case proceedings take place in the court with jurisdiction over the charge. Utah district courts handle felony prosecutions and class A misdemeanors; justice courts generally handle class B and class C misdemeanors, infractions, and ordinance violations within their jurisdiction. — Utah Code §§ 78A-5-102 and 78A-7-106.

Challenges concerning probable cause, release conditions, or the admissibility of evidence are matters for the criminal court. An administrative complaint to a police agency does not itself dismiss a charge or change a court order. — Utah Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rules 9 and 12.

Complaints about an officer’s conduct may be submitted to the employing law-enforcement agency. Utah’s Peace Officer Standards and Training division also has statutory authority over peace-officer certification and disciplinary matters. — Utah Code § 53-6-211.

sections.heading: Common questions in Utah
bullets: Does every arrest require a warrant? No. Utah Code § 77-7-2 identifies circumstances allowing peace officers to arrest without a warrant.
Is the initial appearance a trial? No. It addresses the charge, rights, representation, and release-related matters rather than deciding guilt. — Utah Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 7.

Does a probable-cause finding mean a conviction? No. Probable cause permits specified criminal proceedings to continue; it is not proof of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. — Utah Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rules 7 and 9.

Is a preliminary examination the same as warrantless-arrest review? No. Arrest review evaluates the basis for warrantless custody; a preliminary examination addresses whether qualifying charges should proceed toward trial. — Utah Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rules 7 and 9.

sources.label: Utah Legislature — Utah Code § 77-7-2
Utah Courts — Utah Rules of Criminal Procedure
Utah Legislature — Judicial Code, Title 78A
Utah Legislature — Peace-officer disciplinary authority, § 53-6-211

criminal-law/south-dakota/domestic-viole.summary: South Dakota prosecutes domestic violence through offenses such as simple assault and aggravated assault; the domestic relationship also matters under the state’s domestic-abuse laws. Simple assault is generally a Class 1 misdemeanor, while aggravated assault is a Class 3 felony, with substantially higher potential punishment. A civil protection order is separate from a criminal prosecution, but knowingly violating an order can create an additional criminal charge under South Dakota law.

sections.heading: How South Dakota defines domestic violence charges

facts.label: Domestic abuse
facts.value: The statutory definition includes physical harm, bodily injury, attempts to cause physical harm or bodily injury, and inflicting fear of imminent physical harm or bodily injury between family or household members. It also includes qualifying protection-order violations — SDCL § 25-10-1.

facts.label: Covered relationships
facts.value: Family or household members include spouses, former spouses, people related by consanguinity, adoption, or law, people who live or have lived together, and people who have a child together — SDCL § 25-10-1.

facts.label: Simple assault
facts.value: The statute covers several forms of conduct, including recklessly causing bodily injury and attempting by physical menace to put another person in fear of imminent serious bodily harm. Visible injury is therefore not required for every form of simple assault — SDCL § 22-18-1.

facts.label: Aggravated assault
facts.value: Aggravated assault includes specified serious-injury and dangerous-weapon conduct. The statute also expressly covers intentionally impeding another person’s breathing or blood circulation by pressure on the throat or neck, or by blocking the nose and mouth — SDCL § 22-18-1.1.

rows: Simple assault, without an applicable enhancement
Up to one year in county jail, a $2,000 fine, or both — SDCL §§ 22-18-1, 22-6-2.
Up to 15 years of imprisonment; a fine of up to $30,000 may also be imposed — SDCL §§ 22-18-1.1, 22-6-1.
Knowing protection-order violation, without an applicable felony provision
Up to one year in county jail, a $2,000 fine, or both — SDCL §§ 25-10-13, 22-6-2.
Protection-order violation whose acts also constitute assault
Up to two years of imprisonment; a fine of up to $4,000 may also be imposed — SDCL §§ 25-10-13, 22-6-1.

sections.heading: Protection orders and criminal cases are separate

facts.label: Civil petition
facts.value: A person may petition for an order for protection under the domestic-abuse chapter. This is a separate proceeding from prosecution for assault or another criminal offense — SDCL § 25-10-3.

facts.label: Available restrictions
facts.value: After the required proceedings, a protection order may prohibit domestic abuse and exclude the respondent from a dwelling. The statute also authorizes temporary custody or visitation provisions and other specified relief — SDCL § 25-10-5.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in South Dakota
bullets: Local police departments and county sheriffs receive reports of suspected criminal conduct. Criminal charges proceed in the name of the State, rather than as a private civil lawsuit.
County state’s attorneys prosecute state criminal cases. South Dakota circuit courts handle felony prosecutions; magistrate courts have misdemeanor jurisdiction.
Domestic-abuse protection-order petitions are filed in circuit court under SDCL § 25-10-3. The South Dakota Unified Judicial System publishes protection-order forms and court information.

sections.heading: Common questions in South Dakota
bullets: Does every domestic assault require an injury? No. Simple assault includes certain attempts and physical-menace conduct without a completed bodily injury — SDCL § 22-18-1.

Is strangulation specifically covered? Yes. Intentionally impeding breathing or circulation through the specified neck, throat, nose, or mouth conduct falls within aggravated assault — SDCL § 22-18-1.1.
Is violating a protection order always a misdemeanor? No. Section 25-10-13 includes felony treatment when the violating acts also constitute assault.

Are these penalties automatic sentences? No. They are statutory maximums for the listed classifications, not mandatory sentences in every case. Enhancements and other sentencing provisions can affect a particular prosecution; talk to a lawyer.

South Dakota Legislature — Chapter 22-6: Classification and Penalties
South Dakota Legislature — Chapter 25-10: Protection from Domestic Abuse
South Dakota Unified Judicial System

criminal-law/utah/drug-charges.summary: Utah drug charges are governed primarily by the Utah Controlled Substances Act, and the charge depends on the substance, quantity, conduct, and applicable statutory enhancements. Possession, distribution, possession with intent to distribute, and drug-paraphernalia offenses are separate crimes; a sale is not required for every distribution charge. Utah also distinguishes authorized medical cannabis activity from unlawful marijuana possession, so medical cannabis status does not provide blanket immunity from drug prosecution.

sections.heading: Utah drug offenses and important distinctions

facts.label: Main criminal statute
facts.value: The Utah Controlled Substances Act prohibits unauthorized manufacture, distribution, and possession with intent to distribute controlled substances. It separately prohibits knowingly and intentionally possessing or using a controlled substance without statutory authorization. The substance and conduct determine the applicable offense classification. — Utah Code § 58-37-8.

facts.label: Distribution does not require payment
facts.value: Utah defines distribution by reference to delivery, and delivery includes an actual, constructive, or attempted transfer of a controlled substance. An unlawful transfer can therefore support a distribution charge even when no money changes hands. — Utah Code §§ 58-37-2 and 58-37-8(1).

facts.label: Marijuana possession
facts.value: Unauthorized possession of less than 100 pounds of marijuana is generally a class B misdemeanor under the possession provision. That classification is not a universal rule for cannabis-related conduct: distribution, possession with intent to distribute, and applicable enhancement provisions are treated separately. — Utah Code § 58-37-8.

facts.label: Drug paraphernalia
facts.value: Using drug paraphernalia, or possessing it with intent to use it for the unlawful controlled-substance activities listed in the statute, is a class B misdemeanor. The statutory definition and contextual factors matter; an object's appearance alone does not state every element of the offense. — Utah Code §§ 58-37a-3, 58-37a-4, and 58-37a-5(1).

sections.heading: General incarceration ranges for relevant offense classes

rows: Indeterminate prison term of 1 to 15 years
Indeterminate prison term not exceeding 5 years

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Utah
bullets: Criminal drug allegations are investigated by law enforcement and prosecuted by the appropriate public prosecutor. A private complaint does not itself create a criminal court case.

Utah district courts handle felony criminal cases and class A misdemeanors. Justice courts generally handle class B and class C misdemeanors and infractions, subject to statutory jurisdictional exceptions.
Utah's appellate courts review qualifying criminal appeals; they do not serve as the initial filing court for a drug prosecution.

The Utah Department of Health and Human Services administers the state's medical cannabis patient program. Medical cannabis registration questions are distinct from defending a criminal charge; talk to a lawyer about a pending prosecution.

sections.heading: Common questions in Utah
bullets: Is every Utah drug charge a felony? No. Utah law includes misdemeanor drug offenses, including the general less-than-100-pound marijuana possession provision and unlawful use or possession-with-intent-to-use drug paraphernalia.

Does sharing drugs count as distribution? It can. Utah's delivery and distribution definitions do not require a commercial sale. The prosecution must still establish the applicable statutory elements.

Does a medical cannabis card protect all cannabis possession? No. Utah's authorization depends on compliance with applicable medical cannabis laws; a card is not unrestricted permission to possess, use, or distribute cannabis.

Are the listed incarceration ranges automatic sentences? No. They describe general statutory incarceration ranges for the classifications, not a guaranteed outcome. Probation, suspended sentences, and offense-specific provisions can affect the actual sentence.

Is possession with intent to distribute the same as simple possession? No. Utah separately criminalizes possession with intent to distribute. The prosecution must prove the distribution intent required for that charge.

Utah Legislature — Controlled substance definitions, § 58-37-2
Utah Legislature — Punishments, Title 76, Chapter 3
Utah Legislature — Drug paraphernalia offenses, § 58-37a-5

criminal-law/vermont/arrest-process.summary: In Vermont, an arrest can be made under a warrant or, in circumstances authorized by law, without one; an arrested person who remains in custody must be brought before a judicial officer without unnecessary delay. The Superior Court’s Criminal Division handles criminal prosecutions, including arraignment and release decisions. Vermont law generally favors release on personal recognizance or an unsecured appearance bond, but courts may impose conditions or, in specified cases, hold a defendant without bail.

sections.heading: Arrest and the first court appearance

facts.label: Arrest authority
facts.value: Vermont Rule of Criminal Procedure 3 governs arrests without a warrant and the use of citations. A warrantless arrest requires a legally authorized basis; the rule distinguishes felonies from misdemeanors and limits when officers may arrest for a misdemeanor committed outside their presence. — V.R.Cr.P. 3

facts.label: Appearance after arrest
facts.value: An arrested person who is not released must be brought before a judicial officer without unnecessary delay. The initial-appearance process addresses the accusation, access to counsel, and release or detention. — V.R.Cr.P. 5

facts.label: Access to counsel
facts.value: A defendant entitled to appointed counsel who cannot obtain counsel is entitled to representation at every stage of the proceeding, from the initial appearance through appeal, unless that right is waived. — V.R.Cr.P. 44

rows: Depending on the circumstances, an officer may issue a citation to appear rather than continue custodial processing.
A judicial officer addresses the charge and the defendant’s procedural rights.
The charge is read or its substance stated, and the defendant is called upon to plead.
The court determines whether release is appropriate and what conditions, if any, are authorized.
A not-guilty plea leaves the charge for further proceedings; arraignment itself does not determine guilt.

facts.label: Ordinary release standard
facts.value: For defendants covered by the ordinary release statute, the starting point is personal recognizance or an unsecured appearance bond unless that release will not reasonably mitigate the risk of flight. Conditions addressing flight must be the least restrictive necessary; the statute separately permits conditions addressing public protection. — 13 V.S.A. § 7554

facts.label: Life-imprisonment charges
facts.value: A person charged with an offense punishable by life imprisonment may be held without bail when the evidence of guilt is great. This provision does not make every felony a no-bail case. — 13 V.S.A. § 7553

facts.label: Certain violent felonies
facts.value: Detention without bail is also authorized for a felony involving an act of violence against another person when the evidence of guilt is great and the court finds, by clear and convincing evidence, a substantial threat of physical violence that no release conditions will reasonably prevent. — 13 V.S.A. § 7553a

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Vermont
bullets: Criminal charges, arraignments, and motions concerning an existing criminal case are handled in the Vermont Superior Court’s Criminal Division. — Vermont Judiciary, Criminal Division

A request to amend release conditions belongs in the criminal case under the statutory review procedure. Complaints about police conduct do not themselves change a court’s release order. — 13 V.S.A. § 7554

sections.heading: Common questions in Vermont
bullets: Does arrest mean guilt? No. Arrest initiates custody or processing; guilt is determined through later criminal proceedings.
Is cash bail automatic? No. Vermont’s ordinary release statute starts with personal recognizance or an unsecured appearance bond. — 13 V.S.A. § 7554
Can someone be held without bail? Yes, under specified statutory standards, including certain life-imprisonment and violent-felony cases. — 13 V.S.A. §§ 7553–7553a
Is arraignment the trial? No. Arraignment presents the charge and calls for a plea. — V.R.Cr.P. 10

sources.label: Vermont Judiciary — Criminal Division
Vermont General Assembly — 13 V.S.A. § 7554
Vermont General Assembly — 13 V.S.A. § 7553
Vermont General Assembly — 13 V.S.A. § 7553a

criminal-law/vermont/expungement.summary: Vermont provides criminal-record relief under Title 13, chapter 230, but eligibility depends on the offense, the disposition, and the statutory requirements applicable to the record. Expungement and sealing have different legal effects: expungement removes the covered record through the statutory process, while sealing preserves it subject to restrictions on access. Neither remedy should be confused with a pardon, and an order concerning one case does not automatically clear every other criminal record a person has.

facts.label: Governing law
facts.value: Title 13, chapter 230 governs expungement and sealing of Vermont criminal history records. Eligibility is statutory; the existence of an old criminal case alone does not establish entitlement to relief. — 13 V.S.A. ch. 230.

facts.label: Convictions and other dispositions
facts.value: The chapter separately addresses records involving convictions and records arising from proceedings that did not result in a conviction. A dismissal or acquittal and a conviction therefore do not present the same eligibility question. — 13 V.S.A. §§ 7602–7603.

facts.label: Effect of expungement
facts.value: For a covered expunged record, the statute directs that the person be treated as though the arrest, conviction, or sentence never occurred. That protection concerns the record covered by the expungement order, not unrelated cases. — 13 V.S.A. § 7606.

facts.label: Effect of sealing
facts.value: Sealing restricts access rather than destroying the record. Vermont law specifies the treatment of sealed records and the circumstances in which access remains available. — 13 V.S.A. § 7607.

sections.heading: What changes when a record receives relief

rows: Expungement and sealing are different remedies; a sealed record is retained rather than destroyed.
Both remedies restrict ordinary public access to the covered criminal history record.
The statutes protect against being required to acknowledge covered expunged or sealed records in employment and licensing contexts.
The statutes prescribe responses indicating that no criminal record exists for the covered matter.
Later access to a sealed record
Sealing is not an absolute prohibition on access; statutory exceptions apply.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Vermont
bullets: The Vermont Superior Court’s Criminal Division handles petitions under the criminal-record expungement and sealing statutes. The petition concerns the court record of the particular criminal proceeding. — 13 V.S.A. §§ 7602–7603.
The prosecutor has a role in the statutory proceeding, but a prosecutor’s agreement is not itself an expungement or sealing order. Relief is ordered by the court. — 13 V.S.A. ch. 230.

The Vermont Crime Information Center, within the Department of Public Safety, maintains state criminal history information. Its recordkeeping role is distinct from the court’s authority to grant relief.
Eligibility disputes and questions about the scope of an existing order are legal issues; talk to a lawyer.

sections.heading: Common questions in Vermont
bullets: Are sealing and expungement interchangeable? No. Vermont gives them separate statutory treatment, particularly concerning preservation of and access to the underlying record. — 13 V.S.A. §§ 7606–7607.

Can a case without a conviction qualify? Vermont has a separate statutory provision addressing criminal proceedings that did not result in a conviction. The disposition and statutory conditions matter. — 13 V.S.A. § 7603.
Does one order erase every case? No. The order applies to the criminal history record it covers; it is not a blanket clearance of unrelated proceedings. — 13 V.S.A. §§ 7606–7607.

Can an employer require disclosure of a covered record? Vermont’s effect-of-relief provisions protect against required acknowledgment of covered expunged or sealed records in employment inquiries. Questions involving federal requirements or a particular order require separate analysis; talk to a lawyer. — 13 V.S.A. §§ 7606–7607.

Vermont General Assembly — 13 V.S.A. § 7606
Vermont General Assembly — 13 V.S.A. § 7607

criminal-law/vermont/felony-vs-misdemean.summary: Vermont classifies an offense as a felony when its maximum authorized punishment is death or imprisonment for more than two years; every other offense is a misdemeanor. The classification depends on the punishment the law permits, not the sentence actually imposed, so an offense carrying a possible two-year sentence remains a misdemeanor under Vermont’s rule. Individual offense statutes establish the applicable prison terms and fines, and Vermont Superior Court’s Criminal Division handles both felony and misdemeanor prosecutions.

facts.label: Statutory definition
facts.value: An offense whose maximum punishment is death or imprisonment for more than two years is a felony. Any other offense is a misdemeanor. The definition’s reference to death is statutory wording, not a statement that a particular Vermont offense currently carries that punishment — 13 V.S.A. § 1.

facts.label: Two years is still a misdemeanor
facts.value: Vermont does not use a one-year dividing line. An offense allowing imprisonment for more than one year but no more than two years falls within the misdemeanor definition — 13 V.S.A. § 1.

facts.label: Maximum punishment versus actual sentence
facts.value: A sentence below the statutory maximum does not, by itself, change an offense’s classification. The classification turns on the maximum punishment attached to the offense of conviction — 13 V.S.A. § 1.

sections.heading: Examples of Vermont offenses and maximum imprisonment

rows: One year; a specified mutual-fight exception carries a lower maximum
Petit larceny: stolen property worth $900 or less
Grand larceny: stolen property worth more than $900

facts.label: Larceny fines
facts.value: Petit larceny permits a fine of up to $1,000, imprisonment, or both. Grand larceny permits a fine of up to $5,000, imprisonment, or both. The value threshold therefore changes both the classification and the available penalties — 13 V.S.A. §§ 2501–2502.

facts.label: Assault fines
facts.value: The ordinary simple-assault penalty permits a fine of up to $1,000, imprisonment, or both. Aggravated assault under § 1024(a) permits a fine of up to $10,000, imprisonment, or both — 13 V.S.A. §§ 1023(b), 1024(b).

facts.label: Mutual-fight exception
facts.value: Simple assault under § 1023(a)(1), when committed in a fight or scuffle entered into by mutual consent, carries no more than 60 days’ imprisonment, a $500 fine, or both — 13 V.S.A. § 1023(b).

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Vermont
bullets: Vermont Superior Court, Criminal Division: the trial court division that hears felony and misdemeanor criminal cases.
Local police departments and Vermont State Police: agencies that receive reports of suspected criminal conduct and investigate alleged offenses.
County State’s Attorney’s Office: the prosecuting office responsible for bringing state criminal charges in its county; reporting an allegation does not itself initiate a criminal prosecution.

sections.heading: Common questions in Vermont
bullets: Is every offense punishable by more than one year a felony? No. Vermont requires a maximum exceeding two years. — 13 V.S.A. § 1.
Does receiving probation make a felony a misdemeanor? No. A lesser sentence does not change the statutory maximum used to classify the conviction. — 13 V.S.A. § 1.
Is theft of property worth exactly $900 grand larceny? No. The grand-larceny threshold is more than $900; exactly $900 falls within petit larceny. — 13 V.S.A. §§ 2501–2502.
Are misdemeanor cases heard in a separate misdemeanor court? No. Vermont Superior Court’s Criminal Division hears both misdemeanor and felony cases.

sources.label: Vermont Legislature — 13 V.S.A. § 1, felony and misdemeanor definition

criminal-law/virginia/drug-charges.summary: Virginia drug charges depend on the substance’s legal classification, the conduct alleged, and sometimes the quantity and prior convictions. Unlawful possession of a Schedule I or II controlled substance is generally a Class 5 felony, while manufacturing, selling, distributing, or possessing those substances with intent to distribute carries substantially greater penalties under separate provisions. Virginia also permits deferred proceedings for certain first-time possession defendants, with dismissal available after successful completion of court-ordered conditions.

facts.label: Unlawful possession
facts.value: Virginia prohibits knowingly or intentionally possessing a controlled substance unless it was obtained directly from, or under a valid prescription or order of, an authorized practitioner acting professionally, or possession is otherwise authorized by law. — Va. Code § 18.2-250(A)

facts.label: Presence is not automatically possession
facts.value: Ownership or occupancy of premises or a vehicle where drugs are found does not, by itself, create a presumption that the person knowingly or intentionally possessed them. — Va. Code § 18.2-250(A)

facts.label: Separate marijuana rules
facts.value: The general controlled-substance possession statute expressly excludes marijuana, which is governed by separate Virginia provisions. The possession penalties below therefore should not be read as marijuana penalties. — Va. Code §§ 18.2-250(A), 4.1-1100

rows: One to 10 years’ imprisonment; alternatively, up to 12 months in jail, a fine up to $2,500, or both, in the discretion specified by statute.
Up to 12 months in jail, a fine up to $2,500, or both.
Up to six months in jail, a fine up to $1,000, or both.

facts.label: Conduct covered
facts.value: The distribution statute prohibits manufacturing, selling, giving, or distributing a controlled substance, and possessing it with intent to manufacture, sell, give, or distribute it, except as authorized by law. An actual completed sale is not required for an intent-to-distribute charge. — Va. Code § 18.2-248(A)

facts.label: General Schedule I or II range
facts.value: The general penalty is five to 40 years’ imprisonment and a fine up to $500,000. Repeat-offense and specified quantity provisions can produce different penalties; this range does not describe every prosecution under the statute. — Va. Code § 18.2-248(C), (H)

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Virginia
bullets: General District Court: Adult misdemeanor drug cases generally proceed here; the court also conducts preliminary hearings on felony charges. — Va. Code §§ 16.1-123.1, 19.2-186
Circuit Court: Felony drug trials take place here. Circuit courts also hear appeals from General District Court criminal convictions through a new trial. — Va. Code §§ 17.1-513, 16.1-136
Local Commonwealth’s Attorney: This office prosecutes criminal cases for the Commonwealth; it is not the defendant’s legal representative. — Va. Code § 15.2-1627

sections.heading: Common questions in Virginia
bullets: Can a first possession case be dismissed? Yes. Eligible defendants may receive deferred proceedings under § 18.2-251; successful fulfillment of the conditions results in discharge and dismissal without an adjudication of guilt.

Is first-offender treatment automatic? No. Section 18.2-251 sets eligibility requirements, requires the defendant’s consent, and gives the court discretion to defer proceedings and impose probation conditions.
Does giving drugs away count as distribution? Section 18.2-248 expressly covers giving controlled substances; payment is not required.
Does a prescription matter? Section 18.2-250 recognizes possession obtained through a valid prescription or order from an authorized practitioner acting professionally.

Virginia Legislative Information System — § 18.2-251

criminal-law/virginia/bail-and-bond.summary: In Virginia, bail is pretrial release under conditions set by a judicial officer; a bond is the undertaking used to secure compliance, including required court appearances. Under Virginia Code § 19.2-120, a person held pending trial generally must be admitted to bail unless there is probable cause to believe the person will not appear or that release would create an unreasonable danger to the person or the public. Release conditions, review procedures, and consequences for missed appearances are governed by separate statutes.

sections.heading: Virginia’s bail standard and release conditions

facts.label: Bail is not necessarily a cash payment
facts.value: Virginia distinguishes bail, meaning release from custody, from bond, the undertaking associated with release. Release may involve personal recognizance, an unsecured bond, or a secured bond rather than a single statewide cash requirement. — Virginia Code §§ 19.2-119 and 19.2-123

facts.label: Grounds for detention
facts.value: The statutory grounds for denying pretrial bail are probable cause to believe the accused will not appear as directed or that liberty will constitute an unreasonable danger to the accused or the public. — Virginia Code § 19.2-120

facts.label: Individual circumstances
facts.value: The judicial officer considers available information relevant to appearance and safety, including the alleged offense, criminal history, community ties, employment, financial resources, and record of court appearances. — Virginia Code § 19.2-120

facts.label: Conditions beyond money
facts.value: Authorized conditions include supervision, restrictions on travel or associations, restrictions on possessing firearms or dangerous weapons, and other conditions reasonably necessary to assure appearance and good behavior. — Virginia Code § 19.2-123

rows: Release rests on the accused’s undertaking to appear and comply with applicable conditions.
The bond carries a stated monetary obligation but does not require security to be deposited as a condition of release.
Release requires the security or surety required by the judicial officer; the statute permits cash or qualifying property as security.
Both the accused and the Commonwealth have statutory routes to appeal bail decisions.
Failure to appear after release on a felony charge can constitute a Class 6 felony; failure to appear after release on a misdemeanor charge can constitute a Class 1 misdemeanor.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Virginia
bullets: Magistrates and courts make bail decisions within their statutory authority. The criminal court handling the prosecution is the forum for judicial proceedings concerning release, rather than a consumer complaint agency. — Virginia Code §§ 19.2-119 through 19.2-124

An accused’s appeal from a bail decision by a magistrate, clerk, or deputy clerk goes to the appropriate district court. A further appeal from a district court bail decision goes to circuit court. — Virginia Code § 19.2-124

The Virginia Department of Criminal Justice Services regulates licensed bail bondsmen and handles licensing-related complaints. A licensing complaint is distinct from judicial review of bail. — Virginia Code, Title 9.1, Chapter 1, Article 11

sections.heading: Common questions in Virginia
bullets: Is bail guaranteed? No. A judicial officer may deny bail when the statutory appearance-risk or unreasonable-danger standard is satisfied. — Virginia Code § 19.2-120
Does every defendant have to pay cash? No. Virginia authorizes personal recognizance and unsecured bonds as well as secured bonds. — Virginia Code § 19.2-123
Can the prosecutor challenge release? Yes. The Commonwealth may appeal a bail decision under the statutory review procedure. — Virginia Code § 19.2-124
Does forfeiting the bond resolve a missed appearance? No. A willful failure to appear can produce a separate criminal charge in addition to bond forfeiture. — Virginia Code § 19.2-128

criminal-law/virginia/domestic-violence-.summary: Virginia treats assault and battery against a family or household member as a specific domestic violence offense under Virginia Code § 18.2-57.2, ordinarily a Class 1 misdemeanor punishable by up to 12 months in jail and a $2,500 fine. Qualifying repeat offenses can be felonies, and conduct such as strangulation can support separate felony charges. Criminal prosecution and protective-order proceedings are distinct, so an incident may produce both criminal charges and court-ordered restrictions on contact.

facts.label: Basic offense
facts.value: Assault and battery against a family or household member is a Class 1 misdemeanor unless the statute’s repeat-offender provisions apply. The prosecution must prove the criminal offense and the qualifying relationship beyond a reasonable doubt. — Virginia Code § 18.2-57.2

facts.label: Family or household member
facts.value: Covered relationships include spouses and former spouses, parents, children, stepparents, stepchildren, siblings, grandparents, and grandchildren, regardless of residence. The definition also includes people with a child in common, certain in-laws living in the same home, and people who cohabit or cohabited within the previous 12 months. — Virginia Code § 16.1-228

facts.label: Dating relationships
facts.value: Dating alone does not automatically establish family-or-household-member status. The relationship must satisfy the statutory definition for a charge under the domestic assault statute; other criminal offenses can apply without that relationship. — Virginia Code §§ 16.1-228, 18.2-57, 18.2-57.2

rows: Assault and battery against a family or household member
Ordinarily Class 1 misdemeanor: up to 12 months in jail, a fine up to $2,500, or both.
Domestic assault with two qualifying prior convictions
Class 6 felony when statutory prior-conviction requirements are met, including the 20-year window and different offense dates.
Class 6 felony: knowingly, intentionally, and unlawfully applying pressure to another person’s neck that impedes circulation or respiration and results in wounding or bodily injury.
Violation of a family-abuse protective order
Covered violations are generally Class 1 misdemeanors; specified repeat or aggravated violations carry enhanced penalties.
One to five years’ imprisonment, or, in the authorized sentencing discretion, up to 12 months in jail, a fine up to $2,500, or both.

facts.label: Predominant physical aggressor
facts.value: When officers have probable cause for domestic assault or a qualifying protective-order violation, Virginia generally requires arrest of the predominant physical aggressor unless special circumstances dictate another course. Relevant factors include prior complaints, injury severity, future injury risk, and self-defense. — Virginia Code § 19.2-81.3

facts.label: Protective-order duration
facts.value: A final family-abuse protective order may last up to two years. The court may extend it through the statutory process. Such orders can prohibit contact and further family abuse independently of a criminal conviction. — Virginia Code § 16.1-279.1

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Virginia
bullets: Local police departments and sheriffs’ offices investigate domestic assault allegations; magistrates may issue criminal process and emergency protective orders. — Virginia Code §§ 19.2-45, 19.2-81.3, 16.1-253.4

Juvenile and Domestic Relations District Courts handle family-abuse protective orders and generally hear criminal cases involving offenses against family or household members. They conduct preliminary hearings on qualifying felony charges; circuit courts conduct felony trials. — Virginia Code §§ 16.1-241, 16.1-272

sections.heading: Common questions in Virginia
bullets: Can the complaining witness simply drop the charge? No. The criminal case is brought by the Commonwealth; the witness does not independently control dismissal.
Must the parties live together? No. Several covered relationships qualify regardless of shared residence. — Virginia Code § 16.1-228
Is every domestic assault a felony? No. The basic offense is a misdemeanor, but qualifying prior convictions can elevate it to a felony. — Virginia Code § 18.2-57.2
Does a protective order require a criminal conviction? No. Family-abuse protective orders are available through a separate statutory proceeding. — Virginia Code § 16.1-279.1

criminal-law/virginia/traffic-violations.summary: Virginia treats ordinary traffic infractions differently from criminal traffic offenses: an infraction is not a crime, while reckless driving is generally a Class 1 misdemeanor carrying possible jail time and a criminal conviction. Driving at least 20 mph above the posted limit, or faster than 85 mph regardless of the limit, qualifies as reckless driving by speed. Adult traffic cases generally begin in General District Court, and misdemeanor convictions can be appealed for a new trial in Circuit Court.

facts.label: Ordinary infractions
facts.value: Traffic infractions are violations of public order, not crimes. Unless another penalty applies, a violation covered by Virginia’s general traffic-infraction penalty provision carries a fine of no more than $250; court costs are separate. — Va. Code §§ 46.2-100, 46.2-113

facts.label: General reckless driving
facts.value: Driving recklessly, or at a speed or in a manner that endangers life, limb, or property, can constitute reckless driving regardless of the posted speed limit. — Va. Code § 46.2-852

facts.label: Misdemeanor punishment
facts.value: Reckless driving is generally a Class 1 misdemeanor. That classification permits up to 12 months in jail, a fine of up to $2,500, or both; those are maximum penalties, not mandatory sentences for every case. — Va. Code §§ 46.2-868, 18.2-11

rows: Generally a traffic infraction when prosecuted as speeding rather than reckless driving.
At least 20 mph above the applicable limit, or more than 85 mph; generally a Class 1 misdemeanor.
Reckless or dangerous operation can qualify even below the speed limit; generally a Class 1 misdemeanor.
A traffic infraction available when a reckless-driving case involves slight culpability; fine of up to $500.

facts.label: Trial court
facts.value: General District Courts hear adult traffic infractions and misdemeanor traffic prosecutions. These courts do not conduct jury trials. — Virginia Judicial System, General District Courts

facts.label: Appeal deadline
facts.value: A person convicted in district court of a traffic infraction or an offense that is not a felony may appeal to Circuit Court within 10 days of the conviction. The statute also addresses appeals following deferred proceedings. — Va. Code § 16.1-132

facts.label: New trial on appeal
facts.value: The Circuit Court hears the appeal de novo, meaning a new trial rather than review limited to the district-court record. — Va. Code § 16.1-136

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Virginia
bullets: General District Court clerk: Maintains adult traffic case records and processes filings in the court handling the charge. An appeal from a district-court conviction begins in the district court. — Va. Code § 16.1-132; Virginia Judicial System
Circuit Court: Hears appeals from General District Court traffic convictions and conducts the new trial. — Va. Code § 16.1-136

Virginia Department of Motor Vehicles: Maintains driving records and administers the driver-improvement point system; it does not decide whether a defendant is guilty of a traffic charge. — Va. Code §§ 46.2-383, 46.2-492

sections.heading: Common questions in Virginia
bullets: Is exactly 85 mph automatically reckless driving? Not under the absolute-speed threshold, which requires more than 85 mph. Exactly 85 mph can still qualify if it is at least 20 mph above the limit. — Va. Code § 46.2-862
Can driving below the speed limit be reckless? Yes. Dangerous operation can satisfy the general reckless-driving statute regardless of the posted limit. — Va. Code § 46.2-852

Can reckless driving become improper driving? Yes. When culpability is slight, the court may find improper driving; the prosecutor also has statutory authority to reduce the charge before the court’s decision. — Va. Code § 46.2-869

Does every reckless-driving conviction require jail? No. The ordinary Class 1 misdemeanor penalty allows jail, a fine, or both, without making jail mandatory in every case. — Va. Code §§ 46.2-868, 18.2-11

Virginia Legislative Information System — Misdemeanor penalties
Virginia Legislative Information System — District-court criminal procedure and appeals
Virginia Judicial System — General District Courts

criminal-law/washington/bail-and-bond.summary: Washington generally permits pretrial release in criminal cases, but release conditions and any bail depend on the charge, appearance risk, and public-safety concerns. Article I, section 20 of the Washington Constitution recognizes a right to bail subject to specified exceptions, while court rules favor release on personal recognizance when appropriate. A court may impose financial or nonfinancial conditions, and qualifying life-imprisonment cases can involve a separate hearing on detention without bail.

sections.heading: Washington’s right to bail and release standards

facts.label: Constitutional exceptions
facts.value: All persons charged with crimes are bailable by sufficient sureties except in specified capital cases and qualifying cases involving offenses punishable by the possibility of life imprisonment. The life-imprisonment exception requires clear and convincing evidence of a propensity for violence creating a substantial likelihood of danger to the community or any persons, subject to legislative limitations. — Washington Constitution, article I, section 20

facts.label: Personal recognizance
facts.value: For noncapital cases, the superior-court rule starts with release on personal recognizance unless the court finds that release will not reasonably assure appearance or identifies specified risks, including a likely violent crime, witness intimidation, or unlawful interference with justice. — CrR 3.2(a)

facts.label: Financial resources
facts.value: When addressing appearance risk, the court must impose the least restrictive conditions reasonably assuring appearance. If it requires a secured or unsecured bond, it must consider available information about the accused’s financial resources when determining the amount. — CrR 3.2(b)

facts.label: Excessive bail
facts.value: Washington’s Constitution separately prohibits excessive bail. That protection does not establish a statewide dollar ceiling or a uniform bail amount for each offense. — Washington Constitution, article I, section 14

rows: Release rests on the accused’s promise to comply with court requirements rather than a required secured bond. — CrR 3.2(a)
The court may place the accused in the custody of a designated person or organization agreeing to supervise the accused. — CrR 3.2(b)
The court may restrict travel, association, or place of abode during release. — CrR 3.2(b)
The court may require an appearance bond in a specified amount without requiring security to be deposited. — CrR 3.2(b)
The court may require a bond with solvent sureties or a cash deposit in lieu of the bond. — CrR 3.2(b)

facts.label: Detention without bail
facts.value: Washington provides a statutory detention-hearing process for qualifying offenses punishable by the possibility of life imprisonment. The hearing includes rights to counsel, to testify, to present witnesses and information, and to cross-examine appearing witnesses. — RCW 10.21.040

facts.label: Failure to appear
facts.value: Failure to appear as required can result in forfeiture of bail. Washington statutes govern forfeiture, proceedings against sureties, and circumstances involving return or remission of forfeited bail. — Chapter 10.19 RCW

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Washington
bullets: Superior court handles release decisions in its criminal cases under CrR 3.2; requests to change those conditions belong in the pending criminal case.
District and municipal courts use CrRLJ 3.2 for release decisions in criminal cases within their jurisdiction.
The clerk of the court handling the case maintains its court records, including filed release orders and bond documents.

sections.heading: Common questions in Washington
bullets: Is money always required for release? No. Personal recognizance and nonfinancial conditions are available under CrR 3.2.
Does paying bail end the case? No. Bail concerns release while the criminal proceedings continue, not dismissal or acquittal.
Can Washington deny bail? Yes, within the constitutional exceptions and applicable statutory procedures.
Does release eliminate other restrictions? No. Court-ordered supervision, travel restrictions, or other conditions can remain in effect.
