Washington Courts — CrR 3.2, Release of Accused
Washington Legislature — Chapter 10.21 RCW, Bail Determinations
Washington Legislature — Chapter 10.19 RCW, Bail and Appearance Bonds

criminal-law/washington/juvenile-law.summary: Washington generally handles alleged crimes committed before age 18 through juvenile court under the Juvenile Justice Act of 1977, but statutory exceptions place some cases in adult criminal court. Children under eight cannot commit crimes under Washington law, while children eight through eleven are presumed incapable unless the prosecution establishes sufficient understanding. Juvenile proceedings provide rights to counsel and proof beyond a reasonable doubt, but juvenile offense trials are conducted without a jury.

sections.heading: Washington juvenile jurisdiction and basic rights

facts.label: Governing law
facts.value: The Juvenile Justice Act of 1977 governs juvenile offender proceedings, including diversion, adjudication, disposition, and confinement. Juvenile court is a division of Washington superior court. — RCW 13.40.010; RCW 13.04.021

facts.label: Age and criminal capacity
facts.value: Children under eight are incapable of committing crime. Children eight and under twelve are presumed incapable, but that presumption can be overcome with proof that they understood the act and knew it was wrong. — RCW 9A.04.050

facts.label: Adult-court exceptions
facts.value: Juvenile jurisdiction is not automatic for every defendant under eighteen. Washington has statutory adult-court exceptions for specified cases involving sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds, and a juvenile court may decline jurisdiction through the statutory transfer process. — RCW 13.04.030; RCW 13.40.110

facts.label: Adjudication rights
facts.value: Juveniles have rights to counsel, confrontation, and the privilege against self-incrimination. The prosecution must prove the offense beyond a reasonable doubt. Juvenile court cases are tried without a jury. — RCW 13.40.140; RCW 13.04.021

rows: Law enforcement must provide access to an attorney for consultation before a juvenile waives constitutional rights during custodial interrogation, detention based on probable cause, or a request for consent to an evidentiary search. The consultation requirement cannot be waived; the statute contains limited exceptions.

Eligible cases may be handled through a diversion agreement rather than prosecution. Diversion eligibility and agreement conditions are controlled by statute; diversion is not guaranteed for every charge.

Washington uses juvenile disposition standards that consider the offense and criminal history. A court may impose a disposition outside the standard range upon the required manifest-injustice finding.
Juvenile courts generally must order restitution for qualifying loss or damage resulting from an offense. Restitution is distinct from confinement or community supervision.
Juvenile offender records are not automatically confidential merely because the accused is a minor. Washington provides statutory sealing procedures with eligibility requirements and exceptions.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Washington
bullets: Superior court juvenile division: Juvenile offender cases proceed in the juvenile division unless an adult-court jurisdiction rule applies. The superior court clerk maintains the court case file. — RCW 13.04.021; RCW 13.50.010
County prosecuting attorney: The prosecutor reviews referred allegations and makes statutory filing or diversion decisions; the prosecutor does not represent the juvenile. — RCW 13.40.070

Court handling the juvenile record: Requests to seal juvenile court records are judicial matters governed by Washington's juvenile-record statutes, rather than an ordinary agency complaint process. — RCW 13.50.260

sections.heading: Common questions in Washington
bullets: Does turning eighteen erase a juvenile record? No. Turning eighteen does not itself erase the record; sealing and destruction are governed by separate statutory requirements. — RCW 13.50.050; RCW 13.50.260; RCW 13.50.270
Can a parent waive the required attorney consultation? No. The consultation requirement under RCW 13.40.740 cannot be waived.
Is a juvenile entitled to a jury? Not in a Washington juvenile court proceeding. Juvenile cases are tried without a jury. — RCW 13.04.021
Can a juvenile case reach adult court? Yes. Statutory jurisdiction exclusions and judicial decline proceedings can place certain cases in adult criminal court. — RCW 13.04.030; RCW 13.40.110

sources.label: Washington Legislature — Juvenile Justice Act, chapter 13.40 RCW
Washington Legislature — Juvenile Courts and Juvenile Offenders, chapter 13.04 RCW
Washington Legislature — Criminal capacity, RCW 9A.04.050
Washington Legislature — Juvenile records, chapter 13.50 RCW

criminal-law/washington/expungement.summary: Washington generally uses conviction vacation, rather than automatic expungement, to provide relief from an eligible criminal conviction; vacation does not itself erase every record or seal the court file. Separate rules govern sealing court records and deleting certain nonconviction information held by criminal justice agencies. Eligibility depends on the offense, sentence history, waiting periods, and other statutory conditions, with different laws governing felony convictions and misdemeanor or gross misdemeanor convictions.

facts.label: Misdemeanors and gross misdemeanors
facts.value: RCW 9.96.060 authorizes the sentencing court to vacate qualifying misdemeanor and gross misdemeanor convictions. The procedure can include withdrawal of a guilty plea, dismissal of the charging document, and release from penalties and disabilities resulting from the offense, subject to statutory exceptions. — RCW 9.96.060

facts.label: Felonies
facts.value: Washington provides a separate vacation procedure for qualifying felony convictions. Class A felonies cannot be vacated under this statute, and additional restrictions apply to violent offenses, crimes against persons, and specified offenses. — RCW 9.94A.640

facts.label: Disclosure after vacation
facts.value: The vacation statutes generally allow a person to state that they have not been convicted of the vacated crime, including on employment applications. However, the statutes preserve specified uses of the conviction in later criminal proceedings. — RCW 9.96.060; RCW 9.94A.640

rows: Qualifying misdemeanor and gross misdemeanor convictions; eligibility restrictions apply.
Qualifying felony convictions; offense exclusions and waiting periods apply.
Restricts public access to court records through a separate court determination.
Addresses qualifying criminal history information held by criminal justice agencies, not automatic destruction of the court file.

facts.label: Pending charges
facts.value: Pending criminal charges are a statutory barrier under the general misdemeanor and felony vacation provisions. Both statutes address charges pending in Washington, another state, or federal court. — RCW 9.96.060; RCW 9.94A.640

facts.label: Domestic violence cases
facts.value: Misdemeanor domestic violence convictions have additional eligibility restrictions, including a longer waiting period than the ordinary misdemeanor provision. Multiple domestic violence convictions arising from different incidents can bar relief under that provision. — RCW 9.96.060

facts.label: Sealing is not automatic
facts.value: Vacating a conviction does not automatically seal the court record. Sealing generally requires written findings that identified compelling privacy or safety concerns outweigh the public interest in access; agreement between the parties alone is insufficient. — Washington General Rule 15(c)

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Washington
bullets: Misdemeanor and gross misdemeanor vacation applications go to the sentencing court, ordinarily a district or municipal court. — RCW 9.96.060
Felony vacation applications go to the superior court that handled the conviction. — RCW 9.94A.640

Court-record sealing requests are decided by the court maintaining the record; requests to delete eligible nonconviction criminal history information concern the criminal justice agency maintaining that information. — Washington General Rule 15; RCW 10.97.060

sections.heading: Common questions in Washington
bullets: Does vacation erase the entire case? No. Vacation and sealing are different procedures, and vacation alone does not remove the court file from public access.
Can every felony be vacated? No. Class A felonies and other statutorily excluded convictions are ineligible under RCW 9.94A.640.
Can a dismissed charge qualify for record relief? Certain nonconviction information can qualify for agency deletion under RCW 10.97.060, subject to its conditions and exceptions.

Does Washington have special relief for marijuana possession? Yes. RCW 9.96.060 contains a special vacation provision for qualifying marijuana possession convictions involving people who were at least 21 when the offense occurred.

sources.label: Washington Legislature — RCW 9.96.060
Washington Legislature — RCW 9.94A.640
Washington Legislature — RCW 10.97.060
Washington Courts — General Rule 15

criminal-law/washington/traffic-violatio.summary: Washington distinguishes civil traffic infractions from criminal traffic offenses: ordinary speeding generally follows the infraction process, while reckless driving, driving under the influence, and certain other violations can lead to prosecution and jail. The consequences depend on the offense and criminal history, and a license action can occur separately from the criminal case. District and municipal courts generally handle misdemeanor traffic prosecutions; superior courts handle felony traffic cases.

facts.label: Civil traffic violations
facts.value: Washington generally treats traffic-law violations as infractions unless a statute makes the conduct criminal. A civil traffic infraction does not carry imprisonment as its punishment. — RCW 46.63.020

facts.label: Criminal proof
facts.value: In a criminal prosecution, the state must prove the offense beyond a reasonable doubt. In a contested traffic-infraction hearing, the state must establish the infraction by a preponderance of the evidence. — RCW 9A.04.100; RCW 46.63.090

facts.label: Infraction hearings
facts.value: Traffic-infraction hearings are conducted without a jury. A contested hearing determines whether the infraction occurred; a mitigation hearing addresses the circumstances without contesting that it occurred. — RCW 46.63.090; RCW 46.63.100

rows: Driving with willful or wanton disregard for the safety of persons or property. — RCW 46.61.500
Generally a gross misdemeanor; felony circumstances are specified by statute
Driving while impaired by alcohol or drugs, or meeting specified alcohol or THC concentration thresholds. — RCW 46.61.502

Negligent driving that endangers or is likely to endanger a person or property, together with exhibiting the effects of alcohol, illegal drugs, or specified prescription-drug consumption. — RCW 46.61.5249
Negligent driving that endangers or is likely to endanger a person or property, without the additional substance-related element of first-degree negligent driving. — RCW 46.61.525

facts.label: General criminal maximums
facts.value: A misdemeanor carries up to 90 days in jail and a $1,000 fine; a gross misdemeanor carries up to 364 days in jail and a $5,000 fine. These are general statutory ceilings, not mandatory sentences for every offense. — RCW 9A.20.021

facts.label: DUI sentencing
facts.value: Washington has a separate DUI sentencing statute addressing confinement, fines, license consequences, and ignition-interlock requirements. Applicable consequences depend on factors including qualifying prior offenses and test results or refusal. — RCW 46.61.5055

facts.label: Reckless-driving suspension
facts.value: A reckless-driving conviction results in a 30-day driver's-license suspension by the Department of Licensing. — RCW 46.61.500

facts.label: Separate administrative action
facts.value: Washington's implied-consent law provides for administrative license action arising from qualifying alcohol or drug test results or refusal, separately from criminal prosecution. — RCW 46.20.308

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Washington
bullets: District and municipal courts: Generally handle misdemeanor and gross-misdemeanor traffic prosecutions within their jurisdiction.
Superior courts: Handle felony traffic prosecutions, including felony DUI cases.
Court identified on the notice: Handles responses and hearings for a traffic infraction under RCW 46.63.070.
Washington Department of Licensing: Handles administrative driver's-license actions and implied-consent hearing proceedings under RCW 46.20.308.

sections.heading: Common questions in Washington
bullets: Is every traffic ticket criminal? No. Washington generally classifies traffic violations as civil infractions unless the law specifies otherwise.
Can reckless driving mean jail? Yes. It is a gross misdemeanor, not merely an infraction.
Is DUI always a misdemeanor? No. RCW 46.61.502 specifies circumstances making DUI a felony.
Does a criminal case decide every license issue? No. Department of Licensing proceedings can operate separately under the implied-consent law.

Washington Legislature — Chapter 46.63 RCW, Disposition of Traffic Infractions
Washington Legislature — RCW 9A.20.021, Maximum Sentences

criminal-law/west-virginia/arrest-proces.summary: In West Virginia, an arrested person must be brought before a magistrate without unnecessary delay; the initial appearance addresses the accusation, basic rights, and possible release on bail. A felony arrest does not establish guilt: unless preliminary examination is waived, the magistrate determines whether there is probable cause to hold the accused for further proceedings. Magistrates handle the early stages of many criminal cases, while circuit courts handle felony prosecutions.

facts.label: Arrest warrants
facts.value: A magistrate may issue an arrest warrant when the complaint and supporting material establish probable cause to believe an offense occurred and the defendant committed it. An arrest warrant is not a finding of guilt. — W. Va. Code § 62-1-2

facts.label: Prompt appearance
facts.value: An officer making an arrest under a warrant, or a person making an arrest without a warrant, must take the arrested person before a magistrate without unnecessary delay. For a warrantless arrest, a complaint must be filed forthwith. — W. Va. Code § 62-1-5

facts.label: Information and rights
facts.value: The magistrate must explain the complaint, the right to retain counsel, the right to a preliminary examination, and the right not to make a statement. The magistrate must also warn that a statement may be used against the accused. — W. Va. Code § 62-1-6

facts.label: Opportunity to consult counsel
facts.value: The accused must receive a reasonable opportunity to consult counsel. The initial appearance is not a trial deciding whether the accused committed the offense. — W. Va. Code § 62-1-6

rows: The magistrate explains the accusation and rights and addresses bail under the applicable bail law.
Unless waived, the magistrate examines whether an offense occurred and whether probable cause connects the accused to it.
At the preliminary examination, the accused may cross-examine adverse witnesses and introduce evidence.
The magistrate holds the accused to answer in the court having jurisdiction.
The magistrate must discharge the accused.

facts.label: General entitlement
facts.value: Before conviction, a person arrested for an offense not punishable by life imprisonment is entitled to admission to bail. For an offense punishable by life imprisonment, admission to bail is discretionary with the court having jurisdiction to try the offense. — W. Va. Code § 62-1C-1

facts.label: Setting the amount
facts.value: Bail must be set at an amount that, in the court's judgment, will ensure appearance. Relevant considerations include the seriousness of the charge, previous criminal record, financial ability, and probability of appearance. — W. Va. Code § 62-1C-3

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in West Virginia
bullets: Magistrate court: Criminal complaints, initial appearances, and preliminary examinations are handled through the magistrate-court process. — W. Va. Code §§ 62-1-1, 62-1-5 through 62-1-8.

Circuit court: Felony prosecutions fall within circuit-court jurisdiction; magistrates conduct preliminary felony proceedings rather than felony trials. — W. Va. Constitution, Article VIII, § 6; W. Va. Code § 50-2-3.
Arresting agency: Complaints about an officer's conduct may be directed to that agency. An administrative complaint is separate from the criminal case.

sections.heading: Common questions in West Virginia
bullets: Does arrest mean guilt? No. Arrest and preliminary proceedings address accusations and probable cause, not proof of guilt at trial.
Must the accused make a statement at the initial appearance? No. The magistrate must explain that a statement is not required. — W. Va. Code § 62-1-6.
Is everyone automatically entitled to bail? No. Bail is discretionary before conviction for offenses punishable by life imprisonment. — W. Va. Code § 62-1C-1.
Can the preliminary examination be waived? Yes. West Virginia law expressly permits waiver. — W. Va. Code § 62-1-8.

sources.label: West Virginia Legislature — Criminal Procedure, Article 1
West Virginia Legislature — Bail, Article 1C
West Virginia Legislature — Magistrate criminal jurisdiction

criminal-law/west-virginia/expungement.summary: West Virginia permits expungement of certain dismissed or acquitted charges and certain misdemeanor and nonviolent felony convictions, but eligibility depends on the disposition, offense, criminal history, and statutory exclusions. Conviction petitions generally require waiting one year for a single misdemeanor, two years for multiple misdemeanors, or five years for an eligible felony, measured from the latest applicable statutory event. The circuit court decides whether relief is available; expungement is not automatic simply because a case ended or a sentence was completed.

facts.label: Dismissals and acquittals
facts.value: West Virginia Code § 61-11-25 allows a person acquitted or whose charges were dismissed to request expungement, subject to statutory restrictions. It excludes charges dismissed in exchange for a guilty plea to another offense and excludes applicants previously convicted of a felony. — W. Va. Code § 61-11-25

facts.label: Eligible convictions
facts.value: A separate procedure covers qualifying misdemeanor convictions and nonviolent felony convictions. It does not make every misdemeanor or every offense described as nonviolent eligible; the statute contains offense exclusions and other eligibility conditions. — W. Va. Code § 61-11-26

facts.label: Excluded offenses
facts.value: The conviction-expungement statute excludes driving under the influence of alcohol or controlled substances and offenses involving the use or exhibition of a deadly weapon or dangerous instrument, among other listed categories. — W. Va. Code § 61-11-26

rows: A motion cannot be filed until 60 days after the acquittal or dismissal.
One year after conviction, completion of incarceration, or completion of supervision, whichever occurs last.
Two years after the last conviction, completion of incarceration, or completion of supervision, whichever occurs last.
Five years after conviction, completion of incarceration, or completion of probation, parole, or supervised release, whichever occurs last.

sections.heading: Court review and the effect of an order

facts.label: Proof and review
facts.value: For conviction expungement, the petitioner bears a clear-and-convincing-evidence burden. The court considers statutory eligibility, rehabilitation, and whether expungement is consistent with the public welfare. Prosecutors and other designated participants have an opportunity to respond. — W. Va. Code § 61-11-26

facts.label: Records covered
facts.value: An expungement order can reach court and law-enforcement records associated with the covered matter. The governing statutes provide for sealing records and restrict their inspection; expungement is not simply a change to the sentence. — W. Va. Code §§ 61-11-25 and 61-11-26

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in West Virginia
bullets: For a qualifying dismissal or acquittal, the motion is filed in the circuit court of the county where the charge was filed. — W. Va. Code § 61-11-25

For an eligible conviction, the petition is filed in the circuit court of the county where the conviction occurred, including qualifying convictions originating in a lower court. — W. Va. Code § 61-11-26

The circuit court, rather than a consumer complaint agency or the State Police acting alone, grants judicial expungement under these provisions. Questions about individual eligibility are matters to talk to a lawyer about.

sections.heading: Common questions in West Virginia
bullets: Does a dismissed charge disappear automatically? No. Section 61-11-25 provides a court application process, and statutory exclusions still apply.
Can a felony conviction qualify? Yes. Section 61-11-26 permits expungement of qualifying nonviolent felony convictions, subject to its restrictions.
Does the waiting period always start at sentencing? No. For convictions, later completion of incarceration or supervision can control the starting point.
Does finishing the waiting period guarantee approval? No. The offense and applicant must qualify, and the court must make the required statutory findings.

sources.label: West Virginia Legislature — W. Va. Code § 61-11-25
West Virginia Legislature — W. Va. Code § 61-11-26

criminal-law/wisconsin/bail-and-bond.summary: Wisconsin courts may release a criminal defendant on a signature bond or require monetary bail, with conditions governing the defendant’s conduct while the case is pending. The Wisconsin Constitution generally protects pretrial release, but permits monetary conditions to account for additional public-safety considerations when a defendant is accused of a violent crime. Chapter 969 governs release, changes to bond conditions, and forfeiture; intentionally violating a bond can also produce a separate bail-jumping charge.

sections.heading: Wisconsin’s legal framework for pretrial release

facts.label: Constitutional rule
facts.value: Before conviction, an accused person generally is eligible for release under reasonable conditions designed to assure appearance, protect community members from serious harm, or prevent intimidation of witnesses. The Wisconsin Constitution also provides limited exceptions allowing detention without release. — Wisconsin Constitution, article I, section 8(2)–(3)

facts.label: Monetary conditions
facts.value: Monetary conditions may be imposed when the court finds a reasonable basis to believe they are necessary to assure appearance. For a person accused of a violent crime, the constitution permits additional considerations, including previous violent-crime convictions, community protection, the seriousness of the offense, and the need to prevent witness intimidation. — Wisconsin Constitution, article I, section 8(2)

facts.label: Individual circumstances
facts.value: Wisconsin’s bail statute identifies considerations including the defendant’s ability to give bail, the nature and gravity of the charged offense, criminal record, court-appearance history, community ties, employment, and character. There is no single statewide dollar amount that applies to every criminal charge. — Wis. Stat. § 969.01(4)

facts.label: Commercial bail bonds
facts.value: Wisconsin prohibits compensating a surety for acting as surety on a bail bond. Its system therefore differs from states where commercial bail-bond companies routinely post bonds in exchange for a fee. — Wis. Stat. § 969.12(2)

rows: Release can occur through an unsecured appearance bond rather than an upfront cash deposit. The defendant still must comply with the bond’s conditions.
A court may require a monetary condition subject to constitutional limits; release remains subject to any additional lawful conditions.
Wisconsin Constitution, article I, section 8(2); Wis. Stat. §§ 969.02–969.03
The statutory modification process allows a court to change release conditions or impose additional or different conditions.
A breach of a bond condition can result in forfeiture. The statute also addresses setting aside forfeiture, enforcement, and remission.
Intentionally failing to comply with bond terms is a separate offense: a Class A misdemeanor when the underlying charge is a misdemeanor, or a Class H felony when it is a felony.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Wisconsin
bullets: Circuit court handling the criminal case: Bail and release conditions are addressed in the criminal proceeding. Wisconsin Statutes § 969.08 provides the process for seeking modification of those conditions.

Clerk of circuit court in that county: The clerk maintains the criminal court file, including filed bond documents and court orders. A clerk’s administrative role does not include overruling judicial release conditions.

Wisconsin appellate courts: Review of bail-related orders is governed by Wisconsin’s applicable appellate procedures. Review is a judicial process, not a complaint to a commercial bail-bond regulator.

sections.heading: Common questions in Wisconsin
bullets: Does a signature bond mean there are no restrictions? No. An unsecured bond can still include enforceable release conditions. — Wis. Stat. §§ 969.02–969.03.
Can bond conditions change after release? Yes. Wisconsin law provides for modification of release conditions. — Wis. Stat. § 969.08.
Is missing court the only form of bail jumping? No. The offense covers intentional failure to comply with the terms of a qualifying bond, not just failure to appear. — Wis. Stat. § 946.49.

Does an alleged violation automatically establish bail jumping? No. Bail jumping is a separate criminal charge whose statutory elements must be proved; bond forfeiture is a distinct proceeding. — Wis. Stat. §§ 946.49 and 969.13.

sources.label: Wisconsin Legislature — Wisconsin Constitution, article I, section 8
Wisconsin Legislature — Chapter 969: Bail and Other Conditions of Release
Wisconsin Legislature — Section 946.49: Bail Jumping

criminal-law/wisconsin/domestic-violence.summary: Wisconsin generally prosecutes domestic violence through crimes such as battery, disorderly conduct, or strangulation and suffocation, rather than through a single charge called domestic violence. The domestic-abuse designation depends on the conduct and relationship involved, and it can trigger special arrest procedures, temporary contact restrictions, and a sentencing surcharge. Penalties depend on the underlying offense and applicable enhancements; a misdemeanor battery conviction and a felony strangulation conviction carry substantially different maximum sentences.

sections.heading: What counts as domestic abuse in Wisconsin

facts.label: Covered relationships
facts.value: For Wisconsin’s domestic-abuse arrest law, the alleged conduct must involve an adult against a spouse or former spouse, an adult with whom the person resides or formerly resided, or a person with whom the adult has a child in common. A dating relationship alone does not establish this statutory relationship requirement — Wis. Stat. § 968.075(1)(a).

facts.label: Covered conduct
facts.value: The arrest-law definition includes intentional infliction of physical pain, physical injury, or illness; intentional impairment of physical condition; specified sexual assault; and a physical act that may cause reasonable fear of imminent qualifying harm — Wis. Stat. § 968.075(1)(a).

facts.label: Arrest rules
facts.value: Arrest is mandatory when the statutory criteria are met, not merely whenever someone alleges domestic abuse. The law addresses likely continued abuse, evidence of physical injury, and sexual assault, and contains predominant-aggressor rules when officers identify abuse by multiple people — Wis. Stat. § 968.075(2).

rows: 3 years and 6 months’ imprisonment, $10,000 fine, or both

facts.label: 72-hour restriction
facts.value: Following an arrest for a domestic-abuse incident, the arrested person generally must avoid the alleged victim’s residence and premises temporarily occupied by the victim, and must not contact the victim, for 72 hours. The statute provides a waiver process for the alleged victim; a waiver does not itself cancel a separate court order — Wis. Stat. § 968.075(5).

facts.label: Domestic-abuse surcharge
facts.value: Courts impose a $100 domestic-abuse surcharge for each qualifying offense when the statutory offense, relationship, and conduct requirements are satisfied. This is separate from the offense’s maximum fine — Wis. Stat. § 973.055(1).

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Wisconsin
bullets: Local police departments and county sheriffs investigate reported domestic-abuse crimes; Wisconsin’s arrest procedures appear in Wis. Stat. § 968.075.
The county district attorney prosecutes state criminal cases. The complaining witness does not independently control whether charges proceed — Wis. Stat. § 978.05(1).
Wisconsin circuit courts hear criminal prosecutions. A domestic-abuse restraining-order or injunction proceeding is a separate civil process governed by Wis. Stat. § 813.12.

sections.heading: Common questions in Wisconsin
bullets: Is domestic violence always a felony? No. Battery under § 940.19(1) is a misdemeanor; strangulation under § 940.235(1) is a felony.

Must there be a visible injury? No. The domestic-abuse definition includes qualifying fear-causing physical acts, and the arrest decision cannot rest solely on the absence of visible injury — § 968.075(1), (3).
Can the alleged victim stop an arrest? Their willingness to participate in prosecution cannot determine the officer’s arrest decision — § 968.075(3).
Does the 72-hour period replace bail conditions? No. Courts can impose separate release conditions, including restrictions on contact — § 969.02.

sources.label: Wisconsin Legislature — Domestic abuse incidents, § 968.075
Wisconsin Legislature — Crimes against life and bodily security, Chapter 940
Wisconsin Legislature — Criminal penalties, Chapter 939
Wisconsin Legislature — Domestic abuse surcharge, § 973.055

criminal-law/wisconsin/drug-charges.summary: Wisconsin prosecutes controlled-substance offenses under Chapter 961 of the Wisconsin Statutes, with penalties depending on the substance, conduct, quantity, and sometimes prior convictions. Possession can be a misdemeanor or felony, while manufacturing, delivering, or possessing drugs with intent to deliver can carry substantially greater penalties. State criminal cases are handled in circuit court, and qualifying first-offense possession cases may receive deferred treatment under Wisconsin Statutes section 961.47 rather than an immediate judgment of conviction.

sections.heading: Wisconsin drug offenses and possession penalties

facts.label: Possession
facts.value: Wisconsin generally prohibits possessing a controlled substance or controlled-substance analog unless obtained through a valid prescription or otherwise authorized by Chapter 961. The applicable penalty depends on the substance and statutory provision. — Wis. Stat. § 961.41(3g)

facts.label: Marijuana or THC
facts.value: A first possession offense is punishable by up to $1,000 in fines, up to six months in jail, or both. A second or subsequent offense can be a Class I felony under the statute's repeat-offense provisions. — Wis. Stat. § 961.41(3g)(e)

facts.label: Cocaine
facts.value: A first cocaine-possession offense is punishable by up to $5,000 in fines, up to one year in county jail, or both. A second or subsequent offense can be a Class I felony. — Wis. Stat. § 961.41(3g)(c)

facts.label: Methamphetamine and narcotic drugs
facts.value: Unauthorized methamphetamine possession is a Class I felony. Possession of a Schedule I or II narcotic drug, including heroin, is also a Class I felony. — Wis. Stat. § 961.41(3g)(g), (am)

facts.label: Delivery and intent to deliver
facts.value: Manufacturing or delivering controlled substances and possessing them with intent to manufacture or deliver are separately prohibited. Felony classifications vary by substance and, for many drugs, quantity; these offenses are distinct from simple possession. — Wis. Stat. § 961.41(1), (1m)

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Wisconsin
bullets: Wisconsin circuit courts hear state criminal drug prosecutions. Criminal case documents are filed with the clerk of circuit court in the county where the prosecution is pending. — Wisconsin Court System, Circuit Courts.
County district attorneys ordinarily prosecute violations of Wisconsin's criminal drug laws. The district attorney's office is a prosecuting agency, not defense counsel. — Wis. Stat. § 978.05.
Wisconsin's State Public Defender provides representation to eligible defendants in criminal cases. Eligibility and appointment are governed by Chapter 977. — Wis. Stat. §§ 977.05, 977.07.

sections.heading: Common questions in Wisconsin
bullets: Is every drug-possession charge a felony? No. First-offense THC and cocaine possession have misdemeanor penalties, while methamphetamine and heroin possession are Class I felonies. — Wis. Stat. § 961.41(3g).

Can a first possession case end without a conviction? In qualifying cases, section 961.47 permits probation without entry of a judgment of conviction, with the defendant's consent. Successful completion results in discharge and dismissal; this disposition is available only once. — Wis. Stat. § 961.47.

Does the felony imprisonment maximum mean that entire time is spent in prison? Not ordinarily. Wisconsin's bifurcated prison sentences include initial confinement followed by extended supervision. The table lists total statutory imprisonment ceilings, not mandatory sentences or confinement-only limits. — Wis. Stat. §§ 939.50, 973.01.
Must prosecutors prove a completed sale for an intent-to-deliver charge? No. Possession with intent to manufacture or deliver is a separate offense from completed delivery. — Wis. Stat. § 961.41(1m).

sources.label: Wisconsin Legislature — Chapter 961, Uniform Controlled Substances Act
Wisconsin Legislature — Section 939.50, Classification of felonies
Wisconsin Legislature — Section 973.01, Bifurcated sentence
Wisconsin Court System — Circuit courts

criminal-law/wisconsin/expungement.summary: Wisconsin permits expungement of certain criminal convictions when the person committed the offense before age 25 and the offense carried a maximum imprisonment term of six years or less, subject to statutory exclusions. For the ordinary adult sentencing procedure, the judge must authorize expungement at sentencing, and the person must successfully complete the sentence. Expungement limits access to the court record; it does not erase every government record of the incident.

facts.label: Age and offense limit
facts.value: The ordinary adult provision covers offenses committed before age 25 for which the maximum period of imprisonment is six years or less. The statutory maximum, rather than the sentence actually imposed, controls this threshold — Wis. Stat. § 973.015(1m)(a)1.

facts.label: Judicial findings
facts.value: The sentencing court must determine that the person will benefit from expungement and society will not be harmed. Meeting the age and offense thresholds does not automatically entitle someone to expungement — Wis. Stat. § 973.015(1m)(a)1.

facts.label: Felony exclusions
facts.value: The statute excludes specified Class H and Class I felony convictions. Restrictions include prior felony convictions and offenses classified as violent under the referenced statute; additional listed offenses are also excluded — Wis. Stat. § 973.015(1m)(a)2.

facts.label: Timing
facts.value: Under the ordinary adult provision, authorization must occur at sentencing. Finishing a sentence does not create a new opportunity to obtain authorization that was never granted — Wis. Stat. § 973.015(1m)(a)1.

sections.heading: What the process does and does not cover

rows: Requires no subsequent conviction, successful completion of probation if imposed, and satisfaction of the sentence's conditions.
The detaining or probationary authority issues a discharge certificate and forwards it to the court of record.
Discharge from probation alone does not establish successful completion when probation conditions were violated.
Expungement restricts access to the court record rather than undoing the historical fact of conviction.
Wisconsin Court System, Expunging court records
Court expungement does not remove records maintained by law enforcement or the Wisconsin Department of Justice.
Wisconsin Court System, Expunging court records

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Wisconsin
bullets: The circuit court handling the criminal prosecution makes the ordinary adult expungement decision at sentencing. Wisconsin does not assign that decision to a separate statewide expungement board — Wis. Stat. § 973.015(1m)(a).
The court of record receives the completion certificate. The clerk of circuit court maintains the case record and associated expungement documentation — Wis. Stat. § 973.015(1m)(b).

The Wisconsin Department of Justice maintains a separate criminal-history repository. A court-record expungement and a dispute about the accuracy of a criminal-history entry are different matters — Wisconsin Court System, Expunging court records.

sections.heading: Common questions in Wisconsin
bullets: Does turning 25 before sentencing make someone ineligible? Not by itself. The statute measures age when the offense was committed, not when sentencing occurs — Wis. Stat. § 973.015(1m)(a)1.

Does a short jail sentence make any felony eligible? No. Eligibility depends on the offense's maximum imprisonment term and the statutory exclusions, not simply the punishment imposed — Wis. Stat. § 973.015(1m)(a).
Is expungement automatic after probation ends? No. Prior sentencing authorization and successful completion are required under the ordinary adult procedure — Wis. Stat. § 973.015(1m).

Does expungement erase a Wisconsin DOJ background-check record? No. Expungement of the court record does not erase the separate DOJ criminal-history record — Wisconsin Court System, Expunging court records.

sources.label: Wisconsin Legislature — Wis. Stat. § 973.015, Special disposition
Wisconsin Court System — Expunging court records

criminal-law/wisconsin/juvenile-law.summary: Wisconsin generally handles alleged crimes committed by children ages 10 through 16 as delinquency cases under Chapter 938, the Juvenile Justice Code, while a person who commits a crime at age 17 generally faces adult criminal jurisdiction. Some younger children fall under original adult criminal jurisdiction for specified offenses, and other juvenile cases can be transferred through judicial waiver. Juvenile proceedings use different adjudication, disposition, and record-access rules from adult prosecutions, although confidentiality is not absolute.

facts.label: General delinquency jurisdiction
facts.value: The court assigned to exercise juvenile jurisdiction generally has exclusive jurisdiction over a juvenile age 10 or older alleged to be delinquent. For investigating or prosecuting criminal-law violations, Wisconsin treats a person who has attained age 17 as an adult. — Wis. Stat. §§ 938.02(1), (10), 938.12

facts.label: Children younger than 10
facts.value: An alleged delinquent act committed before age 10 can support a juvenile-in-need-of-protection-or-services proceeding rather than an ordinary delinquency adjudication. — Wis. Stat. § 938.13(12)

facts.label: Waiver into adult court
facts.value: A waiver petition may concern any alleged criminal-law violation committed at age 15 or older, or specified offenses committed at age 14 or older. The judge considers statutory factors and must find clear and convincing evidence that retaining juvenile jurisdiction would be contrary to the juvenile’s or public’s best interests. — Wis. Stat. § 938.18

facts.label: Original adult jurisdiction
facts.value: Specified cases begin under adult criminal jurisdiction without a juvenile waiver order. These include certain homicide allegations against juveniles age 10 or older; the statute also addresses specified prior adult proceedings and offenses connected to an adult-jurisdiction case. — Wis. Stat. § 938.183

rows: Juveniles alleged to be delinquent have a statutory right to counsel; representation and any permitted waiver are governed by specific statutory requirements.
The allegations in a delinquency petition must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt.
Delinquency fact-finding hearings are conducted by a judge without a jury.
Authorized outcomes include supervision, services, restitution, community service, and qualifying out-of-home or correctional placements, subject to statutory conditions.
A delinquency adjudication is not a criminal conviction, but statutes permit specified later uses of juvenile adjudications and records.

facts.label: Confidentiality has exceptions
facts.value: Juvenile law-enforcement and court records have statutory confidentiality protections, but access and disclosure exceptions apply. A juvenile case does not guarantee that every record or proceeding remains private. — Wis. Stat. §§ 938.396, 938.299

facts.label: Reverse waiver
facts.value: For juveniles subject to original adult criminal jurisdiction, Wisconsin provides a statutory procedure for seeking transfer to juvenile court. Transfer requires the juvenile to establish the statutory criteria by a preponderance of the evidence; it is not automatic. — Wis. Stat. § 970.032

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Wisconsin
bullets: Circuit court: Wisconsin circuit courts exercise juvenile jurisdiction through their assigned juvenile branches or judges. Delinquency petitions are filed with the court under Chapter 938. — Wis. Stat. §§ 938.06, 938.25
Juvenile intake: The county’s designated juvenile intake operation screens referrals and performs the intake functions established by statute. — Wis. Stat. §§ 938.067, 938.24
District attorney: The district attorney represents the public interest in delinquency proceedings. — Wis. Stat. § 938.09

sections.heading: Common questions in Wisconsin
bullets: Is a 17-year-old normally prosecuted as a juvenile? No. Wisconsin generally treats age 17 as adulthood for criminal investigation and prosecution. — Wis. Stat. § 938.02
Can someone younger than 17 face adult charges? Yes. Original adult jurisdiction and judicial waiver provide separate routes into adult criminal court. — Wis. Stat. §§ 938.183, 938.18
Does a delinquency finding equal a criminal conviction? No, although it can have later legal consequences under statutory exceptions. — Wis. Stat. § 938.35

Are juvenile records automatically erased? No. Confidentiality and expungement are different. Section 938.355(4m) provides a conditional process for expunging a delinquency adjudication record. — Wis. Stat. §§ 938.396, 938.355(4m)

sources.label: Wisconsin Legislature — Chapter 938, Juvenile Justice Code
Wisconsin Legislature — Section 938.18, jurisdiction for criminal proceedings
Wisconsin Legislature — Section 970.032, preliminary examination and reverse waiver

criminal-law/wyoming/arrest-process.summary: In Wyoming, an arrest may be made under a warrant or under statutory authority for a warrantless arrest; an arrested person must then be brought before a judicial officer without unnecessary delay. The initial appearance addresses the accusation, rights, counsel, and release conditions, while a felony case ordinarily proceeds through a preliminary examination unless that examination is waived or an indictment makes it unnecessary.

sections.heading: Arrest authority and the first court appearance

facts.label: Arrest warrants
facts.value: A warrant based on a criminal complaint requires probable cause to believe an offense occurred and the defendant committed it. A summons may be issued instead of a warrant under the rule’s procedures. — Wyoming Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 4

facts.label: Warrantless arrests
facts.value: Wyoming law authorizes warrantless arrests in specified circumstances, including when an officer has probable cause to believe a person committed a felony or misdemeanor in the officer’s presence, or committed a felony outside the officer’s presence. Additional statutory grounds apply in particular situations. — Wyo. Stat. § 7-2-102

facts.label: Prompt appearance
facts.value: An arrested person must be taken before a judicial officer without unnecessary delay. When the arrest occurred without a warrant, a complaint must be filed promptly. — Wyoming Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 5(a)

facts.label: Rights explained
facts.value: At the initial appearance, the judicial officer explains the charge, the right to counsel, the right to remain silent, and the circumstances under which pretrial release may be secured. Statements made by the defendant may be used against the defendant. — Wyoming Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 5(b)

rows: The judicial officer addresses rights, counsel, and pretrial release; this is not a trial.
Release may involve personal recognizance, an unsecured appearance bond, or conditions imposed under the criminal rules.
Unless waived or displaced by an indictment, the examination tests whether probable cause supports holding the defendant for further proceedings.
The charge is stated and the defendant is called upon to plead.
The criminal rules generally require trial within 180 days after arraignment, subject to excluded periods and authorized continuances.

facts.label: Constitutional bail protection
facts.value: Wyoming’s Constitution prohibits excessive bail and makes prisoners bailable by sufficient sureties except in capital cases when the proof is evident or the presumption great. — Wyoming Constitution, Article 1, § 14

facts.label: Appointed representation
facts.value: The criminal rules provide for assignment of counsel to financially eligible defendants unless an applicable exception or valid waiver applies. Arrest alone does not establish financial eligibility. — Wyoming Rules of Criminal Procedure, Rule 44

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Wyoming
bullets: Circuit courts handle state misdemeanor cases and preliminary proceedings in felony cases; felony trials occur in district court. — Wyo. Stat. § 5-9-129; Wyoming Constitution, Article 5, § 10
Municipal courts handle prosecutions for municipal ordinance violations rather than state felony trials. — Wyo. Stat. § 5-6-101
The Wyoming Office of the State Public Defender provides representation in qualifying criminal cases under the Public Defender Act. — Wyo. Stat. §§ 7-6-101 through 7-6-114

sections.heading: Common questions in Wyoming
bullets: Does every arrest require a warrant? No. Wyoming expressly authorizes warrantless arrests under specified circumstances. — Wyo. Stat. § 7-2-102
Is the initial appearance the same as a trial? No. It addresses rights and preliminary matters rather than determining guilt. — W.R.Cr.P. 5
Does every felony case require a preliminary examination? No. The examination may be waived, and an indictment removes the requirement. — W.R.Cr.P. 5(c)

Does the 180-day trial period begin at arrest? Not under Rule 48(b); its general period runs from arraignment, with exclusions and continuances. Constitutional speedy-trial protections are separate. — W.R.Cr.P. 48(b)

criminal-law/wyoming/expungement.summary: Wyoming allows expungement of qualifying criminal records, including certain arrests that did not lead to convictions and eligible misdemeanor or felony convictions, through a petition to a court. Eligibility depends on the outcome, offense, statutory waiting period, and other requirements; a dismissal or completed sentence does not automatically erase the record. Wyoming generally treats expunged records as confidential rather than physically destroying them, and authorized criminal justice access can remain available.

facts.label: Arrests without convictions
facts.value: Wyoming provides a petition process for qualifying arrest records when charges were not filed, criminal proceedings were dismissed, or the person was acquitted. The statute imposes additional conditions, so a nonconviction outcome alone does not establish eligibility. — Wyo. Stat. § 7-13-1401

facts.label: Misdemeanor convictions
facts.value: A separate statute governs expungement of qualifying misdemeanor convictions. Eligibility and the court’s authority to grant relief depend on that statute’s requirements, rather than the rules for arrests without convictions. — Wyo. Stat. § 7-13-1501

facts.label: Felony convictions
facts.value: Wyoming permits expungement of qualifying felony convictions but excludes specified offenses and imposes eligibility restrictions. It is not a general right to expunge every felony after completing a sentence. — Wyo. Stat. § 7-13-1502

facts.label: Meaning of expungement
facts.value: The statutory definition focuses on classifying records as confidential and restricting dissemination. Expungement is therefore different from an assurance that every record has been destroyed or that criminal justice agencies can never access it. — Wyo. Stat. §§ 7-13-1401, 7-13-1501, 7-13-1502

sections.heading: Deferred proceedings are a separate issue

facts.label: First-offender deferral
facts.value: For qualifying defendants, Wyoming law authorizes a court, with the required consent, to defer further proceedings without entering a judgment of guilt and place the defendant on probation. Successful completion can result in discharge and dismissal. — Wyo. Stat. § 7-13-301

facts.label: Dismissal versus record relief
facts.value: Discharge and dismissal under the deferral statute are not the same procedural step as an expungement order. The deferral statute addresses the disposition of the prosecution; the expungement statutes separately govern confidentiality of qualifying records. — Wyo. Stat. §§ 7-13-301, 7-13-1401

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Wyoming
bullets: Expungement is a judicial petition process, not an administrative complaint process. Wyoming circuit and district courts handle criminal matters; the applicable statute determines the proper court.
For misdemeanor or felony conviction expungement, the petition is filed in the court where the conviction occurred. — Wyo. Stat. §§ 7-13-1501, 7-13-1502
The Wyoming Judicial Branch’s official website provides court information and directories. Questions about eligibility or the effect of an order are matters to talk to a lawyer about.

sections.heading: Common questions in Wyoming
bullets: Does an acquittal automatically expunge the arrest? No. Section 7-13-1401 establishes a petition process for qualifying records.
Can a felony be expunged? Some qualifying felony convictions can be expunged under § 7-13-1502; statutory exclusions apply.
Does finishing probation automatically erase a conviction? No. Completing a sentence and obtaining an expungement order are different legal events.
Does expungement mean physical destruction? Not necessarily. Wyoming’s statutory framework classifies covered records as confidential while preserving authorized access.
